How to read this

Five parts. The book follows one program, the write counter you wrote for your eBPF playground, kept with this book in program/maps/02-hash-map, through its life one stage a chapter, each stage read in the kernel's own source and measured. Part I takes it from C source to bytecode and into the kernel, Part II through the verifier, and Part III onto a hook, through the calls it makes and into its map. Part IV extends the kernel: memory a program manages itself, a set of programs that schedules the CPUs, and a new data structure built twice. Part V asks how the verifier's checks could be proved sound. The primer before chapter 1 builds the register machine that chapter 1 takes for granted; skip it if you already read assembly.

Two paths. Straight through is the intended path. The second path is by topic. Every reference carries a tag (lineageISAloaderverifierruntimeHW), and the references at the back are grouped by it.

Words. A word in bold is being defined in that sentence or the next. After that it is used without ceremony, and it is in the glossary at the back, under the chapter that defined it.

Figures. The figures are drawn in black and grey with one accent colour, a dark green. The accent marks the thing a figure wants you to watch, such as the path the counter takes or the one row that matters, and whatever it marks is also drawn heavier or dashed, so the figures read the same in greyscale. A figure that uses more than one kind of line names them in a legend.

The ribbon. The strip of dates under each chapter title is the history of eBPF by kernel version, drawn in full in the prologue. The entries set darker, with a filled dot, are the span that chapter covers.

Check yourself. Every chapter ends with two to four questions. Answer out loud first, in full sentences, then turn to the answer key at the back, where the answers are in chapter order. A question you can half-answer is the one worth re-reading the chapter for. If you would rather be quizzed properly, hand the book's source, the src folder beside it, to an agent running the Alvar probe skill and ask it to quiz you chapter by chapter: it asks through a real question tool, scores your reasoning rather than your letter, and writes what it found to .alvar/maps/.

Labs. Most chapters end with one lab, marked with its time and what it needs. Labs run from the book's program folder, whose make builds everything, and work on copies in /tmp, so the originals never change. Those that load a program need root: use sudo, or a throwaway virtual machine of your own kernel, vng -r /boot/vmlinuz-linux --user root, which is how the solutions were run. Each solution in the key says whether it was run, on which kernel and with which tools.

Line numbers. Every file and line of kernel source named in this book is from Linux v7.2, the kernel you run. They drift with every release; the chapter on the verifier's source shows how to find them again.

Printing. The pages you see are the pages that print. Print from Chrome with Margins: None, Headers and footers off and Background graphics on. Hints print in full, so cover them with a hand if you want to try first.

6 min · LINEAGE

Every packet, copied

Picture a campus network in 1992 that is misbehaving, and an administrator running a network monitor on a SunOS workstation to find the host at fault. The monitor wants a handful of packets, while the wire can deliver a new one every few microseconds. SunOS's capture facility, NIT, copies every packet into a kernel buffer and passes it up a chain of modules before any filter looks at it. In the measurements that Steven McCanne and Van Jacobson of Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory published in January 1993, a packet that NIT's filter rejected still cost 136 microseconds, plus 210 nanoseconds for every byte in it.

Their answer was the BSD Packet Filter, which in the same test spent 4.6 microseconds on a rejected packet whatever its size. It makes the decision inside the kernel, on the packet where the network card left it.

Three ways to put code in the kernel

Figure 0.1 sets side by side the choices facing anyone who wants their own code to see what the kernel sees. A kernel extension is code added to a running kernel to change or watch what it does. The oldest kind is the kernel module of the first column, compiled to machine code and loaded with the kernel's full power. A bug in a module is a bug in the kernel, which can take the machine down, and a module has to be rebuilt for each kernel version.

The second column keeps the new code in a user-space program to which the kernel copies everything, so that a bug crashes only that program, at the price of one copy per packet. NIT stood close to this column.

McCanne and Jacobson chose the third column. A filter in their design is a small program, written for an imaginary machine, that the kernel runs on each packet to decide whether to keep it and how many of its bytes to keep.

We can trust the filter because of what its machine cannot do. It can read the packet and sixteen words of scratch memory, and its jumps only go forward, so every run reaches the end. A read past the end of the packet stops the filter and drops the packet, and a wrong filter keeps the wrong packets while the kernel goes on running.

The tap and the machine

Figure 0.2 redraws the paper's overview. When a packet arrives, the network driver calls BPF before the protocol stack sees it. BPF runs every listening program's filter on the packet, copies the bytes each filter accepted into that program's buffer and hands control back to the driver, so that a packet no filter accepts is never copied. We call the place where the driver calls out a hook, a point on the kernel's own path where it stops to run code attached there. The write counter sits on a hook too, at the entry to the write system call.

Section 3.3 of the paper describes the machine, which has an accumulator (the register most instructions read and write), an index register X, the scratch memory and an implicit program counter. That machine is now called classic BPF. The paper draws its programs as a control-flow graph, in which instructions are nodes and jumps are edges, and in 1993 every edge pointed forward.

Read with · The BSD Packet Filter: A New Architecture for User-level Packet Capture, Steven McCanne and Van Jacobson, USENIX Winter 1993

What it is. The eleven-page paper that introduced the filter machine every later BPF descends from.

Why now. Figure 0.2 is redrawn from its Figure 1, and the left column of Figure 1.3 is its section 3.3.

  1. Section 1, introduction. The problem, and the two improvements it claims: a register-based filter machine and a simpler buffer model. Five minutes.
  2. Sections 2 and 2.1, the network tap and packet filtering. Keep its Figure 1 beside Figure 0.2. Ten minutes.
  3. Section 2.2, Figure 3 only. The "reject all" plot, where this prologue's two numbers come from. Three minutes.
  4. Sections 3 to 3.2.2. The expression tree against the control-flow graph, with Figures 4 to 6, then the five design constraints. Ten minutes.
  5. Section 3.3, the pseudo-machine. Figure 7 with Tables 1 and 2. Ten minutes.

Skip. Figure 2 and the measurement setup in section 2.2. Sections 3.4 and 3.5 can wait unless you want to see the IP header length parsed. Section 3.6 and Figure 8 compare against CSPF in detail, and section 4 onward is about tcpdump and availability.

The figure. Figure 7, the filter for "host foo" drawn as a graph, in which every edge points down the page because no jump goes back.

Carry in. Three questions; their answers are in the key under the prologue.

  1. Why does BPF filter a packet in place instead of copying it into a kernel buffer first?
  2. What two shortcomings do the authors find in CSPF's expression-tree model?
  3. In Figure 7, an IP packet sent by host foo arrives. Which nodes does it visit before TRUE?

About 40 minutes · LINEAGE

Linux adopted the design in December 1997, when kernel 2.1.75 added the Linux Socket Filter, which attaches a classic BPF program to one socket once a check has accepted it.

The first checkIn 2.1.75 the check was sk_chk_filter in net/core/filter.c. It tested that every jump lands inside the program, that every scratch-memory index is below 16 and that the last instruction is a return, and its comment reads "If we let some ugly filter code slip through kaboom!" Chapter 4 shows what the check grew into.

"You simply create your filter code, send it to the kernel via the SO_ATTACH_FILTER ioctl and if you[r] filter code passes the kernel check on it, you then immediately begin filtering data on that socket."

Jay Schulist, Documentation/networking/filter.txt, Linux 2.1.75, December 1997

Thirty-two years on one page

Figure 0.3 carries the rest of the story. Its first group shows the machine leaving the network: Linux 3.0 began translating filters into x86-64 machine code in 2011, and Linux 3.5 let seccomp run classic BPF on system calls in 2012. In 2014 the machine itself was rebuilt, and that rebuild, the row in bold, is where we pick up the story in chapter 1.

Most rows after that add a hook or a kind of map, although from 2018 the kernel describes its own types to programs, and from 2021 programs can call ordinary kernel functions.

Recap

There are three ways to run new code where the kernel's data is: as a module with the kernel's full power, by having the kernel copy data out, or as a small program for a limited machine that the kernel runs itself. The 1993 BSD Packet Filter chose the third, a filter run in place on each packet, with forward-only jumps and nothing to read but the packet and its scratch memory. Linux adopted it in 1997 together with a check before attaching, and later used the same machine for system calls. Everything from 2014 on widens that machine.

8 min · ISA

A contract between code and processor

An instruction set architecture (ISA) is the contract between compiled code and the processor that runs it. It fixes the registers, the processor's own named storage slots, the ways of addressing memory, the instructions that exist and the bytes that encode each one. Caches and pipelines stay outside it, so one x86-64 binary runs on old and new chips alike.

Each instruction has an opcode, the number that selects the operation, and operands, the registers, memory addresses or constants it works on. A constant stored inside the instruction is an immediate, like the 4 in eBPF's r1 += 4. Rules that the hardware leaves open, such as which register carries a function's first argument, make up the ABI, the application binary interface that compilers agree on.

One expression, three machines

Figure P.1 computes one expression on three kinds of machine. A stack machine names no registers. Each of its instructions pops operands from an operand stack and pushes the result back, so i64.add has no operand fields, and the JVM, WebAssembly and CSPF, the 1980 filter that the 1993 paper replaced, all work this way.

Classic BPF, in the middle, is the prologue's accumulator machine. Its arithmetic always writes A and takes the second operand from X or from the instruction, so b, c and d wait in scratch memory. eBPF, on the right, is a register machine whose instructions name any of eleven registers, so its inputs arrive in r1, r2 and r3 and never leave the processor.

Counted the way the 1993 paper counts a stack machine run in software, the three columns make 12, 3 and 0 memory accesses. That was the paper's case for registers, since memory was already the bottleneck of the SPARCstation 2 it measured on.

Why one address in 1993The paper also says why it stopped at an accumulator. When software runs the filter one instruction at a time, it decodes each operand field in turn, so "a single address instruction format minimizes the decode" (section 3.2.2). eBPF was designed to be translated into processor instructions before it runs, which removes that cost.

"The operand stack must be simulated. On most modern machines this means generating add and subtract operations to maintain a simulated stack pointer and actually doing loads and stores to memory to simulate the stack."

McCanne and Jacobson, The BSD Packet Filter, section 3.1, USENIX Winter 1993

Arithmetic in registers, memory through loads

Reading AT&T syntaxThe x86-64 listings in this book use AT&T syntax, as clang, objdump and the kernel's documentation do. The destination comes last, % marks a register, $ an immediate and parentheses a memory address, so addq %rsi, (%rdi) adds rsi to the eight bytes at the address in rdi. eBPF assembly reads like C, destination on the left.

In a load/store architecture, arithmetic works only on registers and memory is reached only through loads and stores. RISC-V and eBPF are built this way. x86-64 is not, since its arithmetic may name a memory operand, so in Figure P.2 one x86-64 instruction does the work of three. The processor still loads, adds and stores inside that instruction, and the saving is in code size. In eBPF only loads, stores and atomic operations touch memory, which chapter 4 relies on.

The stack and the frame pointer

A value goes on the stack, the memory where each running function keeps a frame for its locals, when live values outnumber registers or a variable needs an address. A frame pointer is a register holding a fixed address in the frame, so that each local is named as that register plus a constant. Storing a register on the stack to free it is a spill, and loading it back is a fill.

eBPF's stack is 512 bytes (MAX_BPF_STACK in include/linux/filter.h) below r10 (Figure P.3, right). A program can read r10 but never write it, so r10 − 8 names the same eight bytes throughout a function. On x86-64, rbp is a frame pointer only by convention, and clang drops it at -O2.

Calls: who keeps which register

A calling convention is the part of the ABI that says where a call's arguments and result go and which registers the call may overwrite. Those are caller-saved, since a caller that still needs their values must save them first, while the registers that a called function must hand back unchanged are callee-saved. Linux's System V ABI for x86-64 passes six integer arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8 and r9, returns in rax, and keeps rbx, rbp and r12 to r15 callee-saved.

eBPF passes arguments in r1 to r5, returns in r0 and keeps r6 to r9 callee-saved, and the kernel's classic_vs_extended.rst pairs each register with the x86-64 register that already does its job (Figure P.3, left), so a call into a kernel function moves nothing first.

Instructions as bytes

eBPF encodes every instruction in eight bytes: an opcode byte, a byte holding two four-bit register numbers, a 16-bit offset and a 32-bit immediate. Only the load of a 64-bit constant takes two slots. RISC-V's base instructions are four bytes, while an x86-64 instruction takes from 1 to 15 (MAX_INSN_SIZE in the kernel's arch/x86/include/asm/insn.h).

With a fixed width, slot n starts at byte 8n and a hex dump splits by eye. The eBPF bytes 79 13 in Figure P.2 are opcode 0x79, a 64-bit load, then a register byte with the destination in its low four bits and the source in its high four, so they read r3 = *(u64 *)(r1 + 0).

One function, compiled twice

Figure P.4 compiles a three-line function for both targets, row by row. The x86-64 code adds the word at p straight into rbx, where eBPF first loads it into r6, and both compilers keep t in a callee-saved register because t is needed again after next() returns.

Where r6 to r9 are keptWhen the kernel turns an eBPF function into x86-64 code, do_jit() in arch/x86/net/bpf_jit_comp.c starts it with push_callee_regs(), which pushes rbx, r13, r14 or r15 for each of r6 to r9 that the function uses, and the exit path pops them again.

The two differ at entry and exit. The x86-64 code pushes rbx on entry and pops it before retq, since step() owes its own caller an unchanged rbx. The eBPF code has no such pair, because the kernel itself saves whichever of r6 to r9 an eBPF function uses, as chapter 7 shows.

Trace it by hand · Five exercises with a pencil

~45 min · trace by hand · pen and paper; clang, llvm-mc and llvm-objdump only to check

Task. Work the five exercises in order, since each practises one section of the primer, from counting memory accesses to reading the calling convention. Do each on paper before you reach for a tool.

Done when. You have two counts for exercise 1, a filled table for exercise 2, a short program for exercise 3, two decoded instructions for exercise 4 and a corrected program for exercise 5. You can check exercises 2 to 4 with llvm-mc -triple bpfel -show-encoding and clang -O2 -target bpf -S.

1 · Count. Write a = (b + c) * (d + e) for the stack machine and for classic BPF of Figure P.1, with b to e in locals 0 to 3 or in M[1] to M[4], leaving a on the stack or in A. Count instructions and memory accesses for each, with the rules of Figure P.1, and say why classic BPF needs a scratch word that holds none of the variables.

2 · Run. Execute this eBPF code by hand, writing each register's value after its slot runs and leaving the row empty if the slot does not run. All registers start at 0, and > compares two 64-bit values as unsigned numbers. What is r0 at exit, and what is r2, in hexadecimal?

SlotInstructionr0r1r2r10 − 8
0r1 = 5
1r2 = r1
2r2 *= r1
3*(u64 *)(r10 - 8) = r2
4r2 -= 30
5if r2 > 7 goto +1
6r1 = 100
7r0 = *(u64 *)(r10 - 8)
8r0 -= r1
9exit

3 · Translate. Write return (a - b) * (a + b); in eBPF assembly, with a in r1, b in r2 and the result in r0. Use no register except r0, r1 and r2, and as few instructions as you can, then compare your version with what clang -O2 -target bpf -S writes.

4 · Decode. Decode 7b 1a f8 ff 00 00 00 00 and 07 01 00 00 f0 ff ff ff into eBPF assembly with the opcodes below. As in the worked example, the low four bits of byte 1 name the destination register and the high four the source, while bytes 2 and 3 hold a signed offset and bytes 4 to 7 a signed immediate, both little-endian.

OpcodeMeaningOpcodeMeaning
07dst += imm79dst = *(u64 *)(src + off)
0fdst += src7b*(u64 *)(dst + off) = src
b7dst = imm85call imm
bfdst = src95exit

5 · Find the bug. This function receives a pointer to a record in r1. It reads a timestamp from the record's first field, calls kernel function 5, which takes no arguments and returns the current time in nanoseconds in r0, and stores the time elapsed in the record's second field. Which reads break the calling convention? Rewrite the code so that it is correct, adding as few instructions as you can.

0: r2 = *(u64 *)(r1 + 0)
1: call 5
2: r0 -= r2
3: *(u64 *)(r1 + 8) = r0
4: r0 = 0
5: exit
Hint 1 · direction

1 · A stack-machine instruction touches memory for every value it pushes or pops; an accumulator machine has two registers and parks everything else.

2 · Work one slot at a time; a jump's offset counts from the slot after the jump.

3 · a and b are each needed twice, so decide which value you can afford to overwrite first.

4 · Cut the eight bytes into their four fields before you look anything up.

5 · For each register read after slot 1, ask whether the convention promises that it comes back from a call.

Hint 2 · mechanism

1 · In classic BPF, A holds one sum and X the next operand, so the other sum needs somewhere to wait.

2 · 25 − 30 is −5, which read as an unsigned 64-bit number is 264 − 5.

3 · Put a − b in r0 first; after that, a is no longer needed in r1.

4 · f8 ff read little-endian is 0xfff8, and as a signed 16-bit number that is 0xfff8 − 0x10000.

5 · r1 to r5 are caller-saved and r6 to r9 callee-saved.

Hint 3 · nearly there

1 · In classic BPF, compute d + e, store it with st M[5], compute b + c, then ldx M[5] and mul x.

2 · The jump at slot 5 is taken, so slot 6 never runs.

3 · Start with r0 = r1 and r0 -= r2; two more instructions finish it.

4 · In the first, the destination is r10 and the source r1.

5 · Copy r1 into r6 before the call, and load the field into r7 instead of r2.

Solutions in the answer key under the primer.

What it costs

CPU
On this book's machine, an AMD Ryzen 7 8845HS (Zen 4) at about 5 GHz, a chain of dependent register adds runs at one cycle, 0.2 ns, per add. A dependent load took 4–5 cycles from the L1 cache, about 14 from L2, 50–60 from L3 and about 110 ns, some 550 cycles, from main memory, measured with a pointer chase through 16 KiB, 192 KiB, 6 MiB and 256 MiB buffers on one pinned core.
Spills
A spill and its fill add two instructions and an 8-byte slot. In the same test the pair added about one cycle of delay when the store and the load named the same register and offset, as stack slots do, and about seven cycles when the same address came through two different registers.
Calls
A call costs the call, the return and any moves that put arguments in place. eBPF's r1 to r5 already sit in the x86-64 argument registers, so a call into the kernel adds no moves, and a value kept in r6 to r9 needs no spill around it.

Count memory accesses before instructions: a register operand costs nothing extra, a cache hit a few cycles and a miss hundreds. Build with -O2 so that values stay in registers, and keep a value that must outlive a call in r6 to r9.

Recap

An ISA fixes a processor's registers, memory addressing, instructions and their encoding, and the ABI's calling convention adds where arguments and results go and which registers a call may overwrite. A stack machine keeps its operands in memory, an accumulator machine in one register and scratch memory, and a register machine in named registers, which for a = (b + c) * d means 12, 3 and 0 memory accesses. eBPF is a load/store register machine with r0 to r9, a read-only frame pointer r10 over a 512-byte stack, and a convention shaped like x86-64's: arguments in r1 to r5, the result in r0, r6 to r9 kept across calls. Its instructions are eight bytes each, where x86-64's take 1 to 15.

New words in this chapter

instruction set architecture
the contract between compiled code and a processor: registers, memory addressing, instructions and their encoding
register
one of the processor's own named storage slots
opcode
the number that selects an instruction's operation
operand
a value or place an instruction works on
immediate
a constant stored inside the instruction
ABI
the application binary interface: conventions compilers agree on above the ISA
load/store architecture
an ISA whose arithmetic uses only registers and whose memory is reached only by loads and stores
stack
memory in which each running function keeps a frame for its locals
frame pointer
a register holding a fixed address in the current frame; r10 in eBPF
spill
storing a register on the stack to free it; loading it back is a fill
calling convention
where a call's arguments and result go, and which registers it may overwrite
caller-saved
a register a call may overwrite; r0 to r5 in eBPF
callee-saved
a register a call must hand back unchanged; r6 to r9 in eBPF

Check yourself

  1. Predict the value: a C function takes seven long arguments and returns the last one. Besides retq, clang -O2 -S writes one x86-64 instruction for it. Which one, and at what address relative to rsp does the seventh argument arrive?
  2. A colleague writes scramble() in x86-64 assembly. It multiplies rdi by 12345, using rbx to hold the constant, and returns without restoring rbx. A C loop that adds scramble(i) & 1 for i from 0 to 9 prints sum 5 when built at -O0 and sum 12347 at -O2. What went wrong, and how is it fixed?
  3. Built at -O0, the eBPF code of Figure P.4 grows from 6 instructions to 12, and among the new lines are *(u64 *)(r10 - 0x18) = r1 before the call and r1 = *(u64 *)(r10 - 0x18) right after it. What is the compiler doing with t, and why may -O2 keep t in r6 instead?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under the primer.

  • ISACompiler Explorer, Matt Godbolt. Compiles C in the browser for many targets, including "BPF clang 23.1.0" and "BPF gcc". Paste Figure P.4's function into an x86-64 pane and a BPF pane, then switch -O2 to -O0 and watch the spills appear.
  • ISABPF Instruction Set Architecture (ISA), Linux kernel documentation. The kernel's copy of the instruction-set text from the standardisation work with the IETF that produced RFC 9669. For now read section 1.2 on encoding and the table in 1.3.1; chapter 1's read-with card covers the rest.
  • ISABPF ABI Recommended Conventions and Guidelines v1.0, Linux kernel documentation. The companion page from the same IETF work, one screen long, listing eBPF's registers and calling convention. Two minutes, and worth keeping beside Figure P.3.
  • ISAProject 4: Machine Language Programming, From Nand to Tetris, Noam Nisan and Shimon Schocken. Two small programs for the 16-bit Hack computer, run in the course's free, open-source CPU emulator. Hack does its work with two registers and memory, so the exercise shows from the inside why the middle column of Figure P.1 needs so many loads; an evening.

Chapter 1

The machine: instruction set and calls

The write counter reaches the kernel as 216 bytes, and every one of them belongs to a field with a fixed place in an eight-byte slot. We read all 27 slots, follow the kernel's copy of them down to 152 bytes of x86, and see what the kernel says about bytes that break the rules.

Spine. The primer built a register machine on paper and decoded two instructions with a table of eight opcodes. Now we take the machine that Linux runs, read the write counter in it byte by byte, and follow those bytes as far as the kernel's own copy of them, before chapter 2 goes back to the compiler that chose them.

32 min · ISA · LINEAGE

The counter as 216 bytes

We start from the bytes. Compiled as in Lab 1.1 and disassembled with llvm-objdump -dr, the write counter is the listing of Figure 1.1. Each line is one slot, with its number on the left, its eight bytes in the order they sit in the file, and clang's reading of them on the right. The slots run from 0 to 26, yet the numbers 7, 14 and 22 never appear, because the instructions at 6, 13 and 21 take two slots each. The section that holds the code is 216 bytes long (0xd8 in llvm-readelf -S), which makes 27 slots and 24 instructions.

Slots 6 and 21 load the address of a map, a kernel object of keys and values that programs and user space both read and write. Here it is the table write_counts, in which the counter keeps one count per thread. Slot 13 loads the address of the format string that bpf_printk prints. All three hold zeros in the file, and the line under each, a relocation of type R_BPF_64_64, names what belongs there once the map and the string exist in the kernel, which happens only when the counter is loaded (chapter 3).

The other slots are complete as they stand, and Figure 1.2 takes twelve of them apart field by field. Four rules decode every row.

The low three bits of the opcode byte name the instruction's class, and the other five bits mean different things in different classes. The register byte holds the destination in its low four bits and the source in its high four, so a2 in slot 4 is destination 2 and source 10. The offset and the immediate are signed and little-endian, which makes both fc ff and fc ff ff ff read as −4. A field the instruction does not use is zero, a rule the kernel enforces (the section "When it goes wrong").

Two rows read differently from the rest. The offset of slot 9 is a distance in slots, counted from the slot after the jump. So goto +2 skips slots 10 and 11 and lands at 12, where the counter goes on whether or not the lookup found an entry. The immediate of slot 11 is no number to add: its 1 names an operation, a fetching add, and the value added comes from r1.

Two machines, twenty-one years apart

Still runningThe left column has not gone away: tcpdump -d 'tcp port 22' prints the classic program that tcpdump compiles, and Linux rewrites such filters into the new instructions before it runs them.

The bytes of Figure 1.1 belong to a machine with a history. The left side of Figure 1.3 is the 1993 machine from the prologue, with its accumulator A, an index register X, a few words of scratch memory and one packet as input. Linux ran it for years for tcpdump's socket filters and seccomp's system-call filters.

In 2014 Alexei Starovoitov rebuilt that machine inside the kernel. LWN called the result "internal BPF" at the time, and the kernel documentation now calls it eBPF, extended BPF. Linux 3.15 shipped it in June 2014 and converted every classic filter into the new instructions, so tcpdump never saw a difference.

The conversion still runs, in bpf_convert_filter() in net/core/filter.c, and it shows how the old machine fits inside the new one. A lives in r0 and X in r7 (BPF_REG_A and BPF_REG_X in include/linux/filter.h). Each word k of classic scratch memory becomes four bytes of stack at r10 − (4k + 4), so the new machine needed no scratch memory of its own.

We can read the right column from the top, since each row answers a limit of the left one. Ten 64-bit registers, r0 to r9, match the registers of a modern 64-bit CPU, and r10 is a read-only frame pointer to a small stack. A call instruction reaches into the kernel, and since Linux 3.18 added maps in December 2014 a program can keep state between runs. Both machines still end by handing one value back out.

"The latter expands the set of available registers from two to ten, adds a number of instructions that closely match real hardware instructions, implements 64-bit registers, makes it possible for BPF programs to call a (rigidly controlled) set of kernel functions, and more."

Jonathan Corbet, "BPF: the universal in-kernel virtual machine", LWN, 21 May 2014

Eight bytes per instruction

Every eBPF instruction is eight bytes, cut into the fields that Figure 1.4 marks out. The first byte is the opcode, and the next holds two register numbers of four bits each, a source and a destination. After them come a signed 16-bit offset, the field eBPF uses for memory addresses and jump distances, and a signed 32-bit immediate. The counter's instructions, as clang -target bpf writes them into the object file and the kernel receives them, are its bytecode.

The classic layout above it in the figure is also eight bytes, cut differently: a 16-bit opcode, two one-byte jump distances and a 32-bit constant. The new machine kept the size and moved the fields, so a classic filter's bytes read as nonsense to it, as the second row of Figure 1.13 shows. The kernel declares the new layout in include/uapi/linux/bpf.h at line 80:

struct bpf_insn {
        __u8    code;           /* opcode */
        __u8    dst_reg:4;      /* dest register */
        __u8    src_reg:4;      /* source register */
        __s16   off;            /* signed offset */
        __s32   imm;            /* signed immediate constant */
};

One declaration serves every architecture, and the host's byte order decides where its fields land. On a little-endian host such as x86-64, the destination sits in the low four bits of the register byte, and the offset and the immediate are stored low byte first. A big-endian host swaps the two register numbers and stores the longer fields high byte first, and the RFC prints one instruction both ways.

Read with · BPF Instruction Set Architecture (ISA), RFC 9669, D. Thaler (editor), IETF, October 2024

What it is. The standard that fixes eBPF's instructions, so that Linux and other platforms run the same bytecode. Linux v7.2 keeps the same text in Documentation/bpf/standardization/instruction-set.rst, with one addition: the results of dividing the most negative number by −1.

Why now. Figure 1.4 is drawn from its section on instruction encoding, and the counter's disassembly can be checked against its tables line by line.

  1. Section 3.1, basic instruction encoding. The five fields, and one example printed little-endian and big-endian. Five minutes.
  2. Section 3.2, wide instruction encoding. Why some instructions take sixteen bytes. Three minutes.
  3. Section 3.3, instruction classes. The low three bits of every opcode. Five minutes.
  4. Section 4, then 4.3 and 4.3.1. How an arithmetic or jump opcode splits into code, source bit and class; then find CALL and EXIT in the jump table and read the paragraph on helper functions. Ten minutes.

Skip. Section 7 on registries, which matters to people writing a new runtime, and section 5.5, the legacy packet loads, which exist to keep 1993-style programs working. Sections 2.4 on conformance groups and 5.3 on atomics are worth a second sitting after this chapter, which covers both.

The figure. The example at the end of section 3.1, one add instruction printed twice. The two register numbers swap places between the rows, and x86-64 uses the first.

Carry in. Three questions; their answers are in the key under chapter 1.

  1. Which class does opcode 0x85 belong to, and what do its other bits say?
  2. Why does the standard need a second eight bytes for some instructions?
  3. What does a helper call carry in its immediate, and what does the standard leave to each platform?

About 25 minutes · ISA

Eight classes

The low three bits of every opcode name one of eight instruction classes, which Figure 1.5 lists with the counter's slots in each. Six of the eight come from 1993 with their numbers unchanged, since include/uapi/linux/bpf_common.h still serves classic and extended BPF alike. The classic RET and MISC, 6 and 7, became JMP32 and ALU64 in bpf.h. The counter uses six classes, and most of its 24 instructions are 64-bit arithmetic and jumps.

The other five bits are split in one of two ways. In the arithmetic and jump classes, the top four bits name the operation. Bit 3 says where the second operand comes from, the immediate (K, 0) or the source register (X, 1), so b7 is 1011 0 111, a move from the immediate in ALU64, and bf differs from it only in that bit. In the load and store classes, the top three bits are a mode and the next two a size of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes. So 7b is 011 11 011, a plain memory access (MEM) that stores eight bytes (DW) from a register (STX).

ALU and ALU64 hold the same operations at two widths. A 32-bit operation reads the low halves of its registers and writes zeros into the upper half of its destination. Clang gives such operations the w names, so the counter's w2 = 0x1a at slot 15 sets all 64 bits of r2. JMP and JMP32 differ in the same way, except that the calls, the exit and the 16-bit goto live in JMP alone.

Arithmetic, and how far a jump reaches

Arithmetic offers the operations of a small integer CPU, fourteen codes from add (0x0) to byte swap (0xd). Signed division, signed modulo and the sign-extending move reuse the codes of division, modulo and move, and the offset field tells them apart: 1 for the signed operations, and 8, 16 or 32 for the width a move extends from. Division by zero does not trap, since division writes 0 and modulo leaves the destination as it was. The kernel's copy of the document adds one rule that RFC 9669 leaves out, for the most negative number divided by −1, which stays itself and leaves a remainder of 0.

A jump's offset counts slots from the slot after the jump, as slot 9 showed, and sixteen signed bits reach 32,767 slots forward or 32,768 back. For anything farther, the standard defines a goto in the JMP32 class that takes its distance from the 32-bit immediate, which llvm writes gotol. It also suggests turning a long conditional jump into a short one over a long goto. Few programs are long enough to need it, although a loader with CAP_BPF may hand the kernel up to a million instructions (syscall.c line 3034).

Linux v7.2 decodes two jumps that neither RFC 9669 nor its own copy of the document describes. may_goto, opcode 0xe5, is a JMP-class jump with the code JCOND that the kernel itself decides to take, so that a loop the program cannot bound still ends (the section "Loops" of chapter 4). gotox, opcode 0x0d, is a goto with the X bit set. It jumps to an address held in a register, read from a jump table that the kernel keeps in a map (kernel/bpf/bpf_insn_array.c), and it came with Linux 6.19.

Memory, and the atomic at slot 11

As the primer put it, only loads, stores and atomic operations touch memory. A load or a store adds the offset to a base register, and the counter reaches its whole stack this way, the key at r10 − 4 and the value at r10 − 16. A load zero-extends what it reads into the 64-bit register. Version 4 of the instruction set, accepted from Linux 6.6, added a mode that sign-extends, MEMSX. A byte loaded with it is opcode 0x91, where clang's default version spends three instructions, a byte load and two shifts.

An atomic operation is a read, a change and a write that no other CPU can come between. eBPF encodes every one of them as a store, the class STX with the mode ATOMIC (0xc0), and names the operation in the immediate. The immediate takes the arithmetic codes for add, or, and and exclusive or, plus 0x01, FETCH, when the old value should come back in the source register. Exchange (0xe1) and compare-and-exchange (0xf1, which compares with r0 and leaves the old value there) always fetch. They come in 32 and 64 bits only, so llvm's assembler and the kernel both refuse lock *(u8 *)(r10 - 8) += r1.

The counter's slot 11, db 1a f0 ff 01 00 00 00, is a 64-bit fetching add into its value on the stack. Chapter 2 traces it back to __atomic_fetch_add() in the C source and to the version of the instruction set clang was asked for. Linux 6.15 added two operations under the same class and mode that RFC 9669 predates and v7.2's document does not list. Load-acquire (immediate 0x100) and store-release (0x110) are a load and a store with the memory ordering their names describe, and they alone among the atomics accept 8- and 16-bit widths (bpf.h lines 54 and 55).

The wide instruction

One instruction does not fit the eight-byte mould. A wide instruction takes two slots and sixteen bytes, because it loads a 64-bit value into a register and the immediate holds only 32 bits. Its first half is an LD instruction with the mode IMM and the size DW, opcode 0x18. The second half is a pseudo-instruction whose fields are all zero except the immediate, next_imm in the ISA document, which holds the upper 32 bits. The kernel's C joins the two halves in one line (Figure 1.10).

Most of the time the 64 bits are not a constant at all. The first half's source field, of no use to a load from the immediate, says what the immediate means, and Figure 1.6 lists the seven meanings that Linux v7.2 knows. A map is the commonest. The loader writes the map's file descriptor into the immediate and 1, BPF_PSEUDO_MAP_FD, into the source field. While it checks the program, the kernel swaps the descriptor for the map's address in check_and_resolve_insns(), which writes the address's low half into insn[0].imm and its high half into insn[1].imm.

Form 2 does the same for a place inside a map's value, and that is how the counter's format string arrives, since the loader keeps the object's read-only data in a map of its own. The other forms reach things the kernel already has. Form 3 loads the address of a kernel variable named by its type ID, a number from the kernel's own description of its types that chapter 2 introduces. Form 4 loads the address of one of the program's own functions, for a helper that calls it back, such as bpf_loop() in chapter 4. Forms 5 and 6 name a map by its index in fd_array, an array of descriptors that the loader passes beside the program, and a load that uses them without one fails with fd_idx without fd_array is invalid.

Calling into the kernel

The counter's slot 1Slot 1 stores w0, the low 32 bits of r0, and every register has a w name for its low half. Helper 14 puts the thread ID in that low half and the process ID in the high half, so the counter's table counts writes per thread, although in a single-threaded process the two numbers are the same.

The write counter calls into the kernel four times, at slots 0, 8, 16 and 24 of Figure 1.1. Each call goes to a helper function, a function inside the kernel that a program may call by number. The program names it by a small integer, the helper ID, which clang stores in the call instruction's immediate. Helper 14 returns the process and thread IDs of the running task, and helper 1 looks up a key in a map. The IDs are the values of the BPF_FUNC_ enumeration in vmlinux.h, a header the counter already includes, and Lab 1.1 names all four.

"Introduction of bpf_call insn and register passing convention for zero overhead calls from/to other kernel functions"

Alexei Starovoitov, "net: filter: rework/optimize internal BPF interpreter's instruction set", commit bd4cf0ed331a, March 2014

Linux v7.2 numbers its helpers from 1 to 211, the last being bpf_cgrp_storage_delete(), and the comment under the list in bpf.h says that it "is effectively frozen". New ways into the kernel arrive as the third kind of call in Figure 1.7, which chapter 9 follows from the inside. All three kinds use the opcode 0x85, and the source field tells them apart, as it does for the wide instruction. With 1 there, the immediate is a distance in slots to another function of the same program, counted like a jump's, and that function's exit returns to the caller. Linux has accepted such calls since 4.16.

With 2 in the source field, the immediate is the type ID of a function inside the kernel. The offset says whose types to look it up in, 0 for the kernel's own and any other value an index into fd_array for a module (find_kfunc_desc_btf()). These calls came with Linux 5.13. RFC 9669 describes the first and third kinds by their encoding alone, and leaves to each platform what the functions behind the numbers do.

Arguments reach a helper through eBPF's calling convention, which Figure 1.8 lays out register by register. Registers r1 to r5 carry up to five arguments and r0 carries the answer back, and after the call r1 to r5 cannot be read; in the words of the kernel documentation they are "reset to unreadable". Registers r6 to r9 are callee-saved, in the primer's terms, so they keep their values across the call, and r10 never changes. The rule holds for all three kinds of call, and a comment in kernel/bpf/core.c states it in one line: a call "scratches BPF_R1-BPF_R5 registers, preserves BPF_R6-BPF_R9, and stores return value into BPF_R0".

We can watch the rule at work in the counter's listing, where the map goes into r1 at slot 6 and again at slot 21, because no value in r1 is kept across a call. Figure 1.8 shows the map gone from r1 after the call, so a value the program needs later has to be parked in r6 to r9. Five argument registers are enough for every helper. Since r1 to r5 sit in the registers where x86-64 already passes arguments (Figure P.3), a call moves nothing before it jumps.

Inside the v7.2 source

Figure 1.9 lists the files behind everything so far. The two headers under include/uapi are the format itself, shared with user space. filter.h adds the kernel's own names, among them two registers beyond r10. BPF_REG_PARAMS, register 11, may appear only in the 8-byte loads and stores that pass a call's arguments beyond the fifth on the stack (is_stack_arg_ldx() and its two neighbours, filter.h lines 753 to 772), and BPF_REG_AX, register 12, is a spare that no program can name and the kernel uses when it rewrites a program. The rest of the table is code that carries the bytes out.

An interpreter runs a program by reading one instruction at a time and doing what it says. The machine's interpreter is ___bpf_prog_run() in core.c, which came with the machine in 2014, inside net/core/filter.c, and later moved to kernel/bpf. Figure 1.10 shows its outline, a jump table and a loop.

The jump table has 256 entries, one for every value of an opcode byte, each the address of a label inside the function, a C extension written &&label. Every entry starts as default_label, and BPF_INSN_MAP then overwrites the 121 opcodes the interpreter runs. At select_insn the interpreter looks up the slot's opcode and jumps there. The code at the label does the work, and CONT moves insn to the next slot and jumps back, so every instruction costs a table lookup and an indirect jump before it does anything. LD_IMM_DW steps over a wide instruction's second half with an extra insn++.

A loader may send 129 opcodes, eight more than the interpreter runs. bpf_opcode_in_insntable() adds the six classic packet loads, may_goto and gotox, and the kernel rewrites the packet loads and may_goto into ordinary instructions before the program runs (fixups.c). Any other opcode is refused at load as unknown. default_label should therefore never be reached, and if it is, BUG_ON(1) ends the run with a kernel bug report, since the comment above it warns that returning 0 could let a broken program keep running.

JMP_CALL shows what became of the helper ID. The interpreter calls __bpf_call_base + insn->imm, and the immediate it adds is no longer 14. While the kernel checks the program, it replaces each helper ID with the distance in bytes from __bpf_call_base, a function in core.c that only returns 0, to the helper's code (fixups.c line 2341), so that one addition finds any helper. Figure 1.11 shows the counter's copy after the load, where slot 0 holds 260,144 in place of 14.

The dump differs from the object in three ways. The calls carry distances, the third one negative because bpf_trace_printk() lies below __bpf_call_base in memory. The wide instructions show source field 1 with map 2, and source field 2 with map 4 and offset 0 for the string.

The tagbpftool prints a tag for every program, 0b348880a0a9dde6 for the counter. It is the first 8 bytes of a SHA-256 over the slots as loaded, with each map descriptor set to zero so that the same bytes give the same tag in every process (bpf_prog_calc_tag(), core.c line 301).

The kernel holds addresses in those slots, but bpf_insn_prepare_dump() in syscall.c turns each one back into a map ID for the reader, and it shows a call's rewritten immediate only to a reader allowed to see kernel addresses. The lookup at slot 8 has become a direct call into the hash table's own code, followed by two new slots that turn the element it finds into the address of its value. That is why the kernel's copy is 29 slots and 232 bytes where the object held 27 and 216, and chapter 10 explains the two slots.

The interpreter is entered through one of sixteen small functions, __bpf_prog_run32 to __bpf_prog_run512, one for each multiple of 32 bytes of stack. Each declares the program's stack as an array on the kernel stack, points r10 at its end and r1 at whatever the hook passed, and calls ___bpf_prog_run() (core.c lines 2400 to 2410). bpf_prog_select_interpreter() picks one by the program's stack depth rounded up to 32, so the counter's 16 bytes would run in __bpf_prog_run32.

None of this runs on the kernel used in this book. Arch Linux builds 7.2.15 with CONFIG_BPF_JIT_ALWAYS_ON=y, which compiles the interpreter out (the #ifndef at core.c line 1833) and has every program translated into x86 when it loads; the section "A kernel with no interpreter" of chapter 7 shows the evidence. Even a kernel that keeps the interpreter translates a program that calls a kernel function by type ID, since __bpf_prog_select_runtime() marks it jit_needed (core.c line 2679).

The ISA document closes the loop from the other side, because it does not ask every runtime to run every instruction. A conformance group is a named set of instructions that a runtime supports whole or not at all. Every runtime must support base32, and it may add base64 for the 64-bit instructions, atomic32 and atomic64, divmul32 and divmul64 for multiplication, division and modulo, and packet for the legacy packet loads (section 2.4 of RFC 9669). Linux accepts instructions from all seven, the packet loads only in the three kinds of program that are handed a socket buffer. Beyond them it accepts the five additions this chapter has met, may_goto, gotox, load-acquire, store-release and register 11, and a sixth, a cast between address spaces written as a 64-bit move with offset 1 (BPF_ADDR_SPACE_CAST in bpf.h).

What a fixed width costs

The encoding's price and its return are both in Figure 1.12. A fixed eight bytes is generous for exit, which uses one byte of them, and a 64-bit constant takes sixteen. The counter's eBPF is therefore larger than its x86, 232 bytes against 152, where x86 spends from one byte (leave) to ten (a movabsq carrying a 64-bit address, one for each wide instruction). What the fixed width buys is a decoder with no state: slot n starts at byte 8n, a jump can be checked by arithmetic on slot numbers, and an interpreter needs one table lookup per instruction. The 26 instructions of the kernel's copy became 36 of x86, one for most slots, two for each conditional jump and for the exit, and seven at the function's entry.

What it costs

CPU
Kernel 7.2.15 in a VM with 16 vCPUs, 12 November 2026. Decoding costs nothing per run, since the counter's 29 slots became 36 x86 instructions when it loaded; an interpreter would spend a table lookup and an indirect jump on every slot, and this kernel has none to measure (CONFIG_BPF_JIT_ALWAYS_ON=y). A run of the counter takes 144 to 162 ns without bpf_printk and 0.48 to 0.54 µs with it (chapter 8), and a helper call about 4.1 ns (chapter 9).
Memory
Eight bytes a slot, sixteen for a wide instruction: 216 B in the object, 232 B in the kernel's copy, 152 B of x86. The program and its slots fit one 4 KB page (bpftool's memlock 4096B); the stack is at most 512 B (MAX_BPF_STACK), and the counter uses 16.
Switches
One copy of the slots into the kernel at load (copy_from_bpfptr(), syscall.c line 3123). None at run time: every call is a function call inside the kernel, on the thread that reached the hook.
Locking
None in the encoding. Slot 11, the counter's only atomic, becomes one locked x86 instruction, lock xaddq, 6 bytes.

Count a program in slots and calls: a slot becomes one or two x86 instructions and a helper call costs a few nanoseconds, so a program of a few dozen slots runs in well under a microsecond unless it prints. Build with clang's default version of the instruction set unless every kernel the program must load on is 6.6 or later, and check the object with llvm-objdump -d for opcodes an older kernel lacks.

When it goes wrong

The rows of Figure 1.13 come from small programs written byte by byte and handed to the kernel by rawload.c, a loader of about a hundred lines that calls bpf() directly, so no compiler or library stands between the bytes and the kernel. Most of them are refused before the kernel walks a single instruction, as the last line of each log, processed 0 insns, says.

bpf_check() runs its passes over the bytes in a fixed order. It first checks that every jump lands inside the program and that the last slot is an exit or a jump. check_and_resolve_insns() then checks every slot's register numbers, opcode and unused fields and turns map descriptors into addresses, and bpf_check_cfg() follows the jumps to find unreachable slots and jumps into a wide instruction's second half. That order explains the second row, where a classic filter's unknown opcode at slot 13 goes unreported because its jump at slot 1 fails first.

The error code sorts the rest. EINVAL marks bytes the machine does not define or a call it cannot resolve. EACCES marks a rule about registers broken on a path the kernel walked, such as reading r1 after a call or writing r10, and chapter 4 and chapter 5 read such logs in full. Two rows are loads that succeed, which only the bytes explain. An immediate written big-endian loads and returns 16,777,216, and a sign-extending load runs on 7.2 but is an unknown opcode to any kernel before 6.6, so a program meant for old kernels should be loaded on the oldest one before it ships.

Try it · Name every helper call in your own object

~20 min · read the source · needs clang and book/program

Task. Compile your hash-map program into an object in /tmp, disassemble it, and name the helper behind each call. You are checking the helper-ID idea against your own bytes.

Done when. You can point at call 0x1, say what r1 and r2 hold at that moment, and name all four helpers.

Hint 1 · direction

The number after call is printed in hexadecimal, and it indexes a list of helpers that your program's headers already carry.

Hint 2 · mechanism

Compile with the flags in program/Makefile but write the object to /tmp, so the program folder stays untouched. Then run llvm-objdump -dr on it, and search the header your program includes for names that start with BPF_FUNC_.

Hint 3 · nearly there

llvm-objdump -dr /tmp/hashmap.bpf.o | grep 'call 0x' gives the four calls; grep -nE 'BPF_FUNC_[a-z_]+ = (1|2|6|14),' vmlinux.h names them.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 1.

Try it · Break the machine on purpose

~40 min · break a real one · needs gcc, llvm-mc and root in a throwaway VM (virtme-ng) or on a test machine

Task. Write four small programs byte by byte, predict what the kernel will say about each, and load them with rawload: r1 = 1 with the two register numbers swapped; a jump onto the second half of a wide instruction; a call to helper 212; and a sign-extending load of a byte that holds 0xff, which should load. You are checking that you can write every field of an instruction without a compiler.

Done when. You have written down four predictions before loading anything, matched each against the kernel's log or the program's return value, and can say why the fourth program returns 4294967295.

Hint 1 · direction

Three of the four are refused for their bytes alone. For each, ask which field is wrong and whether the kernel must run anything to see it.

Hint 2 · mechanism

A case file holds one slot per line, eight hex bytes in memory order, with # for comments; book/labs/machine/cases/ok.txt is a two-slot example. bash book/labs/machine-root.sh build builds rawload into /tmp/machinelab, and llvm-mc -triple bpfel -mcpu=v4 -show-encoding prints the bytes of any instruction you can write in llvm's syntax.

Hint 3 · nearly there

For the jump, put a conditional jump in front of the wide instruction so that its first half is reachable, and count the target from the slot after the jump. Helper 212 is 85 00 00 00 d4 00 00 00. A byte of 0xff loaded as s8 is −1, and the return value is printed as the low 32 bits of r0.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 1.

Check yourself

  1. Predict the value: the disassembly of your program ends at slot 26, so it has 27 slots, and three of its instructions are wide. How many instructions does it have, and how many bytes does its section hold?
  2. A hand-written program does call 1, then reads r1 to use the map again, and the kernel refuses to load it with R1 !read_ok. What happened?
  3. Just before call 0x1 your listing shows r1 = 0x0 ll. Is your program about to pass a NULL map to the helper?
  4. Predict the value: bpftool prog show reports xlated 232B for the loaded counter, against 216 bytes of code in its object file. How many slots does the kernel's copy hold, and where did the extra ones come from?
  5. A tool built with -mcpu=v4 loads on your 7.2 laptop, but a server running 6.1 refuses it with unknown opcode 91, and the same source built with clang's default loads on both. What does the server lack?
  6. Predict the value: slot 9 of the counter is 15 00 02 00 00 00 00 00. Which slot does it jump to when r0 is 0, and what is the farthest slot a jump at slot 9 could reach forward in this encoding?
  7. A script turns the output of tcpdump -dd into a byte file and loads it with BPF_PROG_LOAD. The kernel answers jump out of range from insn 1 to 1538 for a program of 20 slots. Where does 1,538 come from?
  8. Predict the value: the counter's x86 code holds three 10-byte instructions, the longest in it. Which eBPF instructions do they come from, and how many bytes do the three save against the slots they replace?
  9. Your hand-written socket filter, meant to return 1, loads without complaint and returns 16777216. Its first slot is b7 00 00 00 00 00 00 01. What went wrong, and why did the kernel not refuse it?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 1.

Recap

The write counter is 27 slots of eight bytes, 24 instructions of which three are wide, and every slot splits into an opcode, two four-bit register numbers, a signed 16-bit offset and a signed 32-bit immediate, little-endian on x86-64, with every unused field zero. The opcode's low three bits name one of eight classes, and the other five hold an operation and a source bit in arithmetic and jumps, or a mode and a size in loads and stores; atomics are stores whose immediate names the operation, and a wide instruction's source field says whether its 64 bits are a constant, a map, a value inside a map, a kernel variable or a function. A call carries a helper ID, a distance to a function of the same program or a kernel function's type ID, takes its arguments in r1 to r5 and answers in r0, and leaves r1 to r5 unreadable. The kernel checks every slot's opcode and fields before it walks anything, rewrites helper IDs into distances and map descriptors into addresses, and on the kernel used here translates the result into x86, since its interpreter is compiled out.

New words in this chapter

map
a kernel object of keys and values that programs and user space both read and write
eBPF
extended BPF: the 64-bit instruction set Linux has run since 3.15
offset
a signed 16-bit field for memory addresses and jump distances
bytecode
a program's instructions as stored in the object file and handed to the kernel
instruction class
the kind of instruction named by an opcode's low three bits: LD, LDX, ST, STX, ALU, JMP, JMP32 or ALU64
wide instruction
an instruction of two slots, sixteen bytes, that loads a 64-bit value: a constant, or a map or other address the kernel fills in
helper function
a kernel function a program may call by number
helper ID
that number, carried in a call's immediate
interpreter
code that runs a program by reading one instruction at a time and doing what it says; in Linux, ___bpf_prog_run()
conformance group
a named set of instructions, such as base32 or atomic64, that a runtime supports whole or not at all

Chapter 2

From C to an object: clang, BTF and CO-RE

Before the kernel sees any of the write counter, clang has chosen its 27 slots, its registers and its stack, and has written beside the code a description of every type the program uses, which is also what lets one object load on kernels laid out differently.
