Spine. In chapter 1 the write counter was 27 slots of the machine's instructions, three of them wide and holding zeros where a map or a string belongs. This chapter goes back to the compiler that chose those slots, then follows its output, the object file, up to the moment the loader hands it to the kernel.

22 min · ISA · LOADER

The counter's C, and what one command makes of it

Figure 2.1 is the whole write counter, with the command that compiles it. That command writes an object file of 8,112 bytes, of which the 27 slots of chapter 1 take 216, so most of what clang produces is something other than code. This chapter is about the other 7,896 bytes, and about the choices clang made on the way, from the stack slot it gave to pid to the instruction it picked for line 19.

Three lines of the source decide most of what follows. Line 12 puts the function into a section of the object named after the hook it runs at, the sys_enter_write tracepoint, a fixed, named hook that kernel developers placed in the source at the entry to write(). Lines 4 to 9 declare the map, yet no instruction creates it, and the declaration reaches the object only as a description of types. Line 17 calls a helper by its ID and passes it the map, whose address nobody knows until the kernel has created the map.

The object is read by libbpf, the C library that the counter's loader links against, which reads an object file, creates what it describes in the kernel and attaches it. Part of the object is meant for libbpf alone, while the code and a description of the program's types in BTF, the BPF Type Format, go on into the kernel. BTF is a compact record of types, each struct with its fields and their offsets and each function with its signature. The kernel describes its own types in the same format, which starts to matter as soon as a program reads a kernel struct, as the fork tracer does later in this chapter.

Three stages inside clang

Inside clang the counter passes through three stages, which Figure 2.2 draws from top to bottom. The front end is the part of clang that parses C and writes it out as LLVM IR, the typed intermediate code that every LLVM target shares, with unlimited virtual registers, each assigned once. The middle runs the general optimisations of -O2, and the back end in llvm/lib/Target/BPF turns the IR into BPF instructions and writes the object.

The BPF target also hooks passes into the shared middle. BPFCodeGenPassBuilder.cpp places BPFAbstractMemberAccess and BPFPreserveDIType at the start of the pipeline, so that reads of kernel struct fields and __builtin_btf_type_id() become records before any optimisation can fold them away. BPFAdjustOpt holds back rewrites that would leave code the kernel's checker cannot follow, the checker that runs at load and that chapter 4 walks through.

"In particular, if bpf program tries to access a particular kernel data structure member, the details of the intermediate member access will be remembered so bpf loader can do necessary adjustment right before program loading."

Header comment of llvm/lib/Target/BPF/BPFAbstractMemberAccess.cpp, LLVM 23.1.4

The counter in IR

Figure 2.3 is the counter's IR at -O2. The map is a global variable in a section named .maps, the license is a four-byte string in license, and the function carries its SEC() name as its section. A helper has no symbol to call, because bpf_helper_defs.h declares bpf_map_lookup_elem as a constant function pointer whose value is 1. The IR therefore calls inttoptr (i64 1 to ptr), and a pattern in BPFInstrInfo.td turns a call to a constant into call 1, the helper ID of chapter 1.

The NULL test is an icmp eq against null and a branch, and the atomic add is an atomicrmw add with sequentially consistent ordering. Only pid and updated_val still live in memory, as alloca slots, because their addresses go to helpers. At -O0 every local keeps its stack slot, and the program grows to 38 slots and 56 bytes of stack.

Registers, the stack and the atomic

Six and moreIn v7.2, MAX_BPF_FUNC_ARGS in include/linux/bpf.h is 12: a call to another BPF function or to a kernel function exported for programs may pass arguments six to twelve through a hidden register, r11, and clang 23 announces this with __BPF_FEATURE_STACK_ARGUMENT. Helpers keep five.

Instruction selection matches IR operations against the patterns in BPFInstrInfo.td, and register allocation then maps the virtual registers onto r0 to r9, spilling to the stack when they run out. BPFRegisterInfo.cpp reserves r10 as the read-only frame pointer, so every stack slot is an offset below it. BPFCallingConv.td passes arguments in r1 to r5 and returns in r0, the convention that chapter 1 read from the kernel's side.

A helper takes at most five arguments because struct bpf_func_proto, its prototype in the kernel, has five argument slots (arg_type[5] in include/linux/bpf.h). Once the program is compiled to machine code (chapter 7), each of them reaches the helper in an x86 argument register. The 512-byte stack is MAX_BPF_STACK in the kernel, and BPFRegisterInfo.cpp checks the same number while it lays out the frame, so an oversized buffer stops the build before the kernel could see it.

The -mcpu option picks the version of the instruction set, and clang 23 defaults to v3 (BPFSubtarget.cpp; clang -target bpf -dM -E prints __BPF_CPU_VERSION__ 3). Version 2 adds less-than jumps, version 3 adds 32-bit jumps and the w registers, and version 4 adds sign extension, byte swaps and signed division; Linux has accepted them since 4.14, 5.1 and 6.6. Only for v4 does clang 23 store a constant to memory in one instruction, without first moving it into a register (HasStoreImm), and Figure 2.4 compares four builds.

The atomic add is where the version matters most. On v3 the atomicrmw becomes XFADDD, a fetch-and-add with opcode 0xdb and the fetch bit in its immediate. Version 1 has no fetching 64-bit add, so clang emits the older add without fetch while the result goes unused, as here, and BPFMIChecking.cpp stops the build when the result is read.

What the object holds besides code

The map's address is unknown until the kernel creates the map, so each reference to it, prepared by LowerGlobalAddress() in BPFISelLowering.cpp, is selected as LD_imm64, the wide instruction of chapter 1, with its constant left at zero. BPFELFObjectWriter.cpp records a relocation of type R_BPF_64_64 for each, the note under slots 6 and 21 in the listing of chapter 1 that tells libbpf which instruction to fill in. Two map loads and one .rodata load are why 24 instructions fill 27 slots.

As Figure 2.5 shows, BTFDebug.cpp also turns the debug information into .BTF, the types, and .BTF.ext, which holds one func info record with the function's type, eleven line info records tying slots to source lines, and no CO-RE records. Each line-info record points at the source text among the BTF strings, which is where the C lines come from when the kernel explains a rejection in chapter 5. The map definition exists only as BTF, because __uint() turns each number into the length of an array type.

Both sections are made from the debug information, so the -g in the Makefile is what creates them. Built without it, the object has neither, and libbpf refuses the counter as soon as it opens the file, with libbpf: BTF is required, but is missing or corrupted., because the 32 zero bytes of .maps say nothing about the map on their own. We checked this with clang 23.1.4 and bpftool 7.8.0 on 2026-11-12; the same build takes something less visible from the fork tracer, which the section "One relocation, from clang to the running kernel" comes back to.

Why a field offset cannot be fixed at build time

The counter reads no kernel struct, so it cares little which kernel it meets. The fork tracer, a smaller program from hello_world/03-tracepoint, runs at the sched_process_fork tracepoint and prints the pid fields of parent and child, so it reads child->pid. To do that the compiled program needs the byte offset of pid inside struct task_struct. That offset is a fact about one kernel build, and it moves when fields are added or removed and when the kernel's configuration switches fields on or off.

Figure 2.6 compares three ways to get the right offset into the program. The first compiles on every machine against that machine's headers, which is how BCC worked for years: it ships clang and LLVM inside each tool, compiles at start-up and needs the kernel's headers installed on every host.

Where CO-RE stopsCO-RE fixes offsets, but it cannot bring back a function the compiler inlined, which a probe on that function needs. A EuroSys 2025 study found that biotop broke that way in Linux 5.16, and that 83% of 53 real programs depended on something that changed between kernels.

The second compiles once, against one kernel, and hopes. On a kernel with a different layout the program reads whatever now sits at the old offset, and nothing warns anyone. The third is CO-RE, compile once, run everywhere, which Andrii Nakryiko described for libbpf in February 2020. The compiler records a question beside each field read, and the loader answers it on the target from that kernel's BTF, so that CO-RE moves some work to load time but keeps it to one lookup for each field the program reads.

"After libbpf processed BPF program code, to kernel it looks like any other valid BPF program code. It is indistinguishable from a BPF program compiled right there on the host with up-to-date kernel headers."

Andrii Nakryiko, "BPF CO-RE (Compile Once – Run Everywhere)", section "Kernel", 19 February 2020

Read with · BPF CO-RE (Compile Once – Run Everywhere), Andrii Nakryiko, nakryiko.com, 19 February 2020

What it is. The design of CO-RE explained by the person who built it into libbpf, first published on Facebook's BPF blog.

Why now. Figure 2.6 is its first two sections in one figure, and its running example is the field the fork tracer reads, task_struct's pid.

  1. "The problem of BPF portability". What BCC did, and the four costs it paid. Five minutes.
  2. "High-level BPF CO-RE mechanics", all four parts. BTF, the compiler, the loader and the kernel, and what each contributes. Ten minutes.
  3. "Getting rid of kernel header dependency" and "Reading kernel structure's fields". Where vmlinux.h comes from, and one read of pid written six ways. Ten minutes.

Skip. "Dealing with kernel version and configuration differences" and "Altering behavior based on user-provided configuration" until a program needs them; "BPF CO-RE as of 2021" is a status report.

The figure. The post has no figures; study the run of one-line code blocks in "Reading kernel structure's fields". The "BPF_PROG_TYPE_TRACING + BPF CO-RE way", which is the kind of program the fork tracer is, comes down to BCC's one line wrapped in one compiler built-in, and the book's vmlinux.h applies that built-in automatically.

Carry in. Three questions; their answers are in the key under chapter 2.

  1. What did BCC need on every machine, and what did that cost?
  2. Which four parts does CO-RE need, and which of them needed the fewest changes?
  3. Why does vmlinux.h lack the #define constants you might expect from kernel headers?

About 25 minutes · LOADER

BTF, and the 3.5 MB vmlinux.h

The answers come from the kernel's own BTF. As Figure 2.7 shows, the kernel build makes BTF from the compiler's debug information with a tool called pahole, and the running kernel publishes it at /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux, which is 6.5 MB on the 7.2 kernel we use. The same file is read twice, once when a header is written from it and again by libbpf on whichever machine loads the program. BTF went into Linux 4.18 in 2018.

The program folder's Makefile writes that header with bpftool btf dump file /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux format c. The result is vmlinux.h, which holds every type in the kernel, 166,183 lines and 3.5 MB of C for our kernel, so that no kernel headers need to be installed, and both of our programs include it. Its fifth line, a #pragma clang attribute that adds preserve_access_index to every struct and union in the file, tells clang to treat each of them as relocatable, and the next section follows what that does to one field read.

One relocation, from clang to the running kernel

Because of that pragma, the front end writes every read through such a struct as a call to llvm.preserve.struct.access.index. The counter has none, since it never reads through ctx, but a read of ctx->args[2] would add one. BPFAbstractMemberAccess then replaces the call with a global whose name spells out the path to the field, BPFMISimplifyPatchable folds that global into the load instruction, and BTFDebug writes a record about the load into .BTF.ext.

The fork tracer has two such reads. When we run llvm-objdump -dr on it, slot 2 reads w4 = *(u32 *)(r1 + 0xb38), with a line under it: CO-RE <byte_off> [6] struct task_struct::pid (0:95). That line is a CO-RE relocation, a record kept in the object's .BTF.ext section. It says that slot 2's offset field, the 16-bit field of Figure 1.4, holds the offset of pid and must be checked at load.

Asking about another kernelUbuntu 20.04's first kernels shipped without BTF. BTFHub, kept by Aqua Security, publishes BTF files for kernels like that, and libbpf can read one in place of /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux through its btf_custom_path option. Lab 2.2 uses one to ask libbpf what it would do there.

Figure 2.8 follows the record from compile to load. The offset 0xb38, byte 2872, is right for the kernel the header came from, so on that kernel libbpf writes the same number back. Suppose we copy the object to a server running Ubuntu 20.04's first kernel, 5.4.0-26. libbpf looks up struct task_struct in that kernel's BTF by name and then pid by name, finds it as field 65 at byte 2264, where our 7.2 kernel has field 95, and writes 0x8d8 into slots 2 and 3. Because libbpf matches by name, the field can move without anything breaking.

In an ordinary libbpf load the kernel never sees the record, and as the field note says, it receives a plain load with the right offset. When the running kernel has no field of that name, libbpf replaces the instruction with a call to a helper that does not exist, number 195896080, and the load fails with failed to resolve CO-RE relocation. That loud failure is what CO-RE offers in place of silence, because the fixed-offset build would have loaded and read the wrong four bytes.

The silence comes back when a build loses -g. Without debug information clang writes no BTF and no relocations, yet the fork tracer still compiles with the same 0xb38 in both loads. libbpf opens and loads it without a warning, since the tracer defines no map that would need BTF. We loaded such a build in a VM running our 7.2.15 kernel on 2026-11-12, and its instructions reached the kernel with 2872 fixed in them, which is right for this kernel and wrong for the 5.4 one.

Stable: what the record asksDrifting: the answer, kernel by kernel (checked November 2026)
A struct by name, task_structIts type number: 6 in the object, 135016 in the 7.2 kernel's BTF, 147 in the 5.4 kernel's
A field by name, pidIts position: field 95 in 7.2, field 65 in 5.4
What to patch: the offset field of slot 2The value: 2872 in 7.2, 2264 in 5.4

Inside libbpf and the kernel: who answers the record

The matching we have followed lives in two files of the v7.2 tree. In tools/lib/bpf/libbpf.c, bpf_object__relocate_core() walks the CO-RE records of every program and hands each to bpf_core_resolve_relo(). That function collects the candidates, every type in the kernel's BTF and in its modules' BTF, whose name matches the record's struct once any suffix that starts with three underscores is ignored (bpf_core_essential_name_len()). That rule lets a second definition such as task_struct___old stand for the same kernel struct.

bpf_core_calc_relo_insn() in tools/lib/bpf/relo_core.c then works out the answer for each candidate and stops with field offset ambiguity when two of them disagree, and bpf_core_patch_insn() writes the answer into the instruction. When nothing matches, bpf_core_poison_insn() writes the call to helper 195896080 instead, a number that its comment in the source spells out as 0xbad2310, "bad relo".

The kernel compiles the same matching code, since kernel/bpf/relo_core.c is one line that includes ../../tools/lib/bpf/relo_core.c. check_core_relo() in kernel/bpf/check_btf.c applies records that arrive in the core_relos array of BPF_PROG_LOAD, through bpf_core_apply() in kernel/bpf/btf.c. libbpf takes that path when it writes the whole load as a small BPF program that makes the bpf() calls itself (tools/lib/bpf/gen_loader.c), since such a loader has no copy of libbpf in user space to do the matching for it. In an ordinary load, as for both of our programs, the records stay in user space.

The kernel's own BTF reaches user space through a short file. CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF builds kernel/bpf/sysfs_btf.c, which publishes the bytes between __start_BTF and __stop_BTF, the section that pahole wrote into the kernel image during the link, as the read-only file /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux. That file has an mmap handler, btf_sysfs_vmlinux_mmap(), so libbpf 1.8 maps the 6.5 MB instead of copying them (btf_parse_raw_mmap() in tools/lib/bpf/btf.c) and reads the file only when mapping fails.

libbpf opens that file only for an object that needs it. obj_needs_vmlinux_btf() in libbpf.c asks for kernel BTF when the object has CO-RE records or typed kernel symbols, or a program that attaches through the kernel's BTF, as the fork tracer's tp_btf program does and the counter's program does not. We traced both loads with strace in a VM running our 7.2.15 kernel on 2026-11-12. The counter's loader never opened /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux, while bpftool prog load of the fork tracer opened it once, mapped all 6,532,544 bytes and logged patched insn #2 (LDX/ST/STX) off 2872 -> 2872.

The object's own BTF goes into the kernel and stays there. libbpf hands .BTF over with BPF_BTF_LOAD, and the kernel checks it in btf_parse() before it returns a descriptor. That descriptor goes with each map, so that the map's key and value have types. It also goes with each program, together with the func info and line info from .BTF.ext, which check_btf_func() and check_btf_line() in check_btf.c check against the program's instructions. None of this has happened yet, because everything in this chapter took place before the first bpf() call, and chapter 3 follows the loader through those calls.

What it costs

CPU
Each slot becomes one or a few x86 instructions (chapter 7), so slots are a fair measure of run time: -O0 spends 38 slots on what -O2 does in 27, the extra ones mostly stack stores and reloads, and v4 saves one more. CO-RE is paid at load only. libbpf reads the running kernel's BTF, 6,532,544 bytes and 147,680 types on our 7.2 kernel, in about 10 ms (btf__load_vmlinux_btf(), timed three times), then makes one lookup by name per relocation; a run pays nothing, and the counter, which needs no kernel BTF, skips the 10 ms as well.
Memory
The object is 8,112 bytes, of which 216 are code. The kernel keeps the 1,502 bytes of BTF and the func and line info for the program's life; the 4.5 KB of DWARF stays in the file, and llvm-strip -g removes it while keeping .BTF and .BTF.ext (3,624 bytes left). During a load that needs kernel BTF, libbpf 1.8 maps the file read-only, which grew our process by about 1.1 MB, and frees it when the load ends.
Switches
None per event. Per load, an openat() and an mmap() of /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux when the object needs kernel BTF, and neither for the counter (strace in the VM, kernel 7.2.15).
Locking
Slot 11 is a locked read-modify-write, lock xadd in x86, although its target is the program's own stack, which no other CPU can see; updated_val += *curr_val would be a plain add.

Build with -O2 -g and the default v3, or v4 when every target kernel is 6.6 or newer, and never drop -g, which takes the BTF, the map definition and every CO-RE record with it. Use CO-RE for any program that reads kernel structs, since it costs milliseconds once per load and nothing per event, and keep atomics for memory that other CPUs share.

When it goes wrong

Problems at this stage show up at three moments: while clang builds, while libbpf opens the object, and while the load runs on a kernel other than the one the header came from. The first two are loud, and the message usually names its cause. The quiet failure is a program that loads and runs on the wrong offsets, and the fourth row of Figure 2.9 is the reason to keep -g in every build. The table gathers the failures met in this chapter and its labs, each with a command that tells its cause apart from the others. Only the last three need the target kernel or its BTF, and none of them needs root.

Try it · Compile the counter four ways

~25 min · measure · needs clang, llvm-objdump and bpftool; no root

Task. From book/program, compile hashmap.bpf.c four times into /tmp/ch10: with the Makefile's flags, at -O0, with -mcpu=v1 and with -mcpu=v4. For each object, find the code section's size in slots and the deepest stack offset. Then find the instructions that differ between v1 and the default, and the place in the BTF where max_entries is kept. This rebuilds Figure 2.4 from your own objects.

Done when. You have four rows of slot counts and stack depths that match Figure 2.4, you can point at the instruction that changes between v1 and v3, and you can show the BTF line that holds 1024.

Hint 1 · direction

A slot is eight bytes, so the size of the code section is enough to count slots. The section is named after the SEC() string. Change one compiler option at a time.

Hint 2 · mechanism

Start from the Makefile's BPF_CFLAGS. llvm-size -A lists section sizes, llvm-objdump -d --no-show-raw-insn prints instructions you can diff, and the stack offsets are the r10 - 0x… operands. bpftool btf dump file reads the object's BTF without root.

Hint 3 · nearly there

clang -g -O0 -target bpf -D__TARGET_ARCH_x86 -I/usr/include/bpf -I. -c maps/02-hash-map/hashmap.bpf.c -o /tmp/ch10/O0.o, then llvm-size -A /tmp/ch10/O0.o | grep sys_enter_write and llvm-objdump -d /tmp/ch10/O0.o | grep -o 'r10 - 0x[0-9a-f]*' | sort -u. For the map: bpftool btf dump file /tmp/ch10/O2.o | grep nr_elems.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 2.

Try it · Ask libbpf about a kernel you do not run

~25 min · read the source · needs clang, llvm-objdump, bpftool and a download; no sudo

Task. Compile your fork tracer into /tmp, find its CO-RE relocations, and ask libbpf what it would write into slot 2 on two kernels: yours, and Ubuntu 20.04's 5.4.0-26, whose BTF you download from BTFHub. Nothing is loaded. You are running Figure 2.8 on your own object.

Done when. You can say which offset slot 2 carries, which offset each kernel gives pid, and show the libbpf line that matches each.

Hint 1 · direction

The object carries one answer and the question behind it. Each kernel's BTF holds its own answer, and libbpf compares by name. A kernel you do not run can still be asked, through its BTF file.

Hint 2 · mechanism

From book/program, compile the tracer into /tmp/ch03. llvm-objdump -dr prints each record under its instruction. bpftool gen min_core_btf runs libbpf's matching against any BTF file, and bpftool -d prints each step. BTFHub's archive on GitHub keeps the 5.4 file as ubuntu/20.04/x86_64/5.4.0-26-generic.btf.tar.xz.

Hint 3 · nearly there

llvm-objdump -dr /tmp/ch03/tracepoint.bpf.o | grep -B1 CO-RE; download the file from raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/btfhub-archive/main/ plus that path, unpack it with tar xJf; then bpftool -d gen min_core_btf BTF_FILE min.btf tracepoint.bpf.o 2>&1 | grep 'relo #0: matching', once with /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux and once with the 5.4 file.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 2.

Check yourself

  1. Predict the value: you add u64 n = ctx->args[2]; to the counter. At what byte offset from ctx does clang put the load, and what access string does the CO-RE record carry?
  2. You add char buf[600];, filled by bpf_probe_read_kernel(), and the build stops with error: Looks like the BPF stack limit is exceeded. Please move large on stack variables into BPF per-cpu array map. … Which part of the toolchain refused, and why before the kernel was involved?
  3. To support an old kernel, a colleague builds with -mcpu=v1 a version of the counter that keeps the result of __sync_fetch_and_add(), and clang stops with error: Invalid usage of the XADD return value. What happened?
  4. Predict the value: in the 5.4 kernel's BTF, pid sits at bits_offset=18112. What does libbpf write into slot 2's offset field, in hex?
  5. A tool that reads task->__state loads on your 7.2 laptop. On a server running Linux 5.10, built with BTF, it fails, and the log ends with failed to resolve CO-RE relocation and struct task_struct.__state. What happened?
  6. Your write counter includes the same vmlinux.h as the fork tracer. How many CO-RE relocations does its object carry, and what could still stop it loading on another kernel?
  7. To make the objects smaller, a colleague removes -g from the Makefile. The counter now fails when libbpf opens it, with libbpf: BTF is required, but is missing or corrupted., while the fork tracer still builds and loads. Which of the two is worse off, and what should the colleague have done instead?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 2.

Recap

Clang's front end writes the counter as LLVM IR, in which a helper call is a call through a constant pointer and the atomic add is an atomicrmw; the BPF back end selects instructions for the chosen -mcpu version, allocates r0 to r9 with r10 as the frame pointer, and refuses frames of 512 bytes or more before the kernel sees anything. Map references become wide instructions with R_BPF_64_64 relocations, and BTFDebug writes .BTF and .BTF.ext from the debug information, so the map definition, the line info and every CO-RE record exist only when the build has -g. A read of a kernel struct field cannot keep a fixed offset, because offsets differ between kernel builds, so vmlinux.h, the kernel's BTF printed as C, makes clang record each such read as a CO-RE relocation. libbpf answers each record at load, by name, from the running kernel's BTF, fails the load loudly when the field is missing, and hands the kernel plain instructions, which chapter 3 follows through bpf().

New words in this chapter

tracepoint
a fixed, named hook that kernel developers placed in the source, such as sys_enter_write
libbpf
the C library that reads an object file, creates its maps and programs, and attaches them
BTF
BPF Type Format: a compact description of structs, fields, offsets and function signatures, written by clang for a program and by pahole for the kernel
front end
the part of clang that parses C and writes LLVM IR
LLVM IR
the typed intermediate code that all LLVM targets share, with unlimited virtual registers each assigned once
back end
the target-specific part of LLVM; for BPF, llvm/lib/Target/BPF
instruction selection
the back-end step that matches IR operations to BPF instructions
register allocation
the back-end step that maps virtual registers onto r0 to r9, spilling to the stack when needed
func info
a .BTF.ext record giving the BTF type of a function that starts at a slot
line info
a .BTF.ext record tying a slot to a source line, with the line's text
CO-RE
compile once, run everywhere: field offsets recorded at build and corrected by libbpf at load
vmlinux.h
the kernel's BTF printed as one C header by bpftool btf dump … format c
CO-RE relocation
a record in .BTF.ext that names a struct and field by name and says which instruction to patch

Go deeper

  • ISAClang implementation notes, Linux kernel documentation. Two short sections: the CPU versions, and which atomics each version can emit. Five minutes.
  • ISAeBPF instruction set extensions, Paul Chaignon. What v2, v3 and v4 add, the kernel and LLVM version each needs, and their effect on Cilium's largest programs.
  • LOADERBPF LLVM relocations, Linux kernel documentation. Every BPF relocation type with a worked example; read it beside llvm-readelf -r on your own object. Its "CO-RE Relocations" and "CO-RE Relocation Record" sections decode the (0:95) in the objdump line.
  • LOADERBPF Type Format (BTF), Linux kernel documentation. Section 4, on the ELF file format, describes .BTF.ext with its func info, line info and CO-RE records.
  • LOADERBPF CO-RE (Compile Once – Run Everywhere), Andrii Nakryiko, 2020. The read-with card in this chapter says which sections.
  • LOADERBPF CO-RE reference guide, Andrii Nakryiko. Read it when a field is renamed or missing; the section on the "ignored suffix rule" is the fix for question 2.5.
  • RUNTIMERevealing the Unstable Foundations of eBPF-Based Kernel Extensions, Zhong, Liu, Arpaci-Dusseau and Arpaci-Dusseau, EuroSys 2025. Where CO-RE stops helping; read the introduction and the study of 53 programs.
  • LOADERbpf: btf: Introduce BPF Type Format (BTF), Martin KaFai Lau, Linux 4.18, 2018. The commit in which kernel/bpf/btf.c is born; at first BTF described only map keys and values, and type information for the whole kernel came in 5.2.
  • LOADERlibbpf: implement BPF CO-RE offset relocation algorithm, Andrii Nakryiko, libbpf for Linux 5.4, 2019. The first version of the matching that relo_core.c now holds; its message explains the candidate search by name.

Chapter 3

Into the kernel: bpf(), the load path, and who holds what

The write counter's loader creates two maps and a program through one system call, and the kernel hands back a descriptor for each and counts everyone who holds them. Given only CAP_BPF, the same loader creates both maps and is then refused the program with an empty log, because the line that refuses it runs before the program is checked at all.

  • What the counter's loader asks of the kernel, and why a load can fail with no log at all

Spine. In chapter 2 clang wrote the counter's object: 27 slots with zeros where the maps belong, the types that describe them, and the func and line info that tie each slot to the source. Now the loader hands all of it to the kernel through one system call, and we follow the kernel's side of the load, from that call to the descriptor it returns, and back out again when the loader exits.

22 min · LOADER · RUNTIME

What the loader asks the kernel

We start with the loader run without sudo, whose failure in Figure 3.1 shows the shape of every request. The loader reaches the kernel through a single call, the bpf() system call, whose first argument names a command such as BPF_PROG_LOAD and whose second points to that command's attributes in a union bpf_attr. Linux 3.18 added it, with maps, in December 2014.

The first programs in the trace are not the counter. They are two instructions long, and libbpf loads them first to ask whether this process may load at all. On our test kernel kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled is 2, so only a privileged process may load, and each probe comes back with EPERM.

With sudo the probes pass. The trace of the same loader then holds 33 calls before its read loop starts, eight of them BPF_PROG_LOAD and five BPF_MAP_CREATE, and only one and two of those belong to the counter. The rest are libbpf asking what this kernel supports, along with BPF_BTF_LOAD calls that hand over the types chapter 2 described. Lab 3.1 picks the counter's own calls out of that trace.

Root is more than a loader needs, so we run the counter's loader the way a careful deployment would, as an ordinary user that holds one capability, CAP_BPF, which Linux 5.8 added in 2020 (commit a17b53c4a4b5) so that loading BPF would not need the rest of root's powers. Figure 3.2 shows the result on kernel 7.2.15 in a virtme-ng VM. Both maps are created, and then the program is refused twice with -EPERM: libbpf loads once without a log and, after the failure, once more with a 16 MB log buffer so that it can print the kernel's reasons.

The buffer comes back empty, and libbpf has nothing to print. Something refused the program before the kernel had begun to check it, and to find the line that did, we first follow a load that succeeds, from the loader's side and then through the kernel's source.

Load: the maps first, then the program

With sudo, the loader calls hashmap_bpf__open_and_load(), as Figure 3.3 shows, from the skeleton, a header that bpftool gen skeleton wrote from the counter's object, with the object inside it as bytes. Open parses those bytes, and load creates everything in the kernel, each map with BPF_MAP_CREATE and then each program with BPF_PROG_LOAD.

Numbers before mapslibbpf 1.8, the version used in this book, picks each map's number before the map exists. At open it reserves a descriptor per map and patches the instructions with it, and when BPF_MAP_CREATE returns, it moves the real map onto that number with dup3().

A map is a kernel object of keys and values that programs and user space both read and write, and the loader knows each one by the file descriptor that BPF_MAP_CREATE returned. libbpf writes that number into every wide instruction that named the map, the zeros at slots 6 and 21 of Figure 1.1 (bpf_object__relocate_data(), libbpf.c line 6434). It also sets the instruction's source-register field to 1, BPF_PSEUDO_MAP_FD, which marks the constant as a descriptor.

The object also holds a map the source never declares, the read-only hashmap_.rodata, which holds bpf_printk's format string and which slot 13 points into. BPF_PROG_LOAD then carries the program type, BPF_PROG_TYPE_TRACEPOINT, the kind of program, which fixes what it receives when it runs and which helpers it may call, and all 27 slots. The kernel checks every path through the program, which chapter 4 follows, and swaps each descriptor for the map's address, as the comment above check_and_resolve_insns() promises: "if it accesses map FD, replace it with actual map pointer". It then hands back a descriptor for the program, which is loaded and yet runs nowhere.

"In the load phase, libbpf creates BPF maps, resolves various relocations, and verifies and loads BPF programs into the kernel. At this point, libbpf validates all the parts of a BPF application and loads the BPF program into the kernel, but no BPF program has yet been executed."

libbpf Overview, "BPF App Lifecycle and libbpf APIs", Linux kernel documentation

Running is the second half of Figure 3.3. hashmap_bpf__attach() opens a perf event on the tracepoint and joins the program to it with BPF_LINK_CREATE, which returns a link (a bpf_link in the kernel's terms since Linux 5.7), an object whose job is to hold one program on one hook. How the loader finds the hook, and what attaching writes into it, is the subject of chapter 8, and for the rest of this chapter the link matters as one more holder of the program.

From the system call to a descriptor

The kernel's side begins at SYSCALL_DEFINE5(bpf), line 6534 of kernel/bpf/syscall.c; in v7.2 the call has five arguments, the last two for attributes that every command shares. __sys_bpf() copies the attributes in, returns -E2BIG for any nonzero byte beyond the size this kernel knows, lets each Linux Security Module (LSM) see the command through security_bpf(), and calls bpf_prog_load() at line 2972. Figure 3.4 lists what that function does next, and the row in bold is where our loader stopped.

libbpf asks firstBefore its probes, libbpf tried bpf(BPF_TOKEN_CREATE) on /sys/fs/bpf and got EOPNOTSUPP: token.c line 151 refuses a token in the initial user namespace, where it would add nothing. With no token, every check used the initial namespace.

After CHECK_ATTR has rejected unknown fields, the capability tests run, in the user namespace of a BPF token if the caller passed one. A token is an object made from a mount of the BPF file system that was set up to delegate chosen commands and kinds of program into a user namespace, and with one, bpf_token_capable() checks capabilities in that namespace instead of the initial one. Every kind of program except socket filters and cgroup skb programs needs CAP_BPF, and a kind that can read kernel memory, a tracepoint program among them, also needs CAP_PERFMON (is_perfmon_prog_type(), line 2871). Our loader stopped at line 3045, the test for CAP_PERFMON.

Figure 3.5 shows that stop with ftrace's function_graph tracer, which records each function that bpf_prog_load() calls. The refused load asks bpf_token_capable() twice, gets true for CAP_BPF and false for CAP_PERFMON, and returns -1, which is -EPERM, after 3.5 µs. As root, the same load passes both tests and runs to the end in 146 µs.

The steps after the capabilities build the program object. bpf_prog_alloc() takes memory charged to the caller's memory cgroup, the 27 slots and the license string are copied in, and license_is_gpl_compatible() decides whether GPL-only helpers may be called. A signed program, possible since 6.18, has its signature checked here, and security_bpf_prog_load() at line 3192 lets every LSM refuse, including BPF programs that are themselves attached to that security hook.

bpf_check() is the check that walks every path through the program, the subject of chapter 4, and the first thing it does with the caller's buffer is set up the log, in bpf_vlog_init(), 52 lines into the function. Every refusal before that point reaches user space as an errno with an empty log, which is the symptom of Figure 3.2. Inside, the kernel also reads the BTF, func info and line info that clang wrote, replaces map descriptors with map pointers, records the maps the program uses in prog->aux->used_maps, walks the program, and ends by calling __bpf_prog_select_runtime(), which compiles it to x86 code (chapter 7).

Back in bpf_prog_load(), bpf_prog_alloc_id() gives the program the ID that bpftool prints, and bpf_prog_kallsyms_add() names its machine code in /proc/kallsyms. bpf_prog_new_fd() at line 3227 then returns a descriptor for an anonymous inode, a file with no path that the kernel creates to hand an internal object to a process; /proc/PID/fd shows it as anon_inode:bpf-prog.

Each map took a shorter road through the same file before the program did. BPF_MAP_CREATE reaches map_create() at line 1626, where map_create_alloc() checks the attributes and the capabilities and asks the map's own operations to allocate it. On our kernel, with unprivileged BPF off, every map needs CAP_BPF and the socket and device maps need CAP_NET_ADMIN as well, while no step asks for CAP_PERFMON, which is why the loader of Figure 3.2 got both of its maps. The LSMs then see the new map in security_bpf_map_create(), bpf_map_alloc_id() gives it an ID, bpf_map_save_memcg() records the memory cgroup it is charged to, and bpf_map_new_fd() returns a descriptor that shows as anon_inode:bpf-map.

Who holds the program, its maps and its link

Every object in Figure 3.6 counts the references held on it. Each holder is one unit of a reference count, an atomic64_t refcnt in the object, and the object is freed when the count reaches zero. While the counter runs, the program has three: the loader's descriptor, the link, and the perf event, for which bpf_perf_link_attach() takes a reference of its own (bpf_prog_inc(), line 4337, under the comment that perf_event_set_bpf_prog() takes none). Each map has two, the loader's descriptor and the program's used_maps.

Nothing but the loader, or a pin, holds the link. When the loader exits, its descriptors close and the counts fall until the link goes, which detaches the program, and then the program and its maps are freed, in an order that the section "What frees each of them" measures step by step.

An object can also outlive every process. Pinning gives it a file name in bpffs, the BPF file system that Linux 4.4 added, which our test machine mounts at /sys/fs/bpf. The file holds a reference of its own, so sudo bpftool link pin id ID /sys/fs/bpf/wc keeps the counter counting after the loader exits, sudo rm /sys/fs/bpf/wc stops it, and bpf_link__pin() does the same from C. In the kernel, BPF_OBJ_PIN reaches bpf_obj_pin_user() in kernel/bpf/inode.c, which takes a reference through the descriptor it is given and leaves it with the new inode until bpf_destroy_inode() gives it back.

Who holds a map, and how two programs share one

Figure 3.7 shows two programs from two objects, loaded by two bpftool processes, that both name map 2. The second, forget_thread, deletes a thread's count when the thread exits, which keeps chapter 10's hash from filling with threads that are gone. After twenty short-lived writers the map held 4 entries, and 25 once forget_thread was unloaded.

Within one object, libbpf creates each map once and writes its descriptor into every program that names it. Across objects, both definitions ask for LIBBPF_PIN_BY_NAME, so the first loader pins the map at /sys/fs/bpf/write_counts and the second reuses it after map_is_reuse_compat() has compared type, key and value sizes, max_entries and flags. At load, bpf_check() records the map in the second program's used_maps through __add_used_map(), at most 64 maps a program, and takes a reference, so that the map now counts two programs among its holders.

Figure 3.8 lists the holders behind a map's two counts. refcnt counts every holder, while a descriptor or a pin also takes a user reference, counted in usercnt. When the last user reference goes, bpf_map_put_uref() calls the map's map_release_uref, which hashes and arrays use to stop the timers and workqueues in their values. When the last reference of any kind goes, the map is freed.

Why one kind of array emptiesAn array whose slots hold programs, which chapter 7 uses to jump from one program into another, empties every slot when its last user reference goes. A slot holds a reference to its program, and that program may hold the array in its used_maps, so programs that jump into each other could hold each other forever. Emptying the slots when user space lets go breaks every such cycle (commit c9da161c6517, Daniel Borkmann, 2015).

A second process can also reach a map without loading anything. BPF_OBJ_GET opens a pin and returns a new descriptor, and BPF_MAP_GET_FD_BY_ID turns the ID that bpftool prints into one, for a caller with CAP_SYS_ADMIN (bpf_map_get_fd_by_id()). Either way the new descriptor adds one to both counts. The map then stays until that process closes it, even if every program and pin is gone.

What frees each of them

Figure 3.9 follows the counts when the loader is killed. Closing the link detaches the program from the tracepoint, and perf_event_detach_bpf_prog() sleeps about 25 ms in synchronize_rcu_tasks_trace() before it drops its reference, because a CPU may still be running the program. When the last reference goes, bpf_prog_put_deferred() frees the ID at once and passes the memory to call_rcu(), which frees it only after an RCU grace period, the time it takes every CPU to leave any read-side section that could still see the program.

Freeing the program is what releases the maps. bpf_prog_free_deferred() runs in a kworker and puts each map in used_maps, and a map whose count reaches zero is freed in another kworker, from the work that bpf_map_put() queues; write_counts was gone 34.6 ms after the signal.

A pin moves the start of that chain. With the link pinned, nothing happens when the loader exits, and the same sequence begins only when the pin is removed and bpf_destroy_inode() drops the pin's reference; bpf_link_put() hands a last reference to a workqueue, so the teardown then runs in a kworker. A pinned map outlives its programs in the same way, and write_counts, pinned by name in Figure 3.7, stayed while its pin existed after both programs were gone and was freed a second after the pin was removed.

Each kind of object therefore waits for its own last holder. A link goes with its last descriptor or pin and takes the program off its hook as it goes; a program goes once its descriptors, links, perf events and pins have all let go, and only then releases its maps; a map goes when the last of its descriptors, pins and programs has let go.

What it costs

CPU
Kernel 7.2.15 in a throwaway VM, November 2026. The BPF_PROG_LOAD that checks the counter's 27 slots took 0.29 to 0.37 ms of system-call time in five runs and 0.48 ms in another (strace -T), and the whole start-up, 33 calls with libbpf's feature probes, under 3 ms of kernel time. function_graph put 107 µs of a 146 µs load in bpf_check(), which processed 36 instructions (verified_insns in fdinfo); a refused load costs 3.5 µs.
Memory
Charged, with one exception that chapter 10 measures, to the memory cgroup of the process that creates each object (bpf_map_save_memcg(), kernel/bpf/syscall.c): a 4,096-byte page for the program, 83,968 bytes for write_counts, whose 1,024 entries exist from creation, and 336 for .rodata. The object's BTF stays loaded at 1,502 bytes, and the program's x86 code takes 152.
Switches
One system call per command at load and none per event. Teardown runs in the exiting process, an RCU callback and two kworkers, and the exiting loader sleeps about 25 ms in synchronize_rcu_tasks_trace().
Locking
Reference counts are atomic, so a holder comes or goes without a lock. IDs come from an IDR under prog_idr_lock, and bpf_check() takes the global bpf_verifier_lock only for loads without CAP_BPF, so privileged loads are checked in parallel.

Load once at start-up and keep the descriptor or a pin, since every reload pays for a check and a teardown with two grace periods. Count the holders, because any extra one, a pin, a copied descriptor or another map that holds the object as a value, keeps the program running and its memory charged after the loader exits: pin a shared map by name, and remove the pins nothing needs.

When it goes wrong

Most failures of a load show up as an errno and a line from libbpf, and Figure 3.10 pairs each one this chapter met with its usual cause and the command that tells it apart. The first four rows are about getting in: three refusals, and a trace that hides the counter's own load among libbpf's probes. An -EPERM that arrives with an empty log came from a test in bpf_prog_load() that ran before bpf_check() set up the log, the sysctl or a capability, while a refusal that comes with a log came from the check itself, which the next two chapters read. An -EACCES after the program loaded belongs to attaching, and here to the permissions of tracefs.

The capability rows decide how a loader is deployed. Run in the initial user namespace, a tracing loader needs only CAP_BPF and CAP_PERFMON, and the counter's maps need only CAP_BPF. A loader in a container with its own user namespace holds its capabilities only there, while the tests look in the initial namespace, so it needs a BPF token from a bpffs mount that delegates the commands and kinds of program it uses. A token is no use outside such a namespace, since token.c refuses to create one in the initial namespace.

The other rows are about holders. A program that runs when it should have stopped, or stops while it should still run, raises one question, which reference is left, and the answer is always among the holders of Figure 3.6 and Figure 3.8: a descriptor in some process, a link, a pin or a program's used_maps. bpftool lists the objects, ls /sys/fs/bpf lists the pins, and the probes of Lab 3.2 show the order in which the kernel lets go.

One step of the load has stayed closed in this chapter. bpf_check() spent 107 of the counter's 146 µs processing 36 instructions on its two paths, and a load that it refuses comes back with a log in place of an empty buffer. Chapter 4 opens that step and follows the counter through it.

Try it · Watch your loader talk to the kernel, then take its place

~30 min · measure · needs clang, gcc, strace, bpftool and sudo

Task. Build a copy of your hash-map loader in /tmp, run it under strace with sudo, and while it runs, find its program, link and maps with bpftool. Then pin the link, stop the loader, and see who still holds what. You are checking the split between load and attach, and Figure 3.6, on your own machine.

Done when. You can point at the BPF_MAP_CREATE for write_counts, the BPF_PROG_LOAD for count_writes and the BPF_LINK_CREATE that joins it to the perf event; and count_writes keeps counting with no loader running, until you remove the pin.

Hint 1 · direction

Load and attach are made of different system calls, and attach begins with one that is not bpf(). Trace both kinds, then look for your own names among libbpf's probes.

Hint 2 · mechanism

From book/program, compile the object into /tmp/ch02, generate a skeleton from it there, copy hashmap.c beside it and compile. Run the loader under sudo strace -f -o with output to a file, and use a second terminal for bpftool. To take the loader's place, pin the object that holds the program on its hook.

Hint 3 · nearly there

sudo strace -f -o strace.txt -e trace=bpf,perf_event_open ./hashmap > /dev/null; then sudo bpftool prog show name count_writes and sudo bpftool link show. Pin with sudo bpftool link pin id ID /sys/fs/bpf/wc, stop the loader with sudo pkill hashmap (Ctrl-C will not do it: its read loop never looks at the flag the handler sets), and run sudo bpftool map dump name write_counts | grep -c key twice. Read the trace with grep -E 'write_counts|rodata|insn_cnt=27|LINK_CREATE|perf_event_open' strace.txt | cut -c1-120.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 3.

Trace it · Hold the counter with a pin, then let it go

~30 min · measure · needs root in a throwaway VM (virtme-ng) or on a test machine, bpftool and bpftrace

Task. Start the loader, pin its link, and kill the loader. Check what is still loaded. Then trace the release functions of Figure 3.9 while you remove the pin, and read off which thread frees what, and how long after the unlink(). This is the reference count of the section "Who holds the program, its maps and its link", held by a file instead of a process.

Done when. With the loader gone, bpftool still lists count_writes, write_counts and the link; after the pin is removed, your trace shows bpf_link_free in a kworker within a millisecond, and both maps freed several tens of milliseconds later.

Hint 1 · direction

Pin the object that holds the program on its hook, as in Lab 3.1. Removing the pin starts the same chain as closing the link's descriptor, but from another thread.

Hint 2 · mechanism

Find the link's ID with bpftool link show while the loader runs. Probe bpf_link_free, bpf_prog_put_deferred, __bpf_prog_put_rcu, bpf_prog_free_deferred and bpf_map_free_deferred, and set a start time when unlinkat() is called on your pin.

Hint 3 · nearly there

bpftool link pin id ID /sys/fs/bpf/wc, then kill -TERM the loader. The probe script teardown.bt in book/labs/ch11-root.sh starts its clock with tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_unlinkat /str(args.pathname) == "/sys/fs/bpf/wc"/ and prints comm and func for each probe. Run it in the background and rm /sys/fs/bpf/wc.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 3.

Check yourself

  1. Predict the values: in a sudo run of your loader under strace, what does insn_cnt say in the BPF_PROG_LOAD for count_writes, and how many BPF_MAP_CREATE calls carry names from your object?
  2. Predict the value: while the loader runs, what are the reference counts of count_writes and of write_counts, and who holds each reference?
  3. sudo bpftool prog show lists count_writes, yet sudo bpftool map dump name write_counts stays empty however much the system writes. What happened, and which command confirms it?
  4. You give the loader CAP_PERFMON as well as CAP_BPF. Now it prints libbpf: failed to determine tracepoint 'syscalls/sys_enter_write' perf event ID: -EACCES, then failed to auto-attach: -EACCES. Did the program load, and which step failed?
  5. You pin write_counts with bpftool map pin and stop the loader. bpftool map dump still shows the counts, but they never grow again, and bpftool prog show no longer lists count_writes. Why does the map remain when the program does not?
  6. A colleague's copy of forget_thread asks for 2,048 entries, and its loader stops with libbpf: couldn't reuse pinned map at '/sys/fs/bpf/write_counts': parameter mismatch. What did libbpf compare, and what are the ways out?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 3.

Recap

Everything the loader does in the kernel goes through the bpf() system call, driven by libbpf: load creates the maps, writes their descriptors into the wide instructions and loads the program, which the kernel checks and rewrites with real map addresses, and attaching then makes a link that holds the program on its hook. BPF_PROG_LOAD enters at SYSCALL_DEFINE5(bpf), and bpf_prog_load() checks the attributes, a token, the capabilities and the expected attachment, allocates and copies the program, checks the license and any signature, and asks the LSMs, all before bpf_check() creates the log, so a refusal there leaves the log empty. bpf_check() records used_maps, walks the program and compiles it; then the program gets an ID, a kallsyms name and an anonymous-inode descriptor. Descriptors, links, perf events, pins and used_maps are reference counts, a map also counts the user references of its descriptors and pins, and libbpf shares a map between objects by pinning it by name and reusing it when the definitions match. The last put frees the ID at once and the memory only after RCU grace periods, the program first and its maps after it.

New words in this chapter

bpf() system call
the single system call through which user space creates and controls BPF objects; its first argument is a command
skeleton
the header bpftool gen skeleton writes: the object as bytes, plus open, load, attach and destroy functions
load
creating maps and programs in the kernel; nothing runs yet
link
a bpf_link: a kernel object that holds one program on one hook; releasing it detaches the program
program type
the kind of program; it fixes what the program gets and may call
BPF token
an object made from a delegating bpffs mount that lets a process in a user namespace pass the capability checks for the commands and types the mount allows; since 6.9
anonymous inode
a file with no path that the kernel creates to give a process a descriptor for an internal object
reference count
a counter in a kernel object with one unit per holder; the object is freed when it reaches zero
pinning
giving a BPF object a file name, which holds a reference without any process
bpffs
the BPF file system, mounted at /sys/fs/bpf, where pins live
user reference
a reference held from user space, by a descriptor or a pin, counted in usercnt beside the map's ordinary reference count
RCU grace period
the time it takes every CPU to leave any read-side section that could still see an object, after which the object can be freed

Part II

The verifier

Before the counter runs, the kernel proves that it is safe. We watch the verifier walk every path of the program, read the log it leaves when it refuses one, follow that log line into verifier.c, and see how it tracks the values a register can hold.

Chapter 4

The verifier walks every path

Before a program runs once, the kernel follows every path through it and refuses it unless each one is safe. For the write counter that walk took 36 instructions and a fraction of a millisecond; a loop written the wrong way can take a million instructions and half a second, and still be refused.

Spine. In chapter 3 the counter went down the bpf() system call to bpf_check() and came back as a descriptor. Now we go inside that one call, where the kernel follows every path of the counter before it agrees to keep it.

27 min · VERIFIER

What the kernel reports about its walk

The part of the kernel that follows every path through a program is the verifier, and it runs inside bpf_check(), the call that chapter 3 left unopened. We cannot watch it with a tracer, because it is one long computation inside one system call, but it can write a report. The verifier log is the text the verifier writes into a buffer that the loader passes with the load. The log level, a bit mask in the same request, says how much to write: 1 for each instruction walked, 2 for the full state at each one, 4 for statistics. We load the counter with a twenty-line libbpf loader that sets the level and the buffer itself, and Figure 4.1 shows what came back.

The last line matters most. processed 36 insns is the number of instructions the walk went through, counted every time it passes one, and the limit beside it is the budget that count may not exceed. total_states 2 says the walk saved its state twice along the way, peak_states 2 is the most it held at once, and max_states_per_insn 0 is the largest number of checkpoints it found at one instruction without a match among them. mark_read is still printed in v7.2, but nothing in the source sets it any more, so it reads 0 for every program.

verified_insnsThe kernel keeps the count with the loaded program (verifier.c line 19982) and reports it in bpf_prog_info and in the descriptor's /proc/PID/fdinfo entry. bpftool v7.8.0 prints it in neither its plain nor its JSON listing.

The lines above it come only with level 4. The verification time, 146 µs here, is the clock of the whole of bpf_check() from its first line to its statistics (lines 19774 and 19980 of verifier.c), so it includes the setup and the rewriting around the walk. In fifteen loads over three VM runs it ranged from 99 to 551 µs, with a median of 156. The stack depth is 16 bytes, the two slots that hold the key and the value, and insns processed repeats the count for each function the walk verified on its own.

The count is the counter's two paths. The level-6 log in Figure 4.1 ends the first path at the exit in slot 26. It then prints from 9 to 12, walks again from slot 12 and stops at slot 25 with the word safe. The first path is 24 instructions and the second 12, which add up to the 36 of the statistics line; the rest of this chapter explains why the walk went that way.

What the walk proves

The page lagsThe kernel's verifier page still opens by saying that the first step disallows loops, which was true before 5.3. In v7.2, push_insn() in kernel/bpf/cfg.c refuses a backward jump only when the loader lacks CAP_BPF (lines 133 to 139).

The verifier's job is the promise that Figure 4.2 spells out as six things a loaded program never does, and if it cannot show all six on every path, the load fails and nothing runs. Only the last row is about time, and the check behind it is the plain count of the statistics line. The kernel will walk at most one million instructions, a number kept as BPF_COMPLEXITY_LIMIT_INSNS in include/linux/bpf.h next to the comment "yes. 1M insns". Until Linux 5.2 a program could have at most 4,096 instructions.

The verifier works in two steps. The shape check looks at every jump once, making sure that none leaves the program and that every instruction can be reached. Then the walk starts at the first instruction and follows every path, a route from the start to an exit that takes one side at each branch.

The promise is about safety alone. The counter keys its map by thread ID, as chapter 1 pointed out, and the verifier has no opinion about that, because it checks what the program may touch and leaves what the program counts to its author.

Walking the counter

The counter has one branch, the test of r0 at slot 9, so it has two paths, and we follow both in Figure 4.3. At each instruction the verifier updates its verifier state, which records for every register and stack slot what kind of value it holds.

After the lookup at slot 8, r0 is a pointer-or-NULL, a register that points at a map value or holds NULL without the kernel knowing which, so nothing may be read through it. At slot 9 the walk splits. On the fall-through side the test has shown that r0 is not zero, so r0 becomes a plain map value that slot 10 may read. The other side, where r0 is 0, cannot be walked at the same time. The verifier copies the whole state as it stands, notes slot 12 as the place where that side starts, and puts the copy on a stack.

That copy is a pending branch, a side of a conditional jump that the walk has kept for later, together with the state it must start from. The walk is depth first: it follows one path to an exit, then takes the most recent pending branch off the stack and follows it, and it ends when an exit is reached and the stack is empty. Figure 4.4 lists the counter's walk in those terms.

Why 25 and not 12Slot 12 is a jump target, so it could be compared too, but the first path saved no state there. The verifier saves one only after at least two jumps and eight instructions since the last save (bpf_is_state_visited() in kernel/bpf/states.c, v7.2), which on the counter's first path left slots 9 and 25.

The second path starts at slot 12 and stops at slot 25, where the verifier saved its state on the first path, so it never reaches slot 26. The verifier compares the two states, finds that the saved one covers the new one in everything the rest of the program still uses, and treats the rest as already proved. Cutting a path short in this way is called pruning. The 36 of the statistics line are therefore 24 instructions on the first path, 11 on the second and one more for slot 25, counted when it is compared.

What the kernel knows about one register

At level 1 or 2 the log lists, after each instruction, the registers that changed, in the form Figure 4.5 takes apart. The first word of an entry is the register type. A scalar is a plain number that may never be used as a pointer, while map_value points into a value inside a map. The second entry in the figure is the first without _or_null, because the test at slot 9 changed that one flag and left the rest of the entry as it was.

The rest of the entry is what the checks need. The value size, vs=8, is what every read through r0 is measured against, and id=1 is shared by every copy of this pointer, so that a test on one copy clears the NULL flag on all of them. A scalar carries bounds instead, which is how the kernel knows that the key read back at slot 12 lies between 0 and 0xffffffff; chapter 6 explains how it works out such bounds.

Why now. Every idea of the first half of this chapter is on it in the kernel's words: the two steps, register types, the id shared by copies, and pruning.

About 35 minutes · VERIFIER

Checkpoints, and when two states are the same

The walk does not compare states at every instruction. During the shape check, kernel/bpf/cfg.c marks the places where a comparison can pay off, every conditional jump, the target of every jump and the instruction after every call, and only at those does do_check() call bpf_is_state_visited(). A checkpoint is a copy of the verifier state saved at such a place, kept in a list per instruction so that every later path reaching it can be compared with it. Figure 4.6 draws the three questions the walk asks there.

"For each new branch to analyse, the verifier looks at all the states it's previously been in when at this instruction. If any of them contain the current state as a subset, the branch is 'pruned' - that is, the fact that the previous state was accepted implies the current state would be as well."

Documentation/bpf/verifier.rst, section "Pruning", Linux v7.2

"Equal" is the wrong word for what the first question asks, although the function is called states_equal(). The comment above regsafe(), which compares one register, says it returns true "if (rold safe implies rcur safe)". A saved state covers the current one when it is at least as general, so that whatever the saved path proved for every value it allowed also holds for the narrower set of values the current path brings. A register that was never written in the saved state covers anything, because the path that went on from there never read it.

Only what is still to be read takes part. A register or stack slot is live at an instruction when some path from there may read it before writing it. In v7.2 the verifier works out the live registers of every instruction before the walk starts (bpf_compute_live_registers()), prints them at level 2 and compares only those. Figure 4.7 shows the counter's: at slots 12 and 25 no register is live, which is why the pending branch could drop r0 and why slot 25 matched whatever the two paths held. At each checkpoint clean_verifier_state() also forgets dead registers and stack slots in the current state, so that they cannot make two states look different.

For a scalar the comparison has a second side. Its range is compared only if some check further on depended on it, and the walk records that dependency as it goes, which is the subject of chapter 6. A pointer must keep its type, flags included, so a pointer-or-NULL never stands in for a map value, nor the other way round.

The third question decides when to save. Saving a checkpoint at every prune point would cost memory and comparisons for little gain. The walk therefore saves one only when at least two jumps and eight instructions have passed since the last, a rule that the comment beside it credits with saving up to half the memory and a fifth of the time in the kernel's tests. A checkpoint that keeps failing to match is moved out of the list once its misses exceed three times its hits plus three, and a loader without CAP_BPF stops adding checkpoints at an instruction that already has more than 64.

Loops

A loop is a branch that jumps backwards, and the shape check sees it as a back-edge, a jump to an instruction that is still on its own path. Before Linux 5.3 every back-edge was refused. Since then the verifier accepts a bounded loop, one whose last round it can see, by walking it. Each round is a further stretch of the same path, with a new state, until the loop's test is decided as false and the walk goes on past it.

The second question of Figure 4.6 is the guard against a loop that never ends. When the walk reaches a checkpoint saved earlier on the same path, it may not prune against it, because that path has not reached an exit and has proved nothing yet. If the two states are identical in every register and slot, the loop has made no progress, and the verifier refuses the program with "infinite loop detected"; otherwise it goes round again. A counted loop changes its counter every round, so it is walked once per round, and the statistics grow with its bound.

The plain loop of Figure 4.8 costs eight instructions of walking per byte, the eight instructions of its body, plus 19 for the rest of the program, so sixteen times the bytes cost sixteen times the walking. Three later additions let a loop be proved without walking every round. Each one gives the walk a place where it may compare a state with one from an earlier round of the same path, and stop going round once the new round brings nothing the earlier one did not cover.

The bpf_loop() helper, added in 5.17, takes a count and a function, and the kernel calls that function once per round. The walk treats the call as a branch into the function that may be taken again. It walks the function, comes back to the call, and stops once the state at the call falls within the state it saw the round before (push_callback_call(), verifier.c line 9276). The round number reaches the function as an unknown number, so the function must check it before using it as an index, and the hash loop's 4 KB are proved in 63 instructions.

An open-coded iterator, added in 6.4, is a loop in the program's own code that asks a kernel function for each next round. For the numbers behind bpf_for() that function is bpf_iter_num_next(), which returns NULL when the rounds run out. The verifier relies on that contract.

At each such call it walks the side where the iterator has run out and keeps the side where it returned a value as a pending branch. It stops going round once the state at the call repeats. To help that happen, it forgets the range of any number that no check has needed yet, so that a number the loop changes every round, such as a count of its own, does not make every round look new (comment above process_iter_next_call(), line 7532).

may_goto, added in March 2024, is a jump instruction that the program takes only when a hidden count runs out. On x86-64 in v7.2 that count is checked against a clock, and the loop is cut off after a quarter of a second (bpf_check_timed_may_goto(), kernel/bpf/core.c line 3407).

The walk gives it the same treatment as an iterator call, yet in Figure 4.8 it made the plain loop dearer. The loop's test i < N is decided from the known value of i in every round. A register whose value decided a branch is compared by that value at a checkpoint, so no round's state ever falls within an earlier one's. The walk still goes round 256 times, and every round now adds a checkpoint and a pending branch. With the counter kept in the map value, where the walk does not follow it, the same loop is proved in 67 instructions at any size.

Function calls

Since 4.16 a program can call functions of its own. A function marked static in C is walked at each call site, inside the caller's walk, in a new frame of the state that holds its registers and stack. When it returns, the walk continues in the caller with what it learned. Two states can cover each other only if every frame was entered from the same call site, so a function called from four places is walked four times. In our measurement a 32-round loop in a function called four times cost 666 instructions of walking.

A global function, one without static, is verified once on its own, for any arguments that its types in the program's BTF allow. At each call the walk checks the arguments against those types, gives r0 an unknown number and moves on, and at level 1 it prints Func#%d ('%s') is global and assumed valid. Afterwards do_check_subprogs() walks each called global function from its own start (verifier.c line 18525). The same four calls cost 14 instructions in the caller and 163 in the function, 177 in all. The price is everything the caller knew, because a global function that indexes an array with its argument must check the bound itself even when every caller passes a constant.

Both kinds count against one budget. env->insn_processed is not reset between the main program and its global functions, which is why the statistics print one count per verified function after insns processed and their sum on the last line.

The limits, and where they live

The budget is the limit that most programs meet first, and Figure 4.9 puts it beside the others. Each counts something different. The budget counts instructions walked, so it grows with paths and rounds. The jump-sequence limit counts pending branches on the stack at once, which grow when one path passes thousands of branches it cannot decide before it reaches an exit. The call-depth and stack limits bound the frames that a walk must hold.

The stack row has a second form in v7.2. Programs of the tracing types (BPF_PROG_TYPE_KPROBE, TRACEPOINT, RAW_TRACEPOINT and PERF_EVENT, and BPF_PROG_TYPE_TRACING, _LSM and _STRUCT_OPS programs that ask for it; bpf_enable_priv_stack(), verifier.c line 5026) on x86-64 can give each function a stack of its own, and then a function that uses 64 bytes or more is checked against 512 bytes alone, with "stack size of subprog %d is %d. Too large" (line 5138). Three nested functions with 200 bytes of stack each were refused as a socket filter with the message in the table and loaded as a tracepoint program, with a largest frame of 208 bytes.

Inside the v7.2 source

Figure 4.10 lists the code behind everything so far, in the order a load reaches it. bpf_check() runs the shape check in cfg.c and a few passes that prepare the walk, among them the live registers of Figure 4.7. Then do_check_main() builds the first state in do_check_common() and hands it to do_check(). chapter 5 draws the same phases around one log line and follows that line from verbose() into the loader's buffer, so we stay with the loop.

do_check() is one for (;;) over the current instruction. Each pass first increments insn_processed and returns -E2BIG once it passes the budget. At a prune point it calls bpf_is_state_visited(), and a return of 1 sends it to the exit handling. It then gives up the CPU if another task needs it, returns -EAGAIN on a pending signal, prints the instruction when the log asks for it, and hands it to do_check_insn(), which picks a checker by its kind.

A conditional jump goes to check_cond_jmp_op(), which first asks whether the test can be decided from what is known. Only if both sides can happen does it call push_stack() for the jump side and let the walk fall through.

push_stack() allocates an entry, copies the whole current state into it, links it at the head of env->head and counts it in env->stack_size, which is the number the jump-sequence limit tests. At an exit, or after a prune, the loop reaches the label process_bpf_exit, where pop_stack() copies the head entry over the current state and continues at its instruction. When the stack is empty it returns -ENOENT, the loop breaks, and the program is proved.

What it costs

CPU
Kernel 7.2.15 in a VM with 16 vCPUs, 12 November 2026. The counter's walk of 36 instructions sat inside a bpf_check() of 99 to 551 µs, median 156 µs over fifteen loads. Time follows instructions walked: about 0.5 µs each for the hash loops, 1,000,001 in 0.50 s; the plain loop over 4 KB took 16 ms, against 0.2 to 0.3 ms with bpf_loop() or bpf_for().
Memory
A checkpoint is a bpf_verifier_state_list of 256 bytes, a bpf_func_state of 1,032 per frame, which kmalloc rounds up to 2,048, and 96 per 8-byte stack slot (BTF of 7.2.15), about 2.4 KB; a pending branch is the same around a 256-byte stack entry. The loop that hit the budget held 10,001 checkpoints, about 24 MB, charged to the loader's memory cgroup until the load ended.
Switches
One bpf() call, the walk running in the loader's thread throughout; do_check() yields between instructions when another task needs the CPU and stops with -EAGAIN on a signal.
Locking
None with CAP_BPF. Without it every load takes the mutex bpf_verifier_lock: two loads as the user nobody, started together, took 30.7 and 60.7 ms of verification time, the second waiting for the first, while as root both took 30.8 ms.

Read the statistics line of every program at log level 4 before it ships. If the count grows with a loop's bound, or passes about 100,000, rewrite the loop with bpf_for() (6.4 and later) or bpf_loop() (5.17 and later), whose walk does not grow with the round count; keep plain loops for a dozen rounds or fewer.

When it goes wrong

The rows of Figure 4.11 come from programs we wrote to hit each limit, loaded one at a time with book/labs/walk-root.sh. The first three refuse loops, and they fail in different ways. The budget is met by a loop the walk follows round by round, and its statistics show thousands of checkpoints spread evenly along the walk. The jump-sequence limit is met far below the budget by a loop whose body holds a branch the walk cannot decide, because each round leaves one pending branch that nothing removes until the first path reaches an exit. The infinite-loop message arrives within a few instructions, as soon as a round brings the walk back to a checkpoint with nothing changed.

The error code sorts most of these before any reading. -E2BIG means a limit on size or depth, -EINVAL a loop the verifier will not walk, and -EACCES the stack, as it does for the broken rules that chapter 5 reads. The last four rows are loads that succeed, which only the statistics can explain, so a loader in production should record the statistics line of every load and not only of the ones that fail.
