Hint 1 · direction

The walk follows the fall-through side of a branch first and keeps the jump side for later. A wide instruction counts once.

Hint 2 · mechanism

Count the first path from slot 0 to slot 26. The second path starts at slot 12 with the state from the jump side of slot 9, and it stops at the first slot where a state saved on the first path covers it. The margin note on slot 25 says where states were saved.

Hint 3 · nearly there

Twenty-seven slots minus three second halves of wide instructions gives the first path's count. On the second path, slots 12 to 24 are walked, and slot 25 is counted once, when it is compared.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 4.

Try it · Measure one loop written three ways

~40 min · measure · needs clang, libbpf and root in a throwaway VM (virtme-ng) or on a test machine

Task. Load the hash loop of Figure 4.8 written three ways, at 256 and at 4,096 bytes, with the log at level 4, and fill in a table of instructions walked, states saved and verification time. Before each load, predict whether its count will change with the size. The three loops are in book/labs/walk/loops.bpf.c; their bodies are below.

/* 1. plain: the walk goes round once per byte */
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
        h = step(h, s->b[i]);

/* 2. bpf_loop(): the body becomes a callback */
static long one_byte(u64 i, void *data)
{
        struct lctx *c = data;

        if (i >= MAXB)
                return 1;
        c->h = step(c->h, c->s->b[i]);
        return 0;
}
        bpf_loop(N, one_byte, &c, 0);

/* 3. an open-coded iterator */
bpf_for(i, 0, N)
        h = step(h, s->b[i]);

Done when. You have six rows, three loops at two sizes, and the plain loop's count has grown about sixteen times while the other two have not moved.

Hint 1 · direction

The statistics line counts instructions walked. Ask, for each loop, whether the walk needs to know which round it is in.

Hint 2 · mechanism

Build the object twice, with -DN=256 and -DN=4096, and the loader book/labs/walk/stats.c with -lbpf. Load one program at a time with ./stats OBJ PROG 4, where PROG is plain, helper or iter. book/labs/walk-root.sh, run in the VM, does all of it and writes /tmp/book-labs/walk/loops.txt.

Hint 3 · nearly there

Compile from book/program, so that vmlinux.h is found: clang -g -O2 -target bpf -D__TARGET_ARCH_x86 -I/usr/include/bpf -I. -DN=256 -c ../labs/walk/loops.bpf.c -o /tmp/loops256.bpf.o. Time a load by the verification time line, not by the loader's wall clock, which includes libbpf's own work.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 4.

Check yourself

  1. Predict the value: a program has three independent if/else blocks in a row, and nothing set inside them is read after them. How many paths does it have, and how few walks could the verifier get away with?
  2. A program copies the lookup's result, w = v, tests only w against NULL, then reads through v. You expected a rejection, but the kernel loads it. Why?
  3. Your loader shows one count per thread where you wanted one per process. The program passed every check at load time. Is the verifier broken?
  4. Predict the value: the plain loop of Figure 4.8 walks 2,067 instructions at 256 bytes and 32,787 at 4,096. How many will it walk at 1,024 bytes, and about how many bytes could it hash before the budget refused it, if the buffer had no 4 KB limit?
  5. A socket filter that loads as root is refused for your service account with back-edge from insn 10 to 3 and processed 0 insns. Which step refused it, and why did the walk never start?
  6. A small function called from four places gives your program insns processed 666; removing static from it brings that to 14+163. Why does the count fall, and what can the function no longer rely on?
  7. Predict the value: a loop of 10,000 rounds tests a random bit in every round and is refused with The sequence of 8193 jumps is too complex. after processed 73734 insns. How many rounds had the walk gone through, and how many instructions does one round cost?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 4.

Recap

The verifier runs inside bpf_check() and refuses any program it cannot prove safe on every path, with a shape check over the jumps and then a depth-first walk that keeps a type for every register and stack slot, pushes the other side of each undecided branch onto a stack and pops it at the next exit. At prune points it compares the current state with saved checkpoints and stops a path that a finished one covers, comparing only what is live, which cut the counter's second path to 12 instructions and its walk to 36. Loops are walked round by round unless they give the walk a point where rounds can be compared, as bpf_loop(), bpf_for() and may_goto do, and static functions are walked at every call while global ones are verified once. The budget of one million instructions, 8,192 pending branches, 16 frames and 512 bytes of stack bound the walk, and log level 4 shows how close a program came to each.

New words in this chapter

verifier
the part of the kernel that walks a program at load time and refuses it unless every path is safe
verifier log
the text the verifier writes into the loader's buffer: each instruction walked, the reason it stopped, and statistics
log level
how much the verifier writes: 1 for the instructions walked, 2 for the full state at each one, 4 for statistics
shape check
the verifier's first step: every jump lands inside the program and every instruction is reachable
path
one route from the first instruction to an exit, taking one side at each branch
verifier state
what the verifier knows at one instruction: a type, and bounds or sizes, for every register and stack slot
pointer-or-NULL
a pointer that may be NULL, such as a map lookup's result; it cannot be read through until a test on that path
pending branch
a side of a conditional jump that the walk keeps on a stack, with a copy of the state, to follow after the current path ends
pruning
stopping a path where it matches a saved state already proved safe
register type
the kind of value a register holds: never written, a scalar, or one of many pointer types
scalar
a plain number, with bounds, that may never be used as a pointer
checkpoint
a verifier state saved at a prune point, for later paths to be compared with
live
of a register or stack slot at an instruction: some path from there may read it before writing it
back-edge
a jump to an instruction still on the jump's own path; the shape of every loop
bounded loop
a loop whose last round the verifier can see; accepted since Linux 5.3
open-coded iterator
a loop in the program's own code that asks a kernel function for each next round, such as bpf_for(); since 6.4
global function
a function of the program without static, verified once for any arguments its BTF types allow
instruction limit
one million instructions walked, across all paths, before the verifier gives up

Chapter 5

Reading a rejection, from log line to source line

A refused load comes with a log, and every line of that log was printed by one call in the kernel source. This chapter reads three logs from the write counter, each changed in one line, from the bottom up, and then follows one of them to the line of verifier.c that printed it, to the test that pins it and to the road a change to it would take.

Spine. In chapter 4 the kernel walked both paths of the counter and accepted it. Now we break it on purpose, read what the kernel writes when it says no, and follow one of those lines back to the source that wrote it.

21 min · VERIFIER

Three logs from one program

We made three copies of the write counter, changed one line in each and loaded them on kernel 7.2.15, in a throwaway virtual machine on 12 November 2026. Figure 5.1 shows the last lines the kernel wrote for each. That text is the verifier log, which the verifier writes as it walks, one line per instruction, followed by the reason it stopped and a line of statistics. Every log in the figure ends with the statistics, and the reason sits just above them.

The log never reaches the kernel's own message buffer. The load call carries a buffer, its size and a level, the fields log_buf, log_size and log_level in include/uapi/linux/bpf.h, and the verifier writes only there. libbpf first loads with no log at all, and only if that fails does it load again with one and print the result between BEGIN PROG LOAD LOG and END PROG LOAD LOG.

Tracing bpftool prog load of log (a)'s copy with strace -e trace=bpf in the same VM shows both loads, after six small programs with which libbpf probes the kernel's features. The copy goes in with log_level=0 and comes back EACCES, then again with log_level=1 and a buffer of 16,777,215 bytes. The counter's loader sets no print function of its own, so the log lands on standard error, just above the loader's "Failed to open and load BPF skeleton".

Three error codesThe two rule breaks fail with -EACCES and the loop with -E2BIG, and libbpf prints the code on its "failed to load" line. A helper the program type does not allow gives -EINVAL, so the code alone says which kind of no it was.

How much the verifier writes is set by the log level. Level 1, which libbpf asks for after a failure, prints each instruction walked and the registers it changed; level 2 prints the full state at every instruction, 4 adds the statistics, and bpftool -d asks for 1, 2 and 4 together. Level 1 also forgets, because each time a path is proved safe and the walk goes back for another, the verifier rewinds the log to where that path began, so that what remains is the path that failed. The section "How a log line reaches the loader" shows the lines of source that do the rewinding.

Reading one log from the bottom

We read a log from the bottom up, as Figure 5.2 does with log (b). The last line is statistics, printed even when the load fails, and it matters only when the reason is the limit. Above it is the reason, and above the reason is the instruction the walk stopped at, with its slot and opcode. Above that is the walk itself, interleaved with the C lines that the kernel takes from the object's BTF.

The reason names a rule and usually a register, and from there the search goes upward until it finds where that register took on the state the rule refused. In log (b) the entry at slot 9 already holds half of the answer, vs=8, and the reason supplies the other half with off=8 size=8. Eight bytes read from offset eight end past the end of an eight-byte value. There is a second reason to start at the bottom, which we meet in the source: a log too long for the loader's buffer keeps its end and drops its beginning.

"However, when the verifier rejects a program, the unclear error makes repair challenging: the error reports where verification stopped, not where the program lost the proof the verifier required."

Yusheng Zheng and seven co-authors, "Characterizing and Bridging the Diagnostic Gap in eBPF Verifier Rejections", arXiv 2607.02748, July 2026 (abstract)

From message to rule

Figure 5.3 puts the three side by side, and we take them in order. Log (a) breaks the pointer-or-NULL rule of chapter 4, yet the read at slot 10 is a correct read of a map value; what is missing is the test that should come between the lookup and the read.

The other side of the logResearchers find verifier bugs by running this chapter backwards. They generate programs, then flag any where the verifier's verdict disagrees with what the program really does or with a written specification, as State Embedding (OSDI 2024), BVF (EuroSys 2024) and Veritas (SOSP 2025) do. Between them they found more than two dozen verifier bugs.

Log (b) breaks the bounds rule, and it is the only one of the three whose fix sits on the line the log quotes, the + 1. Log (c) breaks the instruction limit. The loop's bound is read from the map, so no round can be shown to be the last, and r7 had reached 0x1e841, about 125,000 rounds, when the walk gave up. With the loop capped by i < *curr_val && i < 16, the same copy loads after 190 instructions.

The study behind the field note found single messages with as many as nine different causes, so the message names the rule while only the walk above it shows where the proof was lost. The rest of the chapter goes the other way, from the message of log (a) back into the kernel that printed it, and then on to the test that keeps that message from changing.

One log line, one source line

The reason of log (a), R0 invalid mem access 'map_value_or_null', was printed by a single verbose() call, and the code around that call holds the condition that sent the walk there, which the message leaves out. Searching the v7.2 tree for the fixed middle of that message, as in Figure 5.4, brings back two lines of kernel/bpf/verifier.c.

We read upward from each hit to the branch around it. Line 6164 sits in the branch for a different kind of pointer. Line 6322 is the last else of check_mem_access(), the function that checks every load and store through a pointer, and it catches every pointer type that no earlier branch accepted.

The broken copyThe broken copy also shows the calling convention of the Primer at work. Clang moved the key pointer into r6 before the call, because the program needs it again afterwards and r1 to r5 do not keep their values.

Line 6106 says why r0 was not accepted. The map-value branch compares the type with ==, so it takes only a plain map value, and r0 still carried the maybe-NULL flag from the lookup, which log.c prints as the suffix _or_null. The kernel never says that the program forgot a check; what it says is that this type may not be read through here.

How a log line reaches the loader

Every line of a log, the walk as well as the reason, passes through the same two functions. verbose(), at line 327 of verifier.c, returns at once when the loader asked for no log and otherwise hands its format to bpf_verifier_vlog() in log.c. That function formats the line into a 1,024-byte buffer inside the kernel and copies it into the loader's buffer with copy_to_user(). Each line therefore crosses into user space as it is written, and none waits for the end of the walk.

The parts of Figure 5.2 come from separate calls in do_check(), made for each instruction before its checker runs. verbose_linfo() prints the C line that the object's BTF ties to the slot, and bpf_verbose_insn() prints the instruction itself through disasm.c. The register state after the semicolon arrives one round later, because only when the next instruction comes up does do_check() know which registers the last one changed. print_insn_state() then rewinds the log by one byte, over the newline, and appends the state to the line above. That is why the instruction where a walk stopped, such as slot 10 of log (a), never has a state after it.

The loader's buffer has a fixed size, and a long walk writes more than fits. In v7.2 the kernel treats the buffer as a ring unless told otherwise. Once it is full, each new line overwrites the oldest bytes, so what is left when the walk stops is its last stretch, the reason and the statistics included. A loader that adds BPF_LOG_FIXED, the value 8, to the level keeps the start of the log instead and loses everything after the buffer fills, which for a rejection means losing the reason. Figure 5.5 shows both on log (a) with a 256-byte buffer.

Either way the load then fails with -ENOSPC, which bpf_check() returns in place of the verifier's own error (line 19985). The kernel also writes the size the whole log needed into log_true_size, a field of the load call's attributes. libbpf's low-level bpf_prog_load() hands that size back, yet its object loader ignores it and doubles its own buffer instead, walking the program once more each time.

The size the kernel compares is the longest the log ever grew, before any rewinding, so the unchanged counter, which the verifier accepts, fails to load with a 64-byte buffer, the third block of the figure. The ring also costs time on a long walk. With a 64 KB buffer the unbounded copy of log (c) failed in 3.7 to 4.2 s, three runs in the same VM, against 2.8 s with BPF_LOG_FIXED, which stops copying once the buffer is full.

The forgetting of level 1 lives in the same code. When the walk finishes a path and takes the next branch from its stack, pop_stack() (line 1705) calls bpf_vlog_reset() with the log position saved alongside that branch, unless the level includes 2. When a whole walk at level 1 succeeds, line 18499 resets the log to its start, and the counter, accepted, leaves 98 bytes, its statistics line and no walk at all.

The map around that line

check_mem_access() is one stop on a longer trip, which Figure 5.6 draws. Each load runs bpf_check() once, and it checks the program's shape, walks every path and then rewrites the program for running. In v7.2 those phases live in separate files, with the shape check in cfg.c, the state comparison behind pruning in states.c, the rewrites in fixups.c and the log's wording and copying in log.c. Of the rejection, only what log.c does comes from outside verifier.c.

The walk itself stays in verifier.c. Its loop, do_check(), hands each instruction to do_check_insn(), which picks a checker by the kind of instruction: arithmetic, load, store, call or jump. The counter's call, its test and its load therefore go to three different checkers.

Figure 5.7 follows them. At the call, check_helper_call() resets r1 to r5 at line 10414 and gives r0 the map-value type, flag and all, at line 10455, so the doubt about NULL is recorded before any test is seen. At the test, check_cond_jmp_op() splits the state in two, making r0 a plain map value on one branch and the number 0 on the other, which removes that doubt without adding any check of its own. At the load, line 6106 accepts only the first of the two.

"When type PTR_TO_MAP_VALUE_OR_NULL passes through 'if (reg != 0) goto +off' insn, the register holding that pointer in the true branch changes state to PTR_TO_MAP_VALUE and the same register changes state to CONST_IMM in the false branch. See check_cond_jmp_op()."

The design comment at the top of kernel/bpf/verifier.c, lines 155 to 158, Linux v7.2
Stable since 2014: learn itDrifting, as of v7.2 (August 2026): look it up
One entry, bpf_check(): check the shape, walk every path, rewriteWhich file each phase lives in; moved functions gain a bpf_ prefix
A rejection is one verbose() call and an error codeLine numbers: verifier.c is 20,065 lines in v7.2 and 25,732 in bpf-next at 7.4-rc1
Every register carries a type and boundsType names: the design comment still says CONST_IMM
A change in behaviour needs a testWhere tests live: 121 progs/verifier_*.c files in v7.2
A comment that is wrongNo code in v7.2, or in bpf-next on 11 November 2026, uses CONST_IMM. Line 15689 makes the false branch a scalar known to be zero. A comment that disagrees with the code is a classic first patch, best written after a search of the list archive.

The left column of that table is worth learning and the right one worth looking up each time. The two passes date from 2014, but the line numbers here are true for v7.2 only, since in today's bpf-next tree verifier.c is about 5,700 lines longer.

The test that pins the message, and the road upstream

A message that users can hit is pinned by a selftest, a test kept in the kernel tree under tools/testing/selftests/bpf. Searching the v7.2 selftests for the full message brings back six files under progs/. One of them, verifier_map_ret_val.c, holds a test called "don't check return value before access", whose body is the counter's bug in BPF assembly: r2 = r10, a call to the lookup, then a write through r0 with no test.

The test annotations above it, __failure and __msg("R0 invalid mem access 'map_value_or_null'"), tell the test runner to load the program, expect a rejection and find that text in the log. A patch that rewords the message in check_mem_access() makes this test fail, which is what the test is for. The BPF maintainers' guide asks for a test with every change to verifier behaviour, because behaviour that no test tracks "could potentially be subject to change".

The runner, test_loader.c, gets its log the way the counter's loader does. It gives each program a 2 MB buffer of its own with bpf_program__set_log_buf() and leaves the level at 0 unless the test asks for more with __log_level() or test_progs runs with -v. libbpf therefore loads the program once without a log and, on the failure the test expects, again at level 1 into that buffer. Each __msg() is then searched for in the log starting where the previous one matched, so a test with several messages expects them in the order the walk prints them.

Figure 5.8 is the rest of the trip, also from that guide. Fixes go to the bpf tree and features and cleanups to the bpf-next tree. An author can run BPF CI, the maintainers' test system on GitHub, before anyone reads the patch. The patch then goes to bpf@vger.kernel.org with PATCH bpf-next in its subject, waits in patchwork, the review queue, and reaches mainline through net-next.

Read with · HOWTO interact with BPF subsystem, Documentation/bpf/bpf_devel_QA.rst, Linux kernel documentation (v7.2)

What it is. The BPF maintainers' answers to the questions every new contributor asks: where to send patches, which tree, how to test.

Why now. Every step of Figure 5.8, and the rule that verifier changes need tests, come from it.

  2. "How do I indicate which tree (bpf vs. bpf-next)…". The subject prefixes, with the git format-patch lines to type. Five minutes.
  3. "Verifier changes and test cases". Three minutes.
  4. "What is the minimum requirement before I submit my BPF patches?" Testing is "a hard requirement"; fixes need a Fixes: tag. Five minutes.

Skip. The questions on samples/bpf, bpftool and iproute2, the stable-backport questions, and the LLVM section, which matter later and are not on this road yet.

The passage. The guide has no figures; study the answer to "How do the changes make their way into Linux?", which names two trees and has both drain into networking trees before mainline.

Carry in. Three questions; their answers are in the key under chapter 5.

  1. Your first patch only corrects a wrong comment. Which tree does it target, and what goes in its subject?
  2. What must a patch that changes the verifier's behaviour include, and what happens if it does not?
  3. You run kernel 7.2. Which version of the BPF selftests should you run against it, and why not the newest?

About 35 minutes · VERIFIER

What it costs

CPU
Kernel 7.2.15 in a throwaway VM, November 2026. Verification time follows the instructions walked: the counter's 36 took 107 µs of a 146 µs load (chapter 3), and the unbounded copy reached the one-million limit in 3.9 s. A refused load is walked again for the log, because libbpf retries at level 1 with its own 16 MB buffer (BPF_LOG_BUF_SIZE) and doubles it on each ENOSPC: that copy failed after 36 s, about 8 s at each of 16, 32, 64 and 128 MB (strace -T). Level 2 slowed verification of the counter from 221 to 591 µs and of the bounded copy from 586 to 2,844 µs.
Memory
53,728 bytes for struct bpf_verifier_env, 136 per instruction for its side data and at least 1,288 per saved state (BTF of 7.2.15), charged to the loader's memory cgroup and freed when the load ends. The log buffer is the loader's, capped at UINT_MAX >> 2 bytes, about 1 GB (kernel/bpf/log.c); level 2 wrote 6.7 KB for the counter and 62 KB for the bounded copy.
Switches
One bpf() call per load and one per retry. Inside it each log line is its own copy_to_user(), so with a 64 KB buffer the unbounded copy failed in 3.7 to 4.2 s with the ring and 2.8 s with BPF_LOG_FIXED. Between instructions do_check() gives up the CPU when another task needs it and stops with EAGAIN on a signal (line 17402).
Locking
None for loaders with CAP_BPF; the others share bpf_verifier_lock (chapter 3).

Load without a log first, as libbpf does, keep level 2 for small programs, and keep a program's paths few so that its load stays in microseconds. For a program near the limit, a buffer set with bpf_program__set_log_buf() stops libbpf's retries, and the ring still keeps the reason. Before sending a verifier change, run the 1,860 or so test programs in the 121 progs/verifier_*.c files and compare processed instructions and states before and after with veristat.

When it goes wrong

Most of what goes wrong with a rejection goes wrong in the reading, and Figure 5.9 collects the cases this chapter met, from the three logs, the three copies of the lab below, the measurements and the source. The first six rows are reason lines. For each of them the confirming command is the load that printed the reason, and the evidence is a line above it, found by reading upward as in the section "Reading one log from the bottom". Before any reading, the error code already sorts most failed loads: -EACCES for the broken rules of this chapter, -EINVAL for a helper the program type may not call, -E2BIG for the instruction limit and -ENOSPC for a log that did not fit.

The next four rows are about the log rather than the program. A log that shows one side of a branch, starts in the middle of a line or arrives after half a minute is still telling the truth. The level, the size of the buffer and libbpf's retries decide how much of it reaches the screen, and when. The last two rows are about the source, whose line numbers change from release to release, so that a search for the fixed words of a message finds the code in any release while a search for a function's name can come back empty.

The row about accepted programs matters most for loaders that run in production. A loader that always passes a log buffer, so as to keep the log for its own error reports, turns any program whose log once grew past that buffer into a failed load, even though the verifier accepted it. Such a loader should load without a log first and ask for one only after a failure, as libbpf does, or size its buffer from log_true_size.

Two of the rows rest on numbers the verifier keeps for every register, the smax=8 of the lab's third copy and the r7 that climbs in log (c). Where those bounds come from, and why the kernel may trust them, is the subject of chapter 6.

Task. Make three more one-line changes, each to a fresh copy of your program in /tmp. Before each load, predict which row of Figure 4.2 it breaks. Then read the log from the bottom up and say where the proof was lost. You are filling in your own version of Figure 5.3.

  1. Pass the thread ID itself as the key: bpf_map_lookup_elem(&write_counts, (void *)(long)pid).
  2. Add bpf_redirect(0, 0); on the line after u64 updated_val = 1;.
  3. Read the value at an offset that depends on the thread ID: *(curr_val + (pid & 1)) in place of *curr_val.

Done when. For each copy you have the reason line, the rule in one sentence, its row in Figure 4.2, and the instruction where the proof was lost.

  1. Predict the value: log (c) stopped with r7 at 0x1e841, which is 124,993, after 1,000,001 instructions. About how many instructions of walking did each round of the loop cost, and which were they?
  2. A changed copy of your program is refused with R1 invalid mem access 'scalar'. Which rule is it, and where in the log do you look for the lost proof?
  3. Your program has a branch, so the walk must have taken both sides, yet the log your loader printed shows only one of them. Where did the other side's lines go?
  4. Predict the value: log (a) prints the read at slot 10 with the opcode (79). Which three fields of the instruction add up to 0x79, and what would the brackets show for a four-byte read, r1 = *(u32 *)(r0 +0)?
  5. A blog post from a few years ago tells you to read check_cfg() in verifier.c. In the v7.2 tree, grep -rn check_cfg kernel/bpf finds nothing. Was the shape check removed?
  6. You reword the message at line 6322, rebuild, and run ./test_progs -t verifier_map_ret_val. The test fails and prints expect_msg. What happened, and what does your patch need?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 5.

Recap

A refused load returns a verifier log, which libbpf asks for at level 1 only after a failure and which level 1 trims to the path that failed. Read from the bottom, the reason names a rule and a register, and the walk above shows where that register lost what the rule needed; of the three broken copies, only the bounds fix sat on the line where the walk stopped. Each line is one verbose() call copied into the loader's buffer, which in v7.2 is a ring, so that a log too long for it keeps its end and the load fails with -ENOSPC. The reason of log (a) is line 6322 of verifier.c, the last branch of check_mem_access(), reached because line 6106 accepts only a plain map value and only a test of r0 clears the lookup's maybe-NULL flag. A selftest pins that message, and a change to verifier behaviour goes upstream with a test, to bpf for fixes and bpf-next for everything else.

bpf-next tree
the git tree for BPF features, cleanups and improvements
BPF CI

the web queue where patches sent to the list wait for review

Chapter 6

How the verifier tracks numbers

The verifier never runs the write counter, yet it knows that a number in it is below 8, because it keeps two descriptions of every number and lets each test narrow them. It also remembers which numbers a check has relied on, and in one program of sixteen tests that memory decided between a walk of 174 instructions and one of 163,929.

Spine. In chapter 5 the third copy of Lab 5.1 was refused with R0 max value is outside of the allowed memory range, which the kernel could say only because it knew that r1 might be as large as 8. This chapter shows where such knowledge comes from, how far it reaches and what it costs.

35 min · VERIFIER

What the log says about a number

We load the counter as the section "What the kernel reports about its walk" did, with the small libbpf loader that sets the log level itself, at level 6: every state and the statistics. Figure 6.1 keeps the lines that hold numbers. After the semicolon the log lists what each instruction changed, one entry per register or stack slot, and each entry is what the verifier knows about that register at that point on that path.

Three kinds of number appear in part (a). A constant prints as its value, as R1=1 does at slot 2, because every bit of it is known. A pointer prints as its kind with what is known of its offset, so R2=fp-4 at slot 5 is the frame pointer minus four, the address of the key. Any other number prints as scalar(…) with the bounds the verifier has worked out. At slot 12 the key read back from the stack lies between 0 and 0xffffffff, since four bytes hold no more, while the bare scalar() that r0 receives at slot 0 is a number about which nothing is known.

Part (b) comes from a copy of the counter that we follow through the rest of the chapter. Suppose the write counter kept eight counters per thread, one for each of the file descriptors 0 to 7, and picked one with the descriptor that write() was called with, as in if (s && fd < 8) s->n[fd]++;. When the kernel loads this per-descriptor copy, the descriptor could be any number at all, as slot 3 says. After the test at slot 10 it has the busiest entry in either log, which Figure 6.2 takes apart.

The fields are bounds, each the smallest or the largest value the register can hold, read in one of four ways: signed or unsigned, over all 64 bits or only the low 32. print_scalar_ranges() leaves out every bound that says nothing, such as an unsigned minimum of 0. It writes equal minimums once and equal maximums once, joined by equals signs, so eight bounds print as two groups. The last field is of another kind, which the next section explains.

Two descriptions of every number

For each register on each path the verifier keeps an abstract value, a description of every value the register could hold at that point. A scalar's abstract value has two parts, and the log prints both. The range holds the smallest and the largest value possible, which the log calls smin and smax when it reads the bits as signed and umin and umax when it reads them as unsigned. The tnum, short for tristate number, describes each bit as 0, 1 or unknown (written x). It uses two 64-bit words, value and mask, declared in include/linux/tnum.h, and the log prints it as var_off=(value; mask).

Figure 6.3 shows why neither part is enough alone. After fd < 8 both say 0 to 7. After fd <= 8 the range says 0 to 8 while the tnum can only say that the low four bits are unknown, since no pattern of known and unknown bits stops at 8. After every step, therefore, the verifier corrects each part from the other, in reg_bounds_sync() in kernel/bpf/verifier.c.

In v7.2 that function, at line 2073, makes four moves. It narrows the bounds to what the tnum allows, and lets the 64-bit and 32-bit bounds narrow each other twice. It then intersects the tnum with the unsigned range, so that bits the range rules out become known, and narrows the bounds once more from the new tnum. In the copy, this is what turns the test's bound of 7 into the tnum (0x0; 0x7).

Version 7.2 draws the range on a circle

Up to Linux 7.1 a register carried four ranges, signed and unsigned for all 64 bits and for the low 32, which made eight numbers kept in step by hand. In April 2026 Eduard Zingerman replaced them with two arcs, r64 and r32 in struct bpf_reg_state. Each is a circular range (struct cnum64 in include/linux/cnum.h), a first value and a count read clockwise round a circle on which the largest number is followed by 0. The count leaves out the first value, so that all 264 values still fit (the header's comment, lines 20 to 23).

A page that lagsThe kernel's verifier page, Documentation/bpf/verifier.rst, still lists "minimum and maximum values as unsigned" and "as signed" at lines 159 and 160. That was so in v7.2 and in the BPF development tree on 12 November 2026. A documentation fix is a small first patch; search the list archive first.

As Figure 6.4 shows, one arc answers the signed and the unsigned question together. The arc from 14 to 2 is the signed range −2 to 2, but read as unsigned it wraps past 15, so the unsigned minimum and maximum of those five values span the whole circle, 0 to 15. The log has not changed: accessors such as reg_umin() in include/linux/bpf_verifier.h work each bound out from the arcs when it is read. The commit says that the operations on arcs were checked with the CBMC model checker.

Arithmetic moves both descriptions

Every arithmetic instruction on a scalar reaches adjust_scalar_min_max_vals() (verifier.c line 14591), which rewrites both descriptions of the destination register. For each operator it calls a helper for the two arcs and a function from tnum.c for the tnum, as Figure 6.5 lists. It ends with reg_bounds_sync(), so that each description can correct the other.

Slot 11 of the copy, a left shift by three, can be followed through both halves. tnum_lshift() moves the value and the mask three places, turning (0x0; 0x7) into (0x0; 0x38). __scalar64_min_max_lsh() shifts the unsigned bounds, so 0 to 7 becomes 0 to 56; had the maximum been able to lose its top bit, it would have allowed every value instead.

Two rules keep the operators simple. A shift, a division or a remainder gets a range only when its second operand is a constant, and a shift only by less than the register's width. Anything else gives an unknown scalar (is_safe_to_compute_dst_reg_range(), line 14508). A 32-bit operation clears the upper half of its destination, as the machine does, and zext_32_to_64() tells both descriptions.

Sound first, then precise

Each helper in Figure 6.5 may give an abstract value that is too wide, but it must never miss a value the program can really produce. In Figure 6.6 we add 1 to a register whose tnum is 00x1, which holds 1 or 3, so the real results are 2 and 4. The kernel's tnum_add() answers 0xx0, which allows 0, 2, 4 and 6.

Who checks the checkerPREVAIL (PLDI 2019) is a verifier built on abstract interpretation from its first line; eBPF for Windows uses it. The tnum paper (CGO 2022) proved tnum_add() sound and as precise as a tnum can be, and its multiplication went into the kernel. Agni, in the card below, checked the ranges.

That answer is sound, because every real result lies inside it. It is not precise, because 0 and 6 can never happen, and precision measures how few such extras a description carries. An imprecise verifier refuses some safe programs, which costs their authors an afternoon, whereas an unsound one accepts a program that reads outside its map value, which is a security bug. Running a program on descriptions of its values in this way is called abstract interpretation. Chapter 14 writes these definitions as logic and shows how an operator is proved sound; this chapter stays with what the kernel does.

Read with · Verifying the Verifier: eBPF Range Analysis Verification, Harishankar Vishwanathan, Matan Shachnai, Srinivas Narayana and Santosh Nagarakatte, CAV 2023

What it is. The paper that turned the kernel's range code into logic formulas, checked them with an SMT solver on sixteen kernels from 4.14 to 5.19, and for almost every bug it found built a program of at most three instructions that shows it.

Why now. It defines sound and precise in the sense this chapter uses, and it studies the eight-number ranges that v7.2 replaced.

About 45 minutes · VERIFIER

A test narrows both sides of a branch

We follow the copy through the walk in Figure 6.7. At slot 3, r6 receives the descriptor as scalar(), a number with no bounds at all. At slot 10, if r6 > 0x7, the walk splits into two paths as it did in Figure 4.3, and the side that jumps, where r6 is at least 8, goes straight to the exit. On the side that falls through, r6 is at most 7; the shift at slot 11 makes that an offset of 0 to 56, which slot 12 adds to r0, the pointer into the map value.

Older kernelsIn v6.12 the narrowing lived in reg_set_min_max(), which check_cond_jmp_op() called after it had decided that both sides could happen and pushed the jump side. v7.2 has no function of that name: the narrowing has moved into the decision itself.

In v7.2 one call does the work for both sides. check_cond_jmp_op() (line 15945) copies the two compared registers once for each side and asks is_branch_taken() whether the bounds already decide the test. For two scalars it compares the bounds and then tries the test on the copies. simulate_both_branches_taken() (line 15192) narrows the fall-through copies with the reversed comparison, r6 <= 7 for if r6 > 7, and the jump copies with the comparison itself, each through regs_refine_cond_op() (line 15517) and a sync. An arc that comes out empty is a side that cannot happen; otherwise push_stack() saves the jump side with its narrowed copies (lines 16088 to 16101).

Figure 6.8 shows what each side gets. An unsigned 64-bit test gives the side that jumps only umin=8. Every number of 263 or more passes that test and is negative when read as signed, so the signed reading learns nothing. The side that falls through gets a maximum in all four readings, and the sync adds the tnum.

A 32-bit test, which clang emits for a u32 index, narrows only the 32-bit arc and the low half of the tnum. When the upper half is already known to be zero, as after the zero-extension in the second row, the sync carries the bound into all 64 bits. When it is not, as in the third row, the 64-bit view learns only that the low half is at most 7. Its largest value becomes 0xffffffff00000007, and it takes the two shifts after the test to bound the whole register.

Copies share what a test learns

Clang often tests a value in one register and uses it from another, and the verifier follows that through ids. When a scalar is copied with a 64-bit move, assign_scalar_id_before_mov() (line 3364) gives the source a fresh id if it has none, and the copy takes the same one. For a loader with CAP_BPF, a store to the stack that keeps all the value's bits, and a load back, do the same for the slot (lines 3502 to 3508). At a conditional jump collect_linked_regs() (line 15852) gathers every live register and spilled slot that carries a compared register's id, and sync_linked_regs() (line 15885) copies the new bounds into each. Registers and stack slots that share an id in this way are linked registers: a bound learned on one reaches all the others.

Figure 6.9 shows the two common cases. In (a) the barrier_var() of libbpf, an empty asm statement, made clang keep a copy in r1 while the index stayed in r6; the test of r1 at slot 10 narrows r6 as well. In (b) the descriptor is a volatile local, so the test and the index are two loads from fp-8. The test's bound is written into the slot, and the second load takes it from there.

A link also holds across the addition of a constant, which the copy records as a delta, printed after the id as in id=2+1 (log.c line 667), so a test on i + 1 narrows i. Anything else ends it. Other arithmetic on a copy clears its id (line 14911), and so does a 32-bit move of a value that may not fit in 32 bits (line 15029). One refused program of Figure 6.15 lost its test in this way, when clang tested a masked copy of the index.

A pointer plus a number, checked at the access

The addition at slot 12 of the copy, r0 += r6, adds a scalar to a pointer and goes to adjust_ptr_min_max_vals() (line 13664). Some pointers may not move at all; a pointer-or-NULL is refused with R0 pointer arithmetic on map_value_or_null prohibited, null-check it first. Then check_reg_sane_offset_scalar() (line 13296) looks at the scalar's signed minimum. With no minimum the load fails with math between map_value pointer and register with unbounded min value is not allowed. With one further than 229 below zero (BPF_MAX_VAR_OFF, include/linux/bpf_verifier.h line 17) it fails with value … makes map_value pointer be out of bounds, and both return -EINVAL before any memory is touched.

A scalar that passes becomes the pointer's variable offset. After slot 12 the log prints r0 as map_value(id=1,…,smin=smin32=0,smax=umax=smax32=umax32=56,var_off=(0x0; 0x38)), a pointer somewhere in the first 56 bytes of the value, and no check of size has happened yet. That waits for the access.

At the access check_mem_access() (line 6078) hands the pointer to a checker for its kind of memory, and Figure 6.10 lists the three this chapter met. For a map value, check_mem_region_access() tries both ends of the offset. It refuses a minimum that could reach below the value, checks the smallest offset, calls an unsigned maximum of 229 or more unbounded, and last checks that the largest offset plus the size of the access ends inside the value. In the copy the largest offset is 56, and eight bytes read from 56 end at 64, the value's size, so the range alone lets the read at slot 13 pass. With fd <= 8 the largest offset becomes 64, and the kernel refuses the copy as it refused the third broken copy of Lab 5.1.

A packet is measured differently, since its length is known only when the program runs. A pointer into it carries a range, the r= of the log, which a test against the packet's end sets for every pointer with the same id (find_good_pkt_pointers(), line 15106). After if (data + 1 > end), pkt(r=0) becomes pkt(r=1), and check_packet_access() runs the region check against that range. On the stack, the 512 bytes below r10, an offset that is not a constant is checked by its signed bounds in check_stack_access_within_bounds().

Which numbers must be exact

Pruning, as the section "Checkpoints, and when two states are the same" showed, ends a path where a saved state covers the current one. For scalars that comparison would rarely succeed if every bound counted, because two paths that differ only in a counter or a length would never match. The verifier therefore lets a scalar's bounds count only once some check has relied on them, and records that in a flag, precise, in struct bpf_reg_state. regsafe() in kernel/bpf/states.c (line 551) lets any current value match a saved scalar whose flag is clear. This record of which scalars' bounds a check has relied on is precision tracking, and the log marks a scalar with the flag set by a P, as in R6=Pscalar().

The word is the kernel's, and it means more here than it did in the section on soundness. There a description was precise when it held few values that cannot happen; here a scalar is precise when its bounds must be kept and compared as they are, however wide they may be.

A scalar becomes precise when its value starts to matter for safety. That happens when it is added to a pointer (line 14817), when its bounds decide a conditional jump (line 16035), when it is the size passed to a helper, and when the kernel restricts what a program returns. Every earlier scalar it was computed from must then become precise too, in the saved states along the path, since a checkpoint whose proof rested on those bounds must not cover a state with wider ones. mark_chain_precision() (line 3294) hands the register to bpf_mark_chain_precision() in backtrack.c (line 790). That function works by backtracking, walking back over instructions already verified to find which registers and stack slots the value came from.

Each instruction changes the set still to be marked, in backtrack_insn() (line 267). A copy r1 = r6 passes the mark from r1 to r6, r6 += r2 adds r2, and an operation with a constant, such as r6 <<= 3, keeps r6. A constant moved into the register ends its search, a load from the stack passes the mark to the slot, and a load from other memory ends it. Figure 6.11 is the walk for r6: back to slot 9, where the current state began, then through the parent state, whose r6 now prints as Pscalar(), to the load at slot 3. The jump history kept with each state says which instruction came before which.

The marks then change what pruning can do. A checkpoint on that path keeps r6 precise, so a later path that reaches it with a different range for r6 is not pruned there. Before each new checkpoint is saved, mark_all_scalars_imprecise() (states.c lines 1213 and 1570) clears the marks it inherited, so that only what a later check proves necessary is kept.

Figure 6.12 puts numbers on it. The two main programs differ in their last line. In matters, s->n[k & 7] += 1 adds k to a pointer, so k is marked precise back to its start, and paths that left different constants in it no longer prune each other. At sixteen tests the walk took 163,929 instructions and 8,827 states; at twenty it hit the budget of one million. In never, which only stores k, each later path is pruned at the first checkpoint it reaches, and the walk grows by ten instructions a test.

Taking the index out of the path's history removes the cost. A variant that indexes with x & 7, a bound of the input that is the same on every path, walked 185 instructions at sixteen tests. Writing the sum without if helps less, because clang turns each conditional addition into a shift and an AND. v7.2 splits a register that can only be 0 or −1 into two paths at such an AND (maybe_fork_scalars(), line 14558), so matters_flat still walked 14,696 instructions at sixteen tests and failed at twenty-four.

"all scalars are assumed imprecise initially (unless unprivileged, in which case everything is forced to be precise)"

kernel/bpf/verifier.c, __mark_reg_const_zero(), lines 1847 and 1848, Linux v7.2

A loader without CAP_BPF gets no precision tracking at all. bpf_mark_chain_precision() returns at its first test (backtrack.c line 805), and every new scalar starts precise (verifier.c line 2166), as the comment above says. The last column of Figure 6.12 is never loaded so, as a socket filter by the user nobody. It saved the same 8,827 states as matters and walked 122,185 instructions, seven hundred times its cost for a privileged loader.

Masking against speculation

Everything so far concerns what the program does. A CPU also does work that no program asked for: it guesses the outcome of a branch and runs ahead on the guess, discarding the results if the guess was wrong. Running ahead in this way is speculative execution. The commit that brought this section's masking, in January 2019, gives a recipe for abusing it. Load an index, compute the limit slowly so that the CPU guesses the outcome of the test against it, read at the untested index, then read again at an address made from the byte that came back.

The kernel calls this Spectre variant 1, and whether the verifier defends against it is decided once per load (verifier.c line 19810). bpf_bypass_spec_v1() (include/linux/bpf.h line 2867) lets the load skip the defence if its loader holds CAP_PERFMON, or CAP_SYS_ADMIN, which passes every BPF capability test (token.c line 14). A kernel booted with mitigations off skips it too. Tracing programs need CAP_PERFMON to load at all (syscall.c line 3045), so the masking falls on socket filters and network programs loaded without it.

The masking is decided during the walk and written after it. When a scalar that is not a constant is added to a pointer, sanitize_ptr_alu() (line 13451) records how far the pointer may move, alu_limit, in the instruction's side data. retrieve_ptr_limit() (line 13356) works it out from the pointer's bounds and the size of what it points into: 56 for r0 += r7 into the 64-byte value. After the walk, bpf_do_misc_fixups() in fixups.c (from line 1703) puts six instructions before the addition.

The walk also takes up one more path, in which the pointer has not moved, as if the masking had made the offset 0, so that what a mispredicting CPU would run is checked too. That is why the second load of Figure 6.13 walked 23 instructions and saved 2 states, against 17 and 1.

The six compute the offset again without a branch, in r12, the verifier's own register BPF_REG_AX (include/linux/filter.h line 63). Slots 19 to 21 leave the sign bit of r12 clear when the offset lies between 0 and the limit, and set it otherwise. The negation reverses that, and the arithmetic shift spreads the sign bit over all 64 bits. The AND then keeps the offset when the result is all ones and makes it 0 otherwise, so a path the CPU should never have taken still reads inside the value.

The other two instructions come from elsewhere. The array lookup, which the kernel had replaced with its own instructions at slots 6 to 15, gains an AND that keeps the index inside the array (arraymap.c lines 232 to 234). The store of the key gains a nospec barrier, which the comment at fixups.c line 836 calls a mitigation for Spectre v4. Each run then took 25 ns against 20 (bpftool prog run, three runs of twenty million; other VM runs that day gave 26 and 21).

One limit per instruction is also a restriction. If the same addition is reached on two paths with different limits, the rewritten instruction cannot serve both. update_alu_sanitation_state() (line 13393) notices the difference, and the load fails with R0 tried to add from different maps, paths or scalars, pointer arithmetic with it prohibited for !root. The matters program, as a socket filter without CAP_PERFMON, is refused in this way, because its k & 7 differs from path to path; as root it loads.

Inside the v7.2 source

Figure 6.14 collects the code behind this chapter in the order an instruction reaches it. An arithmetic instruction goes from check_alu_op() (line 14917) to adjust_reg_min_max_vals(), which sends two scalars to adjust_scalar_min_max_vals() and a pointer with a scalar to adjust_ptr_min_max_vals(), after marking the scalar precise. A conditional jump goes to check_cond_jmp_op(), the walk's own code that the section "Inside the v7.2 source" followed as far as the pending branch, and an access to check_mem_access().

v7.2 has moved two parts of this out of verifier.c. Backtracking lives in backtrack.c, whose comment above bpf_mark_chain_precision() (lines 703 to 789) explains why marks in the current state do not matter and marks in saved states do. The comparison that uses the marks lives in states.c, and the arcs have files of their own, cnum.c and include/linux/cnum.h.

What it costs

CPU
Kernel 7.2.15, VM with 16 vCPUs, 12 November 2026. A proved bound costs one compare and jump per event. At load, sixteen tests whose result became an index cost 163,929 instructions walked and 103 ms, against 174 and 0.39 ms when the result was only stored. Without CAP_PERFMON a socket filter grew from 22 to 30 instructions and from 20 to 25 ns a run.
Memory
Each register state is 88 bytes, 40 of them the tnum and the two arcs (BTF of 7.2.15); the precise walk held up to 89 states at once, against 13.
Switches
None: bounds and marks live inside the bpf() call that loads the program.
Locking
A loader without CAP_BPF, which gets no precision tracking, holds bpf_verifier_lock for its whole walk: 80 ms for the sixteen-test never.

Test an index as an unsigned number, on the value added to the pointer, after the last call that could change it. If the statistics grow with the branches an index passes through, derive it from the input instead. Grant CAP_PERFMON only to a loader trusted with kernel memory; otherwise expect six more instructions for each pointer moved by an unknown offset.

When it goes wrong

The rows of Figure 6.15 come from copies of the per-descriptor counter, each changed in one line and read from the bottom up, as the section "Reading one log from the bottom" taught. Most rows ask one question at different places: what bounds did the scalar have when it met the pointer, and which instruction gave it them? The error code sorts them. -EINVAL comes from the addition itself, when the scalar's minimum is missing or absurd, and -EACCES from the access, or from the masking.

Three rows have a test in the source that the log does not honour, for three reasons. In the masked copy the test was on another register, and the AND had ended the link. After the helper call the test was on an earlier load, and memory that other CPUs can write says nothing about the next load. The signed index was tested only from above. In each, the log shows the bound on one line and a register without it on a later one, and the instruction between them is what must change.

Try it · Read the numbers in your own log

~25 min · read the log · needs clang, bpftool and root in a throwaway VM (virtme-ng) or on a test machine

Task. Load your write counter at log level 2 and find three kinds of number in its log: a constant, a pointer with a fixed offset, and a scalar with bounds but no single value. Then build the per-descriptor copy, write down r6's range and tnum after slot 10 and after slot 11, and only then read them in its log. This is Figure 6.7, checked against your own load.

Done when. You can point at R1=1, R2=fp-4 and the R3=scalar(…) at slot 12 in your counter's log, and your two predictions for the copy match its log, or you can say which part was wrong.

Hint 1 · direction

A constant prints as a bare number, a stack pointer as fp and an offset. A register loaded from four bytes cannot be larger than 0xffffffff, and its tnum says so.

Hint 2 · mechanism

bpftool -d asks for log levels 1, 2 and 4, and prints the log on standard error. As root, from book/program: bpftool -d prog load maps/02-hash-map/hashmap.bpf.o /sys/fs/bpf/hm 2> /tmp/hm.log, then rm /sys/fs/bpf/hm. The copy, book/labs/numbers/fdcount.bpf.c, changes the map's value to struct slots { __u64 n[8]; } and reads u64 fd = ctx->args[0];.

Hint 3 · nearly there

Search the copy's log for 10: (25) and 11: (67); the state after each instruction follows the semicolon. From the repository's top directory, vng -r /boot/vmlinuz-linux --user root --rwdir /tmp -- bash book/labs/numbers-root.sh loads both in a VM and writes the logs to /tmp/book-labs/numbers/.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 6.

Try it · Find the line that loses the bound

~35 min · break a real one · needs clang, libbpf and root in a throwaway VM (virtme-ng) or on a test machine

Task. book/labs/numbers/reload.bpf.c adds the time of each write to one of eight counters, chosen by an index that user space keeps in an array map. It tests the index, and the verifier refuses it all the same. Load it at log level 2, read the log from the bottom up to the line where the index loses its bound, say why it is lost there, and change the source so that the program loads. Its body is below.

u32 key = 0, pid = bpf_get_current_pid_tgid();
struct cfg *c = bpf_map_lookup_elem(&cfg_map, &key);
struct slots *s = bpf_map_lookup_elem(&fd_counts, &pid);
u64 t;

if (!c || !s || c->idx >= 8)
        return 0;
t = bpf_ktime_get_ns();
s->n[c->idx] += t;
return 0;

Done when. You can name the slot at which the index gets back the full 32-bit range after the test had narrowed it to 0 to 7, and your changed program loads, with fewer than 30 instructions walked.

Hint 1 · direction

The verifier tracks registers and stack slots. Ask what it can know about memory that user space and other CPUs may write at any moment.

Hint 2 · mechanism

Compile from book/program, so that vmlinux.h is found: clang -g -O2 -target bpf -D__TARGET_ARCH_x86 -I/usr/include/bpf -I. -c ../labs/numbers/reload.bpf.c -o /tmp/reload.bpf.o. As root, load it with the walk chapter's loader (book/labs/walk/stats.c, built with -lbpf): stats /tmp/reload.bpf.o reload 6 /tmp/reload.log. From the reason, go up to the last line that writes the register added to r7.

Hint 3 · nearly there

Two lines load r1 from r6 +0, and the second comes after call bpf_ktime_get_ns#5. A local variable that holds the index lives in a register the call does not change.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 6.

Check yourself

  1. Predict the value: r1 has the tnum 01x0 and r2 has 0x01, on four bits. What does tnum_add() return for r1 + r2, and which of the values it allows can never happen?
  2. The per-descriptor copy with fd <= 8 is refused. The log gives the reason as invalid access to map value, value_size=64 off=64 size=8, followed by R0 max value is outside of the allowed memory range. The instruction reads at r0 + 0. Where does off=64 come from?
  3. You delete the test on fd, and the load fails at r0 += r6 with math between map_value pointer and register with unbounded min value is not allowed. fd is a u64. Why does the kernel talk about a minimum?
  4. Predict the value: r6 holds a number about which nothing is known, and the walk falls through if w6 > 0x7 goto pc+7. What are r6's umax and var_off on that side, and why is the 64-bit maximum not 7?
  5. The spill program of show.bpf.c tests a volatile index and loads it again for the access, and it is accepted; the program of Lab 6.2 tests an index in a map value and loads it again, and it is refused. What does the verifier know about the stack slot that it cannot know about the map value?
  6. Predict the value: in Figure 6.12, never walks 174 instructions at sixteen tests for root and 122,185 for a user without CAP_BPF. Why does the same program cost so much more, and which column does it come close to?
  7. matters, as a socket filter, loads as root and is refused without CAP_PERFMON with R0 tried to add from different maps, paths or scalars. What differs between the paths, and why does it matter only without CAP_PERFMON?
  8. Predict the value: in part (b) of Figure 6.13, what does r12 hold after slot 24 when r7 is 40, and when r7 is 64? At which offset of the value does slot 26 then read?
  9. In Figure 6.11, why does the walk back for r6 end at slot 3 and not at slot 10, where r6 got its bound, and what would it have done at slot 3 if r6 had been loaded from the stack?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 6.

Recap

For every register on every path the verifier keeps an abstract value; for a scalar that is a range, stored in v7.2 as two circular arcs, and a tnum, and after each step each description corrects the other. Arithmetic moves both, a test narrows both on each side of its branch, in 32 or 64 bits, and copies that share an id share what a test learns. A scalar added to a pointer must have a sane minimum, and the access checks both ends of the offset against the size of what is read. A description must be sound; precision tracking keeps exact only the scalars a check relied on, found by walking back through the instructions, and that choice decides how well paths prune. A loader without CAP_PERFMON also gets masking against speculation, six instructions for each pointer moved by an unknown offset.

New words in this chapter

abstract value
the verifier's description of every value a register could hold at one instruction on one path
range
the smallest and largest possible value, read as signed or as unsigned
tnum
tristate number: each bit known 0, known 1 or unknown, stored as a value and a mask
circular range
a first value and a count on a circle where the largest number is followed by 0; v7.2's form of the range
sound
of a description: it holds every value the program can really produce
precise
of a sound description: it holds few values the program cannot produce
abstract interpretation
running a program on descriptions of its values instead of on the values
linked registers
registers and spilled stack slots that share an id, so that a bound learned on one reaches the others
precision tracking
the verifier's record of which scalars' bounds a check has relied on; only those are compared when pruning
backtracking
walking back over instructions already verified to find which registers and stack slots a precise value came from
speculative execution
the CPU running ahead on a guess about a branch before it knows the outcome, and discarding the results if the guess was wrong

  • VERIFIERSound, Precise, and Fast Abstract Interpretation with Tristate Numbers, the same authors, CGO 2022. Section 2: the tnum and its addition. Twenty minutes.
  • VERIFIEReBPF verifier, Linux kernel documentation. The paragraph on individual bits under "Register value tracking", left for this chapter by the card in chapter 4.

Part III

Running

A program that passed is compiled to machine code, attached to an event and run each time the event fires. We follow the JIT, the hooks, the helpers and kfuncs the program calls, and the maps where its data lives, with what each one costs.

Chapter 7

The JIT, and tail calls as patched jumps

The kernel this book runs on cannot execute bytecode, so every program it accepts is translated into x86 before it runs: the write counter's 29 checked instructions become 152 bytes of machine code in 7 to 17 µs, and a jump from one program into another becomes five bytes that the kernel rewrites whenever the target changes.
