  • What the kernel changes in a checked program, and how the JIT turns it into x86 in a few passes
  • Where the machine code lives, what constant blinding does to it, and what both cost
  • Tail calls: the checks the JIT writes, the direct jump it patches, and what changing a slot costs

Spine. In chapter 6 the verifier finished proving that every number in the write counter stays in bounds. What it hands on is still bytecode, a list of checked instructions that no CPU can run, so before the counter can count a single write the kernel turns that list into machine code.

30 min · RUNTIME · LINEAGE

What the kernel shows of the counter's machine code

We load the write counter and ask the kernel about it in Figure 7.1. bpftool reports two sizes, 232 bytes of instructions after the kernel's rewrites, which makes 29 slots of 8 bytes, and 152 bytes of x86. The x86 also has a name in /proc/kallsyms: bpf_prog_, then the program's tag, a hash of its instructions, then its own name. Every tool that reads kernel symbols therefore sees the counter as one more function of the kernel.

perf is one of those tools. While dd made its writes with the counter attached, 1.31% of the samples fell inside the counter's own code. The functions it calls took more, 5.65% in htab_map_update_elem() alone and several percent in the machinery behind bpf_printk(), so the program's own instructions are a small part of what it costs. perf could name the program but could not show its instructions, because the perf of this distribution is built without the disassembler that annotating BPF code needs. bpftool prog dump jited prints them instead, and the rest of this chapter reads that dump.

A kernel with no interpreter

In Figure 7.2 we ask the kernel how it runs programs. The switch bpf_jit_enable reads 1, and even root cannot set it to 0, because this kernel was built with CONFIG_BPF_JIT_ALWAYS_ON. Nor can root set it to 2, the value that prints every image to the kernel log on kernels that allow it. Its symbol table holds no interpreter at all, so every program is translated when it loads or the load fails.

An interpreter runs bytecode by reading one instruction at a time and doing what it says. Linux has one, ___bpf_prog_run() in kernel/bpf/core.c, but that build option leaves it out. A JIT compiler, named for working just in time, instead translates the whole program into native code, the CPU's own instructions, once and at load time. Figure 7.3 sets the two approaches side by side.

"Enables BPF JIT and removes BPF interpreter to avoid speculative execution of BPF instructions by the interpreter."

Help text of CONFIG_BPF_JIT_ALWAYS_ON, kernel/bpf/Kconfig, Linux v7.2

Speculative execution, which the section "Masking against speculation" met as the CPU running ahead on a guessed branch, can be steered by an attacker. An interpreter in kernel memory is a ready-made machine for running bytecode in that state, which is why this kernel has none. When the JIT cannot translate a program, the load fails with -ENOTSUPP, error 524, in __bpf_prog_select_runtime() in core.c, which bpf_check() calls as its last step (verifier.c line 20036 in v7.2).

Without the option the interpreter is built, and it has limits of its own. bpf_prog_select_interpreter() picks one of sixteen copies of it, one for each 32-byte step of stack up to 512 bytes. For a program the JIT did not take, bpf_fixup_call_args() refuses calls to kernel functions, callbacks, and bpf-to-bpf calls in a program that also makes tail calls. With the option set, bpf_prog_select_interpreter() stores a placeholder that returns 0 and warns, and it should never run.

What the kernel changes before the JIT

The JIT does not see the program clang wrote. Between the end of the walk and the call to the JIT, bpf_check() runs the passes of Figure 7.4 over the instructions. The verification time printed with the log's statistics stops after them, before the JIT starts (verifier.c line 19980). One pass ran before the walk. Each 64-bit load that named a map by its descriptor now holds the map's address, and the load of the bpf_printk() format string holds the address of those bytes inside the .rodata map.

We follow four of the counter's instructions through both steps in Figure 7.5. The map load at slot 6 now carries the map itself. The call 0x1 at slot 8 has become a direct call to __htab_map_lookup_elem(), the hash map's own lookup, followed by two instructions that move r0 from the map's entry to the value inside it. htab_map_gen_lookup() in kernel/bpf/hashtab.c writes those three, and the JIT later turns them into four x86 instructions.

The other three calls changed only their immediate, which now holds the distance of the helper or the map function from __bpf_call_base, so that the JIT can write a plain x86 call. Chapter 9 follows a helper call from both sides.

Every rewrite that turns one instruction into several goes through bpf_patch_insn_data() in fixups.c. It copies the program with the new instructions in place, corrects the jumps that cross the patched spot, and moves the verifier's record of every later instruction along. For the counter that happens once, at slot 8, and costs nothing worth measuring; we meet it again where it happens once for every instruction.

The counter in x86, and the frame around it

The JIT in arch/x86/net/bpf_jit_comp.c then turns each instruction into x86. Each bytecode register lives in one x86 register for the whole program. These are the pairs of Figure P.3, which the JIT keeps in its table reg2hex[]: r0 in rax, r1 in rdi, r2 in rsi and r10 in rbp. So r2 = r10 becomes the three bytes 48 89 ee, which bpftool prints source first as movq %rbp, %rsi. A helper call becomes a plain x86 call with its arguments already in place, because r1 to r5 sit in the registers that the x86-64 calling convention uses for a function's first five arguments.

Figure 7.6 shows the 27 bytes the JIT writes before slot 0. An endbr64 comes first, because this kernel is built with indirect branch tracking (CONFIG_X86_KERNEL_IBT=y), and a CPU that enforces it faults when an indirect call lands anywhere else. A five-byte no-op follows as room for a call that may be patched in later.

Then come a three-byte no-op, which becomes xorq %rax, %rax in a program that makes tail calls, the usual frame setup, a second endbr64 at offset 0x10, and room for the counter's 16 bytes of stack. No register is saved, since the counter never uses r6 to r9. A program that does gets a push of rbx, r13, r14 or r15 for each one it uses, which is the saving the primer said the kernel does on a program's behalf.

Who checks the translatorJitterbug (OSDI 2020) wrote down what a correct BPF JIT must do and checked JITs against it automatically. With it the authors built a verified JIT for 32-bit RISC-V, and found and fixed 16 bugs in five other JITs, all upstream.

At the end, w0 = 0 becomes xorl %eax, %eax, and exit becomes leave and a jump to the kernel's return thunk. emit_return() writes that jump in place of ret on CPUs where the kernel sends every return through the thunk as a defence against speculation. Altogether, 232 bytes of bytecode became 152 bytes of x86. The image is smaller even though one instruction may become several, because most x86 instructions take fewer than the eight bytes of a BPF slot. The counter averages 5.2 bytes a slot, and a long run of additions of 32-bit constants takes 6.

The five-byte no-op serves a trick that the kernel's own functions use too. When a program is attached to the entry of a kernel function, the kernel writes a trampoline, a short piece of x86 that saves the function's arguments, calls the program and then lets the function run. It patches a call to the trampoline over a five-byte no-op at the start of that function, and the no-op at the start of a BPF program lets another program attach to it in the same way. The JIT's source explains it with a network function, eth_type_trans(). Chapter 8 attaches programs this way and follows a trampoline as the kernel builds it and patches it in (the section "What attaching writes into the kernel").

"eth_type_trans has 5 byte nop at the beginning. These 5 bytes will be replaced with 'call generated_bpf_trampoline'. When it returns eth_type_trans will continue executing with original skb and dev pointers."

Comment before the trampoline code in arch/x86/net/bpf_jit_comp.c, Linux v7.2

Passes until the length settles

x86 instructions have different lengths, and the length of a jump depends on how far it goes: a conditional jump to a place within 127 bytes takes two bytes, a farther one six. The JIT cannot know a distance before it knows the length of everything in between. So bpf_int_jit_compile() starts from a guess of 64 bytes for every instruction and translates the whole program again and again, each pass working from the addresses the previous one produced, until the length stops changing.

Figure 7.7 follows the counter through those passes. In the first, the test at slot 11, which skips two instructions, seems by the guess to aim 128 bytes ahead and gets the six-byte form. In the second the real distance is known, and the test shrinks to two bytes. The third pass gives the same 152 bytes, so the JIT asks for memory for the image and runs a fourth pass that writes into it. A program with no such jumps has its final length after the first pass and needs three in all.

Lengths can only shrink from one pass to the next, so the loop ends, but the code does not rely on that alone. After 15 passes (PADDING_PASSES) do_jit() pads every jump that would shrink with no-ops up to its previous length. After 20 (MAX_PASSES) without an image the program is left untranslated, which on this kernel fails the load with error 524.

Where the image lives

The 152 bytes cannot go just anywhere, because kernel code must be executable and should never be writable at the same time. The JIT's last pass writes into an ordinary, writable copy, and bpf_jit_binary_pack_finalize() then copies the image with text_poke_copy() into memory that is mapped read-only and executable. That memory comes from a program pack, a 2 MB block of executable memory that the images of many programs share. bpf_prog_pack_alloc() in core.c hands it out in 64-byte chunks.

The counter asks for its 152 bytes of code, an 8-byte header and 16 spare bytes, rounded up to three chunks, 192 bytes. Its code starts at a random offset inside the spare bytes, and every byte of the pack that holds no code is 0xcc, the x86 breakpoint instruction int3. Before our loads, /proc/vmallocinfo in the VM listed one pack, at 2,101,248 bytes, 2 MB and a guard page. Loading 1,000 small programs of 146 bytes each added 192,000 bytes to the kernel's running total, bpf_jit_current, and no pack. Twenty programs of 300,026 bytes each needed three more packs, and all three were freed with the programs (step 4 of book/labs/jit-root.sh, 12 November 2026).

Until 2022 every image had whole pages of its own. Song Liu's commit that brought the pack, in February 2022, gives the reason. Most programs are small but took a page each, and many of them put pressure on the instruction TLB, the CPU's cache of address translations for code, which slows the whole machine.

Every image is also charged against net.core.bpf_jit_limit, which the kernel sets at boot to half the range of addresses that x86-64 keeps for modules and BPF code, 528,482,304 bytes in the VM (bpf_jit_charge_init()). A loader with CAP_BPF may go past it. For any other, bpf_jit_charge_modmem() refuses, the JIT treats the refusal as a failed allocation, and the load fails with error 524 because the program was not translated. That includes an ordinary user's classic socket filter and seccomp filter, which the kernel converts to eBPF and gives to the same JIT. With the limit set to 1, both failed for the user nobody and worked for root.

Constant blinding

Every constant in a program becomes bytes in executable memory, and the loader chooses those bytes. JIT spraying is an attack that loads programs whose constants, read from the middle of an instruction, are themselves x86 code, and then uses some other kernel bug to jump there. The random start and the int3 filling of the previous section were the first answer, after Keegan McAllister published the attack against the BPF JIT. Constant blinding, added by Daniel Borkmann in May 2016, is the second: a rewrite just before the JIT that never puts a loader's constant into the image as it was written.

bpf_jit_blind_constants() in core.c draws a random number for each instruction with a constant and writes the instruction as three. The first moves the constant XORed with the random number into a hidden register, AX, the second XORs AX with the same random number, and the third is the original operation with AX in place of the constant. A 64-bit load of an address becomes seven instructions, and a move of zero becomes an XOR of the register with itself. bpftool prints AX as r12, and the x86 JIT keeps it in r10, as Figure 7.8 shows for four of the counter's slots.

Blinding is off by default. net.core.bpf_jit_harden at 1 blinds the programs of loaders without CAP_BPF, and at 2 it blinds every program (bpf_jit_blinding_enabled() in include/linux/filter.h). Either value also takes every BPF program out of /proc/kallsyms, because bpf_get_kallsym() lists none while hardening is on, so at 1 bpftool printed the counter's x86 under a bare address although nothing in it was blinded.

At 2 the counter grew from 29 slots and 152 bytes to 60 slots and 333 or 334 bytes, the length changing from load to load with the random constants. It ran in the same 499 to 509 ns as with hardening off. The counter without bpf_printk(), measured in an earlier session the same day, doubled to 48 slots, grew from 129 to 269 bytes and kept its 155 ns a run.

The price is paid at load time, and it grows fast. Each rewrite goes through bpf_patch_insn_data(), which moves everything after the patched instruction, so the work grows with the square of the program's length. Blinding took 11 to 12 µs for the counter, 4.2 ms for 1,000 additions, 0.39 s for 10,000, 5.1 s for 30,000 and 58 s for 100,000 (bpftrace on bpf_jit_blind_constants(), same VM).

Tail calls, and the count the JIT keeps

A tail call ends one program by jumping into another, which reuses the first one's stack frame and never returns to it. The programs to jump to sit in a program array, a map whose values are programs, and the call names a slot by number. User space fills a slot with a program's descriptor, and prog_fd_array_get_ptr() in arraymap.c takes a reference on the program. It then asks bpf_prog_map_compatible() in core.c whether the program matches the array's owner, the first program to use the array, in type, in having been translated by the JIT, in its sleepable flag and in its expected_attach_type, among other properties. A socket filter offered to the array of a tracepoint program was refused with ‑EINVAL.

"The kernel stack is precious, so this helper reuses the current stack frame and jumps into another BPF program without adding extra call frame."

Alexei Starovoitov, commit message of 04fd61ab36ec, "bpf: allow bpf programs to tail-call other bpf programs", Linux 4.2
2022 and nowThe Cloudflare post shows the tail-call count passed between programs in rax. In v7.2, rax carries a pointer to the count, which lives on the first program's stack. The three checks have not changed.

Figure 7.9, redrawn from a Cloudflare post that read the x86 the JIT writes for a tail call, shows what happens at run time. Before the jump, the JIT's code checks that the slot exists, that the chain has made fewer than 33 tail calls, and that the slot holds a program. If any check fails, the program goes on at its next instruction. The limit is MAX_TAIL_CALL_CNT in include/linux/bpf.h, and it is counted while the program runs, because the array can change after the verifier has finished. The jump lands 16 bytes into the target, at the second endbr64 of Figure 7.6, past the target's own frame setup, because the target keeps the caller's frame.

The jump itself goes through a register that holds the target's address. On the VM's CPU, which has enhanced IBRS, emit_indirect_jump() writes a plain jmpq *%rcx. Where the kernel uses retpolines, it writes a jump to a retpoline instead, a sequence that keeps the CPU from speculating through the jump.

We split the counter into count_writes, which only calls bpf_tail_call(ctx, &jmp_table, 0), and count_update, which counts. The x86 JIT pops the first program's saved registers, frees its stack and jumps past the second's frame setup. Only r1, the program's argument, is passed on, so count_update must call bpf_get_current_pid_tgid() again. A program that tail-called itself ran 34 times for one event, its first run and 33 tail calls.

The direct form, patched in place

Because the counter's slot is a constant, record_func_key() in verifier.c remembers it. For a loader with CAP_BPF and constant blinding off, bpf_do_misc_fixups() gives the call a poke descriptor, a record of where the jump for that map and slot lies in the program's code. The JIT writes a direct tail call there, a five-byte jump pointed at the target or turned into a no-op (Figure 7.10), and bpf_tail_call_direct_fixup() fills it in from the slot as the image is finished. Only the check on the count remains, because the slot is known and whether it is empty is written into the code.

The direct form costs almost nothing to run. A socket filter's test run took 19 to 21 ns with or without a direct tail call, against 25 to 27 ns with the slot computed from the packet (bpftool prog run, two sessions on kernel 7.2.15 in the VM, 12 November 2026). The split counter cost 157 to 158 ns a run against 155 to 158 for the whole counter (16 virtual CPUs). Reading the slot from a global, which keeps the three checks of Figure 7.9, raised it to 161 to 162.

The price moves to the update, drawn in Figure 7.11. The array lists the programs whose poke descriptors name it, and smp_text_poke_single() rewrites each matching site, writing an int3 first and interrupting every CPU three times. With 16 virtual CPUs a replacement took 0.05 to 1.1 ms for each program with a direct tail call to the slot, and 9 to 30 µs with two virtual CPUs. Emptying the slot took 5 to 7 ms a program, most of it a wait for a grace period.

Two habits of the pair surprised us. bpftool reported run_cnt 0 for count_update, because the statistics are kept around the program the hook calls, whose time then includes the second half. And when the loader exited with only the link pinned, the array lost its last user reference and was emptied, count_update and the counter's map were freed, and count_writes fell through on every write.

Inside the v7.2 source

Figure 7.12 lists the code this chapter has read, in the order a load reaches it. bpf_check() resolves map descriptors before the walk, runs the rewrites after it, stops its clock and hands the program to __bpf_prog_select_runtime() in core.c. That function decides whether a JIT is required, has bpf_prog_jit_compile() blind a copy of the program if hardening asks for it, and calls bpf_int_jit_compile(), the entry of the x86 JIT.

bpf_int_jit_compile() is the loop of Figure 7.7. It allocates addrs[], one entry per instruction holding the offset where that instruction's x86 ends, fills it with the guess, and calls do_jit() until two passes agree. do_jit() writes the prologue with emit_prologue() and then switches on each instruction's opcode; the case for BPF_JMP | BPF_TAIL_CALL calls emit_bpf_tail_call_direct() when the instruction's immediate names a poke descriptor and emit_bpf_tail_call_indirect() otherwise.

When two passes agree, bpf_jit_binary_pack_alloc() charges the size against the limit and takes chunks from a pack. After the last pass, bpf_jit_binary_pack_finalize() copies the image into place and bpf_tail_call_direct_fixup() points each direct tail call at its slot's program. Back in __bpf_prog_select_runtime(), a program left untranslated fails with -ENOTSUPP, and bpf_check_tail_call() runs the owner check against every program array the program uses, which is why a mismatch is reported after a verifier log that ended cleanly.

What it costs

CPU
The JIT took 6.9 to 16.6 µs for the counter, median 8.2 over ten loads, against 100 to 414 µs of verification, median 157; for long generated programs it took 38 to 62 ns a slot against 3 to 4.5 µs of verification (bpftrace on bpf_int_jit_compile(), kernel 7.2.15 VM, 12 November 2026). At run time a direct tail call cost nothing measurable and an indirect one 6 ns. Blinding left run time alone and took 11 to 12 µs to load the counter and 58 s for 100,000 instructions.
Memory
About 5 to 7.5 bytes of x86 a slot, 2.2 to 2.75 times that when blinded, in 64-byte chunks of shared 2 MB packs: 192 bytes for the counter, charged against bpf_jit_limit (528,482,304 bytes in the VM). A program array takes 8 bytes a slot and a 304-byte header.
Switches
None at run time: a tail call is a jump inside the kernel. One bpf() call changes a slot: 0.8 to 3.7 µs, plus 0.05 to 1.1 ms for each direct tail call naming it, or 5 to 7 ms each when emptying it.
Locking
None when the program runs. Loading takes pack_mutex to allocate the image; a slot update takes poke_mutex and, for each call site, text_mutex and interrupts to every CPU.

Keep the JIT's defaults unless untrusted users load programs; at bpf_jit_harden=2 expect lost symbols, no direct tail calls and load times that grow with the square of program size. Give tail calls a constant slot, keep a user reference on every program array while its programs run, and replace programs rather than emptying slots.

When it goes wrong

Most failures in this chapter happen after the verifier has accepted the program, so its log is no help: it ends cleanly, and the load still fails, or the program loads and does less than expected. Figure 7.13 pairs each symptom we met with its usual cause and the command that tells it apart. The first three rows are error 524 in its three forms, each a program the JIT did not translate on a kernel with nothing else to run it. An ordinary user is most likely to meet the third, through a seccomp filter.

The middle rows belong to tail calls, which fail quietly by design: a failed check sends the program on to its next instruction, so a count placed after the call is the cheapest way to see it. The last rows are about reading the machine code. Hardening hides every program's name and changes the code at every load. The perf of this distribution can count samples in a program but cannot disassemble it, which leaves bpftool's dump as the view that always works.

Check yourself

  1. Predict the value: clang wrote your program as 27 slots. bpftool prog show reports xlated 232B. How many slots did the kernel add, and where?
  2. Predict the value: before its first pass the JIT guesses 64 bytes for every instruction, and the counter's test at slot 11 skips two instructions. How long is that jump in the first pass and in the second, and how many passes does do_jit() make over the counter?
  3. Predict the value: a generated program is r0 = 0, then 1,000 additions of a 32-bit constant to r0, then exit, 1,002 slots. Loaded with net.core.bpf_jit_harden=2, how many slots does bpftool report after the rewrites, and why does the length of its x86 differ between two loads of the same file?
  4. On a small board whose kernel is also built with CONFIG_BPF_JIT_ALWAYS_ON, a program's verifier log ends with an ordinary processed … insns line and no reason, yet the load fails with error 524. What happened?
  5. An ordinary user's program fails to install its seccomp filter with errno 524, Unknown error 524, while the same program run as root installs it. The machine's administrator had lowered a setting under /proc/sys/net/core. Which one, and why is the error not EPERM?
  6. On one machine /proc/kallsyms lists no bpf_prog_ symbol at all, although bpftool prog show reports every program as jited. Which two settings could cause it, and does either of them change the programs' code?
  7. Predict the value: a program tail-calls itself through slot 0 of its program array and counts each run in a map. One event arrives. How many times does the program run?
  8. Predict the value: thirty-two programs each make a direct tail call to slot 0 of one program array, on this chapter's VM with 16 virtual CPUs. About how long does deleting slot 0 take, and what makes filling it again faster?
  9. After the split, bpftool prog show name count_update reports run_cnt 0, yet the map's total rises with every write. Is count_update running, and where did its time go?
  10. A socket filter that tail-calls through the counter's jmp_table fails to load with ‑EINVAL, although its verifier log ends with processed 5 insns (limit 1000000). Which check refused it, and why does the log look clean?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 7.

Recap

The kernel used in this book has no interpreter, so a program the JIT cannot translate does not load, and the error, 524, comes after a verifier log that ended cleanly. Between the walk and the JIT the kernel rewrites the program, giving maps and helpers their addresses and writing some map lookups in place, and the JIT then turns each instruction into a few x86 instructions, pass after pass until the length repeats, into 64-byte chunks of a shared pack that is read-only and executable. Constant blinding hides every constant behind a random XOR, three instructions for one, at a cost paid at load time that grows with the square of the program's length. A tail call reuses the caller's frame, at most 33 times in a chain, and with a constant slot the JIT writes a direct jump that costs nothing to run and that the kernel rewrites at every call site whenever the slot changes. The counter is now 152 bytes of x86 with a name in /proc/kallsyms, and nothing calls it yet.

New words in this chapter

JIT
just-in-time compiler: translates a whole program into native code once, when it loads
native code
instructions of the CPU itself, here x86-64
trampoline
a short piece of x86 the kernel writes so that a kernel function's entry can call a program and continue
program pack
a 2 MB block of read-only executable memory that the JIT shares out among programs' images in 64-byte chunks
JIT spraying
an attack that hides machine code in a program's constants and jumps into the middle of an instruction to run it
constant blinding
a rewrite before the JIT that replaces each constant with two random values whose XOR is the constant
tail call
a jump from the end of one program into another, which reuses the first one's stack frame
program array
a map whose values are programs, indexed by slot for tail calls
poke descriptor
a record of where in a program's machine code the jump for one program-array slot lies, so that the kernel can rewrite it
direct tail call
a tail call to a constant slot, compiled to a five-byte jump that the kernel points at the slot's program or turns into a no-op

  • RUNTIMESpecification and verification in the field: Applying formal methods to BPF just-in-time compilers in the Linux kernel, Nelson, Van Geffen, Torlak and Wang, OSDI 2020. Jitterbug; read Sections 1 and 2.
  • RUNTIMEbpf: add generic constant blinding for use in jits, Daniel Borkmann, commit 4f3446bb809f, May 2016. The message tells the history of JIT spraying and of the defences before blinding, and documents the three values of bpf_jit_harden.
  • RUNTIMEbpf: Introduce bpf_prog_pack allocator, Song Liu, commit 57631054fae6, February 2022. A short message with the reason for packs, and the first version of the allocator in core.c.

Chapter 8

Hooks, and what attaching writes into the kernel

The write counter's SEC() line names one of thousands of places where the kernel can call a program, and attaching it there changes the kernel itself, from a flag on every thread to a call written over a no-op. An empty program adds 57 ns to a write() at fentry and 127 ns at the write tracepoint, and none of the difference is in the program.

Spine. In chapter 7 the JIT turned the write counter into 152 bytes of x86 that nothing calls yet. Now we watch the loader attach that code to the write() system call, read what the attachment writes into the kernel, and look at the other places where the kernel can call a program.

24 min · LOADER · RUNTIME

"A tracepoint placed in code provides a hook to call a function (probe) that you can provide at runtime."

"Kprobes enables you to dynamically break into any kernel routine and collect debugging and performance information non-disruptively."

Using the Linux Kernel Tracepoints, then Kernel Probes (Kprobes), Linux kernel documentation

Attaching the counter to its tracepoint

Before linksOn kernels without links for perf events, the program was handed to the event with an ioctl, PERF_EVENT_IOC_SET_BPF, and nothing in the kernel held the attachment as an object. libbpf still falls back to it there (libbpf.c line 11569).

Attach connects a loaded program to its hook so that it runs, and for the counter it comes down to a perf_event_open() and a BPF_LINK_CREATE, which Figure 8.1 shows under strace beside libbpf's own probe of the kernel. hashmap_bpf__attach() reads the tracepoint's number, 827 in this VM, from /sys/kernel/tracing/events/syscalls/sys_enter_write/id, opens a perf event on it with perf_event_open(), and joins program and event with BPF_LINK_CREATE, attach type BPF_PERF_EVENT. The result is the link that chapter 3 counted among the program's holders, and bpftool link show lists it as a perf_event link on the tracepoint sys_enter_write.

Each attachment is a struct bpf_link, 80 bytes with a reference count, an ID, a type, a table of operations and the program, wrapped in a larger structure with what its hook needs. When the last reference goes, bpf_link_free() calls the table's release, which detaches the program, so the holders counted in the section "Who holds the program, its maps and its link" also decide when a program stops running. Neither the perf event nor the link shows what attaching changed inside the kernel, which for this tracepoint is a flag on every thread (the section "What attaching writes into the kernel").

From a section name to a hook

Before the loader can attach anything it must know what kind of program it holds and where the program goes, and both come from one string. In the compiler, SEC("tracepoint/syscalls/sys_enter_write") only names the ELF section, a named block of the object file, that the function's bytecode goes into, and llvm-readelf -S on the counter's object lists a section under that name, 216 bytes long, beside .maps, .rodata and license.

libbpf matches the name against its own table, section_defs in tools/lib/bpf/libbpf.c (116 entries in v7.2), as Figure 8.2 shows for three of the book's programs. The part before the first slash selects the program type, the kind of program, which fixes what it receives when it runs and which helpers it may call. The part after the slash names the hook. For the write counter that is the tracepoint at the entry to write, while the second program hangs on a kprobe, a hook the kernel inserts at run time on almost any kernel function, found by name, here do_sys_openat2.

Some program types also need an attach type, the variant of a hook the program is for. The fork tracer runs at a tracepoint too, yet its tp_btf prefix brings a different program type, TRACING, with attach type BPF_TRACE_RAW_TP fixed at load. The write counter gets its attach type only when it is attached. A prefix that matches no entry leaves the type unset, and libbpf stops before the kernel sees the program, whereas a misspelling after the slash, such as sys_enter_wrte, still loads and fails only at attach, when libbpf looks the tracepoint up in tracefs.

Read with · Program Types and ELF Sections, Documentation/bpf/libbpf/program_types.rst, Linux kernel documentation (v7.2)

What it is. libbpf's own list of every section name it understands, with the program type and attach type each one produces.

Why now. Figure 8.2 is three rows of this table, and when a SEC() line is puzzling, this page has the answer.

  1. The two rules at the top. What a plain type and a type+ entry accept, and what the part after the slash is for. Three minutes.
  2. The three rows of Figure 8.2. Find tracepoint+, kprobe+ and tp_btf+, and read across: program type, attach type. Five minutes.
  3. The footnotes on those rows. The format of what may follow the slash. Five minutes.

Skip. The cgroup, socket and network rows, and the Sleepable column. The network hooks come back in the section "What a program may change" and sleepable programs in the section "Where the program finds itself"; the other rows belong to hooks this book does not use.

The table. The page has no figures; study the rows for BPF_PROG_TYPE_TRACING, where many prefixes share a single program type and differ only in attach type.

Carry in. Three questions; their answers are in the key under chapter 8.

  1. What does the + in kprobe+ mean, and what happens to a program in plain SEC("kprobe")?
  2. Find your write counter's row. Which program type does it give, and which attach type?
  3. Your fork tracer and your write counter both run at tracepoints. Why does the table give them different program types?

About 15 minutes · LOADER

One write, five stops

A write() passes several places where a program can run, and Figure 8.3 puts both kinds of hook just met on one call. The tracepoint sys_enter_write fires as the system call enters the kernel, so the counter runs before the kernel has even found the file, and a kprobe on vfs_write() fires a little later, as that function starts. Further in, security_file_permission() asks the security modules whether this write may go ahead, and on the way back out two more hooks see how the call ended.

At each stop r1 points at something different. It holds the program's context, the data the hook hands over in a shape that the program type fixes. For the counter that is the tracepoint's record, whose fields /sys/kernel/tracing/events/syscalls/sys_enter_write/format lists: the system call number, then fd, buf and count.

A fixed hook or any function

The two quotes at the head of this chapter describe the two kinds of hook in the counter's world. The write counter runs at a tracepoint, a call that kernel developers wrote into the source, and the openat tracer in book/program hangs on a kprobe, which the kernel places at attach time on a function the loader names. Figure 8.4 sets the tracepoint, the only one of the three placed on purpose, beside the two ways to attach to any function. Kernel 7.2.15 has 2,079 tracepoints, whereas a kprobe can go on almost any instruction outside the 751 entries of the kprobe blacklist, code where a breakpoint would trap again.

An fentry program attaches to the entry of a kernel function through a trampoline, the stub of machine code that chapter 7 saw the kernel write. The compiler leaves a five-byte no-op near the start of each function for ftrace, the kernel's function tracer, and attaching rewrites it into a call, so there is no breakpoint to take. Its twin, fexit, runs as the function returns and also sees the return value. A kprobe at a function's entry borrows the same slot, and only a kprobe placed further into the function is a breakpoint, as the next section measures.

A kprobe's context is the saved CPU registers, from which the BPF_KPROBE macro in kprobe.bpf.c reads the arguments back out, whereas an fentry program gets the arguments themselves, typed by BTF.

The fork tracer in book/program sits between the columns. It runs at a raw tracepoint, added in Linux 4.17, which is the same named point with the record left unbuilt, so that the program receives the tracepoint's own arguments. Its section, tp_btf/sched_process_fork, asks for the BTF-typed kind, whose BPF_PROG macro names the two task_struct pointers that the tracepoint passes, and CO-RE fixes the offset of pid inside them.

The bottom row of Figure 8.4 is what reaching any function costs. Nobody keeps a function's name stable for the programs that attach to it, and the next release may rename the function, split it, or let the compiler inline it into its callers. A kprobe on a missing name fails to attach, but on a function that some callers now inline it misses those calls and says nothing.

What attaching writes into the kernel

The three kinds of hook differ most in the code that runs before the program. Timed per one-byte write() on kernel 7.2.15, an empty program added 57 ns at fentry, 114 ns at a kprobe on vfs_write() and 127 ns at the tracepoint, to a call that takes 320 ns alone, while run_time_ns, which starts at the program's first instruction, gave the program itself 33 to 40 ns at every hook over two sessions. Figure 8.5 draws the difference from kernel stacks recorded under the counter's map update.

A static key is a branch that the kernel compiles as a no-op and rewrites into a jump when a feature is switched on. A static call is a direct call whose target the kernel rewrites in place. Attaching the counter switched both on for the tracepoint sys_enter, and its registration hook, syscall_regfunc() in kernel/tracepoint.c, set a work flag on every thread. From then on every system call takes the slower entry path into trace_syscall_enter().

The first eight bytesThe format file calls them common_type, common_flags, common_preempt_count and common_pid. For a program, perf_call_bpf_enter() stores there a pointer to registers saved by perf_fetch_caller_regs(), under the comment "bpf prog requires 'regs' to be the first member in the ctx".

There the static call reaches perf_syscall_enter(), which finds the bit for write set in a bitmap of enabled calls. Then perf_call_bpf_enter() builds the record on its own stack, and trace_call_bpf_faultable() passes the record's address to each program attached to the event. On x86 a function's first argument travels in rdi, and the JIT keeps r1 in rdi (reg2hex in arch/x86/net/bpf_jit_comp.c), so the address arrives in r1 without a copy.

The kprobe and the fentry program both start from ftrace's slot, five bytes near the top of each traceable function that ftrace turned into a no-op at boot. A kprobe asked for at vfs_write lands on it, at vfs_write+0x4. The kernel was built with CONFIG_KPROBES_ON_FTRACE, which lets kprobes use ftrace, so check_ftrace_location() in kernel/kprobes.c makes it an ftrace probe, which /sys/kernel/debug/kprobes/list marks [FTRACE]. The slot then calls a trampoline that ftrace made for kprobes (Figure 8.6), which saves every register as the struct pt_regs that r1 will point at.

Patching live codeEach change in Figure 8.6 goes through smp_text_poke_batch_finish() in arch/x86/kernel/alternative.c: an int3 on the first byte, a cross-call to every CPU, the other bytes, another cross-call, the new first byte and a third. A CPU that meets the int3 in between is steered around it.

Away from the slot there is nothing to borrow. A kprobe at vfs_write+0x9 writes cc, the x86 breakpoint int3, over the first byte of a sub, and each write takes two traps, one at the probe and one after a copy of the sub has run elsewhere. That cost 387 ns per write. Five jiffies and a grace period after the attach, a kernel thread replaced the breakpoint with a jump to a detour buffer that saves the registers and calls the same handler. With this optimised kprobe the cost fell to 89 ns.

For fentry the JIT writes a trampoline of its own, the 132 bytes at the bottom of Figure 8.6, and the slot calls it directly. It stores the four argument registers, asks __bpf_prog_enter_recur() whether the program may run, points rdi at the stored arguments and calls the program. Saving no full register set, taking no trap and looking nothing up by address, it is the cheapest of the three. For fexit the slot becomes a jump, and the trampoline calls the rest of vfs_write() itself.

Timed per byte of dd instead, which makes one read() and one write() a byte, the same empty programs cost 180 ns at the tracepoint, 120 ns at the kprobe and 65 ns at fentry, over 695 ns with none (VM, medians of ten, book/labs/costs2-root.sh). The tracepoint's share grew most because the read() takes the slow entry path too, which every system call does while the work flag is set. In the session of the costs box below, getppid() took 320 ns with nothing attached, 354 ns with the counter at its tracepoint, and 320 again after the detach.

Inside ftraceftrace finds the call sites to change by walking the records of every patchable function, twice, in ftrace_replace_code() (arch/x86/kernel/ftrace.c). available_filter_functions listed 59,017 of them in the VM of Lab 8.1.

Figure 8.7 adds the price of attaching and detaching. A function_graph trace put 0.3 ms of a 3.7 ms fentry attach in building the trampoline and in three rounds of patching; the rest ran in ftrace's own code, which the tracer cannot see. Detaching a tracepoint or kprobe program took 29 to 46 ms, because the detach waits until no task can still be inside the program, in synchronize_rcu_tasks_trace() called from perf_event_detach_bpf_prog().

Where the program finds itself

A program runs in the context of the event that fired it, with whatever the glue adds (Figure 8.8). An NMI, a non-maskable interrupt, can arrive while the CPU holds any lock, even with interrupts disabled, so code in one must never wait. perf_event programs on hardware counters run in one, and on x86 so does a kprobe that fires as a breakpoint, since exc_int3() enters through irqentry_nmi_enter(). A softirq is interrupt work that the kernel completes after the hardware interrupt has returned, and XDP runs in one.

In process context the CPU works on behalf of a task, here the writer that called write(). The kprobe glue disables preemption, but the system-call tracepoint's glue and the trampoline only stop migration and take an RCU read lock, which on this kernel's preemptible RCU lets the scheduler switch tasks in mid-program. There each program keeps a recursion counter for each CPU, so while one task sits switched out inside the counter, every write another task makes on that CPU is skipped and added to recursion_misses. With two writers pinned to one CPU the write counter lost 45 to 55 per cent of its events; with the writers on two CPUs it lost none.

Sleepable programs may fault and wait. can_be_sleepable() in verifier.c decides which programs may be loaded that way: fentry and fexit programs, fmod_ret programs, which may change a function's return value, iterators, LSM programs other than cgroup ones, uprobes, struct_ops, and tracepoint, raw tracepoint and BTF tracepoint programs. The last three may attach only where the tracepoint is allowed to fault, which in v7.2 means a system-call tracepoint. Which maps they may use is decided by check_map_prog_compatibility(), and chapter 10 chooses maps against Figure 8.8.

What a program may change

Figure 8.9 gives, for seven program types, what r1 points at and what the return value does. The top three can only watch, since whatever they return, the write goes on.

An LSM program attaches to a hook of the Linux Security Modules, such as file_permission in Figure 8.3, and refuses the operation by returning a negative error. Linux 5.7 added them, and on kernel 7.2.15 /sys/kernel/security/lsm lists bpf.

Two hooks sit on the packet path. XDP, the eXpress Data Path, runs in the network driver as each packet arrives, before the kernel builds its own structure for the packet. Its return value drops the packet, passes it on, sends it back out, or redirects it. tc programs run later, in the traffic-control layer, where that structure exists.

Programs can also call further into the kernel through a kfunc, a kernel function offered to programs by its BTF type instead of a helper ID, whose documentation warns that kfuncs "do not have a stable interface". A struct_ops program set fills a table of function pointers that a subsystem calls, which lets the program make the subsystem's decision. TCP congestion control came first, in 5.6, and sched_ext, a scheduler class whose policy is such a set, arrived in 6.12.

How a new hook gets into the kernel

Often no new hook is needed, because fentry and kprobes reach tens of thousands of functions. A new tracepoint is a patch to the subsystem that owns the code, a TRACE_EVENT() definition and one call to it, reviewed by that subsystem's maintainers.

A hook where a program decides is bigger, as cache_ext shows (Figure 8.10). Its authors wanted page-cache eviction written as BPF programs, so they added a struct_ops table of five function pointers, calls to it at five page-cache events, and kfuncs for the lists a policy keeps. Teaching the verifier about both took only 80 lines, because struct_ops and kfuncs carry most of the work.

cache_ext was published at SOSP 2025, and its code is a modified Linux 6.6.8 kept in the authors' repository. The whole change came to about 2,000 lines, and to reach mainline it would take the road of chapter 5, with patches on the mailing lists, tests, and review by the maintainers of both subsystems. Once a program runs at its hook, every helper and kfunc it calls has been checked against what that hook allows, and chapter 9 follows those calls from the bytecode into the kernel, with how a kfunc is registered.

What it costs

CPU
Per one-byte write(), an empty program cost 57 ns at fentry, 80 at a raw tracepoint or fexit, 89 at an optimised kprobe, 114 at a kprobe on the slot, 127 at the tracepoint and 387 at a breakpoint kprobe, of which 33 to 36 ns ran in the program. The counter itself takes 144 to 162 ns a run without bpf_printk and 0.48 to 0.54 µs with it, and adds 230 to 245 ns to each write() without it and 580 to 620 ns with it (run_time_ns over run_cnt, alike under dd and a write() loop; kernel 7.2.15, VM, 12 November 2026, book/labs/hooks-root.sh).
Memory
A link is an 80-byte struct bpf_link inside its hook's wrapper. An fentry trampoline is 132 bytes of code in a 196-byte request, carved in 64-byte chunks from a shared 2 MB pack, plus about 1.1 KB of bpf_tramp_image, bpf_trampoline and bpf_tracing_link (BTF sizes).
Switches
A perf_event_open() and a BPF_LINK_CREATE to attach the counter and none per event, but a system-call tracepoint in use slows every system call, getppid() from 320 to 354 ns (syscall_regfunc()). Attaching took 0.3 ms (raw tracepoint) to 3.7 ms (fentry); detaching a tracepoint or kprobe program sleeps 29–46 ms in a grace-period wait.
Locking
No lock per event, only recursion counters. System-call tracepoints (trace_call_bpf_faultable()), raw tracepoints and trampolines keep one per program and CPU; kprobes and the other tracepoints share one per CPU, bpf_prog_active in trace_call_bpf(), so a kprobe program that fires while another of them runs on its CPU is skipped as a miss. Each patch of kernel text cross-calls every CPU three times under text_mutex.

Prefer fentry where BTF has the function, a raw tracepoint where one exists, and a tracepoint where the program must outlive upgrades; keep kprobes where the optimiser can replace them, and count a system-call tracepoint against every system call. On a busy preemptible kernel, watch recursion_misses, and if it grows, attach where preemption is off.

When it goes wrong

Most failures at a hook are quiet, because a program that attached to the wrong place, or to a place the event no longer passes, loads and attaches without an error. Figure 8.11 pairs each symptom this chapter met with its usual cause and the command that tells it apart. The first three rows belong to the section name: a prefix libbpf does not know stops the load before the kernel sees the program, a misspelt hook after the slash loads and fails at attach, and a bare prefix loads and is never attached. Two failures that the counter's tracepoint can cause while loading, tracefs refusing an ordinary user and a program loaded but never attached, stand with the other failures of a load in Figure 3.10.

The middle rows are about where a hook sits. A kprobe follows a function's name and address while the work may move elsewhere, and a tracepoint fires before the checks that may fail a write, so a count that is too low, too high or zero sends us to available_filter_functions and to the order in Figure 8.3 before the program. The last rows are costs and losses: a breakpoint kprobe that the optimiser could not replace, a system-call tracepoint that slows every system call, a detach that waits for a grace period, and recursion misses on a preemptible kernel, which bpftool prints only when there are some.

Try it · Predict, then count the hooks on your machine

~20 min · measure · needs bpftool and sudo

Task. Write down three guesses first: how many tracepoints your kernel has, how many functions ftrace can patch, and how many functions BTF describes. Then count them, and find the hooks your own programs use in the right lists. This is the left two columns of Figure 8.4, checked on your machine.

Done when. You have three counts beside your guesses, and you have found syscalls:sys_enter_write and do_sys_openat2 in the lists they belong to.

Hint 1 · direction

All three are lists the kernel publishes as files: two in the tracing file system, one in the kernel's BTF.

Hint 2 · mechanism

The tracing file system is mounted at /sys/kernel/tracing and only root may read it; look for files whose names start with available_. The BTF list needs no root: dump /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux with bpftool and count the lines that describe functions.

Hint 3 · nearly there

sudo wc -l /sys/kernel/tracing/available_events /sys/kernel/tracing/available_filter_functions; bpftool btf dump file /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux | grep -c "] FUNC '"; then sudo grep -x syscalls:sys_enter_write /sys/kernel/tracing/available_events.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 8.

Try it · Make the counter miss

~25 min · measure · needs root in a throwaway VM (virtme-ng) or on a test machine with a preemptible kernel, bpftool and taskset

Task. Load the write counter and run two processes that each make 3,000,000 one-byte writes to /dev/null, pinned to the same CPU. Compare recursion_misses and the sum of the map's values with the number of writes. Repeat with the writers on two CPUs, and then with the counter's body attached as a kprobe on vfs_write. This makes the recursion counter of the section "Where the program finds itself" visible.

Done when. bpftool reports recursion_misses in the millions for the tracepoint version on one CPU, and the misses plus the map's total equal the writes made; with two CPUs, or as a kprobe, there are none.

Hint 1 · direction

A miss needs a task to be switched out while it is inside the program, so make two tasks compete for one CPU. Check that your kernel lets the scheduler interrupt kernel code: /sys/kernel/debug/sched/preempt should show (full) or (lazy).

Hint 2 · mechanism

taskset -c pins a process to a CPU. The writer is a ten-line C loop around write(fd, "x", 1). bpftool prog load … autoattach attaches the counter without its loader, and bpftool -j map dump name write_counts gives the values to add up.

Hint 3 · nearly there

bash book/labs/ch14-root.sh build leaves wloop, hashmap.bpf.o and the kprobe variant wc_kp.bpf.o in /tmp/c14. In the VM: bpftool prog load hashmap.bpf.o /sys/fs/bpf/wc autoattach, then taskset -c 3 ./wloop 3000000 & taskset -c 3 ./wloop 3000000 & wait, then bpftool prog show name count_writes.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 8.

Check yourself

  1. After an edit, your loader prints libbpf: prog 'count_writes': missing BPF prog type, check ELF section name 'tracepoints/syscalls/sys_enter_write'. Which step failed, and did the kernel ever see the program?
  2. Predict the values: a process opens /etc/hostname read-only and calls write() on it ten times; every call fails. How many times does each of these run: your write counter, an fentry program on vfs_write(), and an fentry program on security_file_permission() that counts only write checks?
  3. On a newer kernel your kprobe program on do_sys_openat2 loads and attaches without an error, yet prints nothing while files are opened. A tracepoint version of the same program works. What happened?
  4. Predict the values: a kprobe program written with BPF_KPROBE and an fentry program written with BPF_PROG, both on vfs_write(struct file *file, const char __user *buf, size_t count, loff_t *pos), read count. At what offset from r1 does each one load it?
  5. A kprobe program on vfs_write+0xc loads, and attaching it fails with libbpf: prog 'e_kpbad': failed to create kprobe 'vfs_write+0xc' perf event: -EILSEQ. The same program attaches at vfs_write+0x9. What is wrong with 0xc?
  6. The same kprobe program at vfs_write+0x9 adds 89 ns per write on one machine and 387 ns on another, where /sys/kernel/debug/kprobes/list shows the probe without [OPTIMIZED]. What does the slow machine do on each write, and what changes for the program besides its speed?
  7. You want to stop every process from writing to one file, whoever runs it. Which kind of program in Figure 8.9 can do it, and what does it return?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 8.

Recap

The SEC() string is an ELF section name whose prefix picks the program type, and sometimes an attach type, while the rest names the hook, and attaching the counter opens a perf event on its tracepoint and joins the program to it with a link. The program type fixes the context r1 points at and what the return value does; tracepoints, placed in the source on purpose, change rarely, while kprobes and fentry programs reach any function by name and break when it changes. The write tracepoint reaches the counter through a work flag on every thread, a static key, a static call and a record built on the stack; a kprobe at a function's entry rides ftrace's slot into a register-saving trampoline and elsewhere is an int3 until the optimiser replaces it, and an fentry program is called from the slot through a trampoline the JIT wrote, the cheapest path of the three. Where the glue leaves a program preemptible, a task switched out inside it turns the other runs on that CPU into lost events. Tracing programs watch, LSM programs can refuse, XDP and tc programs decide a packet's fate, and struct_ops program sets make a subsystem's decisions, and a new hook of that last kind is a struct_ops table, call sites, kfuncs and verifier rules, sent upstream like any other patch.

New words in this chapter

attach
connecting a loaded program to its hook, so that it runs
ELF section
a named block of an object file, chosen with SEC()
kprobe
a hook placed at run time on almost any kernel function, by name
attach type
the variant of a hook a program is for, sometimes fixed at load
context
what r1 points at when a program starts, shaped by its type
fentry
a program run through a trampoline at a kernel function's entry
fexit
the same at the function's return; it also sees the return value
raw tracepoint
a tracepoint whose program gets the tracepoint's own arguments
static key
a no-op branch that the kernel rewrites into a jump when needed
static call
a direct call whose target the kernel rewrites in place
optimised kprobe
a kprobe whose breakpoint became a jump to a detour buffer
NMI
non-maskable interrupt, which can arrive while any lock is held
softirq
interrupt work finished after the hardware interrupt returns
process context
the CPU running kernel code for a task, as in a system call
LSM program
a program on a security-module hook; a negative return refuses
XDP
eXpress Data Path, a driver hook that decides each packet's fate
tc
a hook in the traffic-control layer, later on the packet path
kfunc
a kernel function offered through BTF, with no promise of stability
struct_ops
a program set that fills a subsystem's table of function pointers
sched_ext
the scheduler class, since 6.12, whose policy is a struct_ops set

  • RUNTIMEProgram types (Linux), eBPF Docs. One page per program type, with its context, return values and the kernel version that added each; read the rows of Figure 8.9 first.

Chapter 9

Calling the kernel: helpers and kfuncs

The write counter's slot 8 holds the number 1 when libbpf hands it to the kernel and the number 357,328 when it runs, and between the two the kernel decides what helper 1 means for a tracepoint program, checks the call against that meaning, and rewrites it. A call costs about 4 ns, a lookup the kernel writes in place costs half a nanosecond, and a kfunc that takes a reference and gives it back costs 40.

  • What the counter's four calls look like to the kernel, and which helpers a tracepoint program may name
  • How a helper ID becomes a prototype, a check, and a direct call or no call at all, and what each costs
  • How a kfunc is registered, checked and given back, why it promises nothing, and how both kinds of call fail

Spine. In chapter 8 the loader attached the counter to the write tracepoint, whose program type fixed what r1 points at when the program runs. The same type decides which kernel functions the program may call, so now we follow the counter's four calls from the bytecode into the kernel and then send a kfunc down the same path. Every number here was measured on kernel 7.2.15 in a virtme-ng VM with 16 virtual CPUs on 12 November 2026, by the script that each figure names.

26 min · VERIFIER · RUNTIME

The counter's four calls, as the kernel reports them

Slot 8 or slot 9Log (a) of Figure 5.1 shows the lookup at slot 9. That log comes from a copy of the counter without its NULL test, for which clang keeps the key's address in r6 and adds r2 = r6 at slot 8; the counter itself calls at slot 8 in its object, its log and its dump.

Figure 9.1 shows the counter's calls three ways. In the object they are four instructions with opcode 0x85 at slots 0, 8, 16 and 24, each with a helper ID in its immediate (the section "Calling into the kernel"). The verifier's log names the calls by those IDs, so slot 8 reads call bpf_map_lookup_elem#1, and the state printed after it records what the call returned, a map value or NULL. In the program the kernel kept, two of the calls go to the hash table's own functions instead. Two instructions added after the lookup move every later slot down by two, so the update at slot 24 of the object sits at slot 26 of the dump.

Which helpers the counter may call at all depends on its program type, and bpftool can ask the running kernel. bpftool feature probe kernel full loads a small test program for every pair of program type and helper and reads the refusals. For a tracepoint program it lists 82 of the 211 helpers, against 88 for socket filters, 104 for XDP programs and 139 for tc classifiers, because each type answers for its own set (the section "Which helpers a program type may call"). For tracing, extension, LSM and struct_ops programs libbpf's probe does not try (tools/lib/bpf/libbpf_probes.c, line 447), so bpftool prints that it could not tell.

The list says which helpers the type may name, which is less than which calls a program of that type may make. A test load that fails for any other reason than an unknown or refused helper counts as support (line 478 of the same file). So bpf_copy_from_user() appears in the tracepoint list, yet a counter that calls it is refused, because that helper may sleep and the counter may not (question 9.8).

A helper is a C function and a prototype

We begin with the C behind helper 1 in Figure 9.2. Every helper is written with one of the macros BPF_CALL_0 to BPF_CALL_5, and BPF_CALL_x (include/linux/filter.h, line 611) turns the top five lines into three pieces. The body becomes an always-inline function with the real argument types, and a typedef records the same types. bpf_map_lookup_elem() itself takes five u64 values, one per argument register, and casts the first two before it calls the body. The kernel's BTF keeps both shapes.

That outer function is the calling convention of the section "Calling into the kernel" seen from the kernel's side. Up to five arguments arrive in r1 to r5, and the answer leaves in r0. The x86 JIT keeps r6 to r9 in rbx, r13, r14 and r15, which every x86-64 function preserves, so a helper is an ordinary C function and needs no glue around it.

The verifier never reads that code. A helper prototype is the struct bpf_func_proto beneath it (include/linux/bpf.h, line 968). It gives the helper's address, whether it is GPL-only or may sleep, and the types of its result and of up to five arguments. Linux 7.2 has 23 argument types and 9 return types. Flags such as PTR_MAYBE_NULL widen them, so that ARG_PTR_TO_MAP_VALUE_OR_NULL is the map-value argument with NULL allowed.

An argument type names a class of register state, and check_func_arg() (verifier.c, line 8211) compares each argument register with its type in turn. check_reg_type() looks the type up in compatible_reg_types[] (line 7807), a table from each argument type to the register types that satisfy it. Some types then ask for more. ARG_CONST_MAP_PTR notes which map r1 holds, so that ARG_PTR_TO_MAP_KEY can demand that map's key size at r2 (line 8324), and ARG_CONST_SIZE checks a length against the pointer in the register before it. How the verifier knows that four bytes at fp-4 are written, or that a length stays in bounds, is the business of chapters 4 to 6; the prototype only says which questions to ask.

Which helpers a program type may call

Which prototype an ID stands for depends on the program type. bpf_get_helper_proto() (verifier.c, line 10117) checks that the ID is below __BPF_FUNC_MAX_ID and then asks the type's own get_func_proto() callback. For a tracepoint program that callback is tp_prog_func_proto() in kernel/trace/bpf_trace.c, and Figure 9.3 follows it down. It answers four IDs itself and passes the rest to bpf_tracing_func_proto(), which adds three of its own and passes the remainder on to bpf_base_func_proto() in helpers.c.

bpf_base_func_proto() sorts helpers by what the loader holds. The first 25 are open to every program, 28 more come after a CAP_BPF test at line 2124, and the last 21, among them bpf_trace_printk(), after a CAP_PERFMON test at line 2192. A tracepoint program cannot be loaded without CAP_PERFMON at all (syscall.c, line 3045), so every tier is open to the counter. With bpf_probe_write_user(), which needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN as well, the sum is the 82 that bpftool listed.

A NULL anywhere in the chain becomes one message, program of this type cannot use helper, whatever the reason was. In our runs an XDP program that calls bpf_printk() loaded as root. Loaded by a process that had dropped CAP_PERFMON and CAP_SYS_ADMIN, it was refused with that message, because XDP's chain also ends in bpf_base_func_proto() and its test (question 9.5). An ID beyond the last one the kernel knows fails a step earlier, as invalid func unknown#300 did for a call of helper 300.

check_helper_call() (line 10171) then refuses three kinds of call in turn. A GPL-only helper fails in a program that is not GPL-compatible, then a helper whose own allowed() callback says no, then a helper that may sleep in a program that cannot. Only after that does each argument go to check_func_arg(), as Figure 9.4 shows for two of the counter's calls. At slot 8, ARG_CONST_MAP_PTR finds a map pointer in r1 and notes the map, and ARG_PTR_TO_MAP_KEY finds the four written bytes at fp-4. The return type leaves r0 as map_value_or_null, the state that Figure 5.7 follows to the NULL test, while slot 0 takes no arguments and leaves nothing to check.

From call 0x1 to the code that runs

Reading the offsetIn the VM, /proc/kallsyms put __bpf_call_base at ffffffffb6598d50 and bpf_get_current_pid_tgid at ffffffffb65d8580, 260,144 bytes higher, the number after the #. bpf_trace_printk lies below the base, at −129,920.

After the walk, bpf_do_misc_fixups() in kernel/bpf/fixups.c rewrites every call, one of the passes that the section "What the kernel changes before the JIT" lists. Most helpers reach patch_call_imm (line 2330), which puts the helper's distance from __bpf_call_base in the immediate, and the JIT turns that into a direct x86 call. For a JIT-compiled program on a 64-bit machine, map helpers go straight to the map's own functions instead (line 1984). So the update at slot 24 of the object becomes call htab_map_update_elem at slot 26 of the dump. A lookup in a map whose operations table has map_gen_lookup is written as instructions, for the hash map a call to __htab_map_lookup_elem() and two more.

An array map goes further. Its array_map_gen_lookup() (arraymap.c, line 218) writes seven instructions that point r1 at the values, load the key, test it against max_entries and scale it, and no call remains. This is inlining, replacing a call with instructions that do the callee's work in place. Figure 9.5 measures it in a tracepoint program that repeats one operation 64 times per event, with kernel.bpf_stats_enabled=1.

The inlined lookup costs half a nanosecond. The same array created with BPF_F_INNER_MAP, for which array_map_gen_lookup() declines at its first test, costs 4.9 ns through a call to array_map_lookup_elem(), close to the 4.1 ns of bpf_get_current_pid_tgid(). Hashing the key and walking a hash chain take the hash map to 13.9 ns.

A few helpers are inlined as well, and Figure 9.6 loads a program that calls eight of them once each. bpf_do_misc_fixups() writes bpf_jiffies64() as three instructions for any JIT-compiled program on a 64-bit machine (line 2079). On x86-64 it also writes three each for bpf_get_smp_processor_id() and bpf_get_current_task() (lines 2105 and 2132), which read the processor number and the current task from this CPU's copy of a kernel variable. The other four remain calls. The x86 JIT inlines no helper of its own, since bpf_jit_inlines_helper_call() keeps its default answer, false, in core.c, so they are calls in the machine code too.

In the second run an inlined helper cost about 0.2 ns a call, against 4.1 ns for a called one. bpf_ktime_get_ns() cost 31.3 ns, because on the VM's clock reading the time costs far more than the call. The five variants of the first run came back within 0.9 ns of Figure 9.5, with the lookup through a call at 4.7 ns and the kfunc pair at 38.8.

The prototype of bpf_get_smp_processor_id() also sets allow_fastcall. That tells the verifier that the inlined call changes no register but r0, so spills and fills of r1 to r5 that the compiler placed around it may be removed (bpf_remove_fastcall_spills_fills(), fixups.c line 2566). Inlining makes the program longer, though: 64 inlined array lookups took 7,744 bytes of bytecode, against 4,672 as calls.

kfuncs: kernel functions named by BTF ID

How manyThe vmlinux BTF of 7.2.15 carries 308 bpf_kfunc tags, against 211 helper IDs (bpftool btf dump file /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux | grep -c "DECL_TAG 'bpf_kfunc'"). Modules carry their own.

A kfunc has no helper ID and no prototype struct. Its definition carries __bpf_kfunc, which keeps the compiler from inlining it or dropping it (include/linux/btf.h, line 89). Its name goes into a BTF ID set, a list of BTF IDs with a word of flags for each, between BTF_KFUNCS_START and BTF_KFUNCS_END. The IDs stay zero until the resolve_btfids tool fills them in as the kernel is linked. pahole, run with its decl_tag_kfuncs feature while the kernel's BTF is written (scripts/Makefile.btf, line 17), then tags each function of a set with bpf_kfunc.

A set does nothing until it is registered for a program type. At boot, kfunc_init() in helpers.c (line 4978) passes the generic set, which holds bpf_task_from_pid() and bpf_task_release() among others, to register_btf_kfunc_id_set() for six program types. It registers a common set once more for BPF_PROG_TYPE_UNSPEC, and every type shares that one. Each registration files the set under one of fourteen kfunc hooks, an index that bpf_prog_type_to_kfunc_hook() in btf.c (line 9029) picks for the type. Tracepoint, raw tracepoint, perf event, LSM and tracing programs all map to the TRACING hook, so the generic set registered for tracing programs reaches the counter as well.

A program declares a kfunc as an external symbol marked __ksym. libbpf finds the name in the kernel's BTF and writes its BTF ID into a call with source field 2, the third kind of call in Figure 1.7, as Figure 9.7 shows for bpf_task_from_pid(). The first kfunc call of a program makes bpf_add_kfunc_call() (verifier.c, line 2677) demand kernel BTF, a JIT and a GPL-compatible licence, and look up the function's address with kallsyms_lookup_name(); a program may call at most 256 different kfuncs. check_kfunc_call() (line 12913) asks btf_kfunc_is_allowed() whether the ID is in a set of the common hook or of the program's hook, matches the registers against the BTF prototype and applies the flags. The fixup then writes the address's distance from __bpf_call_base, for the same direct call as a helper's.

What the flags make the verifier check

A BTF prototype says which types a kfunc takes, and the flags in its set say what a prototype cannot (Figure 9.8). An acquire kfunc, flagged KF_ACQUIRE, returns a pointer that holds a reference. The program must pass that pointer to a release kfunc, flagged KF_RELEASE, on every path before it exits, or store it in a map. KF_RET_NULL makes the result maybe-NULL, KF_SLEEPABLE admits only sleepable programs, KF_DESTRUCTIVE only loaders with CAP_SYS_BOOT, and KF_RCU_PROTECTED only calls inside an RCU read section. The generic set gives bpf_task_from_pid() the flags KF_ACQUIRE | KF_RET_NULL and bpf_task_release() the flag KF_RELEASE (helpers.c, lines 4847 and 4830).

Every pointer argument must also be a trusted pointer, one the verifier knows to be valid and unchanged. That is a pointer the kernel passed to a tracepoint or struct_ops program, or one an acquire kfunc returned, used at offset zero and not loaded from a field of another pointer (kfuncs.rst, section 2.2). Until Linux 7.0 a kfunc asked for this rule with a KF_TRUSTED_ARGS flag. Puranjay Mohan's commit 1a5c01d2508a made it the rule for every kfunc, and v7.2's btf.h no longer defines the old flag. KF_RCU now relaxes the rule to pointers that RCU keeps valid.

The verifier keeps references in the state it walks, as Figure 9.9 shows. The call at slot 2 runs acquire_reference() (verifier.c, line 1427), which gives the new reference the next ID, 2, and records the slot. From there on every line of the log ends with refs=2. On the NULL side of the test at slot 3 the reference is dropped, since a NULL pointer holds nothing to release (mark_ptr_or_null_regs(), line 15706).

On the other side the reference lasts until the exit, where check_reference_leak() (line 9946) prints it with the slot that made it. A release kfunc ends it earlier, in release_reference() (line 8951). That function also makes every copy of the pointer, in a register or on the stack, a plain scalar, so a read through a copy after the release fails with R6 invalid mem access 'scalar'.

Adding a kfunc, and what it promises

Adding a kfunc is correspondingly short. Commit 187baa10963a by Kaitao Cheng, merged for Linux 7.2, added bpf_list_del() in fifteen lines: a nine-line function and a BTF_ID_FLAGS line with KF_ACQUIRE | KF_RET_NULL in helpers.c, and five lines in verifier.c. Those five are needed only because the verifier gives list kfuncs extra rules, such as a check that the list's lock is held. An ordinary kfunc needs no verifier change, since its BTF prototype and flags are the whole contract.

"This helper list is effectively frozen. If you are trying to add a new helper, you should add a kfunc instead which has less stability guarantees."

Comment closing the helper list in include/uapi/linux/bpf.h, Linux v7.2, line 6145

That contract carries no promise. The design Q&A counts the "set of helper functions and their arguments" as stable ABI, and the list stops at helper 211 with the comment above. Levi Zim added that comment in 2025 (commit 0abff462d802, Linux 6.15) "to prevent people from trying to add new helpers there and direct them to kfuncs". Section 3 of Documentation/bpf/kfuncs.rst, which David Vernet's commit 16c294a6aad8 added for Linux 6.3, likens kfuncs to EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL and says that a kfunc "will never have any hard stability guarantees". The next kernel may therefore refuse a program that calls one (Figure 9.10).

A program can prepare for a kernel that lacks a kfunc. Declared plainly, a missing kfunc stops libbpf before any program reaches the kernel, with extern (func ksym) '…': not found in kernel or module BTFs. Declared __weak, it lets libbpf go on, writing 0 wherever the program takes the function's address and turning each call into a call of helper 2,002,000,000 plus the symbol's index (poison_kfunc_call(), libbpf.c line 6239). If a path reaches that call, the verifier refuses it as an unknown helper and libbpf reports the refusal as an unresolved kfunc. A test with bpf_ksym_exists() closes the path, because the verifier sees the test compare 0 with 0, and for a loader with CAP_BPF the call is then removed with the rest of the dead code (Lab 9.3).

Inside the v7.2 source

Figure 9.11 lists that code in the order a load reaches it. A helper is defined by BPF_CALL_x and described by its prototype, and the program type's chain picks one prototype per ID. check_helper_call() checks the registers against it, and bpf_do_misc_fixups() writes either the helper's distance from __bpf_call_base or instructions that do its work. A kfunc is defined in a BTF ID set and filed under a kfunc hook at boot. check_kfunc_call() checks it against its BTF prototype and flags, the walk counts its references until every exit, and it is called through the same kind of direct call.

What it costs

CPU
Per operation (Figure 9.5): 0.5 ns for an inlined array lookup, 4.1 ns for a helper call, 4.9 ns for an array lookup through a call, 13.9 ns for a hash lookup and 39.7 ns for a kfunc acquire and release pair, against 48.8 ns for a run without them. An inlined bpf_get_smp_processor_id(), bpf_get_current_task() or bpf_jiffies64() cost about 0.2 ns, and bpf_ktime_get_ns() 31.3 ns on kvm-clock (Figure 9.6). All on kernel 7.2.15 in a 16-CPU VM, 12 November 2026.
Memory
Prototypes are 96-byte constants in the kernel image. A program that calls any kfunc gets a 12,296-byte table of call descriptors (struct bpf_kfunc_desc_tab, 256 entries of 48 bytes), charged to the loader's memory cgroup. Inlining lengthens the program: 64 array lookups took 7,744 bytes of bytecode and 3,838 of x86 inline, against 4,672 and 2,430 as calls.
Switches
None. Helpers and kfuncs run on the program's CPU in its context; only those marked might_sleep or KF_SLEEPABLE may block, and only sleepable programs may call them.
Locking
Map lookups read under RCU with no lock. bpf_task_from_pid() looks the PID up under rcu_read_lock() and takes a reference with an atomic increment of the task's rcu_users, and bpf_task_release() drops it.

Use an array map when keys are small dense integers, because its lookup is inlined at a tenth of the cost of a call, and call a helper whose answer does not change within a run once, keeping the result. Call a kfunc when no helper does the job, release what it acquired on the path that acquired it, and declare it __weak behind bpf_ksym_exists() when the program must also load on kernels that lack it.

When it goes wrong

Most failures of a call are refusals at load, and the verifier's message names the rule that failed (Figure 9.12). The helper rows follow the steps of check_helper_call() in order, from an unknown ID and a NULL from the type's chain to the licence, sleep, and one argument against its type. The NULL from the chain hides its cause. A helper the type never offers and one that the loader's capabilities withhold print the same line, so the feature probe and the loader's capabilities are worth reading before the program is changed.

The kfunc rows follow check_kfunc_call() and the reference rules of the section "What the flags make the verifier check". A kfunc that libbpf cannot find stops the load before the kernel sees anything. One declared __weak fails in the verifier only if a path reaches its call, and bpf_ksym_exists() is there to close that path. The last row is a cost that prints no error at all: a change to a map's flags can turn seven inlined instructions back into a call, and only the dump shows it.
