Recap

A helper is a C function made by a BPF_CALL_x macro, and the verifier checks each call against its struct bpf_func_proto, chosen per program type by a chain of get_func_proto() callbacks whose last step also tests the loader's capabilities. bpf_do_misc_fixups() then turns the ID into a distance from __bpf_call_base, sends a map helper to the map's own code, or writes the work in place, as it does for an array lookup and, on x86-64, for three small helpers. A kfunc is named by BTF ID, allowed by sets registered per kfunc hook, checked against its BTF prototype and KF_ flags, and then called like a helper, while the verifier counts the references that acquire kfuncs open until every exit has closed them. Helpers are stable and frozen at 211; kfuncs promise nothing, and a program that must load on several kernels declares them __weak and tests them with bpf_ksym_exists().

New words in this chapter

helper prototype
the struct bpf_func_proto that gives a helper's address, flags, return type and argument types; the verifier checks calls against it
inlining
replacing a call with instructions that do the callee's work in place, as the verifier does for an array lookup
BTF ID set
a list of BTF IDs, each with a word of flags, built into the kernel; registered for a program type, it makes the functions in it kfuncs for that type
acquire kfunc
a kfunc flagged KF_ACQUIRE, which returns a pointer holding a reference that the program must release
release kfunc
a kfunc flagged KF_RELEASE, which takes such a pointer and drops its reference
trusted pointer
a pointer the verifier knows to be valid and unchanged, such as a tracepoint's argument or an acquire kfunc's result; every kfunc wants its pointer arguments trusted

Go deeper

  • RUNTIMEBPF Kernel Functions (kfuncs), Linux kernel documentation. Section 2 on defining, annotating and registering a kfunc, with every KF_ flag; section 3 on what users of a kfunc may expect. Its section 2.5.8 describes a KF_DEPRECATED flag that v7.2's btf.h does not define.
  • RUNTIMEbpf-helpers(7), Linux manual page. Every helper with its arguments and return value; read the entry before calling a helper you have not used, and its IMPLEMENTATION section for the kernel files to check against.
  • VERIFIERbpf: Support bpf program calling kernel function, Martin KaFai Lau, Linux 5.13, 2021. The commit that introduced kfuncs; in its diff, verifier.c gains check_kfunc_call(), which checks the registers against the kernel function's BTF type.
  • LINEAGEbpf: Add comment about helper freeze, Levi Zim, Linux 6.15, 2025. Three lines of comment that close the helper list; the commit message links the earlier mailing-list messages it follows.
  • LINEAGEbpf/docs: Document kfunc lifecycle / stability expectations, David Vernet, Linux 6.3, 2023. The section of kfuncs.rst that says what a kfunc's users may and may not count on.
  • VERIFIERbpf: Make KF_TRUSTED_ARGS the default for all kfuncs, Puranjay Mohan, Linux 7.0, 2026. Its message lists the cases that already passed the trusted check and the kfuncs that now refuse a NULL argument.
  • VERIFIERbpf: Introduce the bpf_list_del kfunc, Kaitao Cheng, Linux 7.2, 2026. A whole kfunc in fifteen lines; read the BTF_ID_FLAGS line, then the five lines that tell the verifier about the list's lock.
  • LOADERBPF Design Q&A, Linux kernel documentation. The answers on the stable ABI, on new functionality through kfuncs, and on why calling a kernel function makes no ABI.

Chapter 10

Maps: layout, choosing, sharing

The write counter and its loader never talk to each other. They share one hash map, which the kernel built at 83,968 bytes before the first write, and each of the other map types the counter could use moves that cost somewhere else, into memory for every CPU, into a lock, or into the copies that user space makes to read it.

  • What the kernel built when the loader created the counter's map, down to the bucket, and what a lookup gives back
  • How user space reads the same map, and why the loader prints the same line forever

Spine. Chapter 9 followed the counter's helper calls from the bytecode to the kernel functions that run, among them the lookup and the update of write_counts. Now we follow the key those calls carry into the map, read the map from where the loader sits, and choose the map the counter should have had. Every number in this chapter was measured on kernel 7.2.15 in a virtme-ng VM with 16 virtual CPUs on 12 November 2026, by the script that each figure or paragraph names.

26 min · RUNTIME · LOADER

The counter's map, from its loader and from bpftool

We start with the loader as written, run in Figure 10.1 while one shell writes ten times a second. From round 1 on it prints one thread and its count forever, and Ctrl-C does not stop it, which is why chapter 3 stopped it with pkill. bpftool needs nothing from the loader to see the same map, because for root it turns the map's ID into a descriptor of its own and asks the kernel what the map is.

$ sudo bpftool map show name write_counts
7: hash  name write_counts  flags 0x0
        key 4B  value 8B  max_entries 1024  memlock 83968B

The type, the two sizes and max_entries come from the map's definition in hashmap.bpf.c, while memlock is what the kernel made of them (book/labs/ch09-root.sh). A thread ID and its count take 12 bytes, so 1,024 of them would fill 12,288, yet the map was charged 83,968 bytes before the first write was counted. The next two sections account for the difference, and the endless line waits for the section on user space, since its cause lies in how a map hands out its keys.

What BPF_MAP_CREATE built

When libbpf sends BPF_MAP_CREATE, the kernel reads the map type first. BPF_MAP_TYPE_HASH selects htab_map_ops (line 2358 of kernel/bpf/hashtab.c), a table of twenty function pointers for creating, looking up, updating and walking this kind of map, and each of the 35 map types in v7.2 has its own.

htab_map_alloc() (line 545) then builds what Figure 10.2 shows. It rounds max_entries up to a power of two and makes that many buckets, list heads with a lock each. It also makes every element in advance, 64 bytes holding list links, the stored hash, the 4-byte key and the 8-byte value, each rounded up to 8 bytes, with 16 spares beyond max_entries, one per CPU, for updates. htab_map_mem_usage() adds the parts up for the memlock line, 83,968 bytes at the foot of Figure 10.2, and a map created with BPF_F_NO_PREALLOC makes its elements as keys arrive instead.

A key finds its bucket by hashing. While it builds the map, htab_map_alloc() draws a random seed for it. A lookup hashes the 4-byte key with jhash2() and that seed, keeps the low ten bits of the result, since 1,024 is a power of two, and walks that bucket's list, comparing the stored hash before the key bytes. The walk takes no lock and runs under RCU, so an element it is passing may be moved to another bucket while it walks. Each list therefore ends in a marker that names its own bucket, and a walk that reaches another bucket's marker starts again.

The memory is charged to the memory cgroup of the process that created the map, with one exception in v7.2 that the section "What a layout weighs before the first event" measures. The per-CPU values a map makes when it is created are allocated before the map records that cgroup, so they are charged to no group at all.

From the counter to the map, and back

The counter names the map in a wide instruction that holds the descriptor libbpf wrote in. At load, check_and_resolve_insns() (verifier.c line 18095) swaps the descriptor for the map's kernel address, which bpftool prints as map[id:7], and add_used_map() records the map in the program's used_maps with a reference, which makes the program one of the map's holders (the section "Who holds a map, and how two programs share one"). A later pass rewrites the calls, as chapter 9 followed in detail, so that in Figure 10.3 call 1 has become a direct call to __htab_map_lookup_elem() followed by two instructions, and the update a direct call to htab_map_update_elem().

The two added instructions decide what the counter gets back. When no element holds the key, r0 is NULL, the pointer-or-NULL of chapter 4. Otherwise r0 += 56 moves from the element's address to its value's, past the element's 48-byte header and the key rounded up to 8 bytes (htab_map_gen_lookup(), line 776), and the program holds a pointer into kernel memory that it may read and write with no copy.

The atomic add at slot 13 targets r10 -16, a copy of the value on the stack, so the map changes only at slot 26. There htab_map_update_elem() takes the bucket's lock, links in this CPU's spare element holding the new count, and keeps the old element as the next spare. Two threads never share a key in the counter, so this copy-and-update counts correctly, and what it costs when keys are shared waits for the section "Who waits when several CPUs count".

The same map from user space

Only programs get a pointer, and user space reaches the same struct bpf_map in the other ways of Figure 10.4. The loader uses the descriptor that BPF_MAP_CREATE returned and bpftool one it made from the ID, and each descriptor, like a pin, holds a reference that the section "Who holds a map, and how two programs share one" counts among the map's holders.

Every read from user space is a copy. BPF_MAP_LOOKUP_ELEM runs the same lookup from the ops table, then bpf_map_copy_value() (syscall.c line 309) copies the value out, one system call per key. Arrays created with BPF_F_MMAPABLE, ring buffers and arenas can skip the copies through mmap().

BPF_MAP_GET_NEXT_KEY takes a key and returns the key after it, in bucket order, and given NULL, or a key that is not in the map, htab_map_get_next_key() (line 895) returns the first key. The loader passes prev_key, which is 0 and never changes. No thread has ID 0, so every call returns the same first key, and the inner loop never ends or reads the flag that the Ctrl-C handler sets.

Map typeKeys and valuesUsed for
HASHany key → one valuethe counter's write_counts
ARRAYindex 0 … max − 1; every entry existsthe counter's .rodata; counters by index
PERCPU_HASH, PERCPU_ARRAYas above, one value per CPUcounters with no sharing
LRU_HASHany key; when full, the least recently used goestables that must never fill
PROG_ARRAYindex → programtail calls, chapter 7
ARRAY_OF_MAPS, HASH_OF_MAPSindex or key → another mapmaps swapped whole
PERF_EVENT_ARRAYCPU → that CPU's bufferevents, per CPU
RINGBUFno keys: bpf_ringbuf_reserve(), write, bpf_ringbuf_submit()events from all CPUs, in order
ARENAno keys: pagesmemory both sides address with pointers

The other map types in the table change the layout but keep the route. A per-CPU map keeps one copy of every value for each CPU, so that programs on different CPUs never write the same memory, and user space reads all the copies in one call. A perf buffer is an array of per-CPU buffers that programs write events into. A ring buffer, since 5.8, is one buffer for all CPUs, built, its documentation says, to share memory across CPUs and keep events in order. An arena, since 6.9, is a set of pages that the program and the process both map; this chapter weighs only its memory, and the next chapter, on memory a program manages itself, teaches it.

From here on we weigh these types against each other by what they cost in memory, locks and copies, all on the same kernel, before choosing one for the counter.

What a layout weighs before the first event

Figure 10.5 weighs the layouts at the counter's size. An array costs 8.3 bytes an entry, the values alone. A hash costs 82, a 64-byte element and a 16-byte bucket an entry, as drawn in Figure 10.2. The per-CPU forms keep a value for every possible CPU, so the counter's map as a PERCPU_HASH would take 209 bytes a thread.

Hashes and arrays are made in advance by default, so max_entries reserves memory as well as capping it. A hash created with BPF_F_NO_PREALLOC starts at 17,280 bytes and reaches 91,008 when full. The work moves onto the event path, since every update takes a fresh element from a per-CPU cache that kernel/bpf/memalloc.c refills, and frees the old one; the counter's update grew 43 ns slower.

Per-CPU values and the cgroupA preallocated per-CPU hash of 65,536 entries reports 13,632,384 bytes, but its creator's memory.current rose by 5.5 MB, the elements and buckets, and the percpu line of memory.stat not at all. map_create() in syscall.c calls the type's map_alloc before bpf_map_save_memcg() records the cgroup, and bpf_map_alloc_percpu() charges the recorded one, the root until then, which is never charged.

The kernel charges a map's memory to the memory cgroup of the process that created it, while memlock is the map's own estimate from its map_mem_usage function. For a hash of 65,536 entries the two agreed within 2 KB. They part for an arena, whose arena_map_mem_usage() returns 0 while each page is charged as it is first touched.

Who waits when several CPUs count

A lookup walks its bucket under RCU and takes no lock, so the waiting in Figure 10.6 is all on writes. With one writer the counter's lookup and update cost 92 ns more than reading the key alone, for the bucket lock and the swap of the spare element. The lookup and an add through its pointer with __sync_fetch_and_add(), one locked instruction on x86, cost 32.

Eight writers on one key show what the lock does not protect. The counter's lookup, copy and update lost 66 per cent of the counts. Two CPUs read the same old value and each stored its own sum, a lost update, and the bucket lock only made the stores take turns. The atomic add lost nothing. Its price is the cache line, the 64-byte block in which a CPU caches memory, which must travel to whichever CPU writes it next; sharing one took the add from 533 to 714 ns.

Re-entryIn v7.2 the bucket lock is a resilient spin lock, which returns an error where a spin lock would wait forever: ‑EDEADLK when this CPU already holds it, ‑ETIMEDOUT when a wait passes RES_DEF_TIMEOUT, a quarter of a second. Before 6.15 (commit 4fa8d68aa53e) a per-CPU counter returned ‑EBUSY instead.

A per-CPU map gives each CPU its own copy, so no line travels and a plain add is safe from other CPUs. The price is paid on reading, where user space copies all 16 values of a key and sums them. The copy is private to a CPU but shared by every program on it. An NMI or, on this kernel, a task switch (chapter 8) can slip another program between a load and its store, so a value two programs write wants the atomic add too.

What reading the counts costs user space

Every count that user space reads crosses into it as a copy, and the way it asks sets the price. Looking up a known key took 767 ns, and the loader's walk, a next-key call and a lookup for each key, 1,568 ns a key. A per-CPU hash cost 1,084 ns a key for its 16 values, while one BPF_MAP_LOOKUP_BATCH call that fetched all 1,024 keys of a hash came to 95 ns a key. An array created with BPF_F_MMAPABLE and read through mmap() took a quarter of a nanosecond a key, which makes it the place for a count that user space polls often (book/labs/costs-mapread.c, run by book/labs/costs2-root.sh).

A stream is read by a reader that sleeps until data arrives, and each wake-up, the kernel making that reader runnable again, costs it a context switch. A perf buffer is one buffer per CPU, and libbpf asks perf to wake the reader after every event. The ring buffer is one buffer for all CPUs, and bpf_ringbuf_commit() queues a wake-up only when the reader has caught up to the record just committed. With four writers that held the reader to 5 switches per 1,000 events, against 121 for the perf buffer (Figure 10.7).

Queued as interrupt work from inside the program, the wake-up cost the program microseconds per event in this VM. Skipping it trades delay and loss. Submitted with BPF_RB_NO_WAKEUP and read every 10 ms, a ring buffer lost 9.8 per cent of four writers' events when its 256 KiB filled. A perf buffer that woke its reader every 64 events left the last 30 of a paced run unread.

"bpf_ringbuf_commit() implementation will send a notification of new record being available after commit only if consumer has already caught up right up to the record being committed."

Andrii Nakryiko, commit message of 457f44363a88, "bpf: Implement BPF ring buffer and verifier support for it", Linux 5.8

Which contexts may use which maps

Two rules in Figure 10.8 come from check_map_prog_compatibility() in verifier.c. Kprobe, tracepoint, perf_event and raw tracepoint programs may not use a value holding a bpf_spin_lock, a lock inside a map value for changing several fields together. Sleepable programs may use only the types on a list of twenty-one, which takes in queues, stacks, tries, maps of maps and arenas, though its message names only "array, hash, ringbuf and local storage maps"; a perf buffer is not on it.

A map for the counter

A busy server creates thread IDs without end, and each is written by one thread at a time. Figure 10.9 therefore leads the counter to an LRU hash, which evicts the least recently used entry where a full hash refuses a new thread (question 10.2). The listing adds the count in place and updates only to insert.

u64 one = 1, *v = bpf_map_lookup_elem(&write_counts, &pid);
if (v)
	__sync_fetch_and_add(v, 1);        /* no lock, no copy */
else
	bpf_map_update_elem(&write_counts, &pid, &one,
			    BPF_NOEXIST);   /* a new thread */

With one writer at the write tracepoint this cost 81 ns a run against 152 for the counter as written less its bpf_printk(), which alone added 350 to 1,100 ns, and the map holds at 82,816 bytes (Lab 10.2). A per-CPU form would buy nothing, as no key is shared, for 209 bytes a thread. No map recovers chapter 8's lost events, because a run skipped as a recursion miss never reaches the map; only a hook where preemption is off brings them back. An LRU hash forgets the threads written least recently, and keeping a count for every thread a server ever ran, in memory fixed in advance, needs approximate counts, for which chapter 13 builds a map type.

Maps of maps

A map of maps is an array or a hash whose values are other maps, the inner maps; each slot holds a pointer to its inner map and a reference on it (Figure 10.10). Since the verifier cannot know which inner map a slot will hold, the outer map copies the shape of a sample map into a template when it is created (bpf_map_meta_alloc()). The program's second lookup is checked against the template, and bpf_map_meta_equal() refuses any inner map that differs in type, key or value size, flags or special fields. A template hash of 1,024 entries accepted a hash of 64 and refused, with ‑EINVAL, a hash with 16-byte values and an LRU hash.

Where the numbers come fromSteps 2, 3 and 6 of book/labs/ch16-root.sh, run as root in a virtme-ng VM of kernel 7.2.15 with 16 virtual CPUs, 12 November 2026.

The price is the first lookup. By chapter 9's method a hash lookup took 14.0 ns alone, 14.9 through an array of maps, whose lookup the kernel writes in place as index arithmetic, and 28.3 through a hash of maps. An array of 1,024 slots weighs 8,496 bytes, and each inner map is charged as a map of its own.

The return is a swap. One update points a slot at a fresh map, and maybe_wait_bpf_programs() in syscall.c then waits for an expedited RCU grace period. When the call returns, no program other than a sleepable one can still be writing into the old map. The counter could therefore swap in an empty map every second and read the old one at leisure, a snapshot for 7 to 45 µs an update.

Inside the v7.2 source

Figure 10.11 lists the code this chapter has read, in the order a map's life reaches it. map_create() checks the attributes, and map_create_alloc() indexes bpf_map_types[] with the map type to find the ops table and calls the type's map_alloc. Only after that returns does map_create() record the creator's memory cgroup, which is why the per-CPU values made inside map_alloc are charged to no group. The verifier reaches the map when a program names it, swapping the descriptor for an address and checking that the program's type may use the map.

At run time the counter's lookup lands in __htab_map_lookup_elem(), three calls long: the hash, the bucket and the walk. Its update goes through htab_map_update_elem(), which takes the bucket's resilient lock and asks alloc_htab_elem() for an element, the CPU's spare when the key exists, the next free element when it is new, and -E2BIG when none is left. A map of maps adds three steps of its own in map_in_map.c, and an update of one waits in maybe_wait_bpf_programs().

Each keyed map in this chapter hands a program slots that BPF_MAP_CREATE sized in advance, a key and a value of fixed size and at most max_entries of them, and a value holds bytes. A pointer that a program stores into a value is refused, or comes back from a later load as a plain number, unless the map's BTF declares a field for it, a typed slot for a kernel pointer that the next chapter takes up (check_mem_access() in verifier.c). A list that a program grows one node at a time, a tree it keeps in order, or an object it allocates in one run and finds again in the next needs memory that the program allocates and frees itself, and that is where the next chapter starts.

What it costs

CPU
One writer, over 48 ns for reading the key: 92 ns for the counter's lookup and update, 134 without preallocation, 32 for an atomic add in place, 30 for a per-CPU hash, 2 to 6 for arrays (getppid tracepoint). A hash lookup took 14.0 ns alone, 14.9 behind an array of maps and 28.3 behind a hash of maps (kernel 7.2.15, VM with 16 CPUs, 12 November 2026; book/labs/ch15-root.sh, ch16-root.sh).
Memory
Per entry on 16 CPUs, all at creation: 8.3 bytes for an array, 82 for a hash (83,968 for write_counts), 209 for a per-CPU hash; without preallocation a hash grows from 17,280 to 91,008 bytes. A 256 KiB ring buffer takes 275,776 bytes, a perf buffer 266,240 per CPU, an array of maps 304 bytes and 8 a slot (memlock in fdinfo, same VM and day).
Switches
None in the program, which reads through a pointer. User space pays a system call and a copy: 767 ns a key by lookup, 1,568 for the loader's walk, 1,084 for a per-CPU hash, 95 in one batch, a quarter of a nanosecond through mmap(). Four writers woke a ring buffer's reader 5.3 times per 1,000 events and a perf buffer's 121; an inner-map swap took 7 to 45 µs (costs-mapread.c, same VM and day).
Locking
Lookups none; a hash update takes a resilient bucket lock, a ring-buffer reservation one lock for all CPUs, an atomic add a cache line. Eight writers sharing one key lost 66 per cent of the counter's counts under the bucket lock.

Add in place with an atomic and update only to insert. Go per-CPU when many CPUs write one key, use an LRU hash when keys can outgrow the map, read whole maps in batches or map an array that user space polls, stream through the ring buffer, and pay a map of maps' second lookup only where swapping a whole map is worth it.

When it goes wrong

Most failures with a map are quiet. A program that loses counts still loads and runs, and an update that fails returns an error the counter never reads, so Figure 10.12 pairs each symptom this chapter met with its usual cause and the command that tells it apart. The first three rows belong to the counter and its loader as written. The fourth and fifth look alike from outside, a total that falls short of the writes, and bpftool prog show separates them, since run_cnt counts the runs that happened and recursion_misses, printed only when it is not zero, the runs that were skipped.

In the middle rows the kernel's own accounting is the witness, memlock against the cgroup's charge and an error code that names a lock. Two refusals come at load from check_map_prog_compatibility(), as soon as the program names the map, and the last rows are a stream that drops or delays events and a map of maps that refuses an inner map. The failures of creating, pinning and sharing a map stand with the other failures of a load in Figure 3.10.

Try it · Read your map from outside, then fix the loop

~25 min · measure, then fix a real one · needs clang, gcc, bpftool and sudo

Task. Build a copy of your loader in /tmp/ch09 and run it with sudo. From a second terminal, read write_counts with bpftool while the loader spins. Then fix the copy's read loop so that it prints every key once per round and stops on Ctrl-C. This is the iteration rule behind Figure 10.4, met from both sides.

Done when. Your fixed loader prints a table every ten seconds, its counts agree with bpftool map dump to within a few writes, and Ctrl-C ends it.

Hint 1 · direction

The kernel answers one question: which key comes after this one? The loop has to say which key it saw last, and has to start from no key at all.

Hint 2 · mechanism

Build as in the lab of chapter 3, in /tmp/ch09. bpf_map__get_next_key() accepts NULL as the current key. After each key, copy it into prev_key and pass that address on the next call.

Hint 3 · nearly there

Before the inner loop: uint32_t *prev = NULL;, and pass prev instead of &prev_key. At the end of the loop body: prev_key = key; prev = &prev_key;. From outside: sudo bpftool map show name write_counts and sudo bpftool map dump name write_counts.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 10.

Try it · Give the counter its map

~30 min · measure · needs root in a throwaway VM (virtme-ng) or on a test machine, clang, bpftool and taskset

Task. Make a copy of hashmap.bpf.c that uses BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_HASH and adds one in place, as in the section "A map for the counter", and a second copy that only drops the bpf_printk() line. Load each in turn, make 2,000,000 one-byte writes from one thread pinned to a CPU, and compare the nanoseconds per run, the map's total and its memlock.

Done when. bpftool shows a lower run_time_ns per run for the LRU copy than for the copy without bpf_printk(), the map's total is at least the number of writes, and memlock reads 82816B.

Hint 1 · direction

The cost to remove is the update on every event. Change the map type in the map definition, and keep bpf_map_update_elem() only for a thread the map has not seen.

Hint 2 · mechanism

sysctl -w kernel.bpf_stats_enabled=1 turns on run_time_ns and run_cnt. bpftool prog load OBJ /sys/fs/bpf/wc autoattach attaches without the loader; bpftool -j prog show name count_writes and bpftool -j map dump name write_counts give the numbers.

Hint 3 · nearly there

bash book/labs/ch15-root.sh build leaves hashmap.bpf.o, wc_noprintk.bpf.o, counter_lru.bpf.o and the writer wloop in /tmp/c15; step 7 of the script runs all three with taskset -c 1 ./wloop 2000000.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 10.

Check yourself

  1. Predict the value: before a single write is counted, how many bytes does the kernel set aside for write_counts on your 16-CPU machine, and where do they go?
  2. After days on a busy build server, new threads stop appearing in your loader's table, while old ones keep counting. Nothing is logged. What happened?
  3. You change write_counts to BPF_MAP_TYPE_PERCPU_HASH. The program loads, but every lookup in the loader fails with map 'write_counts': unexpected value size 8 provided for per-CPU map, expected 16 * 8 = 128. Where does 128 come from, and what should the loader pass?
  4. Predict the value: what memlock would bpftool map show print for write_counts as a BPF_MAP_TYPE_PERCPU_HASH on a server with 128 possible CPUs, and as the plain hash it is today?
  5. An fentry program on bpf_obj_cancel_fields() calls bpf_map_update_elem() on a hash whose values hold a bpf_timer, and stores the result. After user space replaces an element of that map, the result reads ‑35. What happened, and why does the same call on a second hash return 0?
  6. The counter, given a struct bpf_spin_lock in its value to protect the count, is refused at load with tracing progs cannot use bpf_spin_lock yet. Moved to fentry/vfs_write, the same code loads. Why, and what should the counter use instead?
  7. A colleague keys the counter by process (bpf_get_current_pid_tgid() >> 32) and runs a server with eight busy threads. recursion_misses stays at zero, yet the map's total is a third of the writes made. Where did the counts go?
  8. Predict the value: by this chapter's measurements a hash lookup takes 14.0 ns. About how long does the same lookup take behind an array of maps, and behind a hash of maps, and why do the two differ?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 10.

Recap

A map is a struct bpf_map whose type picks an ops table, and the counter's hash is an array of buckets, each with a resilient lock, whose elements are all made in advance by default, 83,968 bytes for 1,024 entries on 16 CPUs. A lookup hashes the key with the map's seed, walks one bucket under RCU and returns a pointer 56 bytes into the element, or NULL; user space gets copies made by bpf() commands, or the pages of the few map types that allow mmap(), and walking a hash needs the last key it saw. Layouts trade memory for locking: 8.3 bytes an entry for an array, 82 for a hash and 209 for a per-CPU hash, while a lookup, copy and update on a shared key lost two counts in three that an atomic add in place kept. The ring buffer wakes its reader only once it has caught up, the verifier keeps bpf_spin_lock out of kprobe, tracepoint, perf_event and raw tracepoint programs and perf buffers out of sleepable ones, and the counter wants an LRU hash with an atomic add. A map of maps checks each inner map against a template, costs one more lookup, and lets user space swap a whole inner map behind an expedited grace period.

New words in this chapter

map type
the kind of map, which selects the kernel's table of functions for it
bucket
one slot of a hash map's array: the head of a list of elements, with a lock
element
one entry of a hash map: list links, the stored hash, the key and the value
per-CPU
keeping one copy of each value for every CPU
perf buffer
an array of per-CPU buffers that programs write events into
ring buffer
one event buffer shared by all CPUs, in order, since 5.8
arena
pages that a program and a process both map and address with pointers, since 6.9
lost update
two writers read the same old value and each stores its own result, so one result is lost
cache line
the 64-byte block in which a CPU caches memory, which moves to whichever CPU writes it
resilient spin lock
a spin lock that returns an error on a deadlock or after a timeout instead of waiting forever; the hash map's bucket lock since 6.15
wake-up
the kernel making a sleeping reader runnable again when data arrives
map of maps
an array or a hash whose values are other maps, looked up in two steps
inner map
a map held in a slot of a map of maps, which must match the outer map's template

Go deeper

  • RUNTIMEBPF_MAP_TYPE_HASH, with PERCPU and LRU Variants, Linux kernel documentation. The hash map from both sides: its user-space part says how to start an iteration with NULL and what happens when the current key is missing, and its last section draws which locks an LRU update may take on its way to evicting an entry. Fifteen minutes.
  • RUNTIMEBPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAY and BPF_MAP_TYPE_PERCPU_ARRAY, Linux kernel documentation. How an mmapable array lays its values out from the second page, and the per-CPU array's 32 KB limit on a value.
  • RUNTIMEMap types (Linux), eBPF Docs. One page per map type, with the kernel version that added it.
  • RUNTIMEBPF ring buffer, Andrii Nakryiko, 2020. Why the ring buffer replaced the perf buffer for most uses, with code for both.
  • RUNTIMEBPF ring buffer, Linux kernel documentation. "Motivation" and "Semantics and APIs"; skip the implementation section for now.
  • RUNTIMEbpf: Implement BPF ring buffer and verifier support for it, Andrii Nakryiko, commit 457f44363a88, Linux 5.8. kernel/bpf/ringbuf.c is born here, 501 lines, and 195 changed lines in verifier.c make reserve-then-submit a rule the verifier enforces; the message compares the design with the perf buffer.
  • RUNTIMEbpf: Introduce bpf_arena., Alexei Starovoitov, commit 317460317a02, Linux 6.9. kernel/bpf/arena.c is born, with the arena_map_mem_usage() that returns 0 and the page-fault handler that charges each page to the creator's memory cgroup.
  • RUNTIMEbpf: Add array of maps support, Martin KaFai Lau, commit 56f668dfe00d, Linux 4.12. map_in_map.c is born here with the template and its equality check; the hash of maps follows in the next commit, bcc6b1b7ebf8.
  • RUNTIMEBPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAY_OF_MAPS and BPF_MAP_TYPE_HASH_OF_MAPS, Linux kernel documentation. A short page with the user-space side of a map of maps: inner_map_fd, BPF_F_INNER_MAP and a libbpf example.

Part IV

Extending the kernel

Until now the kernel sized every map in advance and called each program to observe or decide one thing. We give programs memory they allocate and link themselves, let a set of programs act as the CPU scheduler, and add a data structure to the kernel twice, first on an arena and then as a map type of its own.

Chapter 11

Memory you manage: allocated objects, kptrs, lists and trees, arenas

Every map so far was a table the kernel sized before the first event. In this chapter the write counter allocates its own memory, first as one node per thread linked into a red-black tree that the verifier follows object by object, then as a hash table inside an arena, a block of pages that the counter shares with user space and that the verifier no longer follows at all.

Spine. Chapter 10 ended on what a map cannot hold: a value is bytes in a slot that BPF_MAP_CREATE sized in advance, and a pointer stored there comes back as a plain number unless the map's BTF declares a field for it. Now the counter allocates memory itself, in the two ways Linux v7.2 offers, and we watch what the verifier checks in each and what each costs a write. Every number in this chapter was measured on kernel 7.2.15 in a virtme-ng VM with 16 virtual CPUs on 13 November 2026, by book/labs/memory-root.sh, whose outputs are in /tmp/book-labs/memory.

30 min · RUNTIME · VERIFIER

The counter keeps its own tree

The counter of the last chapter kept one slot per thread in a hash map, and the kernel made all 1,024 slots when the loader created it. In this version, c_rb.bpf.c in book/labs/memory, the counter makes a node the first time a thread writes. The memory comes from the kernel while the counter runs, and the node goes into a tree ordered by thread ID.

A red-black tree is a binary search tree that recolours and rotates its nodes on every insert. No path from its root to a leaf is then more than twice as long as any other, so a lookup among n nodes takes at most about 2 log₂ n steps. Figure 11.1 shows the node, the map value that holds the tree's root and its lock, and the lookup that runs on every write.

Three things in the listing are new. The node embeds a struct bpf_rb_node, 32 bytes that the kernel uses to link it. The map value embeds a struct bpf_rb_root, whose __contains tag tells the verifier through BTF which type the tree holds and through which field. Every call that touches the tree sits between bpf_spin_lock() and bpf_spin_unlock() on the lock in the same value. The counter has also moved from the write tracepoint to fentry/vfs_write, because in v7.2 check_map_prog_compatibility() refuses a kprobe, tracepoint, perf-event or raw tracepoint program that names a map holding a bpf_rb_root or a bpf_spin_lock, the second of which Figure 10.12 lists.

We load it with mbench, a small loader in the same folder that attaches the counter, runs three writer threads of 1,000 writes each, and holds the program loaded while bpftool looks at it (Figure 11.2). bpftool finds the program and a map with one 40-byte value and a memlock of 344 bytes. Its dump shows nodes at 7, the three writers and four other threads that wrote meanwhile. The root reads as two zeros. The kernel copies a map value out around its lock and root (bpf_obj_memcpy() in include/linux/bpf.h), and the nodes are not in the map at all.

To read the counts, user space runs a program of its own, drain, a syscall program that takes the nodes out in order, copies thread ID and count into a global array and frees them. All 3,000 writes were counted.

The arena version, c_arena.bpf.c, keeps the same counts in the hash table of the v7.2 selftests, bpf_arena_htab.h with its allocator bpf_arena_alloc.h, whose buckets and elements live in an arena of 1,024 pages. Figure 11.3 shows what changes from outside. bpftool reports the arena with a memlock of 0 bytes, and the loader has a 4 MiB shared mapping of it. The loader finds the table at an address inside that mapping and follows its pointers as any C program would, reading every count with no system call between the two markers that bracket the read. The same read made eight bpf() calls for the hash and one for the tree.

Two ways to own memory

The two versions sit at the two ends of a trade, and Figure 11.4 sets them beside the map they replace. An allocated object is memory that a program gets from bpf_obj_new() while it runs, typed by the program's BTF. The verifier knows the type of every pointer to it and who must give it back, so a mistake is a refusal at load time. The price is a lock around every collection, and memory that only programs can reach.

An arena gives the program plain pages to address as C would, and user space maps the same pages. The verifier stops knowing what any byte means, so a mistake becomes a wrong count, or a report in a log, at run time.

What the verifier knows about an object

bpf_obj_new() is a kfunc that takes a type and returns a pointer to an object of that type, or NULL. The program names the type by its ID in its own BTF, and check_special_kfunc() in verifier.c records the type's size. bpf_fixup_kfunc_call() writes that size into the call's first argument, with a pointer to the type's list of special fields in the second. The kernel side, bpf_obj_new() in helpers.c, thus receives a size and never parses BTF.

A type ID becomes a sizeThe counter's log shows r1 = 0x23 before the call, the BTF ID 35 of struct wnode. The fixup puts three instructions in front of the call: one loads 48, the node's size, into the first argument, and two load the address of its field record into the second.

Only the special fields, the lock, list and tree fields and their kin, are set up (bpf_obj_init()). A reused object keeps old bytes elsewhere, so the counter writes every field it later reads.

From the call on, the verifier follows the result down every path. The pointer has type ptr_or_null_wnode with a fresh ID. Once the NULL check passes it is an owning reference, a pointer through which the program may read and write any field without a lock and which it must give away before it exits.

Figure 11.5 draws the three ways. bpf_obj_drop() frees the object, bpf_kptr_xchg() parks it in a map value, and bpf_rbtree_add() or a list push links it into a collection. If a path reaches the exit while the ID is still held, check_reference_leak() refuses the whole program with "Unreleased reference id=2 alloc_insn=2". The alloc_insn is the instruction that allocated the object.

Linking is the interesting case. When bpf_rbtree_add() returns, check_kfunc_call() turns every register that held the object's ID into a non-owning reference. Through it the program may still read and write the node's ordinary fields, but it can neither free the node nor add it again. Figure 11.6 shows the change in a log. Register R7 goes from ptr_wnode(id=3) to ptr_wnode(non_own_ref), and the held references drop from refs=3,1, the object and the lock, to refs=1, the lock alone.

When bpf_spin_unlock() runs, process_spin_lock() invalidates every non-owning reference, since from then on another program may remove the node and free it, so a write through R7 after the unlock is refused.

Lists, trees and the lock that guards them

The lock is how the verifier makes a collection safe without knowing what other programs do. At every list or tree call, __process_kf_arg_ptr_to_graph_root() checks that the program holds the bpf_spin_lock in the same allocation as the root. Otherwise it refuses with "bpf_spin_lock at off=0 must be held for bpf_rb_root". While the lock is held the program may call only the collection's own kfuncs, bpf_kptr_xchg() and the unlock. do_check_insn() refuses anything else, bpf_obj_new() included, with "function calls are not allowed while holding a lock", which is why the counter allocates before it locks.

The lock itself turns off interrupts on this CPU and takes a queued spin lock (__bpf_spin_lock_irqsave() in helpers.c). Every other CPU that wants the tree waits.

A tree helps the counter only if it can be searched. bpf_rbtree_add() places a node by calling the program's less() back at each level of the descent. Since Linux 6.16, bpf_rbtree_root(), bpf_rbtree_left() and bpf_rbtree_right() hand out non-owning references with which a program walks down from the root, one kfunc call per level, as the search in Figure 11.1 does. bpf_rbtree_first() gives the smallest node and bpf_rbtree_remove() takes a node out as an owning reference again. A list works the same way with bpf_list_head and bpf_list_node, pushed and popped at either end.

An object sits in one collection through each node field it has, and after the push the program's pointer to it is non-owning. Sometimes two collections must both own an object, for instance a tree by thread ID and a list of threads to report. Its type then adds a struct bpf_refcount. bpf_refcount_acquire() returns a second owning reference by raising the count, each owner pushes or drops its own, and __bpf_obj_drop_impl() frees the object when the count reaches zero. For a refcounted type the verifier also marks each non-owning reference as protected by RCU, the MEM_RCU flag (ref_set_non_owning()).

The counter never frees a node at fentry, and could not if it tried. In v7.2, check_kfunc_call() refuses bpf_obj_drop() in kprobe, tracepoint, perf-event and raw tracepoint programs, and in fentry and fexit programs that cannot sleep. It does so whenever the type holds a field that is unsafe in an NMI, such as a bpf_rb_node or a bpf_list_node, with the message "bpf_obj_drop cannot be used in tracing programs on types with NMI unsafe fields". The counter's nodes are freed by drain, a syscall program. A thread that exits keeps its node until then.

An object parked in a map value

A kptr is a pointer field in a map value that the map's BTF marks with __kptr, so that the verifier knows which type of object the field holds and that the map owns it. It lets an object outlive a run without joining a collection, and alloc.bpf.c in book/labs/memory parks 100,000 nodes in the slots of an array this way.

A plain store into the field is refused with "store to referenced kptr disallowed" (check_map_kptr_access()). The pointer already there would be lost, and the new one would have two owners. bpf_kptr_xchg() swaps the field and the program's pointer in one atomic exchange. The map owns what went in, and the program owns, and must give away, whatever came out.

struct kslot { struct wnode __kptr *p; };   /* the value of an array */
    ...
    old = bpf_kptr_xchg(&v->p, n);           /* the slot owns n; we own old */
    if (old)
        bpf_obj_drop(old);

The same kind of field can hold an object that the kernel owns, such as a task from the acquire kfunc bpf_task_from_pid() of chapter 9, under the same rule. What no program takes back out, the map frees. bpf_obj_free_fields() in syscall.c drops each kptr when its value is deleted or the map is freed, and it frees every node of a list or tree whose root sits in the value. The counter's tree goes when counts_tree goes.

Where the objects come from

A program at fentry or a kprobe runs in whatever context the probed function runs in, an NMI included, where calling kmalloc() may not be safe. bpf_obj_new() therefore takes its objects from the BPF memory allocator, kernel/bpf/memalloc.c. For every CPU it keeps a cache of free objects in eleven size classes from 16 bytes to 4 KiB, and it refills them from the kernel's slab caches in the background (Figure 11.7).

An allocation turns off interrupts, takes the first object off this CPU's free list for the size class and turns them on again. It takes no lock and makes no call into the slab allocator. Every object carries an 8-byte header in front, so the counter's 48-byte node takes a 64-byte slot.

irq_work on the same CPU keeps each free list between 32 and 96 objects for classes up to 256 bytes. It allocates a batch when the list falls below and gives objects back above. A drop goes through bpf_mem_free_rcu(): the object waits on a list until an RCU grace period has passed, because another program may still be reading it, and only then can it be handed out again.

The measurements show both effects (alloc.txt). Allocating 100,000 nodes in a row cost 128 to 161 ns a node, the refill working all the while, and small batches of 32 took 32 to 520 ns a node, depending on what the free list held. Even 100,000 pairs of bpf_obj_new() and an immediate bpf_obj_drop() grew the kernel's 64-byte slab caches by 59,000 to 98,000 objects during the run.

These objects belong to no loader. The allocator behind bpf_obj_new() serves the whole kernel and was set up at boot (bpf_global_ma_init() in core.c). When the tree counter held 100,000 nodes, the kernel's 64-byte slab caches had grown by 97,440 objects, about 6.2 MB (mem.txt). The memory.current of the loader's cgroup had not moved, and bpftool's memlock for the program and the map counted none of it.

The arena: pages both sides map

An arena is a map of type BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARENA with no key and no value, whose max_entries counts pages, 4 GiB worth at most, and which must be created with BPF_F_MMAPABLE (arena_map_alloc() in arena.c). Creating one allocates almost nothing: the kernel reserves 4 GiB of its own addresses plus a 64 KiB guard, and fills in the page tables above the last level. User space gets a range of its address space when the loader maps the arena, at an address that map_extra may fix in advance. Two more flags change what a user fault and a pointer cast do. arena_map_mem_usage() returns 0, the memlock of 0 bytes that bpftool printed.

Pages arrive one at a time, from either side. A program calls bpf_arena_alloc_pages(), which takes a free range from the arena's range tree, allocates pages and maps them into the kernel's range (arena_alloc_pages()). Or user space touches an address in its mapping, and arena_vm_fault() puts a page there, unless a program reserved the address or the arena was made to fault. Either way the page is charged to the memory cgroup of the process that created the arena.

Since Linux 7.0 the allocation also works in a program that cannot sleep, such as the counter at fentry. The verifier calls bpf_arena_alloc_pages_non_sleepable() instead, and a free from such a program is finished later on a workqueue (commit b8467290edab).

What makes an arena more than shared memory is that one pointer means the same page on both sides. The compiler marks arena pointers with address_space(1), the __arena of bpf_arena_common.h, and every conversion between that space and the kernel's becomes an address space cast, an instruction of its own. A cast into the kernel's space gives the register the type arena (check_alu_op()) and keeps the low 32 bits of the user address. The JIT adds the base of the kernel's range, kept in register r12, to every load and store. A cast back puts the upper 32 bits of the user mapping's address above the low ones.

Figure 11.8 follows one page. The table that user space found at 0x7f5cac7d3fe8 is 0xac7d3fe8 to the program and kern_vm_start plus 0xac7d3fe8 to the kernel, so a pointer that the program stores in user form is one that user space follows unchanged.

Where the globals golibbpf places a program's __arena globals in the last pages of the arena. A test store to the arena's last page, meant to hit an unallocated page, wrote into bpf_arena_alloc.h's per-CPU state instead, and no fault was reported.

What the verifier gives up in an arena

The verifier's whole view of an arena is one register type. check_mem_access() lets a program load and store through a pointer of type arena at any offset, and adjust_reg_min_max_vals() allows any arithmetic on it. A value loaded from the arena is an unknown scalar, whatever was stored there.

It is the first limit Emil Tsalapatis raised when he reported on arenas in sched_ext schedulers at LSFMM+BPF in May 2025: a kernel pointer stored in an arena cannot be used once it is read back. Figure 11.9 shows it in v7.2. The store of a trusted task pointer is accepted, the load gives scalar(), and following it is refused.

The second limit follows from the first. A helper that takes memory accepts a pointer to the stack, a map value, a packet and a few other kinds, and an arena pointer is none of them. Given an arena buffer, bpf_get_current_comm() is refused with "R1 type=arena expected=fp, pkt, pkt_meta, map_key, map_value, mem, ringbuf_mem, buf, trusted_ptr_, ctx" (check_reg_type()). Data bound for a helper goes through the stack, the clumsiness Tsalapatis described.

A function written for both kinds of pointer meets the third limit, because the verifier types an arena pointer and a stack pointer differently. The scheduler authors kept two copies of such a function or inlined it, so that the verifier typed each call site on its own. Alexei Starovoitov answered that work was in progress, and that letting the verifier mix the two kinds of pointer was hard.

The rest of an arena's safety is the program's job. The selftests' hash table takes no lock, so two CPUs inserting into one bucket at once could lose an element. The counter's threads fell into different buckets and lost no count in bench.txt, and bpf_arena_spin_lock.h in the selftests' libarena supplies a lock built in arena memory for structures that need one.

A load or store at an address with no page behind it is caught by the JIT's exception table (ex_handler_bpf() in the x86 JIT). The load gives 0, the store is skipped, and the program continues with a wrong value. Since Linux 6.18 the kernel also writes a report into the program's BPF stream, a per-program log that user space reads with bpftool prog tracelog stderr or bpf_prog_stream_read(), as the second half of Figure 11.9 shows.

Eighteen months after the session, Figure 11.10 sets each point against v7.2. The two limits on programs stand, and the error stream has landed. What moved is the kernel's side. Since Linux 7.2, kernel code that is handed an arena pointer may read and write through it, because a fault there installs a scratch page and is reported to the program's stream (commit dc11a4dba246). sched_ext uses it to place its own data in a scheduler's arena (kernel/sched/ext/arena.c), and the next chapter, on sched_ext, meets arenas inside schedulers.

Inside the v7.2 source

The mechanisms of this chapter live in four files of kernel/bpf and one of the x86 JIT, and Figure 11.11 lists them in the order the counter meets them. The kfuncs and the collections are in helpers.c, the allocator in memalloc.c, the rules in verifier.c and the arena in arena.c; where a function holds one of the checks met above, the table also gives the check's own line.

What the counter pays

Each version of the counter ran with one writer pinned to a CPU, making 2,000,000 one-byte writes to /dev/null by the method of chapter 10. It ran again with 1,000 made-up threads already in the structure, and with eight writers on eight CPUs (Figure 11.12). With one writer and a small tree, the tree's lock and kfunc calls cost about 23 ns a run more than the hash. The arena, whose lookup is plain loads and one atomic add, cost 21 ns less. A thousand more nodes made the tree's search deeper and added 45 ns a run, while the hash and the arena did not move.

Eight writers show what one lock per collection means. Each of them takes the tree's single bpf_spin_lock on every write, a lock that costs 31 to 32 ns uncontended (lock_pair in alloc.txt). They queue for it: a run took 817 ns, seven and a half times the single-writer cost, and each write slowed from 418 to 1,298 ns on the clock. The hash updates each count with an atomic add in place and locks a bucket only to insert, and the arena hash takes no lock at all, so both stayed within a few nanoseconds of their single-writer cost. The host's cores also run slower when eight are busy, as chapter 10 measured, which inflates all three eight-writer numbers alike.

Allocation is the other cost, paid once per thread. A tree node came from the BPF allocator in 128 to 161 ns over a long run, and taking one back out of a kptr slot and dropping it took 26 to 32 ns. An arena page cost 0.7 to 3.5 µs to allocate in a syscall program and 5.7 to 6.1 µs to free. Freeing also removes the page from the kernel's range and from every user mapping (arena_free_pages()). A 32-byte element from bpf_arena_alloc.h's page-fragment allocator took 6.5 to 7.7 ns, since a page is needed only once per 127 elements.

What it costs

CPU
Per run at fentry/vfs_write, one writer: hash 85.5 ns, tree 108.1 (153.1 with 1,000 threads in it), arena hash 64.3. A node from bpf_obj_new() 128 to 161 ns, an arena page 0.7 to 3.5 µs, an arena element 6.5 to 7.7 ns (kernel 7.2.15, 16-CPU VM, 13 November 2026; book/labs/memory-root.sh).
Memory
Tree: 64 bytes of slab a thread, charged to no loader's cgroup and absent from memlock. Arena: about 33 bytes a key, charged by the page to the creator's cgroup, memlock 0. Hash: 82 bytes an entry, from creation.
Switches
Reading all counts: a bpf() call per key for the hash, one program run for the tree, none for the arena.
Locking
One spin lock per tree with interrupts off, 31 to 32 ns alone; eight writers took 817 ns a run. The arena hash has no lock, and its inserts race.

Keep a map while a slot per key will do. Allocate objects when the program needs links, order or ownership that the verifier should check, and keep each collection off paths that many CPUs take at once. Use an arena for large, pointer-rich structures that user space reads without system calls, and take on their locking, bounds and stack copies.

When it goes wrong

The first ten rows are refusals at load. The verifier log names the instruction in each, so the work is reading the register types on the lines before it. The first seven concern the hook, ownership and the lock: which program types may hold a tree at all or free a node, who owns an object at each point, and where the lock is held. The next three are the arena's single type showing through. No helper accepts its pointer, a kernel pointer loads back as a number, and a program that never named its arena may not cast.

The last three rows load and run. An arena access with no page behind it passes the verifier and returns 0. The program's stderr stream is the only witness, and bpftool reads it while the program is loaded. A tree that slows down with more CPUs, and memory that no cgroup seems to pay for, are the costs of the previous section seen from outside; run_time_ns, /proc/slabinfo and memory.current tell them apart.

Try it · Count writes in a tree and in an arena

~30 min · measure · needs root in a throwaway VM (virtme-ng) or on a test machine, clang 18 or later, libbpf, bpftool and strace

Task. Build the three versions of the counter in book/labs/memory, a hash, a red-black tree and an arena hash, all at fentry/vfs_write. Run each with one writer pinned to a CPU making 2,000,000 writes, three times, and compare the nanoseconds per run. Then check from outside that the arena version reads its counts without a bpf() call.

Done when. Each run reports every write counted, the per-run medians order arena below hash below tree, and strace shows no bpf() call between the two getppid() markers of the arena's read.

Hint 1 · direction

One loader, mbench, runs all three objects; it takes the object, the number of writers, the writes each, and the number of made-up threads to put in first.

Hint 2 · mechanism

bash book/labs/memory-root.sh build builds everything into /tmp/mem-lab on the host. Inside the VM, bash /tmp/mem-lab/memory-root.sh lab runs the three versions three times into /tmp/book-labs/memory/bench.txt.

Hint 3 · nearly there

In the VM: cd /tmp/mem-lab; strace -f -e trace=bpf,getppid -o s.txt ./mbench c_arena.bpf.o 3 1000 0, then print what lies between the markers with awk '/getppid/{n++; next} n==1' s.txt.

Try it · Fix three refused programs

~25 min · fix · needs clang 18 or later and root for bpftool prog load (the VM will do)

Task. book/labs/memory/bad holds leak.bpf.c, unlocked.bpf.c and kptrstore.bpf.c, three programs at fentry/vfs_write that the verifier refuses. Change each, as little as you can, so that it loads and still does what its comment says: allocate a node and keep it, set its count, park an object in a map value.

Hint 1 · direction

Read the last lines of each log and place the program on Figure 11.5: which way out does the object take, and where?

Hint 2 · mechanism

An owned object can go into the tree only under the lock. A field can be written freely while the program owns the object. A kptr field changes hands only through bpf_kptr_xchg(), and what comes out is the program's to give away.

Hint 3 · nearly there

The tree's lock and root are in counts_tree's value (bad/common.h). In kptrstore the object has no list or tree field, which is why bpf_obj_drop() is allowed at fentry. Compile with the flags of memory-root.sh and -Ibad.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 11.

Check yourself

  1. Predict the value: the tree counter has counted 1,000 threads. About how many bytes of kernel memory hold their nodes, and which cgroup pays for them?
  2. You add a program at tp_btf/sched_process_exit that takes an exiting thread's node out of the counter's tree, under the lock, and frees it. It is refused with bpf_obj_drop cannot be used in tracing programs on types with NMI unsafe fields. Why, and where can the node be freed?
  3. bpftool's dump of counts_tree shows "root": {"__opaque": [0,0]} while the counter is counting seven threads. Is the tree empty?
  4. Predict the value: with one writer the tree counter costs 108 ns a run and the hash 86. What do they cost with eight writers on eight CPUs, and why do they part?
  5. A colleague stores struct task_struct * in an arena so that a scheduler can find each thread's task later. The store loads fine, but the program that reads it back is refused with R1 invalid mem access 'scalar'. Why, and what should the arena hold instead?
  6. The arena counter has counted 100,000 threads and bpftool map show still says memlock 0B. Where is the memory, and about how much is it?
  7. Two CPUs run the arena counter at the same moment for two new threads whose IDs differ by 1,024. What can go wrong, and why did the verifier let it?
  8. A program allocates 100,000 nodes and drops each one at once. Why do the kernel's 64-byte slab caches grow by tens of thousands of objects during the run?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 11.

Recap

A program can allocate memory in two ways. bpf_obj_new() gives an object typed by the program's BTF from a per-CPU cache of the BPF memory allocator, and the verifier follows it as an owning reference that every path must drop, park in a kptr field with bpf_kptr_xchg(), or link into a list or red-black tree under the lock in the root's allocation, after which it is a non-owning reference until the unlock. Tracing programs may allocate nodes but not free them, and nodes cost 64 bytes of slab that no loader's cgroup pays for. An arena is a map of pages that the program, the kernel and user space address with one 32-bit offset, so user space reads a structure the program built with no system call; the verifier keeps only the type arena, so kernel pointers load back as numbers, helpers refuse arena pointers, a stray access reads 0 and is reported in the program's stderr stream, and locking is the program's job. For the write counter the arena hash cost 64 ns a run and the hash 86, while the tree, whose every run takes the same lock, cost 108 with one writer and 817 with eight.

New words in this chapter

red-black tree
a binary search tree kept balanced by recolouring and rotating nodes, so that a lookup takes about 2 log₂ n steps at most
allocated object
memory a program gets from bpf_obj_new() while it runs, typed by the program's BTF
owning reference
a pointer to an allocated object that the program must drop, park or link before it exits
non-owning reference
a pointer to a node in a collection, usable for its ordinary fields until the collection's lock is released
kptr
a pointer field of a map value, marked in BTF, that owns the object it points to
BPF memory allocator
the kernel's per-CPU caches of free objects behind bpf_obj_new(), safe in any context
address space cast
the instruction that converts a pointer between the arena's user form and the program's 32-bit form
BPF stream
a per-program log, stdout or stderr, that programs and the kernel write and user space reads

Chapter 12

struct_ops through sched_ext: a program as the CPU scheduler

Every program so far ran at a hook and decided one thing there. A struct_ops program set fills a whole table of function pointers that the kernel calls as it calls its own code, and sched_ext makes that table a scheduling class, so that eight small programs choose which task runs next on every CPU of the machine.

  • A scheduler built from the v7.2 tree, loaded in a VM, and what sysfs and bpftool show of it
