Spine. In chapter 11 the counter kept its counts in memory it allocated and linked itself, and it still ran at its tracepoint, once per write. Now a set of programs takes the place of a part of the kernel: the kernel calls them through a table of function pointers whenever it has a scheduling decision to make.

28 min · RUNTIME · LOADER

A scheduler loaded like a program

A scheduling class is a set of functions through which the Linux scheduler core asks one policy what to run. Each task belongs to one class: the fair class for ordinary tasks, the real-time and deadline classes above it, and since 6.12 an extensible class, sched_ext, whose policy is a BPF program set. Its smallest example is scx_simple. We build it with the tree's own makefile, which compiles libbpf and bpftool from tools/ and dumps vmlinux.h from the running kernel's BTF. The host needs nothing beyond clang, gcc, make, Python and the libelf and zlib headers, although the sparse clone this book uses needed more of tools/ and scripts/bpf_doc.py checked out first; book/labs/schedext-root.sh lists the paths.

Started as root, the loader prints two counters a second and the kernel logs one line. Figure 12.1 shows the rest of what changed. /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state went from disabled to enabled, and the scheduler's name sits in root/ops. The shell that typed the commands reports ext.enabled 1, so the scheduling decisions for that shell, for the loader and for every other ordinary task in the VM are now made by BPF programs.

The page lagssched-ext.rst in v7.2 shows the per-scheduler counters in /sys/kernel/sched_ext/simple/events. The kernel names the root scheduler's directory root (ext.c line 6958), and the counters were in /sys/kernel/sched_ext/root/events.

bpftool sees an object of a kind we have not met, a map of type struct_ops named after the scheduler. Its dump lists the members of a C structure, some holding a program's ID and the rest holding zero, and beside it are eight programs of type struct_ops, one per filled member. The link of type struct_ops belongs to the loader's process.

The counter of the earlier chapters keeps working as before. We loaded it with bpftool prog load … autoattach and made 200,000 one-byte writes with dd, once under the fair class and once under scx_simple. Both times the map held 200,003 writes for the dd process, and count_writes took 533 ns a run under the fair class and 543 ns under scx_simple, with its bpf_printk() still in place. That is what we should expect, because the counter runs inside the write() system call of whichever task is on the CPU, and the scheduler only decides which task that is.

A table of function pointers, filled by programs

A struct_ops map is a map with a single entry whose value is a kernel structure of function pointers, filled with BPF programs instead of kernel functions, so that a subsystem written to call a table of operations calls the programs. Figure 12.2 follows the loader through the four system calls that build one. In the object file the table is a global variable of type struct sched_ext_ops in a section called .struct_ops.link, and each program sits in a section named struct_ops/ followed by its name. The macros SCX_OPS_DEFINE() and BPF_STRUCT_OPS() in the tree's headers write both. libbpf matches the variable's type against the kernel's BTF and creates the map from the BTF ID of a wrapper structure that the kernel declares for each table, bpf_struct_ops_ followed by the table's name; then it loads one program per filled member.

The verifier needs to know which member a program is for, because a member's prototype decides what the program may read and what it must return. The loader says so in two fields of BPF_PROG_LOAD, the table's BTF ID and the member's index, which travels in expected_attach_type. strace decodes that field as an attach type, so it printed BPF_CGROUP_INET_INGRESS for select_cpu at index 0 and BPF_XDP_DEVMAP for init at index 33.

check_struct_ops_btf_id() in the verifier then refuses a program without a GPL-compatible licence, checks that the member is a function pointer, asks the subsystem's check_member() whether this program may fill it, and keeps the member's prototype as the program's own. From then on every read of an argument goes through btf_ctx_access(), which gives argument n the type of the prototype's nth parameter. In simple_enqueue, p is therefore a pointer to struct task_struct and enq_flags a scalar.

The map update makes the table callable: bpf_struct_ops_map_update_elem() walks the members of the structure in BTF order. A data member such as name or timeout_ms goes to the subsystem's init_member(), which checks it and copies it. A function pointer holding a program descriptor gets a trampoline, a short piece of machine code of the kind chapter 7 showed for fentry, which saves the arguments where a BPF program expects them and calls the program. The member in the kernel's copy then points at the trampoline. Figure 12.3 shows the result for scx_simple, with eight trampolines of 172 to 188 bytes in one page of executable memory (a map may use up to eight pages) and 29 members left NULL, which the subsystem treats as "not implemented".

The scheduler core does not know any of this. It calls sch->ops.enqueue(p, enq_flags), an indirect call through a structure, as it would call into a table compiled into the kernel, and lands in the trampoline. A map created with BPF_F_LINK stops at the state READY after the update; registration waits for BPF_LINK_CREATE, which calls the subsystem's reg() and returns a link whose release calls unreg(). A map without that flag, written in a section called plain .struct_ops, registers during the update and stays registered until the entry is deleted. sched_ext's reg() is where the scheduler starts, and its unreg() is where it ends, which is why the scheduler disappears when the loader's last reference to the link goes.

Other tables in v7.2

TCP congestion control was the first struct_ops table, added by Martin KaFai Lau in January 2020 for Linux 5.6 together with the map type. It shows how differently two subsystems can use the same mechanism. Its reg() calls tcp_register_congestion_control(), which adds the algorithm to the list of choices and changes nothing else, since a socket uses it only after asking for it by name, through setsockopt(TCP_CONGESTION) or the system-wide default. Its validate() refuses a table without ssthresh, undo_cwnd and one of cong_avoid or cong_control, because TCP has no fallback for those. Its update() swaps a registered algorithm for a new version under the same link.

sched_ext sits at the other end. It asks only for a name, because every callback has a default, and its reg() takes over every ordinary task at once. bpf_scx_update() refuses replacement in place, since enabling a scheduler runs its init() and init_task(), which may fail.

Figure 12.4 lists the tables in the 7.2.15 kernel's BTF. A BPF queueing discipline, fix-ups for one HID device and a step of an io_uring event loop all use the same map type, trampolines and link. This chapter does not teach them. Each file named in the table holds its bpf_struct_ops definition, whose callbacks say what the subsystem lets a program decide.

sched_ext: a scheduling class in eight programs

The table sched_ext asks schedulers to fill, struct sched_ext_ops, has 37 function pointers and eight data members in v7.2, and Figure 12.5 shows how little of it a working scheduler needs. The core callbacks follow a task through its life as runnable. select_cpu runs when the task wakes, and enqueue when it needs a place in a queue. dispatch runs when a CPU has nothing to run, running and stopping around each stretch on a CPU, and tick on every timer tick while the task runs.

Other callbacks report events the scheduler may track, such as a task joining or leaving the class (enable, disable), a change of weight or of allowed CPUs, a CPU going on- or offline, cgroup moves, and the start and end of the whole scheduler (init, exit). The kernel needs none of them. A missing select_cpu or enqueue gets the built-in behaviour, and the documentation notes that scx_simple's own versions of those two behave like the defaults.

A dispatch queue, or DSQ, is a queue of runnable tasks that sched_ext keeps on behalf of the BPF scheduler, ordered first in, first out or by a key the scheduler gives each task. Through these queues a BPF scheduler hands tasks to CPUs without touching the kernel's runqueues. Every CPU has a local DSQ, from which it always takes its next task, and the whole system has one global DSQ. A scheduler may create its own with IDs below 263, and scx_simple makes one, SHARED_DSQ, in its sleepable init.

The scheduler acts through kfuncs. scx_bpf_dsq_insert() puts a task at the tail of a queue with a time slice, the stretch it may run before it must give the CPU back, here the default of 20 ms. scx_bpf_dsq_insert_vtime() orders it by virtual time instead, a per-task clock that advances more slowly for tasks of greater weight, so that the task furthest behind runs next. scx_bpf_dsq_move_to_local() moves the first task of a queue to the calling CPU's local DSQ. v7.2 registers 69 kfuncs for sched_ext, 64 of them named scx_bpf_; in 6.13 the kfuncs whose names used the verb "dispatch" were renamed, as a comment in the tree's compat.bpf.h records, and that header still maps scx_bpf_consume() and the scx_bpf_dispatch_from_dsq() family to the new names for older kernels.

Figure 12.6 puts these pieces in the order a waking task meets them. simple_select_cpu calls scx_bpf_select_cpu_dfl(), the kernel's own search for an idle CPU. When it finds one, it inserts the task into that CPU's local DSQ at once, which tells the kernel to skip ops.enqueue(). Otherwise simple_enqueue puts the task in SHARED_DSQ, ordered by virtual time unless the loader was started with -f. When a CPU looks for its next task, the kernel takes the first one in its local DSQ, then tries the global DSQ, and only when both are empty calls ops.dispatch(), where simple_dispatch moves one task from SHARED_DSQ.

The kernel repeats that call while it keeps yielding tasks, at most 32 rounds in one pass. simple_running and simple_stopping keep the virtual-time clock, charging each task for the part of its slice it used, scaled by its weight.

A task enters the class when the scheduler is enabled. The reg() call runs the scheduler's init and calls init_task for every task in the system. It then moves each task whose policy is SCHED_NORMAL, SCHED_BATCH, SCHED_IDLE or SCHED_EXT into the ext class, unless the table's flags ask for SCX_OPS_SWITCH_PARTIAL, which moves only tasks that chose SCHED_EXT. During the switch the kernel schedules in bypass mode, ignoring the BPF scheduler and running tasks from simple queues of its own; the events file of the run in Figure 12.1 counted one bypass of 13.9 ms while scx_simple was being enabled. Real-time and deadline tasks never leave their classes, which sit above sched_ext.

Taking the CPU back

A scheduler decides whether other tasks run at all, so a wrong one can stop the machine. sched_ext was merged with a promise, in its documentation, that "the system integrity is maintained no matter what the BPF scheduler does". The verifier keeps part of it, since every program is checked like any other. bpf_scx_check_member() refuses a sleepable program in all members except init, exit, init_task, the two CPU hotplug callbacks, three cgroup callbacks and the two sub-scheduler callbacks, because the others are called where sleeping is not allowed, most of them under a runqueue lock. A program may write to a task only in p->scx.disallow, apart from two fields kept for old schedulers, and a scheduler that is safe in the verifier's sense can still make bad decisions; for those the kernel keeps three ways to end it and one way back.

The scheduler may give up by itself by calling scx_bpf_error(), which records a message and starts the exit. The kernel may end it, and the case it watches for is a task that is runnable and never runs; it also gives up the scheduler when a soft or hard lockup or an RCU stall is reported (ext.c lines 5186 to 5241). Each runnable task carries the time it became runnable. The watchdog, a work item that sched_ext queues every half timeout, walks every CPU's list of runnable tasks and ends the scheduler with "runnable task stall" when one has waited longer than the timeout. That timeout is the table's timeout_ms, or 30 seconds when the field is zero, and init_member() refuses anything longer.

A check in the scheduler tick ends the scheduler too if the watchdog itself has not run within the timeout. Finally, an administrator can press SysRq-S, or write S to /proc/sysrq-trigger. Every one of these, and the release of the link, ends in the same kernel work, scx_disable_workfn() and scx_root_disable(), which enters bypass mode, moves every task back to the fair class, calls the scheduler's exit with the reason, and logs it.

We broke scx_simple on purpose to watch the watchdog work. The change replaces the single line of simple_dispatch with a comment, so that tasks enter SHARED_DSQ and nothing takes them out again. Figure 12.7 shows what followed. For half a minute the VM went on working, because most wake-ups found an idle CPU and took the shortcut of Figure 12.6. A task allowed on one CPU only never takes it, since the scheduler core calls a class's select_task_rq() only for a task that may move (core.c line 3618), so such a task always reaches ops.enqueue().

The first such task the watchdog found was a kernel worker bound to CPU 0, waiting in queue 0 while CPU 0 itself sat idle. After 30.336 seconds the watchdog ended the scheduler, and the kernel moved every task back to the fair class. The loader then printed the dump that sched_ext had collected at the moment of the exit.

Arenas in schedulers

A scheduler keeps state per task, per CPU and per group, and the maps of chapter 10 give it fixed tables with keyed lookups. The arenas of chapter 11 let it build the structures schedulers are usually made of, lists, trees and pools of per-task records linked by pointers, in memory that the loader can read as well. At the 2025 LSFMM+BPF summit, as LWN reported, Emil Tsalapatis said that his team had been happy with arenas in several scheduler experiments. He also named the limits they met. A kernel pointer cannot be stored in an arena, data headed for a kernel function has to be copied to the BPF stack first, and because the verifier types arena and stack pointers differently, a helper written for one cannot take the other, so such helpers are duplicated or inlined.

Alexei Starovoitov answered that work on these was in progress and that mixing the two kinds of pointer in the verifier was a hard problem. The v7.2 tree shows how far schedulers have gone since. scx_sdt, by Tsalapatis and Tejun Heo, is scx_simple with its per-task data allocated from an arena when a task enters the scheduler and freed when it leaves. The documentation describes scx_qmap as a five-level FIFO built on arena-backed doubly linked lists.

v7.2 also adds a second table, sched_ext_ops_cid, in which CPUs go by a sched_ext numbering built from the cache and node topology (kernel/sched/ext/cid.c) and CPU masks are a sched_ext type of their own. bpf_scx_reg_cid() refuses a scheduler of that kind unless all its programs share a single arena. The kernel then carves its own per-CPU scratch masks from that arena (kernel/sched/ext/arena.c), so that the scheduler reads them as ordinary arena memory, and scx_qmap is written to this table. The limit LWN reported is still visible here, since what the kernel places in the arena in v7.2 are CPU masks, never pointers to its own objects. The next chapter, the capstone, starts from this point: it builds one data structure on an arena and then builds it again as a new map type inside the kernel.

Inside v7.2: from the map update to a task on a CPU

Figure 12.8 lists the steps with their places in the source. Two details explain behaviour we see from outside. The enable work runs in a kernel thread that scx_enable() creates once and gives a real-time policy. The switch moves the calling thread itself into the ext class, which ranks below the fair class, and a comment in ext.c (line 6787) explains that a thread switched halfway could wait forever behind fair tasks not yet moved. The system call that created the link waits for that thread, so BPF_LINK_CREATE returns the scheduler's own errors, such as the -EBUSY of a second scheduler.

The class switch is a loop over every task in the system under the fork lock, each move made inside a sched_change guard that takes the task out of its old class and puts it into the new one. The disable path in scx_root_disable() runs the same loop in the other direction (ext.c line 6149).

On the wake-up path the line that matters most is 1913 in do_enqueue_task(). If ops.select_cpu() already inserted the task, the kernel finds a dispatch target recorded on the task and inserts it there without calling ops.enqueue(). A task with migration disabled, or one that is exiting, goes to its CPU's local DSQ without the scheduler being asked, unless the table's flags request otherwise, and the events file counts each such case. When ops.enqueue() does not insert the task anywhere, the kernel marks it as being in the BPF scheduler's custody, and from then on only the scheduler can bring it back to a CPU.

What a BPF scheduler costs

On the first two rows of Figure 12.9 scx_simple and the fair class are within each other's noise. messaging starts 400 processes that pass small messages through sockets and measures the total time. pipe passes one token back and forth between two processes, so each round trip is two wake-ups. A global queue and a search for an idle CPU are enough for both on an otherwise quiet machine with 16 CPUs.

The third row is the same pipe test with a busy loop on every vCPU, so that a waking task never finds an idle CPU. The fair class lets the waking task run soon after it wakes, and the vtime policy usually does the same, because a task that slept carries a virtual time behind the spinners'. In FIFO mode the waking task joins the tail of SHARED_DSQ behind spinners whose 20 ms slices run out one by one. Each round trip took about 1.9 ms, fifty times longer than under the fair class.

In Figure 12.10, every switch to a task runs simple_running and simple_stopping. Most of the 112,083 calls to simple_dispatch found SHARED_DSQ empty, since simple_enqueue ran only 36,642 times, and the other wake-ups went straight to an idle CPU from simple_select_cpu. A pass through a task's life on the CPU thus costs a few hundred nanoseconds of BPF. Most of that is spent inside two kfuncs that do work the fair class does in C as well, which is why the first two rows of Figure 12.9 show no penalty. The statistics add two clock reads to each call, so these figures are slightly high.

What it costs

CPU
Per call of scx_simple's programs, 65 ns (running) to 625 ns (dispatch), kfuncs included; messaging 0.178 s against 0.190 s under the fair class and pipe 2.41 µs against 3.11 µs a round trip, medians of five within the run-to-run spread; with every vCPU busy, FIFO mode took 1.9 ms a round trip against 35 µs (kernel 7.2.15, VM with 16 vCPUs, 13 November 2026).
Memory
Eight programs of 4 KiB memlock each; the struct_ops map 6,288 bytes; five other maps 54,136 bytes, of which 36,864 are the exit dump buffer; one 4 KiB page of trampolines; the loader 4.5 MB resident.
Switches
None per scheduling decision: the callbacks run inside the kernel. The loader took 57 to 76 ms from exec to enabled and 38 to 47 ms from SIGINT to disabled (five runs), with one bypass of 13.9 ms while enabling; it then reads its statistics map once a second.
Locking
enqueue, dispatch, running and stopping run with a runqueue lock held and may not sleep; a custom DSQ is one raw spinlock, so scx_simple's single SHARED_DSQ is a lock every CPU takes.

A BPF scheduler pays for itself when a workload needs a policy the fair class cannot express, such as keeping a latency-critical service's threads on chosen CPUs or running a group's threads together, and the decision costs hundreds of nanoseconds that the policy wins back. For a general mix keep the fair class: scx_simple only matched it, its FIFO mode lost by a factor of fifty under load, and a scheduler is one more program whose failure the watchdog has to catch.

When it goes wrong

The rows of Figure 12.11 fall into three groups by when they happen. The verifier rows come first, at BPF_PROG_LOAD, and all three came from code that compiled. BPF_STRUCT_OPS() casts whatever argument list it is given onto the context array, so a wrong signature is caught only when the verifier types a read against the member's prototype in the kernel's BTF. The next two rows come at registration, from init_member() during the map update and from scx_root_enable_workfn() during the link's creation, and libbpf reports both as a failed attach with the kernel's error code.

The last group happens while the scheduler runs. Each ends in the same scx_root_disable() and the same return of every task to the fair class, and the reason in the loader's EXIT: line and in dmesg tells them apart. A scheduler that disappears without an error was unregistered, usually because its loader exited and took the link with it. The pinned TCP congestion control of step 7 in book/labs/schedext-root.sh shows the other side: bpftool struct_ops register with a directory pins the link, bpf_mini stayed in tcp_available_congestion_control after bpftool exited, and removing the pin unregistered it. bpftool alone would load scx_simple with its sched_ext constants left at zero, because the tree's loader writes their values into the object before loading it (SCX_ENUM_INIT(), called from SCX_OPS_OPEN() in tools/sched_ext/include/scx/compat.h).

Try it · Take the CPU away from a scheduler

~40 min · break a real one · needs the v7.2 tree with tools/ checked out, clang, gcc and make on the host, and root in a throwaway VM (virtme-ng)

Task. Build scx_simple from the v7.2 tree, run it in a VM and measure perf bench sched pipe under it and under the fair class. Then change one line so that simple_dispatch never moves a task, run the broken scheduler with two busy loops pinned to one CPU, and read the watchdog's report. This is the safety net of the section "Taking the CPU back", seen from both sides.

Done when. You have a median round trip for each class, and the kernel has ended the broken scheduler with runnable task stall about 30 seconds after it was enabled, with /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state back at disabled.

Hint 1 · direction

The tree builds its own libbpf and bpftool, so the host needs only a compiler; the scheduler needs root, so it runs in the VM. Ask which callback moves a task out of SHARED_DSQ, and which tasks can never avoid that queue.

Hint 2 · mechanism

make -C tools/sched_ext scx_simple builds the scheduler. In the VM start build/bin/scx_simple in the background, wait until the state file says enabled, run the benchmark five times and stop the loader with SIGINT; then run the benchmark again without it. For the broken scheduler, copy scx_simple.bpf.c, empty the body of simple_dispatch, generate its skeleton under the name scx_simple and compile the unchanged scx_simple.c against it.

Hint 3 · nearly there

bash book/labs/schedext-root.sh build does all of the building and leaves var/stall/simple_stall and spin in /tmp/schedext-w. In the VM, STEPS="4 6" bash /tmp/schedext-w/schedext-root.sh runs both halves, or by hand: ./var/stall/simple_stall & taskset -c 5 ./spin & taskset -c 5 ./spin &, then wait and read dmesg | grep sched_ext. When you compile the loader yourself, put the variant's directory first with -iquote.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 12.

Check yourself

  1. Predict the values: scx_simple fills eight members of struct sched_ext_ops. How many BPF_PROG_LOAD calls of type struct_ops does its loader make, how many bpf__sched_ext_ops_* trampolines appear in /proc/kallsyms, and what number does simple_dispatch carry in expected_attach_type?
  2. A scheduler that compiled cleanly stops at load with R1 invalid mem access 'scalar' in simple_dispatch, whose first lines read BPF_STRUCT_OPS(simple_dispatch, struct task_struct *prev, s32 cpu) and if (prev && prev->pid == 1). What did the verifier see?
  3. With scx_simple running, a colleague starts a second copy, which prints Failed to attach struct_ops and Device or resource busy. Which call failed, where in the kernel, and does anything of the second copy stay behind?
  4. Predict the value: a busy loop runs on each of the 16 vCPUs, and two processes pass a token through a pipe under scx_simple in FIFO mode with its 20 ms slices. Roughly how long does one round trip take, and why?
  5. An operator kills scx_simple's loader with kill -9. Within milliseconds dmesg says disabled (unregistered from user space), although nobody unregistered anything. What happened, and how does a struct_ops table outlive its loader?
  6. bpftool struct_ops register of a TCP congestion control fails with Invalid argument and the kernel logs bpf_mini does not implement required ops, while the sched_ext documentation says that a scheduler's only mandatory field is its name. Why the difference?
  7. In Figure 12.10, simple_dispatch averages 625 ns a run and simple_running 65 ns, although simple_dispatch is a single call. Where does its time go?
  8. A scheduler whose ops.dispatch() never moves a task runs for about half a minute before the kernel ends it, and the task named in the report is a kernel worker bound to CPU 0, although the busy loops you started run on CPU 5. Why 30 seconds, why that task, and how would you make the wait shorter?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 12.

Recap

A struct_ops map holds one kernel table of function pointers: the loader creates it from the table's BTF type, loads one program per filled member with the member's index as its attach type, and fills the map's value with program descriptors, whereupon the kernel checks each program against its member's prototype, writes a trampoline per member and points the member at it. The link created next calls the subsystem's reg(), and its release calls unreg(), so the table lives as long as the link. sched_ext is such a table with 37 callbacks, of which only the name is required; its programs place tasks in dispatch queues with kfuncs, a CPU runs what is in its local DSQ, and ops.dispatch() is asked only when that and the global queue are empty. scx_simple matched the fair class on two benchmarks at a few hundred nanoseconds per callback, its FIFO mode lost by a factor of fifty with every CPU busy, and a scheduler that strands a task is ended by the watchdog after 30 seconds, with every task returned to the fair class.

New words in this chapter

scheduling class
the set of functions through which the scheduler core asks one policy what to run
struct_ops map
a one-entry map whose value is a kernel table of function pointers, filled with programs
dispatch queue
a queue of runnable tasks that sched_ext keeps for a BPF scheduler, FIFO or ordered by a key
local DSQ
the dispatch queue of one CPU, from which that CPU always takes its next task
time slice
how long a task may run before it must give the CPU back
virtual time
a per-task clock that runs slower for heavier tasks; the task furthest behind runs next
bypass mode
sched_ext scheduling without the BPF scheduler, while one is enabled, disabled or failing
watchdog
sched_ext's periodic check that ends a BPF scheduler when a runnable task has not run in time

Chapter 13

Capstone: a new data structure, twice

A hash map keeps an exact count for every thread it has room for and nothing for the rest. In this chapter the write counter keeps an approximate count for every thread in memory fixed in advance, first as a count-min sketch that a program builds in an arena on a stock kernel, then as a map type of its own in a kernel we patch, and we weigh what each build costs the counter, the kernel and its maintainers.

Spine. Chapter 12 handed a kernel subsystem to a set of programs through struct_ops, whose schedulers build their structures in arenas. We return to the write counter and to the question chapter 10 left open: a count for every thread a server ever ran, in memory fixed in advance. Part A's numbers were measured on kernel 7.2.15 in a virtme-ng VM with 16 virtual CPUs on 13 November 2026, by book/labs/capstone-root.sh; Part B's on a v7.2 kernel built with the series, in the same kind of VM on the same day. The outputs are in /tmp/book-labs/capstone.

28 min · RUNTIME · VERIFIER

A hundred thousand threads

The workload is the one a hash cannot hold. Four heavy threads each write 100,000 times while 100,000 light threads come and go, 64 at a time, each writing three times, so the counter sees 700,000 writes from 100,004 threads. The loader, cbench in book/labs/capstone, records each thread's ID and writes, so the truth is known exactly, and each version of the counter counts only the loader's own threads. The VM's kernel.pid_max is raised to 4,194,304 first, because at its default of 32,768 thread IDs would be reused long before the hundred-thousandth thread.

Figure 13.1 shows three versions on the stock kernel. The hash of chapter 10, 1,024 entries, kept exact counts for the first 1,024 threads, the heavy four among them, and refused 296,940 inserts with -E2BIG. The LRU hash of the same size kept 740 of the loader's threads and none of the heavy four. They had finished their writes early in the run, and a hundred thousand inserts later they were the entries used least recently, which is what an LRU hash evicts.

The sketch kept an estimate for all 100,004 threads in 110,592 bytes. No estimate fell below the truth, the heavy threads were over by at most 93 writes in 100,000, and the light ones, which wrote three times, by at most 135. The table of the heaviest threads beside it named the heavy four, and user space read the table and every estimate with no system call.

What a count-min sketch promises

A count-min sketch is a table of d rows of w counters with one hash function per row, from which any key's count can be estimated. Cormode and Muthukrishnan introduced it in 2005. To add c to a key, add c to the one counter that each row's hash picks for the key. To estimate a key, read the same d counters and take the smallest, because every counter holds the key's own count plus whatever other keys hashed there.

Two guarantees follow. An estimate is never below the true count, since counts only grow. And if N is the total of all counts, an estimate exceeds the truth by more than εN with probability at most δ when w = ⌈e/ε⌉ and d = ⌈ln(1/δ)⌉, provided the hash functions come from a pairwise-independent family (Theorem 1 of the paper). For ε = 0.001 the width is 2,719, and five rows give δ = e−5, about 0.0067. The sketch then takes 13,595 counters, 108,760 bytes of eight-byte counters, whatever the number of keys.

Figure 13.2 draws the counters of the run, rebuilt from every thread's true count with the program's own hash; the rebuild reproduces all 100,004 estimates. A light thread's five counters held between 93 and 138 and its estimate is the smallest. A counter holds 257 writes on average (700,000 over 2,719), and the minimum of five such counters is what a light thread reads. A heavy thread's estimate is off by the same 90 or so, which is 0.09 per cent of its count. The sketch's error is absolute, so it suits the heavy hitters, the few keys that account for a large share of the total, and says little about a key that wrote three times.

The paper finds the heavy hitters by keeping a heap of the keys whose estimate passes a threshold, checking each key after its update (section 5.2). Our table keeps the 16 largest estimates instead, a choice that needs no threshold set in advance.

The sketch in an arena

The arena version, c_sketch.bpf.c, reserves its counters with one call. A syscall program, init, run once by the loader, asks bpf_arena_alloc_pages() for 27 pages and writes the width and depth into a header before the rows. With the table compiled in, it also takes 16 nodes from bpf_alloc() of the selftests' bpf_arena_alloc.h and links them into a list. The address of the sketch goes into a global in .bss. Figure 13.3 shows the result from the loader's side, with the addresses of the run in see.txt.

The program can use only what it carries. No helper hashes a buffer, so cms.h holds a copy of the kernel's jhash2() for an eight-byte key, seeded with the row number, and picks the slot with the kernel's reciprocal_scale(), a multiply and a shift that maps a 32-bit hash onto 0 to w − 1. They are the functions the map type of the second half uses, so both sketches put a thread in the same counters. jhash with a seed per row is not a family proven pairwise independent, as the paper assumes, so the measured errors are the check that it behaves like one here.

The update in Figure 13.4 is also the query, because __sync_fetch_and_add() returns each counter's old value. Linux v7.2 accepts that on arena memory. atomic_ptr_type_ok() in verifier.c asks the JIT, and the x86 JIT's bpf_jit_supports_insn() refuses only the fetching forms of AND, OR and XOR on the arena; an exchange or a compare-and-swap is accepted, and the table uses compare-and-swap to claim a node. The empty asm statement names the arena map in the program. Without it the verifier refused the counter's first cast with the message chapter 11 met, since the program reached the arena only through a pointer in .bss.

The table walks its 16 nodes on every write. It refreshes the thread's node if it finds one, and otherwise, when the new estimate beats the smallest in the table, claims that node by compare-and-swap on its thread ID. A global kmin lets a light thread skip the walk. No lock is taken, so a node's estimate can trail by a write when two CPUs race, which a table of the heaviest can afford.

The limits of the section "What the verifier gives up in an arena" shaped two choices. The table stores thread IDs and estimates, never a task_struct pointer, which would load back as a scalar. And the key reaches the hash as a number in a register, so no arena buffer is ever handed to a helper, which would be refused, as the tenth row of Figure 13.11 shows.

What the arena sketch costs

Each version ran with one writer pinned to a CPU making 2,000,000 one-byte writes to /dev/null, three times, by the method of chapter 10, and again with eight writers on eight CPUs (Figure 13.5). The sketch cost 70.7 ns a run against 83.7 for the hash. Five hashes and five atomic adds on memory the program addresses directly came out cheaper than one hash lookup, a call into the kernel that hashes the key and walks a bucket under RCU.

The table is the one structure every writer shares. With one writer it added 2.6 ns a run; with eight it added 38, because the 16 nodes sit in a few cache lines that every heavy writer's walk stores into, so the lines travel between CPUs on almost every write. The counters themselves are shared only by chance, when two threads' keys land in one 64-byte line, so the bare sketch rose by only 3.4 ns.

The workload of a hundred thousand threads made every version slower, through cold caches and the creation and exit of threads between writes, but it split them further. The hash paid most, 213.9 ns a run, because each of 296,940 refused inserts searched the free lists of all 16 CPUs before failing (___pcpu_freelist_pop()), and the 262,144-entry hash that held everything paid 153.4 for its inserts.

The same sketch in .bss, which libbpf creates as a one-element array map with BPF_F_MMAPABLE, cost the same as the arena within a nanosecond, and user space reads it through mmap as well. What the arena adds over the array is pointers, which the array version cannot hold, so its table is a fixed array searched by index. The structure the program can grow, link and hand to user space as a graph is what the arena buys, at a few pages of memory charged by the page and no memlock.

Figure 13.6 sets the errors against the bound at three widths. At w = 2,719 every error lay between 33 and 144 against a bound of 700. A sketch ten times narrower, 10,880 bytes, made the typical error about ten times larger, a median of 1,041, as εN predicts. No estimate at any width passed its bound, and the typical error was about a seventh of it, the slack of the Markov inequality behind Theorem 1.

A map type: the API decides the shape

A map type is code in kernel/bpf that programs reach through the map helpers and user space through bpf(), so its design starts with which helpers fit. Figure 13.7 weighs the three choices. Lookup returns a pointer to a value stored in the map, and a sketch stores no value for a key; its answer is computed on each query. The bloom filter of kernel/bpf/bloom_filter.c had the same problem and solved it with a keyless map, one created with a key size of 0, whose value is the item itself, pushed to add it and peeked to test it.

The value of BPF_MAP_TYPE_COUNT_MIN is therefore the key's bytes followed by a u64 count. Push adds the count to the key's d counters, so a program can count bytes as easily as writes, and peek returns the smallest of them. From user space, BPF_MAP_UPDATE_ELEM pushes, and BPF_MAP_LOOKUP_ELEM reads the key from the value buffer and writes the estimate into its count. max_entries is the width, the low four bits of map_extra the depth, five by default as the bloom filter's hash count is, and BPF_F_ZERO_SEED fixes the seed for tests.

cms_map_alloc_check() refuses a key, a value of eight bytes or less, a width of 0, unknown flags, other bits in map_extra, and more counters than a 32-bit slot index reaches. cms_map_mem_usage() reports the header and 8wd bytes, which is the memlock bpftool prints. The counters are shared and updated with atomic64_add(). A per-CPU sketch would cost 16 times the memory on this machine and make every query sum 16 copies of each counter, and the write counter does not need one: a thread runs on one CPU at a time, so two CPUs meet on a counter only when their keys collide, as the eight-writer runs confirm.

The program in c_cms.bpf.c is shorter than the arena version, a struct cms_value on the stack and one push. What the API takes away is the table: push cannot return the estimate, so keeping the heaviest threads costs a second pass of five hashes, a peek, where the arena version had the estimate for free.

What the series touches

Figure 13.8 is the series as git format-patch wrote it into book/labs/capstone/patches, eight patches against the v7.2 tag. Twenty-one files change for 209 lines of map. The uapi header gains an enum value that can never be taken back, and its copy under tools/include must match it, or libbpf's build warns and then fails. syscall.c learns where push and peek replace update and lookup, that map_extra is allowed, and that creating the map needs CAP_BPF. libbpf learns the type's name and how to probe for it, and bpftool its name; until it does, bpftool prints type 36.

The verifier needs the most care, because it must learn the map's rules from us in four places. check_map_func_compatibility() allows push and peek on the new type and refuses every other helper. resolve_map_arg_type() says that peek reads its buffer, where for a queue it writes it. check_map_prog_compatibility() keeps a list of the map types a sleepable program may use, and the first selftest run failed on it: a syscall program sleeps, and it was refused with "Sleepable programs can only use array, hash, ringbuf and local storage maps".

The fourth place was found the hard way, when the counter with its table was refused at its peek. Stack liveness in v7.2 reads a helper's prototype, where peek's buffer is marked write-only, and does not ask resolve_map_arg_type(), so it takes the stored key as dead before the call and poisons it, and the argument check then refuses to read it.

The bloom filter has the same bug on the stock kernel. On 7.2.15 the two smallest programs in book/labs/capstone/bad that peek one with a value on the stack are refused with "slot poisoned by dead code elimination". Mainline fixed it for the bloom filter in commit 830e4372de5c, merged for Linux 7.4 and first tagged in 7.4-rc1. Patches 1 and 2 carry the same rule for a v7.2 tree, and on bpf-next the count-min patch would only add its type to that condition.

The selftests check creation's refusals, user-space access, a program's push and peek against user space, and three programs the verifier must refuse. On the final kernel the seven subtests of count_min_map, the two of verifier_bloom_peek and the bloom filter's own test passed. scripts/checkpatch.pl --strict raised three kinds of complaint, all inherent: no Signed-off-by, since only the author can certify the Developer's Certificate of Origin, a question whether MAINTAINERS needs updating, which its kernel/bpf/ pattern already covers, and the extern declarations by which bench.c registers every benchmark.

The cover letter, the message numbered 0 that explains a series before its patches, says what the map does and why, gives the benchmark's numbers, and asks the maintainers the question the next sections take up. The series was not sent. It is in the book's lab folder to be read, and nothing was mailed, pushed or posted.

The two builds measured

The patched kernel ran the comparison in one VM session (Figure 13.9). Its configuration came from vng and the selftests' fragments, with lock debugging turned off; the fragments as given turn on CONFIG_PROVE_LOCKING, under which the hash's run cost 137 ns instead of 83. Compare the columns of one session only, since the stock and the patched kernels are built differently.

In that session the map type cost 93.1 ns a run with one writer, between the arena sketch at 75.9 and the hash at 89.5. With the table of the heaviest the gap widened, 108.4 against 78.1 for the arena, because every write then pays for a peek, a second pass of five hashes. The first build of the map was slower still. Its push called a slot function five times, and inlining it, the change now in patch 3, took the counter from 108.0 to 86.0 ns a run, each measured beside an arena sketch at 70 to 72, and the benchmark's push from 25.3 to 45.3 million a second. This CPU runs the kernel with the SRSO mitigation in its "Safe RET" mode, which sends each return of kernel C code through a thunk, while the arena version's hashing is compiled into the program itself.

The benchmark takes the hook away and repeats each operation 1,024 times a run from getpgid(). With one producer a push took about 21 ns and the hash's lookup and add, whose lookup the verifier inlines, about 27. Eight producers pushing the same 100,000 random keys reversed the order. Push fell to 19.3 million a second per producer because every push writes five counters that the other CPUs write too, while peek, which only reads, held at 42.1, and the bloom filter's push, which sets bits in one dense bitmap, fell to 7.4. Thread IDs do not collide that way, which is why the counter's eight writers cost the map type only 12 ns more; keys that every CPU updates are the case for a per-CPU sketch.

The map type's errors matched the arena's within the variation between runs, as the same hash with the same seeds should make them. Reading all 100,004 of them took one lookup each, 63.8 ms against the arena's 1.4 ms of loads.

Inside the v7.2 source

Figure 13.10 follows the bloom filter from BPF_MAP_CREATE to its push and peek in Linux v7.2, and then the count-min map along the same path in the patched tree. The two share every step but the last, the map's own file, which is why a new keyless map is mostly a matter of adding its type to lists that already exist.

The rewrite in fixups.c explains the cost of a map helper. Once the verifier knows which map a call names, it replaces the call to bpf_map_push_elem() with a direct call to the map's map_push_elem, so the program pays one call and no indirect jump, and then the op's own loop of d hashes and atomic adds.

What upstream says about new map types

The bloom filter is the closest precedent, and its review is on lore. On 1 September 2021, answering its first version, Andrii Nakryiko wrote that "bloom filter logic is actually simple enough to be implementable by pure BPF program logic", lacking only a helper that hashes memory, and went on: "We could go further, and start implementing other simple data structures relying on hashing, like HyperLogLog. And all with no kernel modifications." The map type was merged all the same, as commit 9330986c0300 for Linux 5.16. A count-min sketch is one of the structures he described, built from hashing and counters.

Two and a half years later the arena gave programs the memory that argument needed. Alexei Starovoitov's commit message for it, 317460317a02 of March 2024, lists as its second use case that "the bpf program builds arbitrary data structures in bpf_arena (hash tables, rb-trees, sparse arrays), while user space consumes it". The kernel's later work on arenas, the error streams and kernel-side faults of chapter 11, makes that use easier.

We found no statement by a maintainer that rules new map types out, and they still land: the instruction array (b4ce5923e780, Linux 6.19) and the resizable hash (16b4d3e2fb24, Linux 7.2) came after the arena. What a map type costs is fixed by its place in the uapi, which kfuncs avoid; Documentation/bpf/kfuncs.rst calls them "a kernel <-> kernel API" that is "not bound by any of the strict stability restrictions associated with kernel <-> user UAPIs". A module can register its own with register_btf_kfunc_id_set(), as chapter 9 showed, so a sketch kept by a module needs no uapi change at all, at the price of no bpf() access and no promise across releases.

What it costs

CPU
Per run with one writer: hash 83.7 ns, LRU hash 84.2, arena sketch of five rows 70.7, with its table of 16 73.3, the same sketch in .bss 70.6 (kernel 7.2.15, 16-CPU VM, 13 November 2026); on the patched kernel, in one session, the map type 93.1, the arena sketch 75.9 and the hash 89.5.
Memory
Sketch: 8wd bytes whatever the number of keys, 108,760 for w = 2,719 and d = 5, held in 27 arena pages that report 0 to memlock, or 109,272 bytes of memlock as the map type. Hash: 82 bytes a thread from creation, about 21 MB to hold 100,004 threads.
Switches
Reading 100,004 estimates: none for the arena or the array, 1.5 ms of loads; one bpf() lookup each for the hash, 69.5 ms, and for the map type, 63.8 ms.
Locking
None: atomic adds on counters that two CPUs share only when keys collide. The table of the heaviest is shared by every heavy writer and cost 38 ns more a run with eight writers.

Count exactly while the keys fit a map; when they do not and an error of ε times the total is acceptable, use a sketch. Build it in an arena when user space reads it often or it needs pointers, as a map type only to give it a uapi of its own and bpf() access for any tool, which means proposing it upstream with tests, documentation and a reason the arena cannot serve; a kfunc module serves a single site without either.

When it goes wrong

The rows fall into three groups. The first three concern a kernel and its tools that disagree about the map type, which is the everyday cost of a new uapi value: every loader, bpftool and header must be rebuilt before the type has a name. The middle rows are refusals by the verifier, half of them rules that a new map type must teach it and half the arena's single type showing through, and each log names the instruction. The last rows load and run. A sketch never errs below the truth, so an estimate that looks high calls for its bound, e·N/w, before suspecting the hash.

Check yourself

  1. Predict the value: the sketch of this chapter, w = 2,719 and d = 5, counts 7,000,000 writes. What error bound does Theorem 1 give, with what probability, and what typical error does the run suggest?
  2. A light thread that wrote three times reads 93. Is the sketch broken, and what would bring the estimate down?
  3. The LRU hash of 1,024 entries kept 740 of the loader's threads but none of the four that wrote 100,000 times each. Why those four?
  4. With one writer, the table of the heaviest added 2.6 ns a run; with eight writers it added 38. Where does the difference come from, and how would you shrink it?
  5. Why does a count-min map use push and peek rather than update and lookup, and how does user space get an estimate back?
  6. A program that peeks a bloom filter with a key on its stack loads on a kernel with the fix merged for Linux 7.4 but is refused on 7.2.15 with "slot poisoned by dead code elimination". What does the verifier get wrong in 7.2?
  7. A colleague's arena program uses __sync_fetch_and_or() to set a flag in a counter and test whether it was set. Why is it refused, and what can replace it?
  8. Your team wants the sketch for one service on its own servers. Arena, map type, or a kfunc module, and what does each cost the team?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 13.

Recap

A count-min sketch keeps d rows of w counters and adds each key's count to one counter per row; its estimate is the smallest of the key's counters, never below the truth and above it by more than εN with probability at most δ when w = ⌈e/ε⌉ and d = ⌈ln(1/δ)⌉. On a hundred thousand short-lived threads, a hash of 1,024 entries refused 296,940 inserts and an LRU hash evicted the heaviest threads, while a sketch of 108,760 bytes kept an estimate for every thread, the heavy ones within 0.1 per cent. Built in an arena, the sketch cost 70.7 ns a run against 83.7 for the hash, user space read it and a pointer-linked table of the heaviest without a system call, and an array map would have held the counters but not the pointers. Built as a map type it became a keyless map reached by push and peek, at the price of eight patches over twenty-one files, a value in the uapi for good, and four rules the verifier had to be taught by hand, one of which v7.2 had already got wrong for the bloom filter. That verifier is a program too, and chapter 14 begins Part V's question of how anyone can know it is right.

New words in this chapter

count-min sketch
d rows of w counters with one hash function per row, from which any key's count is estimated as the smallest of its d counters
heavy hitter
one of the few keys that account for a large share of all counts
keyless map
a map created with a key size of 0, whose value is the item itself, reached by push and peek
cover letter
the message numbered 0 of a patch series, which explains the series before its patches

Part V

Proving the verifier

The verifier is a static analyser, and a static analyser can be proved sound or shown to be wrong. We review the ideas and tools a proof needs, carry out one small proof by hand and with a solver, and then read two papers that apply them to eBPF.

Chapter 14

Formal proving: a refresher, and the reads to do first

A test shows that the verifier was right about one program. A proof shows that it is right about every input, and this chapter collects the few ideas, the notation and the four reads that the papers of this part take for granted.

9 min · VERIFIER

A promise written as a claim

Chapter 4 drew the verifier's promise as six things a loaded program never does. Written so that it can be checked, a promise becomes a specification, a claim about every possible input that a program either meets or breaks. For chapter 6's copy it reads: for every descriptor the copy can receive, the eight bytes read at slot 13 lie inside the 64-byte map value. No finite set of tests can settle "for every".

Figure 14.1 sets out the two ways a verifier can fail such a claim. It is sound, in chapter 6's sense now applied to the whole verdict, when it never loads a program that breaks the specification on some input. It is complete when it never refuses a program that meets it, a property called completeness, and each refusal of a safe program is a false alarm.

Linux keeps the soundness bug's cell empty and pays in the false alarm's. A verifier without false alarms would need to know every value at every instruction without any loss, far more than a load can spend. A loaded unsafe program is therefore a bug, to be fixed and backported, while a false alarm is a limit, and the kernel's source documents one of its own.

"This is a conservative heuristic that allows to verify wide range of programs, however it precludes verification of programs that conjure an imprecise value on the first loop iteration and use it as precise on a second."

Comment above process_iter_next_call(), kernel/bpf/verifier.c, Linux v7.2

Abstract values, formally

The papers relate two kinds of value. Concrete values are the numbers a register really holds, and abstract values are the tnums and ranges of chapter 6. The bridge between them is concretization, written γ (gamma), which maps an abstract value to the set of numbers it stands for: on four bits γ(00x1) = {1, 3}, and γ([2, 5]) = {2, 3, 4, 5}.

An abstract operation is sound when its answer holds every concrete result. With ∀ read as "for every" and ∈ as "is in", the claim for an abstract addition ⊕ and any two abstract values A and B is the line below.

∀x ∈ γ(A),  ∀y ∈ γ(B) :  x + y ∈ γ(A ⊕ B)

Figure 14.2 checks one case. The real sums of 00x1 and 0x10 are 3, 5, 7 and 9, while tnum_add() answers xxx1, the eight odd numbers, and interval addition answers [3, 9]. Both answers are sound and imprecise, and together they allow only the real sums.

Where two paths meet, an analysis may merge their abstract values with a join, the smallest abstract value that holds both. [0, 2] joined with [5, 6] is [0, 6], and tnum_union() in tnum.c joins two tnums. A loop is a path that meets itself, so a joining analysis repeats until the value at the loop's top stops changing: 16 rounds on four bits in Figure 14.3, and 264 on a register. Widening ends the climb by moving any bound that grew to the end of the number line, and the loop settles in two rounds.

PREVAIL, read in chapter 17, joins wherever paths meet and widens at loops. Linux never joins paths. It walks each round as a separate verifier state and prunes a path only when, for every scalar whose range matters, the new γ lies inside the saved one (regsafe() in states.c, with range_within() and tnum_in()), so a loop it cannot prune runs into the instruction limit. For iterator loops and bpf_loop(), widen_imprecise_scalars() forgets the range of every scalar whose range has not yet mattered, a widening straight to "any value" and the cause of the false alarm quoted above.

Three ways to know, and what a solver is asked

Trying every case, the first column of Figure 14.4, is a proof when the cases can be listed: on four bits there are 81 tnums, so 6,561 pairs for a two-input operation. The work grows sixteenfold with each bit. A claim about every width therefore needs a proof on paper, by algebra or by induction over the bit positions, as the tnum paper gives for tnum_add() and chapter 15 writes out for a smaller case.

The third way hands the question to an SMT solver, a program that decides whether a formula over numbers, bits and other theories can be made true. Its answer is satisfiable, printed sat, with a model that gives every variable a value, or unsat when no such assignment exists. Figure 14.5 asserts the claim's negation. A sat answer is then a counterexample, inputs that break the claim, and unsat proves that none exists at that width.

Two multiplicationsThe proved tnum_mul() of 2021 was replaced in August 2025 by commit 1df7dad4d5c4, whose message reports experiments and no proof. On four bits the lab's checker finds both sound; the newer is wider than the best tnum in 227 of 6,561 pairs, the older in 299.

The width matters because the variables are bit-vectors, fixed-width words whose arithmetic wraps round. RFC 9669 §4.1 requires the same of every BPF register, so on four bits 15 + 1 is 0.

For a systems engineer the useful question is which change needs which argument, and the table below is a rule of thumb. A selftest exercises a handful of programs, while a missing value can hide in one pair among billions. Whatever changes what an abstract value stands for deserves more than tests.

A change to …Check it with
an abstract operation in tnum.c or cnum_defs.hevery pair at 4 to 8 bits, a solver query at 64, the selftests; a written proof if the algorithm is new
the precision of an existing operationthe same, since a tighter answer is where a lost value hides
how descriptions are combined: reg_bounds_sync(), narrowing at a branchone query over all descriptions together, as Agni does in chapter 16, and the selftests
a message or the log's formatthe selftests that pin it (chapter 5); no abstract value changes

Four reads, in order

The four reads climb from pictures to formulas: Cousot's page without symbols, the lecture notes with the definitions and the interval domain that PREVAIL builds on, Programming Z3 for the solver, and the tnum paper, which puts all three onto tnum.c in Agni's notation.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 14.

Recap

A specification is a claim about every input; a sound verifier never loads a program that breaks it, a complete one never refuses one that meets it, and Linux chooses soundness and accepts false alarms. An abstract operation is sound when every concrete result lies in γ of its answer. PREVAIL joins paths and widens loops, while Linux walks every round until the instruction limit. Soundness is shown by every case at a small width, a proof for every width, or a solver's search for a counterexample over bit-vectors.

New words in this chapter

specification
a checkable claim about every possible input
completeness
of a verifier: it never refuses a safe program
false alarm
a refusal of a program that is in fact safe
concretization (γ)
γ(A) is the set of values the abstract value A stands for
join
the smallest abstract value that holds two others
widening
jumping a growing bound to the end of its range
counterexample
an input for which a claim is false
SMT solver
a program that decides if a formula can be made true
satisfiable
some assignment makes it true: sat, with a model
bit-vector
a fixed-width word whose arithmetic wraps round

One proof by hand, one bug by solver

Trying every case proves tnum_and() sound on eight bits in sixteen minutes, and at 64 bits the cases number 2256. We prove it for every width on paper, have Z3 prove it at 64 bits in a few milliseconds, and then watch Z3 find the bug in the verifier's 32-bit bounds that Linux shipped from 5.7 until 2021, CVE-2021-3490.
