Spine. In chapter 14 we wrote the verifier's promise as a specification, checked tnum_mul() on four bits by trying every case, and printed a solver query that nobody ran. Now we run it, prove one operation by hand at every width, and turn the same method on a function of the verifier that was wrong for a year.

25 min · VERIFIER

Every case, then a solver

We start where the refresher stopped, with its checker, book/labs/ch17-check.py, and the bitwise AND of two tnums, tnum_and() at line 92 of kernel/bpf/tnum.c. For every pair of tnums the checker lists the values each one stands for, ANDs every pair of those values, and asks whether each result lies inside the tnum that tnum_and() returned. It found no counterexample at 4, 5, 6, 7 or 8 bits. At every width it also found each answer to be the tightest tnum possible, which the line "wider than the best answer: 0" in Figure 15.1 reports.

The price is in the same figure. Each extra bit gives a tnum and one of its members four ways to continue: a known 0, a known 1, or an unknown bit that is 0 or 1. The cases for two inputs therefore grow sixteenfold, from 65,536 at four bits to 4,294,967,296 at eight. The time follows them from 0.02 s to 987 s, about 0.23 µs a case, and at 64 bits there are 1664 = 2256 cases, which at that pace would take about 1070 seconds.

The last two commands hand the same claim to Z3 at 64 bits. It answers unsat for tnum_and() in 6 ms and for tnum_add() in 0.77 s, and the query that the refresher printed without running, Figure 14.5, answers unsat in 0.79 s when it is run as printed. Because the query asks for a counterexample, unsat is a proof at that width. The rest of the chapter shows why the paper proof and the solver agree, how such a query is written, and what the answer looks like when the code is wrong.

What a tnum stands for, bit by bit

Chapter 6 stored a tnum as two 64-bit words, a value and a mask, and the refresher wrote γ for the set of numbers it stands for. A proof needs that set as a test on one number. The membership relation of a tnum (v, m) is the test x & ~m == v, which holds when x, with every unknown bit cleared, equals the value. It is Equation 9 of the tnum paper (CGO 2022).

Figure 15.2 applies it to 1x0x, whose members are 8, 9, 12 and 13. The kernel's own form of the test is tnum_in() at line 210 of tnum.c, which regsafe() calls during pruning to ask whether one tnum lies inside another. Given the constant tnum_const(x) as its second argument, it clears from x the bits unknown in P and compares the rest with P's value.

The paper adds a second test, Equation 10. A well-formed tnum is one whose value has no 1 in a bit the mask marks unknown, v & m == 0, and the kernel builds no other kind. The two tests are not independent, because a number that passes the membership test leaves a value with every masked bit already cleared, so v & m is 0. A pair that breaks the rule, such as value 0010 with mask 0010, therefore has no member at all, and a claim that already says x is in P gains nothing from saying that P is well-formed. The assumption earns its place when membership is written another way, as the first row of Figure 15.11 shows.

tnum_and() proved by hand

We prove tnum_and() rather than tnum_add() because every operation in it works on each bit separately, so the argument never has to follow a carry from one bit into the next. The paper's proof for tnum_add() needs four lemmas about the carries (§III-B, Lemmas 2 to 5) and an appendix for their proofs, while for tnum_and() and the other bitwise operators it relied on the solver at 64 bits (§III-A). The kernel's code at line 92 of tnum.c first computes α = P.v | P.m, the bits that may be 1 in a member of P, and β likewise for Q. It then returns R = (v, m) with v = P.v & Q.v and m = α & β & ~v.

The claim is the refresher's soundness condition for this operation. Take any width n, any well-formed n-bit tnums P and Q, any x in γ(P) and any y in γ(Q). Then x & y must be a member of R: (x & y) & ~m == v.

One piece of notation keeps the steps short. We write a ⊑ b, read "a lies under b", when every bit set in a is also set in b, that is, when a & ~b == 0. Two facts about the relation carry the proof. ANDing both sides with the same word keeps it, and a ⊑ b makes a & b equal to a.

Figure 15.3 sets out the six steps. The first two place each input between the tnum's known 1s and the bits that may be 1. Membership says that P.v is x with the unknown bits cleared, so P.v lies under x. Splitting x into its known part P.v and its unknown part x & P.m shows that x lies under α.

ANDing those relations gives steps 3 and 4, a floor and a ceiling for x & y. Step 5 is the claim itself. By De Morgan's law ~m is ~(α & β) | v, which splits (x & y) & ~m into two parts; the ceiling makes the first 0 and the floor makes the second v.

Step 6 adds that the result is well-formed, which matters because R becomes the input of the next instruction's operation. No step mentions the width, so the argument holds for every n at once, and no step uses the well-formedness of P or Q, which membership already implies. Read bit by bit, the code says that a bit of the result is known 1 when it is known 1 in both inputs. It is unknown when it may be 1 in both and is not known 1, and every other bit is known 0.

The right-hand column is the visible link between proof and checker: steps.py tries each step's claim in all 65,536 four-bit cases, and every true step holds in all of them. The false step in the last row, the rule of the refresher's broken tnum_and_both, fails in 27,120 cases.

Those counts reveal a shortcut, because 65,536 is 164 and 38,416 is 144, the one-bit counts raised to the fourth power. Every word in this claim is computed bit by bit from the same bit of the inputs, so checking the sixteen one-bit cases already proves it for every width. The same argument shows that tnum_and() is as tight as a tnum can be. tnum_add() has no such shortcut, because a carry ties each bit of the sum to all the bits below it.

Read with · Sound, Precise, and Fast Abstract Interpretation with Tristate Numbers, §III-B and Appendices A and D, Vishwanathan, Shachnai, Narayana and Nagarakatte, CGO 2022 (arXiv version 3, 15 December 2021)

What it is. The proof that tnum_add() is sound and as precise as a tnum can be at every width, the paper's Theorem 6, built on four lemmas about carries, with the proofs of the lemmas and the solver encoding in the appendices.

Why now. It is on the list because it is the proof this chapter declined to write: after tnum_and() bit by bit, it shows what a carry adds to the argument.

  1. §III-B up to Lemma 2, with Figure 2. The example 10x0 + 10x1 = 10xx1 in three columns: by hand, the kernel's code, and the carry sequence. Fifteen minutes.
  2. Lemmas 2 to 5 and Theorem 6. The fewest carries come from adding the values, the most from adding the values with every unknown bit set, and the positions where the two carry sequences differ are the unknown carries. Twenty minutes.
  3. Appendix A, then Appendix D. The propositional proofs of the lemmas, and the Z3 encoding with the random tests that compared it with the kernel's C. Thirty minutes.

Skip. §III-C and Appendix B, on the new multiplication, and Appendices E and F, until a change to tnum_mul() is on the table.

The figure. Figure 2(c), where the minimum carries 10000 and the maximum carries 10100 differ in one place, so the carry sequence is 10x00 and the sum has two unknown bits.

Carry in. Two questions; their answers are in the key under chapter 15.

  1. Lemma 2 says that sv = P.v + Q.v produces the fewest carries of any concrete addition p + q from P and Q. Why can no such addition carry less, and which addition does Lemma 3 say carries most?
  2. In Figure 2, why is the carry into bit 2 of 10x0 + 10x1 unknown, and why does the proof of tnum_and() need nothing like Lemma 5?

About 65 minutes · VERIFIER

The same claim as a query

A solver searches for values that make formulas true, so a claim that should hold for every input is handed over turned round, as the refresher explained. Figure 15.4 shows the shape, and Figure 15.5 is the whole script. The variables are six bit-vectors of the chosen width: the two halves of P and of Q, and the two concrete inputs. The function tnum_and() is the kernel's four lines with the C types removed, because Python's |, & and ~ build Z3 expressions when their operands are bit-vectors. Two s.add() lines state the assumptions, and the third states that z = x & y is not a member of R.

An answer from such a query holds for one width only, and checking a claim at a fixed width is what the tnum paper calls bounded verification. Width is also what the solver pays for. Z3 decides bit-vector formulas mostly by bit-blasting, turning each bit into a Boolean variable and each operation into clauses over those variables (Programming Z3, §3.4.1). An AND becomes one small clause set per bit with nothing linking the bits, which fits the 2 to 6 ms that tnum_and() takes at every width, while an addition becomes a ripple-carry adder whose carries tie the bits together.

Figure 15.6 plots the cost against width. The solver's time for tnum_add() rises from 0.012 s at 8 bits to 0.77 s at 64 and its memory from 25.9 MB to 30.3 MB, by its own count. The multiplication that Linux used until 2021 is another matter, since tnum.c in 5.12 multiplied by a loop of tnum additions. Encoded with that loop unrolled once per bit, it is proved at 8 bits in 13 s. At 16 bits Z3 gives up at the 60-second limit we set and answers unknown, and the tnum paper let it run 24 hours at that width without an answer.

A wrong operation turns the answer to sat, and the model is the evidence. Figure 15.7 asks about tnum_and_broken(), which sets α to P.v and so forgets the bits that are unknown in P. Z3 picks a P with every bit unknown and a Q of all 1s, and the values x = y = 11111111.

The broken α is 0, so R claims the result is the constant 00000000 while the real x & y is 11111111. Each bit of z is one that step 2 of the proof would have placed under α. Reading a model means finding that bit and naming the step of the proof the code skipped.

A bug that shipped: the 32-bit bounds of AND, OR and XOR

Before Linux 5.7 the verifier could not follow 32-bit arithmetic and jumps closely, and programs that should have verified were refused, as the commit that changed it says. John Fastabend's commit 3f50f132d840 of 30 March 2020, "bpf: Verifier, do explicit ALU32 bounds tracking", released in 5.7, gave each register signed and unsigned bounds for its low 32 bits as well. It added one function per operator, such as scalar32_min_max_and(). Yonghong Song's 2921c90d4718 added scalar32_min_max_xor() in August 2020, released in 5.10.

The 32-bit functions for AND and OR, and then XOR, returned at once when the low halves of the source and the result were known. Their comment states the assumption: the 64-bit function, called next, would set the bounds.

The assumption was false whenever the low halves were known and the upper halves were not. Daniel Borkmann's fix, 049c4e13714e of 10 May 2021, entered 5.13-rc4 and the stable releases 5.12.4, 5.11.21 and 5.10.37, all checked against the source at those tags on git.kernel.org. The flaw is CVE-2021-3490, and the commit credits reports by Manfred Paul and by Thadeu Lima de Souza Cascardo.

Wrong bounds break the verifier's promise directly. As the section "A pointer plus a number, checked at the access" showed, the verifier allows an access at a pointer plus a scalar when the scalar's bounds keep it inside the object. A bound that leaves out a value the register can really hold therefore lets the check pass for that value. That is the soundness bug's cell of Figure 14.1.

The specification the verifier needs is a claim about every input. For every pair of registers the verifier could describe before the instruction, and every pair of values inside those descriptions, the low 32 bits of the result must lie inside the 32-bit bounds the kernel computes, signed and unsigned. Figure 15.8 sets the C of scalar32_min_max_and() in v5.10 beside its encoding in book/labs/proof/cve.py, which encodes AND, OR and XOR three times each: as v5.10 had them, as the fix left them in 5.13, and as v7.2 has them. A return in the middle of the C becomes a choice at the end of the Python, because a formula has no control flow, and each C comparison has to be read for its signedness before it is written down.

A faithful encoding needs three things beyond the function itself. First, dst_known tests the destination after its tnum has been overwritten with the result of tnum_and() (line 6372 of v5.10), so it asks whether the result's low half is known. Second, scalar_min_max_and() runs next and, when both whole registers are known, calls __mark_reg_known(), which sets the 32-bit bounds as well; there the comment's assumption held. Third, the registers arrive tidied, and the encoding must say how.

An invariant is a fact about the verifier's state that every step leaves true, so the next step may rely on it. After each arithmetic instruction, __reg32_deduce_bounds() (line 1165 of v5.10) makes the signed and unsigned 32-bit ranges equal whenever either one stays on one side of the sign boundary. Then __reg_bound_offset() (line 1240) narrows the tnum to what the unsigned range allows. Without those two invariants, Z3 reports counterexamples against the fixed code as well, in states the verifier never builds. The difficulty is general: one operator cannot be judged apart from the code that tidies its output, which is the problem the work of the next chapter takes on.

Figure 15.9 gives the outcome. Z3 answers sat for all three functions of v5.10 in 0.01 to 0.03 s, and unsat for the fixed 5.13 and for v7.2.

Asked for the smallest counterexample, with bounds as tight as the tnum allows so that the numbers read easily, it returns one for AND. The destination holds 1, known in all 64 bits, and the source has its low half known 0 and bit 32 unknown. The low halves of both operands are known, so v5.10 returns early and keeps the destination's bounds of [1, 1], while the real result is 0. The source is not known in all 64 bits, so the 64-bit function repairs nothing.

The tidy-up that follows takes the larger of each pair of minima and the smaller of each pair of maxima, so it can narrow bounds but never widen them. Here it leaves the impossible state of the fixing commit's own log, a minimum of 1 above a maximum of 0. For OR, Z3 finds the mirror case, a destination of 0 and a source whose low half is 1, with bounds kept at [0, 0] and a real result of 1. The commit's own registers, a destination (0x1; 0xffffffff00000000) and the constant 0x100000002, give the same pattern, and cve.py --example evaluates them in all three kernels.

What v7.2 computes for the same registers

In v7.2 each early return calls __mark_reg32_known() (lines 14170, 14214 and 14257 of verifier.c), and the 32-bit bounds are a single circular range, r32, which chapter 6 introduced. scalar32_min_max_and() at line 14161 sets that arc with reg_set_urange32(), from the result tnum's value up to the smaller of the two unsigned maxima, and _or() and _xor() at lines 14205 and 14249 follow the same pattern. The v7.2 encoding needs neither of the tidy-up invariants to come out unsat, because one arc has no second range that could disagree with it.

The running kernel agrees with the formulas. book/labs/proof/v72-log.py builds a socket filter without a compiler and loads it. The filter gives R2 the value of the commit's example, (0x1; 0xffffffff00000000), ANDs it with 0x100000002 and returns 0, reading no memory, and the script prints the verifier's log for the AND. Figure 15.10 shows the result: smin32, smax32 and umax32 are 0, and the log leaves out umin32 because it is 0, the value the commit's "after" line has and the arc of cve.py --example.

What it costs

CPU
AMD Ryzen 7 8845HS, Python 3.14.10, z3-solver 5.4.1, 13 November 2026. The exhaustive check costs about 0.23 µs a case and sixteen times more for each bit: 0.02 s at 4 bits, 3.8 s at 6, 987 s at 8 for tnum_and(). Z3 proved tnum_and() in 2 to 6 ms at every width, tnum_add() in 0.012, 0.062, 0.131 and 0.771 s at 8, 16, 32 and 64 bits (medians of five) and tnum_sub() in 2.7 s at 64; the multiplication of 5.12 took 13 s at 8 bits and had no answer in 60 s at 16. The nine CVE queries took 1.4 s together, with Python's start-up.
Memory
Z3 counted at most 26.0 MB for tnum_and() and 30.3 MB for tnum_add() at 64 bits; the whole Python process peaked at 61, 67 and 77 MB for those two and the nine CVE queries. The checker stayed under 18 MB, since it holds one pair's values at a time.
Script length
tnum_add() is 11 lines of C and 4 of Python. cve.py has 168 lines of code for about 210 lines of C from two kernels: the functions under test and the tidy-up around them.

Check every case at 4 to 8 bits whenever an abstract operation changes, since it needs no tools and runs in seconds. Before posting the change, prove it with a solver at 64 and 32 bits, encoding the code that runs around it; write a proof on paper for a new algorithm whose query does not finish, as the tnum paper did for multiplication, or for a bitwise operation, where the one-bit check already is one.

When it goes wrong

Most failures in Figure 15.11 are failures of fidelity, where the formula says something other than the code. A bogus counterexample is the lucky case, because its model can be checked by hand against the C, as we did for the 32-bit bounds. The dangerous case is an unsat from a formula that says too little, assumes too much or speaks of another width, since nothing in the answer reveals it. For that reason the tnum paper ran its encodings against the kernel's C on random inputs (Appendix D). Each row's command prints its evidence within two seconds, except the timeout, which waits for the limit it is given.

Prove it two ways · A second tnum operation, then a broken one

~45 min · write, then run · needs python3 and a venv with z3-solver; no root

Setup. We ran Z3 from a virtual environment in the book's folder. From book/, run python -m venv .venv and then .venv/bin/pip install z3-solver; we used z3-solver 5.4.1 with Python 3.14.10. Then, from the repository root, PY=book/.venv/bin/python.

Part 1. Pick tnum_or(), tnum_xor() or tnum_sub() from kernel/bpf/tnum.c (lines 102, 111 and 75 in v7.2). Copy book/labs/proof/lab.py, replace its op() and concrete() with your operation and the instruction's effect on numbers, and run python3 -I lab.py check for every four-bit case and $PY -I lab.py prove for Z3 at 64 bits.

Part 2. Break your operation by dropping one term, such as | qm in the mask of tnum_xor() or chi in tnum_sub(). Run both checks again and read Z3's counterexample at eight bits with $PY -I lab.py prove 8.

Done when. You have unsat at 64 bits for the real operation, a counterexample from both checks for the broken one, and a sentence that names the bit of z outside R and says why the dropped term would have marked it unknown.

Hint 1 · direction

The six operators & | ^ ~ + - work unchanged on Python integers and on Z3 bit-vectors, which is why one op() serves both checks. Keep the kernel's variable names so the code can be compared line by line.

Hint 2 · mechanism

For tnum_xor(), the value is pv ^ qv with the unknown bits cleared and the mask is pm | qm. A bit of x ^ y is unknown when it is unknown in either input.

Hint 3 · nearly there

In the model, look for a bit where Q is x. The broken mask copies P's mask only, so R claims to know that bit, and the y Z3 picked has the other value there.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 15.

Check yourself

  1. Predict the value: how many cases (P, x, Q, y) does steps.py try at five bits, and in how many of them does the false step of Figure 15.3 hold?
  2. Sound or not: a patch drops & ~v from tnum_and(), so that the mask is α & β, on the grounds that a wider mask is safer. What does Z3 answer, and why?
  3. A colleague's Z3 query for a new range operation answers unsat in 10 ms, yet a selftest later shows a bound that misses a real value. Give two ways the query could be unsat while the C is wrong.
  4. Predict the value: in the fixing commit's case, R2 is (0x1; 0xffffffff00000000) with 32-bit bounds [1, 1] and R3 is the constant 0x100000002. What 32-bit bounds does v5.10 give R2 after r2 &= r3, before and after __update_reg32_bounds(), and what does 5.13 give?
  5. Z3 answers unsat for the v7.2 encoding of scalar32_min_max_and(). What has been proved about the v7.2 verifier, and what has not?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 15.

Recap

Trying every case proves an abstract operation at small widths and grows sixteenfold a bit, 987 s at eight for tnum_and(). A proof on paper covers every width: with membership x & ~m == v, tnum_and() follows in six steps, each true in all 65,536 four-bit cases, and for a bitwise operation one bit suffices. A solver proves one width per query, tnum_add() at 64 bits in under a second, from the assumptions and the claim turned round, and a sat model names the bit the code got wrong. Encoded with the code around it and the verifier's invariants, the 32-bit bounds of v5.10 give a counterexample for AND, OR and XOR, the fix of 2021 and v7.2 give none, and the next chapter applies the same method to every range operation of the verifier at once.

New words in this chapter

membership relation
the test x & ~m == v, true when the number x is one of the values of the tnum (v, m), agreeing with v on every known bit
well-formed tnum
one with no 1 under its own mask, v & m == 0
bounded verification
checking a claim for every input of one fixed bit width, as a solver query does; it says nothing about other widths
bit-blasting
turning each bit into a Boolean variable and each operation into clauses
invariant
a fact about the state that every step leaves true

Chapter 16

Reading Agni: proving Linux's range analysis

Agni compiles the verifier's own C into logic, checks each arithmetic and branch operator of the range analysis against a claim of soundness on sixteen kernels, and writes a short program for most of the bugs it finds. We read how it does that, re-derive one of its verdicts by hand, and mark what its proofs leave out, v7.2 included.

Spine. In chapter 15 we wrote one function of the verifier into Z3 by hand and found CVE-2021-3490, with two of the verifier's invariants assumed rather than proved. Agni takes the hand out: its formulas come from verifier.c itself, each operator is checked together with the code that tidies its output, and one run covers a whole kernel.

29 min · VERIFIER

Sixteen kernels, two verdicts each

The paper is Verifying the Verifier: eBPF Range Analysis Verification by Harishankar Vishwanathan, Matan Shachnai, Srinivas Narayana and Santosh Nagarakatte, presented at CAV 2023. We read the authors' copy of 30 May 2023 and the repository of its tool, Agni, on GitHub. It checks the part of the verifier that chapter 6 followed through the log: the tnum and the ranges of every scalar register, and the code that updates them. Its scope is 36 instructions, the operations add, sub, and, or, xor and the three shifts in 64-bit and 32-bit form, and ten conditional jumps in both forms.

Figure 16.1 gives the verdicts for seven of the sixteen kernels it checked, from 4.14 to 5.19. Each kernel was checked twice, against a general specification, gen, and a refined one, sro, whose difference is the subject of the section "The shared tail, and bugs no program reaches". Under gen no kernel passed, 5.19 included, while under sro every kernel from 5.13 on passed and every older one failed. The paper reads the second result as a proof that recent kernels are sound with respect to value tracking.

A violation in the table is one operator whose output misses a value the program can really produce, counted once for each of the five descriptions it misses. For each violation left under sro, Agni searched for an eBPF program that reaches it and found one for about 97 percent, never longer than three instructions. Among them the authors count 27 bugs that nobody had reported, all fixed by then in patches written for other reasons. On their test machine, 90 percent of the operators were checked within about 100 minutes, and the slowest checks ran for 2,000 minutes or more.

The artifact's README at tag v1.0 walks through one such search on Linux 5.9, and Figure 16.2 quotes it. For the 64-bit OR the refined check fails in the two 32-bit descriptions, and the search names a skeleton of two instructions, a signed comparison (JSLE) followed by the OR. Its authors built a whole program around that skeleton and ran it in a virtual machine with 5.9. After the OR, R1's tnum knows all 32 low bits to be 1, so the low half is 0xffffffff, or −1 read as signed. The 32-bit bounds say [−1, −2], a range with no value in it.

The log fits the early return of chapter 15. Both low halves are known, so scalar32_min_max_or() keeps the destination's old 32-bit bounds and the tidy-up then narrows them past each other, until commit 049c4e13714e removed the return in 5.13-rc4 as the fix for CVE-2021-3490. What differs is the route. The previous chapter reached the bug by writing one function as a formula and checking it, whereas Agni reached it, with a program, from the compiled C of every operator, run kernel by kernel.

Five descriptions, one claim

The refresher of chapter 14 wrote soundness for one abstract domain: for every x in γ(A) and every y in γ(B), the result of the real operation lies in γ of the abstract one. Chapter 15 proved that claim for tnum_and() alone. The verifier, however, keeps five abstract values for every scalar, as chapter 6 showed. They are the tnum and four ranges, unsigned and signed, for all 64 bits and for the low 32, which Agni names u64, s64, u32 and s32; kernels before 5.7, which added the 32-bit ranges, have only three.

Taken together the five form a product domain, a domain whose values are tuples with one value from each of several domains and whose γ is the intersection of what the parts allow (§2 of the paper). A register P stands for γt(Pt) ∩ γu64(Pu64) ∩ … ∩ γs32(Ps32), so a number belongs to P only if all five descriptions allow it. In the textbook form of such a domain each component has operators of its own, and separate reduction functions narrow one component with another, so that each piece can be proved sound alone.

The kernel does not divide its code that way, and Figure 16.3 follows one 64-bit AND to show where. tnum_and() works on tnums alone, but scalar32_min_max_and() and scalar_min_max_and() take the unsigned minimum from the tnum just computed and copy the signed range from the unsigned one. Code that reads the output of one domain while it computes another is neither an operator of one domain nor a reduction, which takes finished values (Figure 2(b) of the paper). With no pieces to prove one at a time, Agni proves each instruction's code in a single query, which the paper calls one-shot reasoning.

The claim, the paper's Equation 2, lets x range over the numbers that all five descriptions of P allow and y over those of Q, and asks it for each description D of the output in turn.

∀P, Q, ∀x ∈ γ(P), ∀y ∈ γ(Q) :  x & y ∈ γD(AND(P, Q)D).

Here AND is the kernel's whole operator, including the tail of three calls that every ALU operator ends with, and Figure 16.4 sets the claim beside the one of chapter 15 and the variants that follow. A conditional jump writes no register, yet the verifier learns something on each side of it, since after if r1 < r2 the taken branch may lower r1's maximum. Its code therefore returns both registers for both outcomes, twenty abstract values, and the claim for a jump (Equation 3) is that the real x and y lie in the refined values of the branch they take.

The shared tail, and bugs no program reaches

Under Equation 2 every kernel failed, and in 5.19 the six bitwise operators, and, or and xor in both widths, still failed. The precondition was too generous. It admits any five descriptions that share a number, including combinations that no program produces, such as a signed range of [0, 10] beside an unsigned range that reaches past 263.

Such combinations never reach an operator because of the tail. Every ALU operator ends with the same three calls, __update_reg_bounds(), __reg_deduce_bounds() and __reg_bound_offset(), which 5.19 gathered into reg_bounds_sync(), and the paper calls them the shared suffix. Agni treats the suffix as a shared refinement operator, sro for short, a function that narrows each description of a register by the others and runs on every register an operator returns. A program starts with registers that hold constants or unknown values, which the tail leaves unchanged (the authors checked this with the solver), so every register an operator receives has passed through it.

The refined specification, Equation 4, therefore passes the inputs through the tail first, so that x must lie in γ(sro(P)) and y in γ(sro(Q)). It removed every violation from 5.13 to 5.19 and about 6.8 percent of them in older kernels. What gen reports and sro does not is latent unsoundness, a wrong output that an operator gives for inputs no program can feed it, because those inputs never come out of the tail.

Latent did not stay acceptable for long. In AND, OR and XOR the signed range was copied from the unsigned one whenever neither input's signed minimum was negative, which gives a minimum above the maximum when the unsigned range crosses 263. Harishankar Vishwanathan's commit 1f586614f3ff, "bpf: Harden and/or/xor value tracking in verifier", released in 6.10, copies the range only when it stays on one side of the sign boundary. Its message says that earlier work, the CAV paper among it, had reported the case, and that Agni counted it as a false positive because its inputs pass through the tail.

The patch had a second purpose, which Figure 16.5 shows from the follow-up paper of SAS 2024. As the tail grew, a formula holding operator and tail together took 36 hours for 5.19 and 6.3, and from 6.4 on the solver ran for weeks and timed out without an answer. Once every operator is sound alone, the operator and the tail can be proved apart, the tail with the identity as its real operation, and the two results compose. Each kernel then took under 30 minutes, and the artifact's --modular option, which works this way, refuses AND, OR and XOR on kernels before 6.10.

From verifier.c to a formula

Writing each operator out by hand, as chapter 15 did for one, would have to be repeated for every kernel, and the paper calls it tedious and error-prone. Agni compiles the verifier instead, along the path of Figure 16.6. A small wrapper for each instruction marks two registers as scalars and calls adjust_scalar_min_max_vals() with a fixed opcode, and clang turns verifier.c, the wrappers and tnum.c into LLVM IR.

Custom passes then remove every function that writes no register state and inline every call that remains, and LLVM's constant propagation and dead-code elimination delete every case of the opcode switch but one. Inlining everything works because no function on these paths recurses or loops, so each instruction becomes a single function whose control flow is acyclic, and the tool stops with an error when that is not so. A pass taken from the SeaHorn verifier turns each memcpy into plain stores.

The LLVMToSMT pass writes the result in SMT-LIB. Each IR value becomes a bit-vector, each basic block is guarded by the conditions of the paths into it, and a phi node selects its input by the condition of the edge it arrived on. Memory needs no byte array, because these functions reach it only through fields of struct bpf_reg_state. The pass keeps a tree of bit-vectors for each of the two registers and makes a new tree at each store, following the versions of memory that LLVM's MemorySSA analysis computes.

Figure 16.7 shows the result for the 64-bit AND of 5.10 as the repository keeps it, 1,839 lines that declare 548 bit-vectors and make a single assertion. Not all of the path is automatic. The jumps go through wrappers that copy part of check_cond_jmp_op() by hand, in five versions for ranges of kernels from 5.3-rc1 to 6.10-rc5. The tail has wrappers of its own, and when the kernel changes those functions a person writes another copy.

From a failed check to a program

A violation that survives Equation 4 may still be latent, because the tail removes only some of the impossible inputs. Agni settles the question by building a program that reaches the violation, a search the paper calls differential synthesis, finding a program whose real run and whose abstract interpretation by the verifier disagree.

A register's five descriptions are initial when they describe a constant or an entirely unknown value, the only two kinds of register a program starts with. For one instruction, Equation 5 asks Z3 for two initial registers, and values in them, that put the result outside its descriptions. The question has a single ∃ and is easier than the ∀∃ of most synthesis problems, since one input and one program suffice.

For a program of k instructions, Agni enumerates the opcodes of the first k − 1, which form the skeleton. The solver then draws every operand from an initial register or an earlier result, each of which must hold its real value (Equation 6). A branch becomes a choice whose two targets both lead to the next slot, so that its refined registers can feed later instructions (Equation 7).

The search tries one instruction, then two, then three, and at four it timed out. For 5.5 no violation could be shown by a single instruction, and for one known bug Agni produced a program of two instructions where the published proof of concept used four. The authors compiled and booted each kernel in QEMU, ran the programs, and found the verifier's log and the real values in agreement with the solver's model in every case they checked. A violation with no program stays open, since a program of four or more instructions may reach it, or it may be latent after all.

Read with · Verifying the Verifier: eBPF Range Analysis Verification, §2 and §4 to §7, Vishwanathan, Shachnai, Narayana and Nagarakatte, CAV 2023 (authors' copy, 30 May 2023)

What it is. The method behind the results at which the card in chapter 6 stopped: the product domain, the three specifications, the translation from C and the search for programs.

Why now. It is on the list because this chapter has given each part a picture, and the paper gives each part its equation, so the two can be read side by side.

  1. §2 from "Combining multiple abstract domains" to the end, with Figure 2. The Cartesian product, γ as an intersection, reduction operators, and in Figure 2(d) why the kernel's code fits neither. Fifteen minutes.
  2. §4.1 and §4.2, Equations 1 to 4, with Figure 3. Soundness for one domain, for several, for a jump with four outputs, and with the shared suffix as a precondition. Twenty-five minutes.
  3. §4.3, Equations 5 to 7, then §6 from "Generating POCs". Initial values, skeletons, branches turned into choices, and what the search found. Twenty minutes.
  4. §5 with Figure 4, then §7. The passes, MemorySSA and the trees of bit-vectors, then the four caveats. Twenty-five minutes.

Skip. §1 and §3 if the card in chapter 6 was read, and §8 apart from its paragraph on the closest related work.

The figure. Figure 2(c) beside 2(d): grey boxes of modular reasoning, one per domain and one for the reduction, against the kernel's single box that mixes them, which is why Agni reasons one-shot.

Carry in. Three questions; their answers are in the key under chapter 16.

  1. In Equation 5, why are both abstract operands constrained with init(), and what does a model of the formula give?
  2. §5 inlines every function that adjust_scalar_min_max_vals() calls and models memory without a byte array. What about the verifier's code makes each of those possible?
  3. Figure 5(b) shows that no violation in 5.5 could be shown by a single instruction, and that 8 of its 30 could not be shown at all. What does each of those facts say?

About 85 minutes · VERIFIER

One verdict, re-derived by hand

To see what such a verdict asserts, we re-derived Agni's verdicts for the 64-bit AND with the method of chapter 15, as a formula written by hand. book/labs/agni/repro.py encodes the taint check at the top of adjust_scalar_min_max_vals(), then tnum_and(), scalar32_min_max_and(), scalar_min_max_and() and the tail, from verifier.c of v5.12 and v5.13 and tnum.c of v5.13, with the five membership tests of Agni's checker. It takes 97 lines of Python for about 260 lines of C. Diffing those functions between the two versions came first, and only the early return of Figure 16.8 differs.

A hand encoding is what Agni exists to avoid, and writing this one shows the cost. Each comparison had to be read for its signedness again, and the tail had to be copied in its order for that kernel. In 5.12 the tail ends by narrowing the tnum and does not narrow the bounds again, while v7.2's tail does. The v7.2 order copied into a 5.12 encoding would describe a kernel that never existed, and nothing in the solver's answer would say so.

Figure 16.9 gives the verdicts, which agree with Agni's. Under sro, 5.12 fails in u32 and s32 and holds in u64, s64 and the tnum, the pattern the artifact's README reports for AND on 5.9, and 5.13 holds in all five. Under gen, 5.13 fails in s64 and s32, the latent case that commit 1f586614f3ff removed, with signed minima of zero or more beside an unsigned maximum above 263. Modular mode, the operator without its tail, fails for 6.9 and holds for 6.10, which is SAS 2024's before and after for that commit.

The counterexample for 5.12, asked for small numbers with --small, is the early return once more. Both low halves are known after tnum_and(), so 5.12 keeps the destination's 32-bit bounds of [6, 6]. The __update_reg_bounds() call at the end of scalar_min_max_and() then lowers the maximum to 4, the value the new tnum allows, and leaves u32 at [6, 4], while the real low half of x & y is 4.

With --synth the script runs Equation 6 with AND as the only instruction, and Figure 16.10 shows the result. One instruction cannot reach the bug, since an unknown register has an unknown low half and a constant is known in all 64 bits. Two can, because an unknown value ANDed with 0x200000000 is known to be 0 in its low half with one unknown bit above it, and a constant ANDed with that register takes the early return. For 5.13 both searches answer unsat.

The hand encoding is small and fast. The five sro queries for 5.12 take about one second, against 31 seconds for AND on 5.9 in the artifact's README on its authors' machine. The query is 64,414 bytes of SMT-LIB, against 100,001 bytes for Agni's AND on 5.10 plus 48,684 for its tail. The difference comes from choices a person made, a few variables per register and shared subterms, where Agni keeps one variable per IR value. The work moved from the solver to whoever reads the C, and that reader is the part Agni removes.

What a proof by Agni leaves out

The paper's §7 lists four caveats. Only range analysis is covered, so register liveness and the handling of speculative execution are outside. Multiplication is left out because its formula times out at 64 bits, and it was checked with 8-bit vectors only. The trusted computing base, the software that must be correct for a proof to hold, includes LLVM, Z3 and the translation passes, which the authors unit-tested, and the synthesis is incomplete.

The repository narrows the scope further, as Figure 16.11 lists. Division, modulo, negation and the unconditional jump are marked to be skipped, and every wrapper sets both registers to SCALAR_VALUE, so pointer arithmetic, which adjust_ptr_min_max_vals() handles, never enters a formula. Nor do the walk and its pruning, precision tracking, the JIT or the checks on helper and kfunc arguments. Agni proves that the verifier's descriptions of numbers are sound for the instructions it encodes, in the kernels it has checked, if its translation and its glue are right; how the verifier then uses those descriptions lies outside the proof.

One gap appeared after publication. A JNE whose two registers had disjoint ranges produced impossible bounds on the branch that cannot run. Agni's claim for jumps looks only at the branch the real values take, so it accepted them (issue 15 of the repository, November 2023). Such a branch can still run speculatively, which is why the verifier checks it, and the --weak_spec option added in July 2024 also requires well-formed outputs on the other side.

Linux v7.2 differs from every kernel Agni has checked. Eduard Zingerman's commit 256f0071f9b6 of April 2026, first released in v7.2, introduced the circular ranges of chapter 6. A register now holds a tnum and two arcs, r64 and r32, in place of four pairs of bounds (Figure 16.12). Agni's membership tests are written for five descriptions and would need rewriting before it could check v7.2. The commit says that the arc operations were verified with the CBMC model checker, with the tests kept in a separate repository.

Agni's own daily run, over eight trees, passed for the stable kernels 5.4.y to 6.12.y until its last run on 14 May 2026. On bpf-next its jump jobs began to fail on 4 April 2026. By 14 May every job for that tree failed, those we inspected before any formula was written, and GitHub then switched the schedule off for inactivity. The public record holds no Agni verdict for v7.2.

The kernel meanwhile came to rely on the result. Commit b254c6d816e5, in v7.1, refines both sides of every branch and treats an ill-formed result as proof that a side is dead, "because the branch operators are sound (verified with Agni)". v7.2 keeps that reasoning in the comment above simulate_both_branches_taken() at line 15187 of verifier.c. On the public record, its pruning of dead branches therefore rests on Agni's checks of the earlier ranges and on CBMC's checks of the arc operations.

What it costs

CPU
Agni on two 10-core Skylake processors at 2.2 GHz: 90 percent of operators in about 100 minutes (CAV 2023); a whole kernel 2.5 hours for 4.14, 36 hours for 5.19, and no answer after weeks from 6.4 on, with operator and tail in one formula; and under 5, 15 or 30 minutes with them apart (SAS 2024). The README's run on 5.9: AND in 9.5 s (gen) and 31 s (sro), JEQ in 3,911 s (sro). Our reproduction, on an AMD Ryzen 7 8845HS with Python 3.14.10 and z3-solver 5.4.1, 13 November 2026, medians of five runs: five sro queries 1.0 s for 5.12 and 0.88 s for 5.13, gen 0.30 s, modular 0.07 to 0.10 s; the two-instruction search 2.3 s for 5.12 and 3.7 s to answer unsat for 5.13.
Memory
The reproduction's Python process peaked at 92 to 100 MB. The paper names its machine's 192 GB and gives no peak for Agni.
Size
Agni is about 5,000 lines (LSFMM+BPF 2025 slides). Its formulas for 5.10: AND 100,001 bytes, the tail 48,684, JLT 738,840; for 6.12 the tail is 180,891 bytes and JLT 2,160,687. Ours: 97 lines of Python for about 260 lines of C, a 64,414-byte query, 392 lines in the script.
Upkeep
Five copies of the jump code and three of the tail, kept by hand; a daily run of 184 jobs over eight trees, off since 14 May 2026.

Before posting a change to a range operator or to the tail, run Agni in modular mode on the patched tree for the operators the change touches and for BPF_SYNC, which takes minutes, and run the selftests; a change to how ranges are stored or how branches refine needs new glue or a proof of its own, as the arcs got from CBMC, and the cover letter should say which. From "Agni found no bug in X", conclude only that the encoded ALU and jump operators of X are sound at 64 bits under its specification; it says nothing about a kernel it was not run on, nor about pointers, pruning or multiplication.

When it goes wrong

The first two rows of Figure 16.13 are what a hand reproduction most often gets wrong: an encoding that drops the tail, from the inputs or from the operator, reports bugs the kernel does not have. Such a report can at least be checked, by asking the refined question or by searching for a program. The next four rows are the opposite danger, a verdict read for more than it covers. No command run on the verdict will reveal that, and only a look at the specification, the kernel version and the list of encoded instructions settles it.

Run it, then read it · One operator on two kernels

~30 min · run, then read · needs python3 and the venv of Lab 15.1; no root

Task. Agni's refined check finds the 64-bit AND unsound in 5.12 and sound in 5.13 (Figure 16.1). From the repository root, with PY=book/.venv/bin/python, run $PY -I book/labs/agni/repro.py 5.12 --small and $PY -I book/labs/agni/repro.py 5.13. For the 5.12 counterexample, name the line of v5.12's verifier.c that kept the destination's 32-bit bounds and the call that narrowed them, with the bounds before and after. Then run 5.13 with --gen and explain why its counterexample is no bug of 5.13.

Done when. You have the two verdict lines, a sentence that names the early return and the narrowing call with the bounds [6, 6] and [6, 4], and a sentence that explains the gen counterexample from its signed and unsigned ranges.

Hint 1 · direction

The output's u32 range has its minimum above its maximum. Of the two ways through scalar32_min_max_and(), one leaves the 32-bit bounds untouched.

Hint 2 · mechanism

A low half is known when the low 32 bits of the mask are 0, as in src (0x5; 0x100000000) and out (0x4; 0x100000000). In v5.12, scalar32_min_max_and() begins at line 6532 and scalar_min_max_and() ends with a call at line 6600.

Hint 3 · nearly there

In the gen run, compare dst's s64 range with its u64 maximum. With a signed minimum of zero or more, __reg64_deduce_bounds() in the tail would cut the unsigned maximum to the signed one.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 16.

Check yourself

  1. Predict the value: how many abstract values does the kernel's code return for one conditional jump in Agni's encoding, and how many for one ALU instruction? Give the arithmetic, and the counts for a kernel before 5.7.
  2. A colleague encodes the BPF_OR of 5.14 by hand, and Z3 returns an output whose s64 minimum is above its maximum, from inputs whose signed minima are 0 and whose unsigned maxima pass 263. Is 5.14 unsound, and what should they run before saying so?
  3. A service stays on 6.6 because Agni's daily run passed for 6.6.y in May 2026. One of its programs multiplies two values from a map and uses the product as an offset into a map value. What has Agni established about that program?
  4. Why could the authors not prove the range analysis the textbook way, one domain's operator at a time and then each reduction, and what made a split possible in 2024?
  5. A reader asks whether "the verifier is verified" holds for the v7.2 kernel on their laptop. What can be said, and on what evidence?

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 16.

Recap

Agni compiles the verifier's C for each of 36 ALU and jump instructions into one SMT formula and checks it against a claim of soundness over the product of the five descriptions, one query per description. Under the general claim every kernel from 4.14 to 5.19 failed; with the inputs passed through the tail that every operator ends with, the refined claim proved 5.13 to 5.19 sound and left the rest of the general claim's reports as latent unsoundness. For the violations that remain, differential synthesis found programs of at most three instructions for about 97 percent, and our hand encoding of the 64-bit AND re-derives the verdicts for 5.12, 5.13, 6.9 and 6.10 in about a second, at the price of reading every line of C. The proofs cover value tracking for the encoded instructions only, and no Agni run on v7.2, whose ranges are arcs, is public, although v7.1 and v7.2 rely on the branch operators being sound. The next chapter reads a verifier built the other way, from abstract interpretation outward, where Linux's grew by patches.

New words in this chapter

product domain
tuples of abstract values, one per domain; a tuple stands for the numbers all its parts allow
shared refinement operator
the tail every ALU operator ends with, which narrows each description by the others
latent unsoundness
a wrong output for inputs that no program can produce
differential synthesis
a search for a program whose real run and abstract interpretation disagree
trusted computing base
the software that must be correct for a proof to hold; for Agni, LLVM, Z3, its passes and its wrappers

Chapter 17

Reading PREVAIL: a verifier built on abstract interpretation

PREVAIL checks an eBPF program the way the textbooks of the refresher describe: it joins the states of paths where they meet, widens at loops, and keeps relations between a packet pointer and the packet's end, so that a loop costs it the same at any bound. We read its PLDI 2019 paper in the paper's own notation, set a toy of its fixpoint beside a toy of Linux's walk on one packet loop, and weigh what each design buys, what it costs and where PREVAIL runs today.
