Spine. Chapter 16 proved Linux's range analysis after the fact, one operator at a time, and left the walk and its pruning outside the proof. PREVAIL starts from the other end, with an analysis built on the theory of chapter 14 from its first line and a soundness theorem for the whole method.

32 min · VERIFIER

One loop, two verifiers

The paper is Simple and Precise Static Analysis of Untrusted Linux Kernel Extensions by Elazar Gershuni, Nadav Amit, Arie Gurfinkel, Nina Narodytska, Jorge A. Navas, Noam Rinetzky, Leonid Ryzhyk and Mooly Sagiv, presented at PLDI in Phoenix in June 2019. We read the copy that the project's site links, dated 5 May 2019 and paginated as in the proceedings, and the repository of its tool, PREVAIL, at commit 97093b5b3264 of 13 November 2026. Its argument begins with loops, and so does ours, with a loop small enough to follow by hand through both verifiers.

Figure 17.1 shows it. An XDP program adds up the first N bytes of a packet, in two versions. sum_once checks once that N bytes are there and then loops, while sum_each checks in every round that the byte it is about to read lies before the end. We compiled both with clang 23 at four bounds and loaded them in a VM running Linux 7.2.15, reading the verifier's statistics as in the section "What the kernel reports about its walk".

Linux walks the loop once per round. Each round runs the seven slots from 8 to 14 with r3 known to the last bit. So sum_once costs seven instructions of walking per byte, 7N + 12 in all, and sum_each about ten. Verification took 0.13 ms at 16 bytes and 3.2 ms at 1,024 for sum_once, and 6.4 ms at 1,024 for sum_each, medians of three loads. The checkpoints grew from 4 to 105, about one every ten rounds, because inside a loop the walk saves a new one only after 20 jumps or 100 instructions (kernel/bpf/states.c, line 1397).

The last two lines of the figure show how the walk keeps the fact that makes the read in sum_each safe. After the check at slot 8, r0 prints as pkt(r=1) in the first round and pkt(r=2) in the second, since every packet pointer carries the number of bytes known to lie before the end (the section "A pointer plus a number, checked at the access"). That number changes every round, so no round's state falls within another's and the walk cannot stop early.

We did not build PREVAIL. In its place, book/labs/prevail/toy.py reads the same slots twice. Its abstract interpreter keeps one interval per register on the schedule PREVAIL uses at loop heads, and its walk follows one path at a time, as Linux does. The walk counts 124, 460, 1,804 and 7,180 instructions for sum_once and 168, 654, 2,568 and 10,254 for sum_each, the kernel's numbers to the instruction. The fixpoint evaluates 47 and 53 at every bound, and Figure 17.2 plots both.

The paper makes the same comparison at a larger scale. On a synthetic program with two strncmp loops, its Figure 11 shows the Linux 4.19 verifier's time climbing faster than the bound until the complexity limit stopped it at 69 iterations. PREVAIL's time grew in proportion. Our flat line hides a price: on sum_once as compiled the toy's fixpoint refuses the read at slot 10, and on sum_each the read at slot 9, both of which Linux proves.

The program as a graph of states

PREVAIL reads bytecode, as Linux does, because the compiler is no part of the trusted computing base (§2 of the paper). It turns the program into a control-flow graph over a core language, eBPFPL (§4.1). The commands are assignments, loads and stores of 1 to 8 bytes, a request for a shared region, and assume(B), which lets through only the states in which B holds. They sit on the graph's edges, so the two edges out of a conditional jump carry the assume of its test and of its negation. A value is a number or a pointer, and a pointer pairs a region (the context, the stack, the packet or a shared region such as a map value) with an offset.

The packet's start and end live in the context, yet the model keeps them in two registers that never change, data_start and data_end, which no instruction names. Such a register is a ghost variable, one that the analysis adds to describe the program and that the program never reads or writes. With it the pointer data + 8 of the paper's Table 2 becomes the pair (pkt, 8), and the packet check compares 8 with the end's offset, which is at most 64 KB, the bound Linux assumes (§6.1).

The analysis keeps one abstract state for each point of the graph, and a point's state is the join of the states its incoming edges bring. Figure 17.3 shows the states the toy keeps for sum_once at N = 16, with its test rewritten as r3 >= 16 for reasons the next section gives. The read at slot 10 is checked once, against a head state that holds r3 anywhere from 0 to 15, where the walk checked it sixteen times against one value each time.

An analysis is path-sensitive when it keeps a separate state for each path that reaches a point, as Linux's walk does until pruning shows that one path's state covers another's. PREVAIL is not, so its cost depends on the size of the graph and the price of the domain's operations. The number of paths does not enter, although on a loop with branches inside it multiplies with every round. The paper's bet, stated in §8, is that eBPF programs can be proved safe without path sensitivity.

Join, widen and narrow at the loop head

A loop head is the point where a back-edge lands, slot 8 in sum_once. Its state must hold for the first round and for every later one, so the analysis starts from what the entry brings, runs the body, joins what comes back and repeats until a round adds nothing. A state that one more round leaves unchanged is a fixpoint of the loop. Joining alone climbs one round at a time, as Figure 14.3 showed on four bits, and on our loop it would not end in practice. The sum in w2 grows by up to 255 a round, so its interval reaches the 32-bit ceiling only after about 16.8 million rounds; the toy, run with --widen-after 0, gives up after 100,000.

PREVAIL's schedule is in Extrapolator::compute_fixpoint() (src/crab/extrapolator.cpp, line 13), and the toy copies it. The first round back is joined, and from the second on the new state is widened against the old (widening_delay_ is 2). At the first widening it is also met with limits, registers within 32-bit ranges and offsets within their regions (calculate_constant_limits(), src/crab/ebpf_domain.cpp, line 164), a guess that later rounds keep only if the loop respects it. The climb stops on the first round whose result lies within the current state, and keeps that round's result. A descending phase follows, a meet with the next round and then narrowing, for at most 2,000,000 rounds.

A narrowing operator lowers a bound that widening raised to infinity to the value the next round gives it, and never raises one, so the descending phase can only gain precision. Figure 17.4 follows r3 at the head of sum_once. The join of round 1 gives [0, 1], and the widening of round 2 sends the upper bound to infinity. In round 3 the back-edge passes only the states where r3 >= 16 failed, so it brings [1, 15]. The round's result, [0, 15], lies within [0, +∞], and the climb stops there, which makes the read at slot 10 safe.

Two changes undo that. With --no-narrow the toy keeps the widened state, as the textbook widening of chapter 14 does, and the head stays at [0, +∞]. With the test as clang compiled it, r3 == 16, the back-edge carries the states where r3 is not 16. An interval cannot hold "any number but 16", since it is one unbroken stretch of the number line, so the round brings [1, +∞] and the read is refused. Both refusals are false alarms, and Linux raises neither, because in each round it knows r3 to the bit and decides the test.

The precision lost on the way shows elsewhere too. After the fixpoint the sum in w2 lies anywhere in [0, 232 − 1], where the walk leaves the loop knowing [0, 4,080]; no check reads the sum, so nothing is refused because of it. Linux has meanwhile borrowed a little of the idea. v7.2 compares a loop's state with the previous round's at the next call of an iterator, the return from a bpf_loop() callback and a may_goto (the section "Loops"). There widen_imprecise_scalars() (kernel/bpf/verifier.c, line 7494) forgets the range of every scalar that no check has needed yet, a widening straight to "any value".

Four domains in one state

Intervals alone were not enough for the authors either. §3 of the paper draws three observations from the programs they studied: the analysis must track relations between pairs of registers, it must track values spilled to the stack as if they were registers, and enumerating paths is becoming infeasible as programs grow. A relational domain is one whose abstract values relate two or more variables, and the paper tried three, from cheapest to most expressive: Zone, Octagon and Polyhedra.

The zone domain keeps constraints of the form x − y ≤ c for pairs of variables, and a bound for each variable alone. It stores them as a matrix, or as a graph whose edges carry the constants. New constraints come from adding the constants along a path and keeping the smallest sum, a shortest-path closure whose cost is at worst cubic in the number of variables. On the check of sum_each in Figure 17.5, slots 5 to 8 give three constraints, and their sum along the path from r5's offset to the packet's length is r5.off − len ≤ −1. That is the condition of the read at slot 9, in every round and whatever widening has done to r3.

Zone and Octagon proved 191 of the paper's 192 programs and intervals 128 (§7.2). Polyhedra proved 21 fewer than Zone, because its implementation stores coefficients in 64 bits and gives up when they do not fit, and Octagon cost more than Zone and proved nothing more, so Zone was chosen. Table 3 of the paper shows why a relation is needed at all. With a variable offset in r5, the safety condition data + r5 + 8 ≤ data_end has three variables; the offset encoding removes data, and the two that remain form a difference constraint.

A whole abstract state of the paper is a product domain, as in chapter 16, with four components (§5.2), and Figure 17.6 lists them with their counterparts in today's code. Two components say what may hold: the tag of each register and stack cell, and the numbers, in the chosen numeric domain. The other two say what must hold, namely the stack bytes that hold only numbers and the cells that hold a whole stored value, so a join intersects them and keeps what both sides guarantee. Each stack cell is a variable of the numeric domain, which is how a value spilled to the stack keeps its relations.

The memory model is where PREVAIL's rules on information flow live. A store to the stack removes every cell it overlaps. A load of bytes that no single store wrote yields a number only if every byte held one, and an invalid value otherwise, so a program cannot read a pointer back a byte at a time (§4.2). Shared regions such as map values are tracked by size alone, since another program may change them at any moment (§5.1).

What it checks, and what its proof covers

The paper asks three things of a program (§2). Memory safety means that every access lies within its region. Information-flow security means that a program run for an unprivileged user cannot learn a kernel address. Reading an uninitialised register or stack byte therefore counts as a violation, a pointer may be compared only with one into the same region or with zero, and it may be stored only to the stack. Termination means that every run ends, and the tool of 2019 did not check it: "For programs with loops, our algorithm verifies safety, but not termination."

Today's PREVAIL checks termination when asked (--termination; by default it ignores it). It adds a ghost counter at each loop head, incremented every round, and asserts that the fixpoint bounds it by 100,000 (BoundedLoopCount, src/ir/syntax.hpp, line 500, checked in src/crab/ebpf_checker.cpp, line 281). The counter can be bounded only through its relation to a variable the loop tests, which the zone domain keeps. The repository's test of a loop of 1,000,001 rounds ends with r0 equal to the counter, and fails for passing the limit (test-data/loop.yaml). The toy, which has no relations, widens its counter to infinity and reports that each of our loops may not end.

The namePREVAIL's README spells it out as "a Polynomial-Runtime EBPF Verifier using an Abstract Interpretation Layer".

The soundness argument is Theorem 5.6: if a program is verified safe, it is safe. It rests on three steps, from the concrete semantics of eBPFPL over mathematical integers, through a semantics in which each shared region is replaced by its size (Lemma 5.4), to the abstract transformers (Lemma 5.5). Machine integers enter only in §6.1, where a result that does not fit in 64 bits becomes an arbitrary value and pointer comparisons that might pass the 64 KB packet bound are refused. In 2019 unsigned comparisons could go either way, and bitwise operations were over-approximated. The theorem covers the model of §4, while the C++ code is tested, on files of small programs and the benchmark set.

The gap between model and code has shown itself in advisory GHSA-65rv-h458-cq99 (CVE-2026-53671, published in September 2026) reports that before release 0.2.4 a store through a pointer to the context was modelled as doing nothing. A program could overwrite ctx->data, load it back as a packet pointer and read any address while PREVAIL answered PASS. In the paper's model the packet's bounds sit in ghost registers that no store reaches, so the proof could not see the case. Release 0.2.4 of 1 June 2026 fixed it with two other soundness bugs, and release 0.2.6 of 3 August lists fifteen more, most of them programs that passed while making an unsafe access. The lesson of chapter 16 holds here too: a proof covers its model.

Inside the two sources

Figure 17.7 sets side by side the places where each verifier handles loops, Linux in v7.2 and PREVAIL at the commit we read. At each prune point Linux's bpf_is_state_visited() chooses among pruning, refusing an infinite loop and saving a checkpoint, with three special cases for the loop forms of the section "Loops". PREVAIL keeps no checkpoints and no budget of instructions. Its loop-specific code is the fixpoint at each head, run for each loop in the weak topological order that its docs credit to Bourdoncle (src/fwd_analyzer.cpp, line 204), and its only bound on a loop is the counter of the termination check.

A toy fixpoint beside a toy walk

The reproduction is about 600 lines of plain Python that need no packages. Both halves read the slots of Figure 17.1 as text, with N filled in, and share one transfer function that applies an instruction to a state of intervals. A pointer is a region with an interval of offsets, as in §4 of the paper, and the packet's length is a ghost variable in [0, 65,535]. The fixpoint half handles one loop on the schedule of the section "Join, widen and narrow at the loop head" and then checks every read against the final states. The walk half keeps a stack of pending branches and, at prune points, asks the three questions of the section "Checkpoints, and when two states are the same", with Linux's two rules for saving checkpoints and a comparison of live registers only.

Figure 17.8 shows two runs. That the walk's counts match the kernel's at all eight measurements says that the toy reproduces the arithmetic of the walk on this program: the rounds, the pending branches that end at once at sum_each's exit, and the spacing of checkpoints. It says nothing about programs with helpers, maps or precision tracking, which the toy lacks. The fixpoint takes 0.3 to 0.5 ms at any bound and the walk 0.5 ms at 16 bytes and 30 ms at 1,024, and the process peaks at 16 MB, which is the interpreter's own.

What the toy leaves out decides what it can show. Without the zone domain it refuses sum_each and cannot prove that any loop ends, where PREVAIL would keep the relations of Figure 17.5. Without the memory model a value spilled to the stack, such as the packet's end in the paper's Table 4, would be lost, and with four kinds of value it cannot follow a map lookup or its null check. Its walk compares every live scalar by range, where Linux skips those that no check has needed (the section "Which numbers must be exact"), so on programs where that matters it would prune less than the kernel. It also omits the checkpoints Linux forces when a path's history of jumps grows long.

The evaluation, read critically

The benchmark set has 192 programs from six projects: 86 from the Linux tree, 23 from linux-prototype, 18 from Open vSwitch, 5 from Suricata, 24 from Cilium and 36 from Cilium's tests (§7.1). The introduction counts 111 used during development and 81 more for the final evaluation, while §7.1 names Linux, Open vSwitch and Suricata as the projects that guided the design, which together make 109. Every program had passed the Linux verifier, so the set cannot show a safe program that Linux refuses, and Chaignon's summary adds that it is small and networking-heavy, with no large tracing program. Figure 17.9 collects the results.

On cost, PREVAIL verified each program in 5.2 seconds or less, at about 1,500 instructions a second. The Linux verifier was faster on every benchmark, which the authors expected, since the programs had been shaped to fit its limits (§7.3.1). Memory is the weak point: read from the paper's Figure 10, the zone domain used up to about 1.5 GB for the largest programs, of some 3,400 instructions. The authors call that "still unacceptable for an in-kernel verifier" and propose to compute the fixpoint in user space, leaving only a final check to the kernel. Alexei Starovoitov's commit c04c0d2b968a of April 2019 gives a scale for comparison: a non-debug kernel walked its whole budget of 1,000,000 instructions in a tenth of a second on a typical x86 machine.

One program of the 192 stayed unproved, and the paper does not say which or why. Nine commits in the projects' histories had reshaped code to pass the Linux verifier, and PREVAIL proved the original version of each. In one of them the kernel recognised data + X > data_end but not data + X <= data_end, which the authors read as a sign of "syntactic pattern matching and ad hoc case analysis". Six more commits had cut loop bounds or moved branches to fit the complexity limit, and PREVAIL proved each earlier version without taking longer. Cilium, for one, had capped a loop over IPv6 extension headers at four rounds (Figure 12).

The experiments ran on 4.19, which refused every back-edge, and Linux has changed since. 5.2 raised the budget to 1,000,000 instructions, 5.3 added bounded loops by walking every round (commit 2589726d12a1), and bpf_loop() in 5.17, bpf_for() in 6.4 and then may_goto gave loops a place where the walk can stop going round. Those forms proved the hash loop of chapter 4 in 63 to 91 instructions at any bound, may_goto only with its counter kept in a map value (Figure 4.8). A plain loop such as ours or the paper's is still walked once a round. We did not re-run the 192 programs or Figure 11 on v7.2, so the comparison of verdicts stands for 4.19 alone.

Read with · Simple and Precise Static Analysis of Untrusted Linux Kernel Extensions, Gershuni, Amit, Gurfinkel, Narodytska, Navas, Rinetzky, Ryzhyk and Sagiv, PLDI 2019 (copy of 5 May 2019)

What it is. The design of PREVAIL: a core language for eBPF, a concrete semantics with safety built in, an abstract semantics that takes the numeric domain as a parameter, a soundness theorem, and an evaluation on 192 programs.

Why now. This chapter has given each part of the design a picture and a run of the toy, and the paper gives each part its definition, so the two can be read side by side with the refresher's γ and join at hand.

  1. §1 and §3, with Tables 2 to 4 and Figure 1. The four complaints about the Linux verifier of 2019, and the three observations that choose the domain. Twenty minutes.
  2. §4.2 and §4.3, with Figures 3 to 5. Regions, tags, the safety condition of each command, and the loads that yield an invalid value. Thirty minutes.
  3. §5, with Figure 6 and Theorem 5.6. Shared regions replaced by their sizes, the abstract state of four components, the transformers for the stack. Thirty minutes.
  4. §6 and §7. What the implementation adds and leaves out, then the results, with Figures 9 to 12 beside Figure 17.9. Twenty-five minutes.

Skip. §2, which earlier parts of this book cover, and §8 apart from its paragraphs on Astrée and on Miné's memory domain.

The figure. Figure 11 beside Figure 12: the time of the Linux 4.19 verifier rising until its limit at 69 iterations, and the two Cilium loops whose bounds were cut to stay below such a limit.

Carry in. Three questions; their answers are in the key under chapter 17.

  1. Table 3 needs data + r5 + 8 ≤ data_end at line 9. Why does the offset encoding turn that into a constraint on two variables, and why is a constraint on two variables still beyond the interval domain?
  2. §5.2's abstract state has two components of "may" information and two of "must" information. Which are which, and why does the join intersect the last two?
  3. §7.3.1 reports the Linux verifier faster on every benchmark. What about the benchmark set makes that unsurprising, and which experiments of §7.3 escape that bias?

About 105 minutes · VERIFIER

Where PREVAIL runs

The repository is github.com/vbpf/prevail. The paper's link, github.com/vbpf/ebpf-verifier, now redirects there, and the README names commit d29fd26345c3 as the version the paper describes. The code is C++23, has 2,431 commits on its main branch and builds on Linux, Windows and macOS, and its latest release, 0.2.6, is of 3 August 2026.

Its main user is eBPF for Windows, whose README of 13 November 2026 describes three ways to run a program, listed in Figure 17.10. In the preferred one, the bpf2c tool passes the bytecode to PREVAIL and, if it passes, translates each instruction into C, which is built into a Windows driver. The JIT mode verifies in a user-mode service, eBPFSvc, and compiles with uBPF's JIT, so in both modes PREVAIL runs in user space, where the paper's memory figures said it belonged. uBPF, the user-space library behind that JIT, has no static verifier of its own. It offers instead an interpreter-only profile that checks pointers at run time.

The project does not aim to agree with Linux on every program. Its parity notes, written against Linux 6.18, list the instructions, helpers and map types still missing. They put "complete precision parity with the Linux verifier" among the non-goals, since the two use "fundamentally different analysis strategies with different precision profiles", and they do not plan to unroll loops as the walk in effect does. A pass from one verifier therefore shows a program safe under that verifier's model of its platform, and only a load on the other platform gives the other's verdict.

The instruction set both read is the one standardised in RFC 9669 (October 2024), whose read-with card is in chapter 1. PREVAIL's options take the RFC's conformance groups by name, from base32 to packet, plus a callx group that the RFC does not list. The RFC's §6 names Linux and PREVAIL as the verifiers that "provide many details" of what a verifier checks, and leaves those details to future IETF work. The standard thus fixes what an instruction means, while what a program may do stays each verifier's decision.

Research has continued from PREVAIL's design. VeRefine (OOPSLA 2025, by Hamza, Zavalía, Gurfinkel, Navas and Fedyukovich) replaces the fixpoint with a flow-sensitive refinement type system. Its types are inferred in user space as a proof certificate, so that only a checker must run in the trusted environment, the split the 2019 paper proposed for its memory problem. Its authors report it faster than PREVAIL on most of their industrial benchmarks; we read its abstract and introduction only.

Why Linux kept its walk

Linux answered the loop problem in the month the paper was presented, and in its own way. Alexei Starovoitov's commit 2589726d12a1, "bpf: introduce bounded loops", of 15 June 2019, lets "the verifier simulate all iterations of the loop" and credits the key idea to an earlier approach of Edward Cree's. It adds that "additional state pruning heuristics make such brute force loop walk practical even for large loops". The walk of chapter 4 is that decision, grown since.

"Our conclusion was that the best use we could make of PREVAIL was to incorporate some of its detail ideas, while rejecting the overall architecture."

Comment by ecree on "Bounded loops in BPF for the 5.3 kernel", LWN.net, 5 August 2019

The most direct account we found of why the design was not adopted is that comment, posted as ecree in reply to one by anadav that had pointed to the paper. Its writer gives the analysis as their own and believes the other developers broadly agree. The comment lists four obstacles. The zone domain cannot hold difference constraints together with the congruences that alignment checks need, and the paper does not explain how a fixpoint would prove termination. The defences against speculative execution may have no abstract semantics, and the memory use is large.

What the writer wanted to take was the proposal of §7.3, a proof supplied from user space and only checked by the kernel. We found no later statement, and two obstacles have moved since: PREVAIL now proves termination with its loop counter, and v7.2 widens imprecise scalars at three loop forms.

What it costs

CPU
PREVAIL with Zone, 2019: 5.2 s or less a program, about 1,500 instructions a second, roughly linear in size (Core i7 at 3.4 GHz, Linux 4.19). Linux v7.2 on our loop (7.2.15 VM, 16 vCPUs, 13 November 2026, medians of three loads): 0.13 to 3.2 ms for 124 to 7,180 instructions of sum_once, 0.15 to 6.4 ms for 168 to 10,254 of sum_each; its whole budget of 1,000,000 instructions took a tenth of a second in 2019 (c04c0d2b968a). The toy, Python 3.14 on a Ryzen 7 8845HS: the fixpoint's 47 or 53 transfers in 0.3 to 0.5 ms at any bound, the walk 0.5 to 30 ms.
Memory
PREVAIL: up to about 1.5 GB resident at 3,400 instructions (Figure 10 of the paper). Linux: 4 to 106 checkpoints on our loop. The toy: 16 MB, the interpreter's own.
False alarms
Zone and Octagon 1 program in 192, intervals 64, Polyhedra 21 more than Zone (§7.2). The toy's intervals: 2 of our 3 loop programs, and no loop proved to end. Linux 4.19: 9 programs reshaped to pass it, all 9 proved by PREVAIL.
Upkeep
PREVAIL: 2,431 commits; three soundness fixes in release 0.2.4 (June 2026) and fifteen in 0.2.6 (August 2026); parity with Linux 6.18 tracked by hand. The toy: about 600 lines.

On Linux, write loops in a form the walk can stop early, bpf_loop(), bpf_for() or a small constant bound, and otherwise expect it to cost about the body's length per round. PREVAIL's design is the better trade when loops have large or variable bounds and verification runs outside the kernel, at build time or in a user-mode service, where seconds and hundreds of megabytes are affordable; for a fixpoint verifier, keep each length check next to the read it guards. Treat a pass from either verifier as evidence about that verifier alone.

When it goes wrong

The first five rows of Figure 17.11 are costs of abstraction, facts that a joined and widened state cannot hold, and the toy shows each in a second; PREVAIL's answers are a relation, a descending phase and a counter tied to the loop. The last three compare a verifier with something outside it, the other verifier or its own proof, and only the source, the changelog or a load on the other platform settles them.

Run it, then read it · One loop, two verifiers, three bounds

~30 min · run, then read · needs python3; no root, no packages

Task. From the repository root, run python3 -I book/labs/prevail/toy.py once-ge 16 64 256 and note, for each bound, the fixpoint's rounds and transfers and the walk's instructions and checkpoints; set the walk's counts beside the kernel's in Figure 17.1. Then run python3 -I book/labs/prevail/toy.py once-ge 16 --no-narrow -v, and explain from its rounds why the read at slot 10 is now refused, and why the first run accepted it.

Done when. You have a table of three bounds with four numbers each, a sentence on which numbers depend on N and why, and a sentence that names the round where the two runs part and the interval each keeps.

Hint 1 · direction

The walk goes round once per byte; the fixpoint goes round until a round adds nothing. Only one of them can depend on how many bytes there are.

Hint 2 · mechanism

Compare the line "up 3" in the two runs with -v. In the first run the climb keeps the result of the round that proved it had stopped; with --no-narrow it keeps the widened state.

Hint 3 · nearly there

The back-edge leaves slot 13 only when r3 >= N failed, so it carries r3 in [1, N − 1]. Join that with the entry's [0, 0], and compare the result with what the read needs.

Solution in the answer key under chapter 17.

Check yourself

  1. Predict the values: for sum_once at N = 4,096, how many instructions will Linux v7.2 report as processed, and how many transfers will the toy's fixpoint make? What does each number depend on?
  2. An interval analyser refuses the read at slot 10 of sum_once as clang compiled it, and accepts the same bytecode with one operator changed at slot 13. Which change, why does it matter to the analyser, and why does it not matter to Linux?
  3. A team ships one XDP program to Linux and to Windows, and their Windows CI runs it through PREVAIL, which passes it. What has that shown about the program on Linux, and what should they also run?
  4. The paper proves Theorem 5.6, yet a 2026 advisory shows PREVAIL passing a program that reads an address of its choosing. How can both be true, and what does the fix tell a reader of any verifier's proof?
  5. A colleague proposes moving Linux to PREVAIL's design so that loops cost the same at any bound. Give two costs of the move that this chapter can source, and one thing Linux has taken from the design instead.

Answers unfold under each question here; in print they are in the answer key under chapter 17.

Recap

PREVAIL keeps one abstract state per point of a program's control-flow graph, joins where paths meet, widens at loop heads from the second round and then narrows, so on our loop its toy settled in four rounds at every bound while Linux v7.2 walked 7N + 12 instructions. Its state combines tags, numbers in the zone domain and two sets about the stack, and the zone domain keeps facts such as r5 + 1 ≤ end that intervals lose. Theorem 5.6 makes the method sound for a model of eBPF, the code is tested, and a 2026 advisory showed the gap between the two. On Linux 4.19 and 192 programs that Linux had passed, the paper found one false alarm and used up to about 1.5 GB. PREVAIL now runs in user space under eBPF for Windows, Linux kept its walk and borrowed a widening for its loop forms, and the epilogue looks back at the limits of all of this.

fixpoint
a state that one more round leaves unchanged
narrowing operator
lowers bounds widening raised, never raises one
relational domain
a domain whose values relate several variables
zone domain

Epilogue

Limits, traps, and where it went

Thirteen chapters followed one small program through every stage of its life and measured each stage, and four more asked whether the verifier at its centre can be trusted. The epilogue puts those measurements on one page, gathers the traps, weighs the case against the verifier and follows eBPF out of Linux, as far as an FPGA.

19 min · VERIFIER · HW · LINEAGE

The counter's life on one page

The write counter is the program of chapter 2, 27 slots of bytecode on the sys_enter_write tracepoint. It keeps one count per thread in a hash map of 1,024 entries, which its loader reads. Each chapter from chapter 1 on took it through one more stage and measured what that stage cost. Figure E.1 stacks those measurements in the order the counter meets them, from clang's output to the last grace period after the loader exits.

The rows fall into three prices by when they are paid. Every write pays for the run, 144 to 162 ns, which adds 230 to 245 ns to the write() around it. At a million writes a second that is about a quarter of one CPU. A load pays once for the walk, the JIT and the attach, from about a hundred microseconds to a few milliseconds, and a detach waits 29 to 46 ms for a grace period. The last three rows fall on whoever changes the verifier and never on the program.

Figure E.2 gathers the decision rule that closed each costs box, one line a chapter. Most of the rules turn on a number the running kernel reports. The run's cost is run_time_ns over run_cnt once kernel.bpf_stats_enabled is 1, and the walk's size is the processed count in the verifier's statistics line. Skipped runs show as recursion_misses in bpftool prog show, and memory as memlock beside the cgroup's memory.current. Each was read in a lab of this book with one command.

Thirteen traps

The chapters' "When it goes wrong" tables hold 172 rows. Most are messages from the verifier or libbpf that name their own cause once the chapter has been read. Figure E.3 keeps thirteen of the other kind, chosen for how often an engineer with a working program meets them: on a busier machine, on the next kernel, or after the loader exits. Eleven of the thirteen print no error at all, so the first sign is a wrong total or a loader that never stops.

Three rows share one symptom, a total short of the writes, and two counters tell them apart. If run_cnt matches the writes, every run happened, and CPUs overwrote each other's updates to a shared key. If recursion_misses grows, runs were skipped at a preemptible hook before the map was reached. If new threads are missing while old ones count on, the hash is full and refuses new keys. The fixes differ as much as the causes, an atomic add or a per-CPU map for the first, a hook where preemption is off for the second, and an LRU hash or a sketch for the third.

What the verifier cannot promise

Part V held the verifier to the standard of a proof, and every result came with a boundary. Chapter 15 proved tnum_add() at every width and watched Z3 find CVE-2021-3490 in the 32-bit bounds Linux shipped from 5.7 until 2021. Chapter 16 showed that Agni's proofs cover the range operators it encodes, on the kernels it ran on, and leave pruning, pointers and multiplication outside. Chapter 17 found a soundness theorem that holds for a model of eBPF, and a 2026 advisory that marked the gap between that model and PREVAIL's code. Four recent papers argue about what such boundaries mean for the verifier as a design.

The SoK on eBPF memory safety by Huang, Payer, Qian, Sampson, Tan and Jaeger (IEEE S&P 2025) gathers the evidence. It counts 325 bugs caused by memory errors that Syzbot has reported in the eBPF subsystem, 169 of them since 2023 and 45 still unfixed. It sorts the verifier's failures into checks that "are unsound, incomplete, and have a limited scope that prevents comprehensive validation of memory safety". Its measurement of real programs is milder: only 1.62 to 3.74 per cent of the memory operations in public eBPF programs, 37 to 85 a program on average, could not be shown safe by any existing defence. The authors take that share as grounds for enforcing full memory safety in ways that keep today's programs fast and loadable.

Jia, Sahu, Oswald, Williams, Le and Xu went further in "Kernel extension verification is untenable" (HotOS 2023). They "argue that eBPF's verifier—the source of its safety guarantees—has become a liability", first because static checking of bytecode has soundness and completeness problems that grow with the verifier. Their second reason is that each limit the verifier imposes gets worked around with a new helper, a way into the kernel that the verifier never checks. They counted 249 helpers in Linux 5.18 and at least 18 security bugs fixed in helpers over two years. In place of the verifier they sketch extensions in safe Rust, signed by a trusted toolchain and checked at load, with light run-time mechanisms to make programs end.

KFlex, by Dwivedi, Iyer and Kashyap (SOSP 2024), keeps the verifier and narrows its job. It "separates the safety of kernel-owned resources (e.g., kernel memory) from the safety of extension-specific resources (e.g., extension memory)". The first is proved statically, and the second is guarded by cheap run-time checks on an extension heap and by a mechanism that cancels an extension that runs too long. The paper reports several of its mechanisms upstreamed. It describes the arena of chapter 11, which Alexei Starovoitov contributed in parallel, as reaching feature parity with its heaps at a limit of 4 GB.

Rex, by Jia, Qin, Craun, Lukiyanov, Bansal, Phan, Le, Franke, Jamjoom, Xu and Williams (USENIX ATC 2025), builds safe Rust extensions on Linux 6.11. It calls the problem the "language-verifier gap". The evidence is 72 commits to Cilium, Aya and Katran in which programs that were already safe had to be reshaped until the verifier accepted them, the work that chapter 5 and chapter 6 did by hand. Rex extensions call the kernel through a crate of safe wrappers, with a small run-time for exceptions, stack safety and termination and no separate static verification. The price, which the paper states, is a Rust toolchain inside the trusted computing base.

What Linux changed instead

Linux kept its verifier and changed what surrounds it. Figure E.4 lists the changes this book covered, each with the first release whose tag contains its commit. Several move the way the papers asked. may_goto puts a run-time bound on a loop, which on x86-64 in v7.2 cuts the loop off after a quarter of a second, and the arena gives a program memory whose bounds and locks it manages itself, as KFlex's heaps did. Signed programs, from 6.18, let a loader prove where a program came from, the role the HotOS design gave to its toolchain's signature.

None of these removes the walk. A signature is checked inside BPF_PROG_LOAD before bpf_check() runs, and the walk still follows every path of the signed program afterwards. The helper list stops at 211, and the comment that closes it in include/uapi/linux/bpf.h sends new work to kfuncs. A kfunc's body is ordinary kernel C that the verifier never reads, so the way around the verifier that the HotOS paper warned about has moved from helpers to kfuncs, checked at the call by BTF type and flag. Tokens and private stacks answer narrower complaints, who may load in a container and how much stack a tracing program's nested calls may use, and neither changes what the walk proves.

Running it in production

For an engineer deciding whether to run eBPF code in production, the evidence points at the loader as much as at the program. A program the verifier accepts is safe under the verifier's model of that kernel, a model that Part V could prove only in parts, inside a subsystem where Syzbot has found 325 memory-error bugs. The risk therefore sits in two decisions, who may load programs and which kernels a program is tested on: the first is set by kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled, the capabilities of chapter 3, tokens and signed loaders, and the second matters because several traps in Figure E.3 appear only on a newer kernel.

eBPF beyond Linux

The instruction set the counter is written in became a standard in October 2024 as RFC 9669, whose read-with card is in chapter 1. It defines conformance groups, so that a runtime can say which instructions it supports. Every implementation must support base32, while base64, the atomic groups, the division and multiplication groups and the deprecated packet group are optional. Its security section leaves what a verifier must check to future IETF work, so two runtimes can agree on every instruction and still accept different programs.

eBPF for Windows runs the same bytecode with PREVAIL as its verifier, in the modes that the section "Where PREVAIL runs" described. In the preferred native mode, bpf2c verifies a program and turns it into C that is built into a driver. A JIT mode verifies and compiles in a user-mode service, and an interpreter is kept for debug builds. In user space, uBPF is an Apache-licensed library because the kernel's implementation is GPL and, in its README's words, "can't be used in many projects". It has an interpreter and a JIT for x86-64 and Arm64, and in place of a verifier it offers a safe profile that checks pointers at run time.

Two other runtimes show the range. rbpf is a virtual machine in Rust with an interpreter, an x86-64 JIT and a small verifier, which its authors call "nothing close to the one for Linux kernel" and which users may replace. bpftime runs uprobes, system-call hooks and XDP programs in user space, compiled with LLVM or uBPF and checked by PREVAIL or by the kernel's own verifier. Figure E.5 sets these beside Linux and the two hardware designs of the next section.

eBPF on an FPGA

A field-programmable gate array, or FPGA, is a chip of logic blocks and memories whose connections are set by loading a hardware design. One chip can thus become many different circuits. Network cards built around an FPGA can process a packet before it crosses PCIe to the host, and two research groups have run XDP programs on such cards. Figure E.6 draws their two designs side by side.

hXDP, by Brunella and colleagues (OSDI 2020), starts from the finding that "the iterative execution model of eBPF is not a good fit for FPGA accelerators". Their clocks run five to ten times slower than a server CPU's. A one-instruction-a-cycle executor at 156 MHz would reach at most 2.8 million packets a second on a simple firewall that one 3.7 GHz core runs at 7.4 million. To close that gap the authors built a compiler, a core, and hardware for XDP's maps and helpers as the kernel defines them. The compiler removes instructions the hardware makes unnecessary, among them the bounds checks the verifier demands, and packs independent instructions together.

The core is a VLIW processor, short for very long instruction word, which issues several instructions in one cycle because the compiler grouped them ahead of time. Theirs, Sephirot, has four lanes, and on a NetFPGA board at 156.25 MHz the design used about 15 per cent of the FPGA to run the firewall at 6.53 million packets a second. Parallelism, helpers and maps were the hard parts. The core cannot reorder instructions at run time, so the compiler must find all the parallelism, and its single helper unit takes one call a cycle. Every map lives in one FPGA memory area, which a configurator shapes from the program's maps section.

eHDL, by Rivitti, Bifulco, Tulumello, Bonola and Pontarelli (ASPLOS 2023), builds a circuit for each program instead. It is a tool for high-level synthesis, the generation of a hardware design from a program written in a software language. It turns an unmodified XDP program into a pipeline whose stages each run one group of independent instructions, so that the pipeline holds a packet in every stage. Bounded loops make this possible, since a loop the verifier can bound unrolls into stages, and each helper call becomes a hardware block of its own. Maps are the hard part again, because "since programs are unrolled as a pipeline in hardware, this effectively means that race conditions might arise" between stages that read and write one entry.

On a Xilinx Alveo U50, a 100 Gb/s FPGA card, its five test programs used 6.5 to 13.3 per cent of the FPGA. They forwarded 64-byte packets at line rate, 148 million a second, with about a microsecond of latency, 10 to 100 times the throughput of processor-based offloads such as hXDP. The price is flexibility, because hXDP loads a new program at run time while synthesising an eHDL pipeline usually takes a few hours. Its map hazards are the counter's lost updates of chapter 10 in another form, two writers to one key, here two pipeline stages where the counter had two CPUs.

About 6 hours · VERIFIER · HW

The counter, thirty-three years on

The prologue began in 1993 with a filter that could read one packet and sixteen words of scratch memory. Its jumps all went forward, and Linux 2.1.75 checked it with three rules before attaching it. The write counter reads the arguments of a system call, calls four helpers and keeps a map that user space reads. It passes a walk of 36 instructions by a verifier whose main file alone, kernel/bpf/verifier.c, has 20,065 lines in v7.2. Figure E.7 sets the two programs side by side.

The design between the two has held. In both, the kernel runs a small program for a limited machine at a hook on its own path, and checks the program before its first run so that a mistake costs wrong answers and leaves the kernel running. What grew is how much the check must know, from three rules that fit in a margin note to a walk of every path that tracks ranges and tnums for every register. That walk is where the SoK's bugs and the proofs of Part V both sit.

A reader who has followed the counter can follow a verifier log down to the source line that wrote it and choose a hook and a map from measured costs. The same reader can tell which proof covers which part of the verifier, and can add a data structure to the kernel twice, as chapter 13 did. The next program will meet the same stages in the same order, and the tables of this epilogue say what each stage costs and how it can fail.

Check yourself

  1. A tool must count, per cgroup, the write() calls of every process on 64-CPU hosts that run kernels from 6.1 to 7.2. Choose a hook, a map and a way to read it, and give the per-event costs you expect from the book's measurements, with the chapters they come from.
  2. A program uses bpf_for(), an arena and the kfunc bpf_task_from_pid(), and it must load on every kernel from 5.15 to 7.2. Which of the three must it give up or guard on older kernels, and how?
  3. A security team asks whether a third-party program that the verifier accepted is safe to run as root on production hosts. What can you claim from Part V and this epilogue, what can you not, and which settings from earlier chapters narrow the risk?
  4. Predict the outcome: a workload runs 100,000 short-lived threads and four that write constantly, and an operator wants per-thread write counts. Compare the counter's hash, an LRU hash of the same size and the count-min sketch on memory, the cost of reading every count, and what each loses.
  5. hXDP runs unmodified XDP programs. Why could it not run the write counter, which is also eBPF bytecode for the same instruction set?

Recap

The write counter's life costs nanoseconds per event, from microseconds to milliseconds per load and attach, and tens of milliseconds per detach, and every chapter's costs box ended in a rule that a number from the running kernel can test. Most traps a working program meets print no error, and a total short of the writes has three causes that run_cnt and recursion_misses tell apart. The verifier's subsystem has had hundreds of memory bugs: KFlex would narrow its job, while the HotOS paper and Rex would replace it with a safe language and a small run-time. Linux kept the walk and added may_goto, arenas, kfuncs, tokens, private stacks and signing around it. Beyond Linux, RFC 9669 fixes the instructions, Windows verifies with PREVAIL, user-space runtimes range from no verifier to PREVAIL, and on FPGAs hXDP built a processor while eHDL builds a circuit for each program.

Appendix

The lineage in commits

Most rows of Figure 0.3 began as a patch posted to a mailing list, were reviewed there, and were applied as a commit that is still in the kernel's history. This appendix gives both for each row, in date order, so that the lineage can be read as code. The first code beside an entry opens the commit on git.kernel.org, with its message, the files it touched and the diff. The second opens the patch on lore.kernel.org, the archive of the kernel's mailing lists, where the review and the other patches of its series sit in the same thread.

Three habits make a commit quick to read. The message comes first, because in this subsystem it often explains the design and the alternatives at more length than any document does. The list of changed files comes next, since a new file under kernel/bpf/ means a new mechanism and a large change to verifier.c means a new rule that loaded programs must follow. Sizes are worth comparing as well. Attaching to tracepoints in 4.7 took 19 added lines because the kprobe commit of 4.1 had already built the plumbing, while the scheduler class of 6.12 arrived as a new file of 4,256 lines.

The first two entries are older than git and link to the paper and to the release patch instead. Entries marked with an asterisk are not in Figure 0.3; later chapters cite them. Line counts are for the single commit shown, and a feature usually needs the rest of its series as well.

Answer key

Prologue

0.1

About 346 microseconds, roughly 75 times BPF's 4.6. NIT's line in the paper's Figure 3 starts at 136 microseconds and climbs 210 nanoseconds per byte, so 136 + 0.21 × 1,000 = 346. BPF's line is flat at 4.6 microseconds for a rejected packet of any size, because it reads only the bytes its filter tests, in place, and copies nothing, whereas NIT copies every packet before any filter sees it and so pays for each byte. It is tempting to reach for the "accept all" numbers in section 2.2, about 6 and 89 microseconds, but those measure the cost of buffering a packet that is kept.

0.2

Thirty. Every classic BPF jump goes forward, because the paper's jump fields are offsets from the next instruction and Linux treats them as unsigned, so a run visits each instruction at most once and ends at or before the last one. The kernel can know this from the program text alone by checking that every jump lands inside the program and that the last instruction is a return, which in Linux v7.2 is the work of bpf_check_classic in net/core/filter.c. A common mistake is to answer 4,096, the BPF_MAXINSNS limit; that number caps how long a program may be, while the forward jumps cap the steps of one run.

0.3

The kernel requires the last instruction to be a return. bpf_check_classic in Linux v7.2 net/core/filter.c ends with the comment "Last instruction must be a RET code" and returns -EINVAL for anything else, at attach time and before any packet. Because jumps only go forward, every run ends at the last instruction or earlier, so if that instruction is a return every path produces a verdict; if it were a jump, a path could run off the end of the program with no answer and no next instruction. Nothing ran here, since the error came from reading the program's text, so a guess that the filter failed on some packet mistakes when the check happens.

0.4

Because memory traffic is the bottleneck and most packets are rejected. Section 2.1 says the packet should be filtered "in place", where the network interface's DMA engine put it, so that a rejected packet costs only the bytes the filter read. SunOS's NIT copied every packet into an mbuf and then into a STREAMS message before its filter module saw it, so even unwanted packets paid for two copies. Section 3 adds why this matters: packet capture rejects far more packets than it accepts, so the cost of rejecting dominates. "To save buffer space" sounds plausible, yet the paper's argument is about the time spent copying.

0.5

A simulated stack and redundant work. Section 3.1 says CSPF's expression tree needs an operand stack, which on a register machine becomes loads, stores and pointer arithmetic in memory, the bottleneck again. It also says the tree often computes what it does not need: the tree for "IP or ARP" still evaluates the ARP test when the IP test is already true. A control-flow graph keeps values in registers and lets each test send the packet straight to its next step, so a packet answers only the tests on its own path. An answer of "it was slow" names the symptom; the authors go further and pin down where the time goes.

0.6

Two nodes, then TRUE. The root, ldh [12] and jeq #0x800, loads the Ethernet type and finds IP. The true edge leads to ld [26] and jeq #foo, which loads the IP source address, at byte 26 of an Ethernet frame, and finds foo, and its true edge goes straight to TRUE. That makes four instructions and the return, while the destination test at byte 30 and the ARP and RARP nodes never run. Counting every node in the figure gives too many, because a control-flow graph is walked along one path, which is why the paper prefers it to a tree.

Primer

P.1

The instruction is movq 8(%rsp), %rax, so the seventh argument sits at rsp + 8. The System V convention has six integer argument registers, rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8 and r9, so the caller stores the seventh on its own stack, and callq then pushes the eight-byte return address below it. At entry rsp points at that return address and the argument is one slot above. Compile long seventh(long a, long b, long c, long d, long e, long f, long g) { return g; } with clang -O2 -S to see it. A common slip is to answer 0(%rsp), which forgets the return address; eBPF has only five argument registers, and chapter 2 shows what clang does beyond them.

P.2

rbx is callee-saved under the System V ABI, and scramble() broke its promise to hand it back unchanged. At -O2 clang unrolls the loop and keeps the running partial sums in rbx and r14 across the calls (movq %rax, %rbx, callq scramble, addq %rax, %rbx), so each call overwrites a partial sum with 12345. At -O0 the sum and i live on the stack, which hides the bug. Fix it with pushq %rbx on entry and popq %rbx before retq, or by using a caller-saved register such as rcx or r11. It is tempting to blame the optimiser, but -O2 only relied on a rule that the assembly broke.

P.3

At -O0 clang gives every argument and local its own slot below r10 and writes each value back as soon as it changes, so t lives at r10 − 24 and is read back from memory after the call. The slot keeps its value because the called function gets a frame of its own and r10 comes back unchanged. At -O2, t stays in r6, which the calling convention promises to return intact, so the store and both reloads disappear. Check with clang -O0 -target bpf -c and llvm-objdump -d. A common misreading is that the convention demands the store; it only forbids keeping t in r0 to r5, and r6 and the stack both satisfy it.

Lab P.1

1 · Count. The stack machine needs 7 instructions and 17 memory accesses: local.get 0, local.get 1, i64.add, local.get 2, local.get 3, i64.add, i64.mul. Each local.get reads a local and pushes it, two accesses, and each arithmetic instruction pops two values and pushes one, three accesses, so 4 × 2 + 3 × 3 = 17; clang writes the same seven, starting with d + e.

Classic BPF needs 9 instructions and 6 accesses: ld M[3], ldx M[4], add x, st M[5], ld M[1], ldx M[2], add x, ldx M[5], mul x. Both sums are live at once and only A and X can hold values, so one sum is spilled to M[5] and filled back into X. eBPF needs four instructions and no access; clang writes r0 = r4, r2 += r1, r0 += r3, r0 *= r2.

2 · Run. r0 is 20 at exit, and r2 is 0xfffffffffffffffb, which is 264 − 5.

SlotInstructionr0r1r2r10 − 8
0r1 = 5050–
1r2 = r1055–
2r2 *= r10525–
3*(u64 *)(r10 - 8) = r2052525
4r2 -= 30050xff…fb25
5if r2 > 7 goto +1050xff…fb25
6r1 = 100not run: the jump goes to 5 + 1 + 1 = 7
7r0 = *(u64 *)(r10 - 8)2550xff…fb25
8r0 -= r12050xff…fb25

Checked by assembling the code with llvm-mc -triple bpfel -filetype=obj and stepping its bytes through a small emulator. The common wrong turn is to read r2 as −5, decide the jump is not taken and run slot 6, which gives 25 − 100 = −75. eBPF's > is the unsigned JGT; the signed comparison is written s> (JSGT), and with it the jump would not be taken.

3 · Translate. Four instructions and three registers are enough, and a = 7, b = 3 gives 40:

r0 = r1        ; a
r0 -= r2       ; a - b
r1 += r2       ; a + b; a is no longer needed
r0 *= r1

Clang 23.1.4 at -O2 writes five, r0 = r1, r1 = r2, r1 += r0, r0 -= r2, r0 *= r1, with the same registers and one copy more, so a compiler's output is a good answer but not always the shortest. The wrong turn is to compute a + b first into r1, which destroys a before a − b needs it and forces a fourth register or a spill.

4 · Decode. 7b 1a f8 ff 00 00 00 00 is *(u64 *)(r10 - 8) = r1: opcode 0x7b stores 64 bits, the register byte 0x1a gives destination 0xa, which is r10, and source 1, and f8 ff is 0xfff8, which is −8. It is a spill of r1 into the first stack slot, and it is the first instruction of Figure P.4's step() at -O0. 07 01 00 00 f0 ff ff ff is r1 += -16, since 0x07 adds an immediate to destination r1 and 0xfffffff0 is −16. llvm-mc --disassemble -triple=bpfel prints both lines the same way. The wrong turns are reading the register byte high half first, which gives *(u64 *)(r1 - 8) = r10, and reading f8 ff as 0xf8ff.

5 · Find the bug. Slot 2 reads r2 and slot 3 reads r1 after the call, and both are caller-saved, so the call may have overwritten them. One added instruction fixes it; any of r6 to r9 will do:

0: r6 = r1
1: r7 = *(u64 *)(r6 + 0)
2: call 5
3: r0 -= r7
4: *(u64 *)(r6 + 8) = r0
5: r0 = 0
6: exit

On x86-64 the same mistake would run and read whatever the callee left in rdi and rsi. eBPF never runs it, because the kernel refuses to load a program that reads r1 to r5 after a call ("After the call the registers R1-R5 contain junk values and cannot be read", classic_vs_extended.rst), as chapter 1 shows. The common wrong turn is to move r1 and leave r2, because r2 was never an argument to the call.

What this shows. Registers are where a machine does its work, memory is where values wait, and the calling convention decides which registers keep their values across a call; every eBPF listing in this book can be read with these five habits.

Chapter 1

1.1

24 instructions in 216 bytes. Every slot is eight bytes, so the section holds 27 × 8 = 216 bytes, and three of the slots are the second halves of wide instructions, which leaves 27 − 3 = 24 instructions. llvm-readelf -S /tmp/hashmap.bpf.o confirms it: the section named after the counter's hook has size 0xd8, which is 216. Answering 27 mixes up slots and instructions; the disassembler numbers slots, and so the line after the wide instruction at slot 6 is slot 8.

1.2

The program read r1 after a call, and after a call r1 holds nothing readable. A helper call leaves r1 to r5 unreadable whatever the helper did, so after call 1 the map is no longer in r1. The fix is to load the map into r1 again before the next call, as the counter's slot 21 does, or to keep a needed value in r6 to r9. The rule is in the kernel's "Classic BPF vs eBPF" page: after a call, "R1 - R5 are reset to unreadable". One might suspect the helper of overwriting r1 with junk, but the kernel never looks at what the helper did and applies the rule to every call.

1.3

No; the zero is a placeholder. The line under it, R_BPF_64_64 write_counts, is a relocation, a note telling the loader that this instruction must point at the map named write_counts, which does not exist yet when clang writes the file. When the loader creates the map, libbpf writes the map's file descriptor into the instruction and marks it as a map reference, and the kernel swaps in the map itself; section 5.4 of the RFC lists that form, and chapter 3 walks through it. Reading 0x0 as NULL would be right for code that runs as written, and nothing runs from this file as written.

1.4

29 slots, two more than the object's 27: 232 / 8 = 29. While it checked the counter, the kernel replaced the call to helper 1 at slot 8 with a direct call into the hash table's own lookup, __htab_map_lookup_elem(), and added two slots after it, if r0 == 0x0 goto pc+1 and r0 += 56, which turn the element found into the address of its value. bpftool prog dump xlated shows them as slots 9 and 10, and the old slots from 9 on move down by two. It is tempting to blame the wide instructions for the growth, but they already took sixteen bytes each in the object.

1.5

The sign-extending load. Opcode 0x91 is class LDX (1) with the size B (0x10) and the mode MEMSX (0x80): one byte loaded and sign-extended, an instruction of version 4 that Linux accepts from 6.6. A 6.1 kernel has no entry for it in bpf_opcode_in_insntable() and refuses the program before walking it; the v6.5 source has no MEMSX at all. With the default version, clang writes the same load as three instructions, a zero-extending byte load and two shifts, which kernels before 6.6 also run. A missing helper is a natural suspect, but a helper fails with invalid func, never with an opcode.

1.6

Slot 12, and slot 32,777. The offset 02 00 is +2, counted from the slot after the jump, so 9 + 1 + 2 = 12. The offset is a signed 16-bit field whose largest value is 32,767, and 9 + 1 + 32,767 = 32,777. A farther jump needs gotol, the goto of the JMP32 class that takes its distance from the 32-bit immediate, and a far conditional jump becomes a short one over a gotol. Counting from the jump itself gives 11 and 32,776, the usual slip; the interpreter's JMP_JA adds the offset to insn, and CONT then adds one more.

1.7

From classic BPF's jump bytes read as eBPF's offset. A classic instruction is a 16-bit code, two one-byte jump distances and a 32-bit constant, so the second instruction of tcp port 22, { 0x15, 0, 6, 0x000086dd }, is stored as 15 00 00 06 dd 86 00 00. eBPF reads bytes 2 and 3 as a little-endian offset, 0x0600 = 1,536, and the jump at slot 1 lands at 1 + 1 + 1,536 = 1,538. The kernel checks jumps before opcodes, so this message hides the unknown opcode b1 at slot 13. Classic filters reach the kernel through SO_ATTACH_FILTER, which converts them with bpf_convert_filter(); BPF_PROG_LOAD takes eBPF only.

1.8

The three wide instructions, and 18 bytes. Each became a movabsq, the x86-64 move that can carry a full 64-bit constant, two bytes of prefix and opcode (48 bf) and eight of address, so 10 bytes replace 16, six saved each and 18 in all. bpftool prog dump jited ... opcodes shows them at offsets 0x33, 0x5d and 0x7f. The calls are a natural guess, since they reach farthest, but a callq is five bytes, an opcode and a 32-bit distance from the next instruction (e8 and four bytes in the dump).

1.9

The immediate was written in big-endian order. On x86-64 the immediate is little-endian, so bytes 4 to 7, 00 00 00 01, read as 0x01000000, which is 16,777,216. The kernel cannot know that 1 was meant, since every 32-bit value is a valid immediate for a move. llvm-objdump -d prints the slot as r0 = 0x1000000, and llvm-mc -triple bpfel -show-encoding gives b7 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 for r0 = 1. A common expectation is that the load step catches such mistakes, but it refuses only fields that must be zero or numbers it does not know.

1.10

The jump class, and a call that takes its target from the immediate. The low three bits of 0x85 are 101, which is 0x5, the JMP class in the class table of section 3.3. The top four bits are 1000, which is 0x8, CALL in the jump table of section 4.3, and the bit between them is 0, which section 4 calls K: the operand is the immediate. CALL is easy to look for among the arithmetic instructions, since a call does work, yet CALL and EXIT both live in the jump class.

1.11

Because the immediate holds only 32 bits. A 64-bit constant, such as an address, cannot fit in one slot, so the wide encoding of section 3.2 appends a second eight bytes whose immediate carries the upper half, and section 5.4 gives the arithmetic: dst = (next_imm << 32) | imm. The counter's object uses it three times, twice for the map and once for the bpf_printk format string. Long jumps are a natural guess for a reason to need sixteen bytes, but in this standard only the 64-bit immediate loads use the wide form.

1.12

An ID, and no other information about the helper. Section 4.3.1 says a helper was identified by a static ID in the immediate, and that platforms with kernel type information may put a type ID there instead. What each helper does, which arguments it takes and what it returns are left to the platform, which on Linux means the kernel's helper documentation and the BPF_FUNC_ list. So helper 1 means "map lookup" on Linux without the standard saying so. Readers who look for a list of helpers in the RFC will not find one, because the standard leaves that to future work.

Lab 1.1

$ cd book/program && make vmlinux.h
$ clang -g -O2 -target bpf -D__TARGET_ARCH_x86 -I/usr/include/bpf -I. \
    -c maps/02-hash-map/hashmap.bpf.c -o /tmp/hashmap.bpf.o
$ llvm-objdump -dr /tmp/hashmap.bpf.o | grep 'call 0x'
       0:	85 00 00 00 0e 00 00 00	call 0xe
       8:	85 00 00 00 01 00 00 00	call 0x1
      16:	85 00 00 00 06 00 00 00	call 0x6
      24:	85 00 00 00 02 00 00 00	call 0x2
$ grep -nE 'BPF_FUNC_[a-z_]+ = (1|2|6|14),' vmlinux.h
13320:	BPF_FUNC_map_lookup_elem = 1,
13321:	BPF_FUNC_map_update_elem = 2,
13325:	BPF_FUNC_trace_printk = 6,
13333:	BPF_FUNC_get_current_pid_tgid = 14,

Expected output. The four calls above, in that order; clang also prints a few warnings from vmlinux.h, which are harmless. The line numbers in vmlinux.h depend on the kernel it was generated from. Run on kernel 7.2 with clang 23, November 2026.

What this shows. call 0xe is helper 14, bpf_get_current_pid_tgid; call 0x1 is the map lookup; call 0x6 is bpf_trace_printk, which is what bpf_printk becomes; call 0x2 is the map update. At slot 8, r1 holds the map loaded at slot 6, and r2 holds r10 − 4, the address of the key on the stack.

Common wrong turn. Reading 0xe as decimal, or as an address, when it is hexadecimal 14, a helper ID. The other is looking for bpf_printk in the list, although it is a macro over helper 6.

Lab 1.2

$ bash book/labs/machine-root.sh build
$ vng -r /boot/vmlinuz-linux --user root --rwdir /tmp -- \
    'cd book/labs/machine/cases && for f in swapped widecut helper memsx;
     do /tmp/machinelab/rawload $f.txt; done'
swapped.txt: 3 slots, load refused, errno 22 (Invalid argument)
BPF_MOV uses reserved fields
processed 0 insns (limit 1000000) max_states_per_insn 0 ...
widecut.txt: 5 slots, load refused, errno 22 (Invalid argument)
jump into the middle of ldimm64 insn 2
processed 0 insns (limit 1000000) max_states_per_insn 0 ...
helper.txt: 2 slots, load refused, errno 22 (Invalid argument)
0: R1=ctx() R10=fp0
0: (85) call unknown#212
invalid func unknown#212
processed 1 insns (limit 1000000) max_states_per_insn 0 ...
memsx.txt: 4 slots, load ok
processed 4 insns (limit 1000000) max_states_per_insn 0 ...
returned 4294967295 (0xffffffff)

Expected output. The four results above, from the case files in book/labs/machine/cases, which are one answer each; the statistics lines are cut short. Run as root in a virtme-ng VM on kernel 7.2.15-arch1-1, 12 November 2026.

What this shows. The first two are refused for their bytes alone, which processed 0 insns confirms: a move from the immediate must leave its source field at zero, and the pass over the jumps knows where every wide instruction's second half lies. The helper ID is checked when the walk reaches the call, after one instruction. The sign-extending load turns the byte 0xff into −1 in all 64 bits of r0, and the test run prints its low 32 bits, 4,294,967,295.

Common wrong turn. Swapping the nibbles of the wrong byte, or counting a jump's target from the jump itself, which lands it on the wide instruction's first half and loads cleanly. The other is expecting 255 from the fourth program, which is what a zero-extending load of the same byte would return.

Chapter 2

2.1

Byte 32, r1 = *(u64 *)(r6 + 0x20), with the access string 0:2:2. struct trace_event_raw_sys_enter starts with an 8-byte struct trace_entry and an 8-byte long id, so args begins at 16, and element 2 of an array of 8-byte longs adds 16 more. The string reads as the pointer itself (0), member 2 (args), element 2; BPFAbstractMemberAccess names its global llvm.trace_event_raw_sys_enter:0:32$0:2:2, and llvm-objdump -dr prints CO-RE <byte_off> [16] struct trace_event_raw_sys_enter::args[2] (0:2:2) under the load. It is tempting to answer 16 by forgetting trace_entry; and 32 holds only for this vmlinux.h, because libbpf rewrites it at load when the running kernel's BTF says otherwise.

2.2

The BPF back end in clang refused, while it laid out the frame. BPFRegisterInfo::eliminateFrameIndex() calls WarnSize(), which reports this error for any offset 512 bytes or more below r10; 512 is the default of the hidden option -bpf-stack-size and matches MAX_BPF_STACK in include/linux/filter.h, which the verifier enforces as well. No object is written, so the kernel never sees the program. Move the buffer into a per-CPU array with one entry and look it up at the start of the program. Raising -mllvm -bpf-stack-size silences clang but only moves the rejection to the verifier.

2.3

On v1 and v2 the only atomic add is BPF_ATOMIC | BPF_ADD without the fetch bit, XADDD in BPFInstrInfo.td, which writes memory and returns nothing. When the program reads the old value, instruction selection still picks that instruction, and BPFMIPreEmitChecking in BPFMIChecking.cpp finds its result in use and stops the build. Build for v3, where atomicrmw becomes XFADDD with the fetch bit, or stop using the result. A common mistake is to blame the kernel; the message comes from clang, and the same source compiles unchanged once the version is v3.

2.4

0x8d8. BTF gives field offsets in bits while the instruction's offset field counts bytes, so 18112 / 8 = 2264 = 0x8d8, and libbpf's matching line in the lab agrees: (0:65 @ offset 2264). Only the 16-bit offset field changes, since the kernel's "BPF LLVM Relocations" page says that for loads it is the offset field that gets patched. Forgetting the division gives 0x46c0, the bit offset written in hex.

2.5

The server's task_struct has no field named __state, because before Linux 5.14 it was called state (commit 2f064a59a11f, "sched: Change task_struct::state"). The 5.4 BTF from the lab shows it, with 'state' at bit 128 and no __state. libbpf found no match by name and replaced the instruction with a call to helper 195896080; the kernel refused that call, and libbpf rewrote the kernel's message into the line in the log. The fix is in Nakryiko's CO-RE reference guide: a second definition, task_struct___old with the old name, chosen at run time with bpf_core_field_exists(). A server without BTF is a reasonable suspect, but that fails earlier and with a different message, failed to find valid kernel BTF.

2.6

None. The write counter never reads a field through a struct from vmlinux.h: its tracepoint argument goes unused, and the rest is helper calls and map access. llvm-objdump -dr on maps/02-hash-map/hashmap.bpf.o shows three R_BPF_64_64 lines, the map and string relocations from chapter 1, and no CO-RE line. So no change of struct layout can break it, although a kernel without the sys_enter_write tracepoint, or without a helper it calls, can. Including vmlinux.h does not by itself tie an object to one kernel, because only field reads create relocations.

2.7

The fork tracer is worse off. Without -g clang writes no .BTF and no .BTF.ext, so the counter's map, which exists only as BTF, cannot be read and libbpf stops at open. The tracer defines no map, so it opens and loads, but it has lost its CO-RE records as well: llvm-objdump -dr shows the same 0xb38 loads with no CO-RE line under them, and on Ubuntu's 5.4 kernel they would read the wrong four bytes without a word. To shrink an object, keep -g and run llvm-strip -g afterwards, which removes the DWARF and keeps both BTF sections, taking the counter from 8,112 bytes to 3,624. It is tempting to call the counter the casualty, because its load stops and the tracer's does not, but a failure that stops the load is the safe kind.

2.8

Clang and LLVM inside the tool, and the kernel's headers installed from the right kernel-devel package, because BCC compiled the program at start-up on each host. "The problem of BPF portability" lists the costs: large binaries, a resource-heavy compile at every start that can take minutes on a busy host, a bet that headers are present, which fails on one-off kernels, and compile errors that appear only at run time. CO-RE moves all of that to the build machine. BCC never got the offsets wrong, which is easy to assume after this chapter; it got them right, at that price.

2.9

BTF, the compiler, the loader and the kernel, of which the kernel changed least. In "High-level BPF CO-RE mechanics", BTF carries the types, clang records the relocations, and libbpf matches the program's types to the kernel's and patches the code. The kernel "doesn't need many changes", because after libbpf the program looks like any other, as the field note in this chapter quotes. It would be easy to picture the kernel doing the patching, since the kernel runs the program, but in the post's design libbpf does it in user space.

2.10

Because BTF, like DWARF, records types and has no place for macros, so a header printed from BTF has no kernel #define lines. The post says so in "Getting rid of kernel header dependency" and points to libbpf's bpf_helpers.h for the most common ones; the rest have to be defined by hand. grep -c '#define' vmlinux.h in book/program prints 5, and all five are bpftool's own lines at the top, the include guard and attribute shorthands. An old or broken header would be the wrong thing to blame, since regenerating it changes nothing.

Chapter 3

3.1

27 and two. The kernel counts eight-byte slots, and the three wide instructions take two each: the section is 216 bytes, and 216 / 8 = 27. The two maps are write_counts and hashmap_.rodata, the read-only map that holds bpf_printk's format string, and grep map_name= strace.txt finds them. The other three BPF_MAP_CREATE lines, and seven of the eight BPF_PROG_LOAD lines, are libbpf's feature probes (run on kernel 7.2 with libbpf 1.8). Two slips are common here: answering 24, which counts instructions where the kernel counts slots, and answering one map, because the .rodata map is easy to forget.

3.2

Three for the program and two for each map. count_writes is held by the loader's program descriptor, by the link that BPF_LINK_CREATE made, and by the perf event, for which bpf_perf_link_attach() calls bpf_prog_inc() (syscall.c line 4337, under the comment that perf_event_set_bpf_prog() takes none of its own). write_counts is held by the loader's map descriptor and by the program's used_maps. The bpftrace probes of Figure 3.9 print refcnt 3 on the program and refcnt 2 on each map. It is tempting to say two for the program, one per descriptor; the perf event's hidden reference is why the detach must drop one too.

3.3

The program was loaded and never attached, so it has never run. Load only creates the program, which runs once a link holds it on its hook, and sudo bpftool link show lists no link whose prog_id is the ID of count_writes. The usual cause is a loader that calls open_and_load() and skips attach(), or ignores the error attach() returned, for example for a tracepoint name that tracefs does not know. Suspecting a bug in the program leads nowhere, since a program that loaded has passed the kernel's checks and this one updates the map on every run, so an empty map means no run at all.

3.4

The program loaded; attach failed, in user space, before any attach call reached the kernel. With CAP_PERFMON the test at line 3045 passes and BPF_PROG_LOAD returns a descriptor. libbpf then needs the tracepoint's number and opens /sys/kernel/tracing/events/syscalls/sys_enter_write/id, and tracefs is mode 0700 for root, so openat() fails with EACCES and perf_event_open() is never called. strace -e trace=bpf,openat shows both: insn_cnt=27 … = 9, then the refused openat. Grant read access to tracefs or attach from a process that has it. A common mistake is to look for a third capability in bpf_prog_load(); the load had already succeeded.

3.5

The pin holds the map, and nothing holds the program. When the loader exits, its descriptors close, the link detaches the program, and the program's count reaches zero; freeing it puts each map in used_maps. write_counts drops from three holders (descriptor, used_maps, pin) to one, the pin's inode, which keeps it until bpf_destroy_inode() runs on rm. Nothing writes to it, so the counts stay where they were, and bpftool prog show name count_writes prints nothing. It is easy to assume that pinning the map keeps the program running; for this program only a pinned link does that.

3.6

libbpf found the pin and compared the existing map with the new definition, and max_entries differed. map_is_reuse_compat() in tools/lib/bpf/libbpf.c reads the pinned map's info and requires the same type, key size, value size, max_entries, flags and map_extra; any difference refuses the load, since the kernel cannot resize a map. The ways out are to make the definitions agree, or to remove the pin so that the next loader creates a new map, which loses the counts and leaves the running counter on the old one. Suspecting the new program is natural, but libbpf creates or reuses every map before it loads any program, so the kernel never saw forget_thread.

Expected output. As above, abridged, with long lines wrapped; IDs, descriptor numbers and the tracepoint's number (827) differ from machine to machine. Run on kernel 7.2.15 with clang 23, libbpf 1.8, bpftool 7.8 and strace 7.3, November 2026, as root in a virtme-ng VM of the same kernel; book/labs/ch02-root.sh repeats it. The full trace holds 33 calls before the loader's read loop starts: eight BPF_PROG_LOAD and five BPF_MAP_CREATE, of which one and two belong to the counter, plus BPF_BTF_LOAD calls that carry type information, the subject of chapter 2.

What this shows. Load is the two maps and the 27-slot program, and attach is perf_event_open and then BPF_LINK_CREATE, several calls later. The first BPF_LINK_CREATE, with target_fd=-1, is libbpf checking that this kernel has perf links; the second is the counter's, and returns the link as descriptor 11. After pkill the pin held the link, so the program kept counting, and each bpftool run is a new process whose own writes add a key. Removing the pin dropped the last reference, and the link, the program and both maps went with it.

Common wrong turn. Taking every BPF_PROG_LOAD in the trace for the counter's, when only the load with 27 slots is. The other is pressing Ctrl-C: this loader's read loop never checks the flag its signal handler sets, so it keeps running, and its bpf() calls fill the trace.
