Removing the pin starts the chain in a kworker, because bpf_link_put() defers to a workqueue, and the program is freed about 7 ms after its last reference, the maps right after it.

What this shows. The pin's inode is one more reference on the link; while it exists the link holds the program and the program holds its maps, with no process involved. The waits are the same as for the killed loader, a tasks-trace grace period in the detach and an RCU grace period before the free.

Common wrong turn. Pinning the program instead of the link: the program stays loaded but is detached when the loader's link closes, so the counts stop.

Chapter 4

4.1

Eight paths, and as few as four walks. Each block doubles the routes, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. The walk follows one full path and keeps the other side of each block for later, and when it comes back for one, that side ends where the blocks meet again if a saved state there covers it, which is likely, since nothing set in the blocks is read afterwards. That gives one full path plus three short arms. The saving rule in the margin note decides where states exist, so a cut can come a few instructions later than the meeting point. A walk that restarted from the top for each kept branch would need six, two per block, but this one resumes from the branch itself.

4.2

Because v and w are the same pointer to the kernel. The copy keeps the id the lookup gave, and when the test on w succeeds, mark_ptr_or_null_regs() (kernel/bpf/verifier.c, line 15706 in v7.2) clears the NULL flag on every register and stack slot with that id. The verifier page says the same in its paragraph on the id field, and in the counter's own log the id is the id=1 inside r0's entry. Expecting a rejection assumes that the kernel tracks only the register named in the test; clang copies pointers between registers all the time, and the id is what makes that harmless.

4.3

No. The verifier proves the six rows of Figure 4.2, which are about jumps, registers, NULL tests, bounds, calls and an end, and the choice of key belongs to the program. The counter stores u32 pid = bpf_get_current_pid_tgid();, and the low 32 bits of that helper's result are the thread ID while the process ID is in the high half, so keying by bpf_get_current_pid_tgid() >> 32 counts per process. "Loaded" is easily read as "correct", but the verifier would accept either key, because both are plain numbers stored on the stack.

4.4

8,211 at 1,024 bytes, and about 125,000 bytes before the budget. Each byte costs the eight instructions of the loop's body, (32,787 − 2,067) / (4,096 − 256) = 30,720 / 3,840 = 8, and the rest of the program costs 2,067 − 8 × 256 = 19, so 19 + 8 × 1,024 = 8,211. The budget allows (1,000,000 − 19) / 8 ≈ 124,997 rounds. A loaded copy at 1,024 bytes printed processed 8211 insns on kernel 7.2.15. It is tempting to expect another limit first, but the loop's test is decided every round, so no pending branch piles up; the cost on the way would be 12,500 checkpoints, one per ten rounds, and about half a second.

4.5

The shape check refused it, before the walk. bpf_check_cfg() in kernel/bpf/cfg.c explores the jumps depth first, and when push_insn() meets a jump to an instruction still on its own path, a back-edge, it returns -EINVAL with that message unless the loader has CAP_BPF (lines 133 to 139). do_check_main() runs only after the shape check, so the statistics show 0 instructions and 5 µs. The fixes are CAP_BPF, or a BPF token that grants it, or a loop the compiler unrolls. A common mistake is to blame the budget, which is the same million for every loader; what changes without CAP_BPF is loops, a program length of 4,096 and 64 checkpoints per instruction.

4.6

Because a static function is walked at every call, and a global one once. The walk enters a static function in a new frame of the caller's state, and states_equal() requires every frame to come from the same call site, so the second call cannot be pruned against the first: 14 instructions in the caller plus four walks of about 163 make 666. A global function is checked once by do_check_subprogs() for any arguments its BTF types allow, and each call only checks the arguments and gives r0 an unknown number (verifier.c line 9398). The function therefore can no longer rely on what its callers pass: if it indexes an array with an argument, it must test the bound itself, even when every caller passes a constant.

4.7

8,193 rounds, at 9 instructions each. Every round's test of the random bit can go either way, so check_cond_jmp_op() pushes the jump side, and nothing is popped until the first path reaches an exit; push number 8,193 passes BPF_COMPLEXITY_LIMIT_JMP_SEQ (8,192). llvm-objdump -d shows a round as two calls, an and, the test, an add, a move, a jump, the decrement and the loop test, nine instructions, with three before the loop: 3 + 8,192 × 9 + 3 = 73,734, the last round stopping at its test. The loop test does not push a branch of its own, because the counter is a known number and the walk takes only the side that can happen.

4.8

Slot 1, *(u32 *)(r10 - 0x4) = w0, which writes the key before the call at slot 8 reads it through r2. The kernel's record shows those bytes as written, fp-8=mmmm????, where m means written and ? never written. The page's example without the store is rejected with "invalid indirect read from stack", and in v7.2 the wording is "invalid read from stack", at line 6725 of verifier.c. Testing the rule as root can mislead, because a loader with CAP_PERFMON may let helpers read unwritten stack (bpf_allow_uninit_stack()), so it is best tried as an ordinary user would hit it.

4.9

Because nothing after that point read the register on the saved path. If any later instruction had read it, the walk from the saved state would have been refused with !read_ok; it was accepted, so every instruction from there on writes the register before reading it, and whatever the current path holds in it is never looked at. In v7.2 the rule is the first test in regsafe(), kernel/bpf/states.c line 514, with the comment "explored state can't have used this". A stricter rule, matching "never written" only with "never written", would also be safe, but the kernel made it looser on purpose, because pruning depends on it.

4.10

Because the only register that differs, r0, is written at instruction 4 before anything reads it. The two states are r0 = 1, r1 = 0 and r0 = 0, r1 = 0, and from the checkpoint on the program reads r1 and overwrites r0, so only r1 matters, and r1 is the same in both. Liveness tracking finds this and drops r0 from the saved state, after which the states are equal and the second arrival is pruned. The write counter has the same shape, since the line from 9 to 12 in the lab solution lists no r0 at all. A comparison register by register would call the states different, which is the error liveness tracking exists to avoid.

Lab 4.1

                                          map=write_counts,ks=4,vs=8)

Expected output. The kernel's own record of the walk, abridged. It was run on 12 November 2026 on kernel 7.2.15-arch1-1 with bpftool v7.8.0, booted in a throwaway virtual machine with virtme-ng (vng) and loaded as root inside it. On an ordinary host, sudo bpftool -d prog load /tmp/hashmap.bpf.o /sys/fs/bpf/hm prints the same lines among libbpf's own, and sudo rm /sys/fs/bpf/hm cleans up.

What this shows. After slot 8, r0 is a pointer-or-NULL. After slot 9 it is a map value on the fall-through side and 0 on the jump side, where the kernel drops it because nothing reads it again. The first path is 24 instructions, and the second walks 11 and is compared once at slot 25, so N = 24 + 12 = 36, and total_states 2 are the states saved at slots 9 and 25.

Common wrong turn. Counting slots instead of instructions, which gives 27 for the first path, or counting the second path from slot 0. The other is expecting the second path to stop at slot 12, the jump target, where no state was saved.

What this shows. The plain loop is walked once per byte, eight instructions a round, so its count grows sixteen times with the size. bpf_loop() and bpf_for() give the walk a call at which a round's state can be compared with the round before, and once it falls within it the walk stops, at any size.

Common wrong turn. Reading the loader's wall clock, about 5 ms for every load, as the cost of verification; most of it is libbpf opening the object and probing the kernel. The other is concluding that bpf_loop() runs its body fewer times: it still calls it N times when the program runs.

Chapter 5

5.1

About eight: 1,000,001 ÷ 124,993 ≈ 8.0. Seven are the loop body, slots 16 to 23 with the wide load at 16 counted once, and the eighth is the exit side of slot 23's test. The walk follows the fall-through first, out of the loop to slot 24, finds a saved state there that covers it, because r7 is never read after the loop, and prunes it on the spot before coming back for the next round. The accepted copy with the cap shows this directly, since at log level 2 its exit side is pruned once per round. Seven, the loop body alone, leaves out the way out that every round also checks.

5.2

A type rule: the instruction reads memory through r1, and r1 holds a scalar, a plain number, which may never be used as an address. The search climbs the log to the last line whose entry after the ; changed R1, because that line is where r1 became a number, often a load from a map value or a helper's return value, such as the counter's slot 10, r1 = *(u64 *)(r0 +0), which leaves R1=scalar(). The fix is wherever the program meant to keep a pointer and kept a number instead. Adjusting the offset on the stopping line misses the cause, because the address was never an address.

5.3

The verifier erased them. At log level 1, which libbpf asks for after a failure, each finished path is wound back out of the log: when the walk returns for a kept branch, pop_stack() in kernel/bpf/verifier.c resets the log to where that branch was saved, and only at level 2 are the lines kept. What remains is the path that failed, while sudo bpftool -d prog load, which asks for levels 1, 2 and 4, shows every path. The missing lines do not mean the other side went unchecked; it was checked, accepted and then removed from the text.

5.4

Class, mode and size, and the four-byte read shows (61). The opcode byte of a load is the three fields added together: class LDX is 0x01, mode MEM is 0x60 and size DW, eight bytes, is 0x18, so 0x01 + 0x60 + 0x18 = 0x79. Size W, four bytes, is 0x00, which leaves 0x61. The values are in include/uapi/linux/bpf_common.h, with BPF_DW in bpf.h, and kernel/bpf/disasm.c prints the line with "(%02x) r%d = *(%s *)(r%d %+d)". Reading the size as the number of bytes, 8 or 4, gives a wrong byte, because the field holds a code for the size.

5.5

No. It moved and was renamed. In v7.2 the shape check is bpf_check_cfg() in kernel/bpf/cfg.c, still called from bpf_check() before the walk, still a depth-first search that reports jumps out of range, unreachable instructions and back-edges. Search for a message instead of the function name: grep -rn "unreachable insn" kernel/bpf finds the code in cfg.c, and otherwise only the design comment. Trusting the old name leads to the conclusion that the check is gone, when function names and files drift between releases and the two-pass design has stayed the same since 2014.

5.6

The test still expects the old wording. Its __msg(...) annotation names the text it wants, the runner searched the new log and did not find it, and test_loader.c reports that as expect_msg. That is the test doing its job, because the message is behaviour and someone depends on it. If the rewording is worth making, the same patch series must update every test that pins the old text, which grep -rln over the selftests finds. The failure can look like a broken kernel, but the program was rejected as before, only in different words.

5.7

bpf-next, with PATCH bpf-next in the subject. The guide sends fixes to the bpf tree and "features, cleanups or other kind of improvements" to bpf-next, and a comment correction is a cleanup. It gives the command, git format-patch --subject-prefix='PATCH bpf-next'. A Fixes: tag is required only for fixes. Before writing the patch, it is worth checking that the comment is still wrong in today's bpf-next and that nobody has sent the same patch to the list. Sending it to bpf because it "fixes" something would misplace it, since the code was never wrong, only its description.

5.8

Test cases in the BPF selftests. The guide says that for a change to verifier behaviour "it is absolutely necessary to add test cases", and that the maintainers "might ask for them before accepting any changes". The reason is in the same answer: behaviour that no test tracks "could potentially be subject to change", because the next person to touch the verifier has nothing to tell them it mattered. In practice the patch adds a function with __success or __failure and __msg(...) to a progs/verifier_*.c file. Small changes get no exemption, and they are the verifier changes most likely to break an existing program.

5.9

The selftests from the 7.2 tree. The guide's rule is "If you run a kernel xyz, then always run the BPF kernel selftests from that kernel xyz as well." Newer selftests are adapted to a newer verifier, which tracks more and accepts programs an older one refuses, so they can fail on 7.2 for reasons that have nothing to do with the change under test. The tag cloned for this chapter, v7.2, already has the matching selftests. Fetching the newest bpf-next tests and reading their failures as bugs in the running kernel is the mistake that rule prevents.

They were run on 12 November 2026 on kernel 7.2.15-arch1-1 with bpftool v7.8.0 and clang 23, in a throwaway virtual machine booted with virtme-ng (vng), as root inside it, using the same script. The map's address differs on every load.

What this shows. Key: a helper's arguments have types, and the key must be a pointer the program may read, such as the stack, while the thread ID is a scalar. That is the second half of the fifth row of Figure 4.2, and the proof was lost at slots 5 to 7, where r2 was built from a number. Redirect: each program type allows its own list of helpers, and the write counter's type may not redirect packets, which breaks the first half of the fifth row, lost at the call itself. Var: the bounds rule again, fourth row. Here the offset is 0 or 8, so the smallest access fits and the largest does not, which is why the reason says max where log (b), with a fixed offset of 8, said min. The proof was lost at slot 13, where the offset joined the pointer.

Common wrong turn. Reading the long expected= list as a list of things to try, when it lists every pointer type the key may be and the fix is to pass &pid again. The other is to read off=8 in the third log as a fixed offset of 8; the instruction says r0 +0, and the 8 is the largest value of the variable part.

Chapter 6

6.1

xxx1: every odd number from 1 to 15. The real sums are 4+1, 4+5, 6+1 and 6+5, so 5, 7, 9 and 11; the values 1, 3, 13 and 15 can never happen. The arithmetic of tnum_add() in kernel/bpf/tnum.c: masks add to 0110, values add to 0101, their sum is 1011, which differs from 0101 in 1110; OR the two masks in and the unknown bits are 1110, leaving bit 0 known as 1. Adding the values and ORing the masks looks reasonable and gives 0xx1, but that misses 9 and 11, so it is unsound: it ignores the carries, which spread the unknown bits upward.

6.2

From the range: 64 is the largest offset the register can add, plus the instruction's own 0. With fd <= 8 the test proves r6 is at most 8, and the shift by three makes that 64; the log line for slot 12 shows umax=64 on r0. check_mem_region_access() tries the largest offset, and eight bytes read from 64 end at 72, past the 64-byte value. Use fd < 8. It is easy to take off=64 for the instruction's offset field, but that field is zero, and the kernel adds the largest value of the range before it checks.

6.3

Because the register holds 64 bits, and the kernel reads them both ways. Without the test, r6 has no bounds, and after r6 <<= 3 the log shows smax=0x7ffffffffffffff8 with no smin printed, which means the signed minimum is the most negative 64-bit number. Adding a number that may be negative could move the pointer before the map value, so check_reg_sane_offset_scalar(), called from adjust_ptr_min_max_vals() in verifier.c, refuses the addition itself, before any read. The C type misleads here, because u64 exists only in the source and the bytecode attaches no signedness to registers.

6.4

umax=0xffffffff00000007 and var_off=(0x0; 0xffffffff00000007), the third row of Figure 6.8. A 32-bit jump compares only the low half, so regs_refine_cond_op() narrows the 32-bit arc to 0 to 7, and the sync makes bits 3 to 31 of the tnum known zeros; the upper 32 bits stay unknown. The largest 64-bit value is then all ones above bit 31 and 7 below. It is tempting to answer 7, as for a 64-bit test, but that needs the upper half known to be zero, which only the two shifts clang placed after the test provide.

6.5

That the slot still holds what the program last stored, with that value's whole state. A 64-bit store of a scalar to the stack keeps its register state in the slot, and a load back links register and slot by id, so the test at slot 11 narrows fp-8 as well and the second load copies the narrowed state (Figure 6.9, part b). A map value is memory that user space and other CPUs can write at any time, so every load from it starts as a fresh scalar with the full range of its size. It is tempting to credit volatile, but the verifier never sees it; it sees two loads from a slot it tracks.

6.6

It comes close to matters, with the same 8,827 states, because without CAP_BPF every scalar is precise from the start: __mark_reg_unknown() sets the flag to !env->bpf_capable (verifier.c line 2166), and bpf_mark_chain_precision() returns at once (backtrack.c line 805). With k precise, paths that left different constants in it cannot prune each other; 122,185 / 174 is about 700. A common mistake is to blame the extra checks an unprivileged load gets; the states column shows that the walk itself grew, as it does for matters, whose last line makes k precise.

6.7

On each path k & 7 is a different constant, so the addition moves the map pointer by a different known amount on each. Without CAP_PERFMON, sanitize_ptr_alu() records one limit and one kind of masking in the instruction's side data, and update_alu_sanitation_state() (verifier.c line 13393) refuses a second path whose record differs, because the rewritten instruction can carry only one. As root bpf_bypass_spec_v1() is true and nothing is recorded. It is easy to read "different maps" and look for a second map; the message covers three causes, and here it is the scalars.

6.8

40, and then 0. For 40: 56 − 40 = 16, 16 | 40 = 56, the negation makes it negative, the shift by 63 gives all ones, and the AND leaves 40, so slot 26 reads at offset 40. For 64: 56 − 64 = −8, −8 | 64 is still −8, the negation gives 8, the shift gives 0 and the AND gives 0, so slot 26 reads at offset 0. The test at slot 17 never lets 64 through on a path the CPU should take; the masking matters only when it runs past that test on a wrong guess. Reading the mask as a clamp to 56 is a common mistake: an offset out of range becomes 0, never the limit.

6.9

Because slot 3 is where r6 was written, and a test does not write the register it tests. Slot 3 loads r6 from memory that is not the stack, the tracepoint's arguments, and backtrack_insn() (backtrack.c line 267) ends the search at such a load: the value's range came from the size of the load, which no earlier register decided. Had slot 3 loaded r6 from the stack, the mark would have passed to that stack slot, and the walk would have gone on to the instruction that stored there. Stopping at slot 10 is a tempting answer, but a test only narrows a value that some earlier instruction made.

6.10

An abstract operator is sound when, for any inputs it is given, every concrete result is inside its abstract result. Equation 1 says it as: for all concrete values inside the input abstract values, the concrete operation's output is a member of the abstract output. The definition is in Section 2 under "Abstract operators", and the SMT form in Section 4.1. Requiring the abstract result to equal the concrete set asks for more than soundness; that is precision, which the paper treats as desirable and the kernel does not promise.

6.11

Because the kernel's code mixes them. Figure 2(b) sets the unsigned minimum from the tnum's value, so an operator on one description reads the output of another. The paper calls these abstraction/reduction operators and checks all five descriptions in one formula, which Section 3 calls "one-shot" reasoning. A reader who knows textbook reduced products may expect independent descriptions that can be proved one by one, but the kernel was never written that way.

6.12

5.13 to 5.19, under the refined specification. The assumption is that every input has already passed through the shared tail of the operators, reg_bounds_sync() in 5.19, which rules out combinations of descriptions no real program reaches (Section 4.2). Under the general specification every version from 4.14 to 5.19 had violations, as Figure 5(a) shows, and the older kernels held 27 bugs nobody had reported. Answering "all of them" overlooks the general check, which the newest kernels still fail, although no real program can trigger those failures.

What this shows. The bound is lost at slot 21. Slot 18 narrowed r1 to 0 to 7, but clang must assume that bpf_ktime_get_ns() may change memory, so it loads c->idx again after the call, and the verifier, which tracks registers and stack slots, gives a load from a map value the full range of its four bytes. The fixed program reads the value once and, as its log shows, adds the tested offset to the pointer before the call.

Common wrong turn. Taking slot 17 for the culprit, since it prints the same full range; the test at slot 18 narrows that load, and only the second one is never tested. Another is to blame the call for changing r1: it does change r1, which is caller-saved, and that is why clang loads the index again.

Chapter 7

7.1

Two slots, both after the map lookup. 232 bytes are 232 / 8 = 29 slots, and 29 − 27 = 2. htab_map_gen_lookup() in kernel/bpf/hashtab.c replaces call 0x1 with a call to __htab_map_lookup_elem() followed by if r0 == 0x0 goto pc+1 and r0 += 56, which moves r0 past the entry's header and key to the value. Check it with bpftool prog dump xlated: slots 9 and 10. Counting the map update as well would suggest more, but the update became a direct call to htab_map_update_elem() in the same single slot.

7.2

Six bytes in the first pass, two in the second, and four passes in all. By the guess the two skipped instructions take 2 × 64 = 128 bytes, one more than a two-byte jump can reach, so do_jit() writes the six-byte form and the first pass gives 156 bytes. The second pass works from real addresses, the jump shrinks by 4 to two bytes, and the image is 152 bytes; the third pass agrees, so the JIT takes memory for the image and writes it in a fourth. bpftrace on the return value of do_jit() showed 156, 152, 152, 152 on all ten loads. An answer of three passes stops at the first pass that agrees, but the image is written in the pass after it.

7.3

3,002 slots. Each of the 1,000 additions becomes three instructions, a move of the constant XORed with a random number into AX, an XOR with the same number, and the addition from AX; r0 = 0 has a zero constant, which bpf_jit_blind_insn() turns into one XOR of r0 with itself, and exit has none, so 3 × 1,000 + 1 + 1 = 3,002, as measured in step 5 of book/labs/jit-root.sh. The x86 length changes because the random values change the encoding: a non-negative value fits the shorter 32-bit move and a negative one needs the sign-extended 64-bit form (emit_mov_imm32()), so 100,000 blinded additions came out at 1,649,911 to 1,650,097 bytes. It is tempting to answer 2,002, two slots for each constant, but the original instruction stays as the third, now reading AX.

7.4

The verifier accepted the program and the JIT could not translate it. Error 524 is ENOTSUPP, a kernel-internal code, and __bpf_prog_select_runtime() in kernel/bpf/core.c, the last step of bpf_check(), returns it when a program was not translated and a JIT is required. With no interpreter to fall back to, the load fails after a clean verifier log. JITs for smaller architectures lack some instructions, such as some atomics. Suspicion falls first on the verifier, yet its log ends without a reason because it found none.

7.5

net.core.bpf_jit_limit. The kernel turns a classic seccomp filter into eBPF and gives it to the JIT, which charges the image against the limit in bpf_jit_charge_modmem(); past the limit that function refuses any caller without CAP_BPF, so the image is never allocated and the program is not translated. With no interpreter, __bpf_prog_select_runtime() reports -ENOTSUPP, and that is the errno the user sees. Root passes because CAP_BPF lets it go past the limit. Step 8 of book/labs/jit-root.sh set the limit to 1 and saw both a seccomp filter and a socket filter fail for nobody. Expecting EPERM is natural, since the refusal inside the kernel is -EPERM, but the JIT treats it as a failed allocation and the caller receives -ENOTSUPP, the error for any program left untranslated.

7.6

net.core.bpf_jit_harden at 1 or 2, or net.core.bpf_jit_kallsyms at 0. bpf_get_kallsym() in core.c lists no BPF program while bpf_jit_kallsyms_enabled() is false, and that function returns false whenever hardening is on or the kallsyms switch is off; sysctl net.core.bpf_jit_harden net.core.bpf_jit_kallsyms tells which. The kallsyms switch changes no code. Hardening at 1 changes none either for a root loader, whose programs are not blinded, although their names vanish; at 2 every program is blinded as well. The likely wrong conclusion is that the programs were never JIT-compiled, but bpftool still prints jited sizes and dumps the x86, only under a bare address.

7.7

34 times: the first run and 33 tail calls. The JIT's code compares the count with MAX_TAIL_CALL_CNT, 33, before each jump and adds 1 after the checks pass. The 34th attempt finds the count at 33, fails the check, and the program goes on after the call, so it ends normally. The check is in emit_bpf_tail_call_indirect() in arch/x86/net/bpf_jit_comp.c. An answer of 33 counts the jumps and forgets the first run, which was not a tail call.

7.8

About 0.18 seconds: 32 grace periods of about 5.6 ms. Emptying the slot makes bpf_arch_poke_desc_update() patch each call site twice and call synchronize_rcu() between the patches, so that no CPU is left inside a half-rewritten site, and it does this once for every program in the array's poke list whose descriptor names slot 0. Step 6 of book/labs/ch16-root.sh measured 180 to 195 ms. Filling the slot again patches two places per site too, but waits for no grace period, which took 57 to 64 ms here, about 1 ms a site for the interrupts to 16 virtual CPUs. Expecting microseconds, as for an ordinary array, is the usual mistake; that holds only while no direct tail call names the slot.

7.9

It runs on every write; its time is counted under count_writes. The statistics are taken in __bpf_prog_run() (include/linux/filter.h), which adds to run_cnt and run_time_ns of the program the hook called. A tail call jumps into count_update's machine code past its frame setup and never passes through that wrapper, so the 157 to 158 ns that count_writes reports cover both halves. It is tempting to conclude that the slot is empty, but then fell_through in the counter's .bss would count the writes, and the map total would stop; in step 4 it stayed at 0.

7.10

The owner check refused it after verification. When bpf_check() has finished, __bpf_prog_select_runtime() in core.c calls bpf_check_tail_call(), which runs __bpf_prog_map_compatible() against every map in the program's used_maps that holds programs. The array's owner is count_writes, a tracepoint program, so a socket filter does not match and the load returns ‑EINVAL with the verifier's log already complete; step 5 printed that log followed by libbpf: prog 'caller': failed to load: -EINVAL. Searching the log for a verifier error finds nothing, because the verifier accepted the program. The same check refuses the filter when user space tries to put it into a slot.

What this shows. Slot 4 is movq %rbp, %rsi and slot 5 is addq $-4, %rsi, because r10 lives in rbp and r2 in rsi. Slot 8 became three bytecode instructions, written by htab_map_gen_lookup(), and four x86 ones: the call, a test of rax, a jump past the add, and the add of 56.

Common wrong turn. Looking for call 0x1 or for helper names in the jited dump. The kernel renamed the call before the JIT ran, and the jited dump shows only addresses; the xlated dump is where the names are.

Expected output. Numbers like these from /tmp/book-labs/jit/time.txt and harden.txt, kernel 7.2.15 in a virtme-ng VM with 16 virtual CPUs, 12 November 2026; the times move by a factor of two between sessions on a busy host, the slots and bytes do not. Each addition takes 6 bytes of x86, and blinded, 16.5 bytes for the three instructions that replace it.

What this shows. The JIT costs about 40 to 60 ns a slot and the verifier 3 to 4 µs for these programs, so translation is about a seventieth of the load; both grow in step with the program. Blinding does not: it took 4.2 ms at 1,000 instructions, 388 ms at 10,000 and, in the same step, 5.1 s at 30,000 and 58 s at 100,000, about ten times as long for each tripling, because every patch moves the rest of the program.

Common wrong turn. Reading the first lines bpftrace prints as the generated program's. libbpf and bpftool load small probe programs of their own, which jit.bt reports too; take the lines that carry the program's name. Timing the whole load from user space is the other trap, since it adds verification to the JIT.

Expected output. Lines like these from step 4 of book/labs/ch16-root.sh on kernel 7.2.15 in a virtme-ng VM. With only the link pinned, jmp_table is empty a second after the loader exits, neither count_update nor write_counts exists any more, and every write falls through, 43 of them from other processes. With the array pinned too, the slot keeps its program and the total grows with the writes.

What this shows. A program holds its program array with a reference but no user reference, so the loader's exit took usercnt to zero and prog_array_map_clear() emptied the slots. The emptied slot dropped the last reference to count_update, and freeing it released write_counts from its used_maps.

Common wrong turn. Pinning only write_counts. The counts stay readable, but the array still loses its last user reference, so the counter stops counting while its map looks healthy.

Chapter 8

8.1

libbpf's load step failed before any BPF_PROG_LOAD, so the kernel never saw the program. The prefix tracepoints has an extra s, and since the table entry tracepoint+ accepts only the bare word, or the word followed by a slash, no entry matches and the program type stays unset. libbpf refuses such a program in bpf_object_load_prog() (libbpf.c line 7939 in v7.2) with that message. A missing tracepoint would fail differently: a wrong name after the slash loads fine and fails later, at attach.

8.2

10, 10 and 0. The tracepoint fires as each call enters the kernel, before anything is checked, so the counter runs ten times. ksys_write() finds the file and calls vfs_write(), which fails its first test, FMODE_WRITE, and returns -EBADF, so the fentry on vfs_write() runs ten times. The permission check comes after that test, in rw_verify_area(), so it never runs. Run with bpftrace on kernel 7.2.15 in a virtme-ng VM: @tracepoint_sys_enter_write: 10, @fentry_vfs_write: 10, @fexit_vfs_write_returned[-9]: 10, and no line for the permission check. Expecting 0 from the counter because the writes failed gets the order wrong, since the tracepoint runs before the kernel knows they will fail.

8.3

The function still exists, so the kprobe attached, but the path that opens files no longer calls it as a separate function. The compiler may have inlined it into its callers in the new build, or the code may have been reorganised so that open goes another way. A kprobe binds to one address in one function and does not follow inlined copies; the kprobes documentation says so. Check with sudo grep -w do_sys_openat2 /sys/kernel/tracing/available_filter_functions and read the new kernel's fs/open.c. The tracepoint syscalls:sys_enter_openat is kept on purpose. Blaming the load or the verifier gets nowhere, since both succeeded and nothing reported an error.

8.4

At 0x60 for the kprobe program and at 0x10 for the fentry program. The kprobe's r1 points at the struct pt_regs that the ftrace trampoline saved; count is the third argument, which x86-64 passes in rdx, and dx is the thirteenth eight-byte field of pt_regs, after r15 to r8, ax and cx, so 12 × 8 = 96. The fentry program's r1 points at the arguments the trampoline stored from rbp − 0x20, eight bytes each, so the third is at 2 × 8 = 16. llvm-objdump -d of the two programs shows r1 = *(u64 *)(r1 + 0x60) and r1 = *(u64 *)(r1 + 0x10). Answering 16 for both is tempting, since the two macros take the same argument list, but BPF_KPROBE hides a PT_REGS_PARM3() read.

8.5

Offset 0xc is inside an instruction. vfs_write+0x9 starts the seven-byte sub $0x88,%rsp, which runs to 0xf, so 0xc is its fourth byte, and an int3 there would change the instruction's immediate instead of stopping the CPU. Before arming, arch_prepare_kprobe() calls can_probe() in arch/x86/kernel/kprobes/core.c, which decodes the function from its start and returns false for an address that is not an instruction boundary, and the kprobe is refused with -EILSEQ, "illegal byte sequence". objdump -d on the kernel's vmlinux shows where the instructions start. It is easy to read EILSEQ as a problem with the encoding of the probe's name, but libbpf parsed the name correctly; the error is about the bytes at that address.

8.6

On the slow machine the probe is still a breakpoint. Each write traps at vfs_write+0x9, where kprobe_int3_handler() runs the program, and traps again after a copy of the sub has run out of line, because on a preemptible kernel prepare_singlestep() ends the copy with a second int3. The trap enters through irqentry_nmi_enter(), so the program runs as if in an NMI, with in_nmi() true, which limits what it may safely do with locks and buffers. On the fast machine the optimiser replaced the int3 with a jump (e9 in the bytes); the slow one has debug.kprobes-optimization set to 0, or an instruction there that cannot be moved. Suspecting the program or the JIT is a common mistake, as both machines run the same code.

8.7

An LSM program, on a hook such as file_permission or file_open, that returns -EPERM when the file matches and 0 otherwise. LSM hooks sit at the points where the kernel asks whether an operation is allowed, and the verifier accepts negative error codes from them. Tracing programs cannot do it, because a tracepoint or kprobe program's return value only decides whether the trace record is kept, and fentry programs must return 0. Check /sys/kernel/security/lsm for bpf, and read the example in the kernel's LSM BPF page. A kprobe program that returns 1 may look like a refusal, yet the write goes on regardless.

8.8

The plus means both forms are accepted: the bare word, or the word, a slash and extras that say how to attach automatically. A program in plain SEC("kprobe") still gets program type KPROBE and loads, but it names no function, so the skeleton's attach() skips it and the loader must attach it by hand, for example with bpf_program__attach_kprobe(). The rules are the two bullets at the top of the page, and libbpf's attach_kprobe() has the comment "no auto-attach for SEC("kprobe")". Anyone expecting a load error will be surprised, because the bare form is legal and only fails to attach itself.

8.9

BPF_PROG_TYPE_TRACEPOINT, reached by two section names, tp+ and tracepoint+, with the attach type column empty, so SEC("tp/syscalls/sys_enter_write") would give the same program. The attach type the write counter ends up with, BPF_PERF_EVENT, appears only at attach, in BPF_LINK_CREATE, which is why this table does not list it. The empty cell can look like "cannot be attached"; what it means is that nothing has to be chosen at load.

8.10

Because they receive different things. tp_btf+ gives BPF_PROG_TYPE_TRACING with attach type BPF_TRACE_RAW_TP, and the program gets the tracepoint's raw arguments, here two task_struct pointers, typed by the kernel's own type information. tracepoint+ gives BPF_PROG_TYPE_TRACEPOINT, and the program gets the tracepoint's formatted record, which is why the write counter's argument is a struct trace_event_raw_sys_enter. The table puts the two prefixes in different rows, and the footnote for tp_btf+ gives its format. Since tp is another spelling of tracepoint, tp_btf looks like a third, and the separate rows show otherwise.

A desktop with more modules loaded lists more functions that ftrace can patch.

What this shows. There are about thirty functions to attach to for every tracepoint, which is the trade in Figure 8.4: many more places, none of them promised. BTF lists more functions than ftrace can patch, because some functions have no ftrace slot, and fentry needs both.

$ cat /tmp/book-labs/ch14/lab-misses.txt

Expected output. As above, from step 11 of book/labs/ch14-root.sh on kernel 7.2.15 in a virtme-ng VM with preemption full; hashmap is the counter at its tracepoint, wc_kp and wc_fe the same body as a kprobe and as an fentry program on vfs_write. Misses and map total add up to 6,000,004 because four other writes happened during each run. The share changes from run to run: six runs of the tracepoint version lost 45 to 55 per cent.

What this shows. Every miss is a write the counter never saw. At the tracepoint and through the trampoline, a writer switched out inside the program leaves the program's counter for that CPU at one, and the other writer's runs on that CPU are skipped until it resumes. The kprobe runs with preemption off, so no task can be switched out inside it.

Common wrong turn. Leaving the writers unpinned: the scheduler puts them on different CPUs and the misses vanish. And bpftool prog show prints recursion_misses only when it is not zero, so a missing field means none.

Chapter 9

9.1

Slot 32, and 0x400. The object has 27 slots; the hash map's rewrite turns slot 8 into three instructions, giving 29 and an exit at 28, while array_map_gen_lookup() turns it into seven, 27 − 1 + 7 = 33, so the exit moves to 32. The seven are r1 += 304, the offset of the values in struct bpf_array, then r0 = *(u32 *)(r2 +0), if r0 >= 0x400 goto pc+3, r0 <<= 3, r0 += r1, goto pc+1 and r0 = 0 (xlated-counter_array.txt from book/labs/ch13-root.sh). Had the map's creator lacked CAP_PERFMON, an eighth instruction, w0 &= 0x3ff, would mask the index against a speculative read, putting the exit at 33. Counting the two-slot map load as replaced is the usual slip; it stays.

9.2

bpf_trace_printk(), helper 6, which bpf_printk() becomes. Its prototype, bpf_trace_printk_proto in kernel/trace/bpf_trace.c, sets .gpl_only = true, and check_helper_call() compares that with prog->gpl_compatible, which bpf_prog_load() set from the licence string (chapter 3); line 10201 of verifier.c prints the message. Slots 0 and 8 passed because their prototypes say false, as does slot 24's, and the log shows 16: (85) call bpf_trace_printk#6 just above the refusal. It is tempting to think the licence refuses the whole program; removing bpf_printk() lets it load, as does a GPL-compatible string such as "Dual MIT/GPL".

9.3

From the second argument type of bpf_map_lookup_elem_proto, ARG_PTR_TO_MAP_KEY. check_func_arg() calls check_reg_type(), which looks the argument type up in compatible_reg_types[] in verifier.c; for a map key that is mem_types, the ten pointer kinds the message lists, starting with fp, a pointer into the stack. Here r2 holds the thread ID as a scalar, and a scalar is never an address, or the helper would read four bytes wherever the number pointed. The cast satisfies clang, which cannot know what helper 1 expects. A common mistake is to suspect the key size; that check comes only after the type check passes.

9.4

The BTF ID sets. check_kfunc_call() asks btf_kfunc_is_allowed() whether ID 82636 is in a set registered for the common hook or for the program type's hook. A socket filter maps to BTF_KFUNC_HOOK_SOCKET_FILTER in bpf_prog_type_to_kfunc_hook(), and kfunc_init() registers the generic set, which holds bpf_task_from_pid(), only for tracing, tc, XDP, struct_ops, syscall and cgroup skb programs, so bpf_fetch_kfunc_arg_meta() returns -EACCES and line 12935 prints the message. In the tracepoint counter the same call loads, because tracepoint programs share the TRACING hook. Whether the function exists was never the question: a kfunc is allowed per hook, much as get_func_proto() allows a helper per program type.

9.5

The loader's capabilities, through the last step of the chain. XDP's xdp_func_proto() passes bpf_trace_printk through bpf_sk_base_func_proto() in net/core/filter.c to bpf_base_func_proto(), which answers it only after bpf_token_capable(…, CAP_PERFMON) at line 2192 of helpers.c; CAP_SYS_ADMIN had to go too, because bpf_ns_capable() in token.c accepts it in place of any other capability. Without them the chain returns NULL, and bpf_get_helper_proto() turns every NULL into the same refusal, which check_helper_call() prints as a matter of program type. bpftool ran its probe as root. It is easy to blame XDP itself, but the same object loaded as root (load-xdp-root.txt against load-xdp-noperfmon.txt, from book/labs/calls-root.sh, step 6).

9.6

About 31.3 ns a call, and about a fifth of the counter's run. The 64 calls added 2,049.0 − 47.5 = 2,001.5 ns, and 2,001.5 / 64 = 31.3 ns. One call per event would add 31.3 / 155 ≈ 0.20 to a run that the costs box of chapter 8 measured at 144 to 162 ns without bpf_printk. The call itself is the 4 ns of any helper call; the rest is reading the clock, which in this VM is kvm-clock, so the number belongs to the clock source as much as to BPF. A common mistake is to expect the clock to be inlined like bpf_jiffies64(); in v7.2 the dump keeps call bpf_ktime_get_ns (Figure 9.6), and a program that needs one timestamp per run should read it once.

9.7

The map's flags, which array_map_gen_lookup() reads. Its first test, at line 227 of arraymap.c, returns -EOPNOTSUPP for a map created with BPF_F_INNER_MAP, which the user-space API header describes as a map that may go into another map "with dynamic max entries": the program may then reach arrays of other sizes through the same call, and seven instructions with one array's max_entries written into them would be wrong for the rest. bpf_do_misc_fixups() falls back to a direct call of the map's own array_map_lookup_elem(), the 4.9 ns bar of Figure 9.5. Nothing in the bytecode differs, so the object's dump looks the same; it is tempting to look for a compiler change, but only bpftool prog dump xlated of the loaded program shows the call where seven instructions stood.

9.8

libbpf's probe counts any refusal other than an unknown or refused helper as support (libbpf_probes.c, line 478), and its test program fails here for another reason, the sleep check. bpf_copy_from_user_proto sets might_sleep, and check_helper_call() refuses it at line 10227 when the program is not in a sleepable context. Making the program sleepable lets the call load: for a system-call tracepoint that is the section SEC("tp.s/syscalls/sys_enter_write"), the prefix under which our copy that calls the sleepable kfunc bpf_copy_from_user_str() loaded (load-sleepkf_s.txt). It is tempting to read the probe's list as a promise for every program of the type, but it lists what the type may name, and the sleep, licence and argument checks still apply.

Expected output. As above, from one run of book/labs/ch13-root.sh (step 3) on kernel 7.2.15 in a virtme-ng VM with clang 23.1.4 and bpftool 7.8.0; offsets after # differ between kernels. The broken copies fail with -EINVAL and -EACCES.

What this shows. In the object a kfunc call is call -0x1 with source register 1 and a relocation; libbpf turns it into source register 2 with the BTF ID, which the verifier log prints as #82636, and the fixup turns that into an offset from __bpf_call_base like any helper's. KF_ACQUIRE created reference 2 at slot 2, and the exit found it unreleased; KF_RET_NULL made the read through r0 illegal until a test.

Common wrong turn. Releasing the task before reading t->tgid. After bpf_task_release() the verifier turns every copy of the pointer into a plain number, and the read fails with R6 invalid mem access 'scalar' (load-kfunc_useafter.txt).

Expected output. As above, from xlated-inline.txt of book/labs/calls-root.sh (step 3) on kernel 7.2.15 in a virtme-ng VM; the constants and addresses differ between boots. The object has eight call instructions in 33 slots, 0 to 32.

What this shows. bpf_do_misc_fixups() replaced four calls with instructions: three each for the processor number and the current task, read through a per-processor address (the __percpu lines), three for bpf_jiffies64(), a wide load of the address of jiffies and a read, and seven for the array lookup. The other four calls stay, one of them under the name of bpf_user_rnd_u32(), the function in bpf_get_prandom_u32_proto.

Common wrong turn. Expecting bpf_get_current_pid_tgid() to vanish, since it reads the current task as bpf_get_current_task() does. It also combines two fields of the task, and no fixup in v7.2 writes it in place, so it stays a call at 4.1 ns.

What this shows. libbpf refuses a missing kfunc itself unless it is __weak; then it writes 0 into the wide load of the function's address and replaces the call with a call of helper 2,002,000,000 plus the symbol's index, whose refusal it rewrites into the two lines above. Chapter 10

10.1

83,968 bytes. The bpf_htab object is 896 bytes; 1024 buckets of 16 bytes are 16,384; 1040 elements of 64 bytes, max_entries plus one spare per possible CPU, are 66,560; and 16 pointers to the spares are 128. That is htab_map_mem_usage() in hashtab.c, and sudo bpftool map show name write_counts prints it as memlock 83968B. Counting only keys and values gives 1024 × 12 = 12,288, which forgets that every element also carries 48 bytes of links and hash and that every key and value is rounded up to 8 bytes.

10.2

The map is full. All 1024 elements were made at creation, and every thread that ever wrote holds one, alive or not. An update for a new key finds no free element and returns -E2BIG (alloc_htab_elem() in hashtab.c), and the counter ignores the return value of bpf_map_update_elem(), so the miss is silent. Updates to existing keys still work, through the per-CPU spares. Check with sudo bpftool map dump name write_counts | grep -c key: it says 1024. Use BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_HASH, delete threads as they exit, or raise max_entries. No verifier or instruction limit is involved, since the program loaded long ago and still runs.

10.3

From one 8-byte value for each of the 16 possible CPUs. A per-CPU map keeps a separate value for every CPU the machine could ever have, and a lookup from user space returns all of them at once, each rounded up to 8 bytes; libbpf checks the size before it calls the kernel (validate_map_op() in libbpf.c). Pass an array of libbpf_num_possible_cpus() values and add them up. Check the count in /sys/devices/system/cpu/possible, which reads 0-15. Sizing the array by the CPUs online now can fall short, because the kernel counts possible CPUs, which can be more.

10.4

1,131,392 bytes as a per-CPU hash and 92,032 as the plain hash. htab_map_mem_usage() in hashtab.c starts from the 896-byte struct bpf_htab and 1,024 buckets of 16 bytes, 17,280 in all. A per-CPU hash adds 1,024 elements of 64 bytes, each holding a pointer where the value would be, and 8 bytes for every value on each of 128 possible CPUs: 65,536 + 1,048,576. The plain hash adds 1,024 + 128 elements, one spare per CPU, and 128 pointers to the spares: 73,728 + 1,024. With 16 CPUs the same sums give Figure 10.5's 213,888 and 83,968. Multiplying the whole 64-byte element by the CPUs, about 8.4 MB, is the usual slip; only the value is kept per CPU.

10.5

The nested update found its bucket's lock already held by its own CPU and gave up with ‑EDEADLK, 35 on x86. Replacing an element whose value holds a timer calls bpf_obj_cancel_fields() from check_and_cancel_fields() inside htab_map_update_elem(), with the bucket locked, so the fentry program runs inside the outer update. Its own update asks for the same resilient lock, and check_deadlock_AA() in rqspinlock.c finds that lock in the CPU's list of held locks. The second hash has its own buckets and locks, none of them held. Step 4 of book/labs/ch15-root.sh prints both results. Reading ‑35 as a full map is tempting, but that is ‑E2BIG, ‑7; before 6.15 the answer was ‑EBUSY, ‑16.

10.6

A tracepoint program may not use a map whose value holds a bpf_spin_lock at all. check_map_prog_compatibility() in verifier.c refuses such a map for every type that is_tracing_prog_type() lists, kprobe, tracepoint, perf_event and raw tracepoint. The source gives no reason beyond the word "yet", but the list holds the types that can fire in an NMI (Figure 8.8), where waiting for a lock the interrupted code holds would never end. fentry is BPF_PROG_TYPE_TRACING, which the list leaves out, so the same code loads there (step 5). The counter needs no lock: __sync_fetch_and_add() changes its one 8-byte count whole, and a lock pays only when several fields must change together. Suspecting the lock helper is natural, but the refusal comes as the map is first named, before any call is checked.

10.7

Into lost updates. Keyed by process, all eight threads share one element, and the counter reads the count, adds one on its stack and writes the sum back with bpf_map_update_elem(). Two CPUs that read the same old value both store old + 1, so one count disappears, and the bucket lock only makes the stores take turns. In Figure 10.6 eight writers on one key lost 66 per cent this way, while run_cnt matched the calls made, which is how to tell this apart from chapter 8's misses. Adding one in place with __sync_fetch_and_add() lost nothing, and a per-CPU hash would count every write too. Blaming the hook is natural after chapter 8, but recursion_misses at zero says every run happened.

10.8

About 14.9 ns behind an array of maps and 28.3 ns behind a hash of maps. The first lookup costs what a lookup in that kind of outer map costs: the kernel writes an array-of-maps lookup in place as a few instructions of index arithmetic (array_of_map_gen_lookup() in arraymap.c), which adds under a nanosecond, while a hash of maps first makes a full hash lookup of its own, about 14 ns more. Step 3 of book/labs/ch16-root.sh measured both on kernel 7.2.15 with 16 virtual CPUs. It is tempting to double the time for both, but only the hash of maps pays for a second hash lookup.

Common wrong turn. Adding a check of running to the inner loop. Ctrl-C then works, but the table still holds one key printed forever.

Expected output. Lines like these, from the third of three rounds of step 7 of book/labs/ch15-root.sh on kernel 7.2.15 in a virtme-ng VM, with recursion_misses 0 on every run. Over the three rounds the LRU copy took 81 to 83 ns a run and the copy without bpf_printk() 151 to 153, once 599 while the host was busy; the counter as written took 500 to 1,242. What this shows. The counter as written pays for an update on every write, a bucket lock and an element swap, although its key already exists; adding through the pointer that the lookup returned leaves only the lookup and one locked add. The LRU hash weighs about the same as the hash and evicts instead of refusing a new thread.

Common wrong turn. Keeping bpf_map_update_elem() after the add. The count stays right, but every write pays for the bucket lock and the element swap again, and the gain disappears. Switching to PERCPU_HASH instead costs 213,888 bytes and a sum on every read, for keys that no two CPUs write at once.

Chapter 11

11.1

About 64,000 bytes, and no loader's cgroup pays. Each node is 48 bytes, a 32-byte bpf_rb_node, the thread ID, padding and the count; the BPF memory allocator puts an 8-byte header in front and serves 56 bytes from its 64-byte class, which the kernel's 64-byte slab cache backs. The allocator behind bpf_obj_new() was set up at boot, so the loader's memory.current does not move: for 100,000 nodes the slab grew by 97,440 objects and the cgroup by nothing (mem.txt). Counting 48 bytes a node, or looking at memlock, misses both the header and where the memory is charged.

11.2

A BTF tracepoint is a tracing program that cannot sleep, and v7.2's check_kfunc_call() refuses bpf_obj_drop() there, as at fentry, when the type holds a field that is unsafe in an NMI; a bpf_rb_node is one. The removal itself is allowed, so the program can take the node out under the lock and add it to a second tree of nodes to free in the same map value. A syscall program that user space runs, as the counter's drain is, or a sleepable program then drops them. Moving to the classic tracepoint makes it worse: there the map cannot even be named.

11.3

No. When the kernel copies a map value out to user space it copies around the special fields, the lock and the root (bpf_obj_memcpy() in include/linux/bpf.h), so those bytes always read as zeros, and the nodes are separate objects that the map does not contain. The counter's own nodes field, an ordinary u64 it updates under the lock, is what reports seven. To see the counts, run a program that walks or drains the tree, as drain does. Taking the zeros as an empty tree is the mistake here.

11.4

The tree took 817 ns a run and the hash 88.5 (bench.txt). Every run of the tree counter takes the tree's single bpf_spin_lock, with interrupts off, so eight CPUs queue for one lock on every write, and the wait is counted in run_time_ns. The hash finds each thread's slot without a lock and adds with an atomic instruction in place, taking a bucket lock only to insert a new thread, so eight writers on eight keys barely touch each other. Expecting the tree's cost to grow with its depth alone misses the lock.

11.5

The verifier types arena memory as plain bytes: check_mem_access() marks any value loaded through a pointer of type arena as an unknown scalar, so the task pointer comes back as a number and following it is refused. Storing it was accepted because a privileged program may write a pointer's value anywhere, which gives the colleague a false start. Keep in the arena what the kernel will not need to trust, the thread ID or an index, and keep the referenced task in a kptr field of a map value, found by that index, as the sched_ext authors described doing in 2025.

11.6

In the arena's pages, charged to the memory cgroup of the process that created the arena, about 3.3 MB: 100,000 keys cost 3,338,240 bytes of memory.current, 33.4 bytes a key, for 32-byte elements packed 127 to a page (mem.txt). arena_map_mem_usage() in arena.c returns 0, so memlock says nothing about an arena, however full. Reading memlock as the arena's size, as one can for a hash, gives the wrong answer; memory.current of the creator's cgroup, read before and after, gives the right one.

11.7

The selftests' hash table picks a bucket by the key's low bits, 1,024 buckets, so the two threads land in one bucket, and htab_update_elem() links a new element at the head of the bucket's list with no lock. Both CPUs can read the same old head and each write its own element in front of it, so one element is lost and its thread is counted again from 1 later. The verifier checks that arena accesses go to the arena and nothing about what they mean, so a race in arena memory loads cleanly. A lock in arena memory, such as the selftests' arena spin lock, would close it.

11.8

A drop does not hand the memory back at once. bpf_obj_drop() frees through bpf_mem_free_rcu(), which puts the object on a waiting list until an RCU grace period has passed, since another program may still hold a pointer to it, so the next bpf_obj_new() cannot reuse it and the CPU's free list runs down. irq_work then refills the list with batches from the slab, which grew by 59,000 to 98,000 objects during 100,000 such pairs (alloc.txt). Expecting a free list to recycle the same object, as a simple cache would, is the trap.

The drop in kptrstore is allowed at fentry because its object, a struct wcount, has no list or tree field; parking a struct wnode the same way would be refused at the drop.

Chapter 12

12.1

Eight, eight and 3. The loader loads one program per filled member, and bpf_struct_ops_map_update_elem() writes a trampoline only for a member that holds a program, skipping a zero descriptor (bpf_struct_ops.c line 797), so the 29 empty members get neither. The member's index travels in expected_attach_type, and the kernel insists on it (line 808); dispatch is the fourth function pointer, after select_cpu, enqueue and dequeue. strace printed it as BPF_CGROUP_SOCK_OPS, the attach type whose value is 3. It is tempting to expect 37 trampolines, one per member, but an empty member stays NULL, and /proc/kallsyms listed eight.

12.2

A scalar where the program expected a pointer. The verifier types each argument from the member's prototype, and the first parameter of dispatch is s32 cpu, so btf_ctx_access() made the value loaded from offset 0 of the context a scalar; the log shows R1=scalar(), and the load at prev->pid, offset 2872, fails. The code compiled because BPF_STRUCT_OPS() casts each 64-bit slot of the context to whatever type the source declares. The verifier never compares the declared signature with the prototype as a whole; it only types each read, which is why the fix is to copy the parameter order from bpftool btf dump file /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux format c.

12.3

BPF_LINK_CREATE failed with -EBUSY. The link's reg() reached scx_root_enable_workfn(), which refuses when the enable state is not DISABLED (ext.c lines 7127 and 7128), and libbpf's bpf_map__attach_struct_ops() reported the error as a failed attach. Before that the second copy had loaded its eight programs and filled its own struct_ops map, which sat in the state READY until the loader exited and closed its descriptors; nothing of it was registered, and the first scheduler stayed enabled under the name simple. In v7.2 a second scheduler can only join as a sub-scheduler of a cgroup, which needs the cid-form table and CONFIG_EXT_SUB_SCHED.

12.4

About 2 ms; the runs took 1.76 to 2.28 ms. A round trip is two wake-ups, and in FIFO mode a woken task joins the tail of SHARED_DSQ and runs only when some CPU's spinner has used up its slice and that CPU calls ops.dispatch(). Sixteen slices of 20 ms that end at scattered times end, on average, one every 20 / 16 = 1.25 ms, so each wake-up waits up to that long and a round trip costs roughly 1.25 to 2.5 ms. A common mistake is to expect 20 ms a wake-up, which forgets that any of the 16 CPUs may pick the task up. Under the fair class the same test took 35 µs, because a woken task does not wait for a slice to end.

12.5

The process exit closed the struct_ops link. The loader held the link's only descriptor, so its release ran bpf_struct_ops_map_link_dealloc(), which calls the subsystem's unreg() (bpf_struct_ops.c lines 1254 and 1263), and sched_ext's unreg() disables the scheduler with the same reason as a clean exit; the run measured 3 ms from the signal to disabled. sched_ext never watches the process. To keep a table registered without its loader, pin the link in bpffs, as bpftool struct_ops register does when given a directory: bpf_mini stayed available after bpftool exited and went when the pin was removed. A map made without BPF_F_LINK instead stays registered until its entry is deleted.

12.6

Each subsystem decides what it needs in its own validate() and reg(). TCP has no fallback for ssthresh, undo_cwnd, and one of cong_avoid or cong_control, so tcp_validate_congestion_control() logs that message and returns -EINVAL (net/ipv4/tcp_cong.c lines 78 to 85), which the map update passes on. sched_ext has a built-in behaviour for every callback, its bpf_scx_validate() returns 0, and the only data it checks is in bpf_scx_init_member(), which refuses an empty name with -EINVAL (ext.c lines 7959 to 7966), the Invalid argument of our run with .name = "". The struct_ops mechanism itself requires no member at all.

12.7

In the kfunc. run_time_ns counts everything between the program's entry and its exit, and scx_bpf_dsq_move_to_local() first flushes the scheduler's pending insertions and then looks at SHARED_DSQ. When the queue is empty it returns after a check without a lock (consume_dispatch_q(), ext.c line 2525); when a task waits it takes the queue's raw spinlock, and a task queued on another CPU's runqueue has to be migrated (line 2552). simple_enqueue ran 36,642 times against 112,083 dispatches, so most dispatches were cheap and the average hides dearer moves. simple_running only compares and stores one number. It would be wrong to blame the BPF code itself, which is one call instruction.

12.8

Thirty seconds is SCX_WATCHDOG_MAX_TIMEOUT (kernel/sched/ext/types.h line 20), used when the table's timeout_ms is 0 (ext.c lines 6886 to 6889). The watchdog runs every half timeout and walks each online CPU's runnable list in order, stopping at the first task over the limit (lines 3475 to 3488). kworker/0:1 may run only on CPU 0, so the core never calls ops.select_cpu() for it (core.c line 3618), every wake-up sends it through ops.enqueue() into SHARED_DSQ, and CPU 0 comes first in the walk, before the busy loop pinned to CPU 5. A shorter wait comes from setting .timeout_ms in the table; above 30,000 ms, init_member() refuses it with -E2BIG.

Expected output. As above, with the timestamps cut, from kernel 7.2.15 in a virtme-ng VM with 16 vCPUs on 13 November 2026: medians of 3.11 µs under the fair class and 2.41 µs under scx_simple, within each other's spread, and an exit 30.4 seconds after the broken scheduler was enabled. Your round trips depend on the host; the 30 seconds do not, since they are the default timeout.

What this shows. A BPF scheduler costs nothing measurable on a quiet machine, and a broken one is contained: the watchdog found a task that had been runnable for longer than the timeout, the kernel moved every task back to the fair class, and the dump named the task, its CPU and the queue it waited in.

Common wrong turn. Compiling the loader with the build's own include directory ahead of the variant's: scx_simple.c then picks up the original scx_simple.bpf.skel.h, the broken scheduler runs as well as the real one, and no watchdog ever fires. Our first runs for this chapter made this mistake; -iquote with the variant's directory, or strings on the binary, settles which object a loader embeds.

Chapter 13

13.1

The bound scales with the total: e × 7,000,000 / 2,719 is about 7,000, exceeded by a given thread's estimate with probability at most e−5, 0.0067. The run at 700,000 writes had a median error of 90 against a bound of 700, so the typical error should be near 900, a seventh of the bound, because a counter holds about N/w = 2,574 writes and the smallest of five such counters is well below the average. It is tempting to think the error stays fixed as the stream grows, but the sketch's memory is fixed and its error grows with N.

13.2

It works as designed: each of its five counters also holds the writes of every other thread hashed there, about 257 on average, and 93 is the smallest of the five. The guarantee is an absolute error of εN, which is large next to three. A wider sketch brings it down in proportion, 272 to 2,719 counters took the median error from 1,041 to 90, and more rows lower the chance of an unlucky thread. A common mistake is to blame the hash; summing a row, which gives N, and comparing with e·N/w shows the error is the expected one.

13.3

An LRU hash evicts the entries used least recently, not the smallest. The heavy threads made their 100,000 writes early in the run, in about 50 ms, and then stopped, while the light threads went on inserting for two seconds. To insert into a full LRU hash, __bpf_lru_list_shrink() in bpf_lru_list.c takes entries from the tail of the inactive list, sparing only those looked up since the last scan, and the heavy threads' entries had not been looked up for most of the run. The count a long-lived, now quiet thread built up is exactly what an LRU hash throws away, and the sketch keeps.

13.4

The sixteen 24-byte nodes sit in a few cache lines of one arena page, and every heavy writer finds its own node and stores a new estimate there on each write. With one writer the lines stay in one CPU's cache; with eight, the lines move between CPUs on almost every write, which is the 38 ns. The counters rarely share a line, since keys land at random among 1,700 lines. Updating the table only every hundredth write, or giving each node a line of its own, would cut the traffic; padding nodes to 64 bytes costs 640 bytes more.

13.5

Lookup must return a pointer to a value the map stores, and a sketch stores nothing per key; its answer is the minimum of d counters, computed on each query. Peek, as the bloom filter uses it, takes the key in a buffer and can return a number, so the estimate comes back as peek's return value. User space has no such return value, so BPF_MAP_LOOKUP_ELEM on the count-min map reads the key from the value buffer and writes the estimate into the count that follows it, a branch the series adds to bpf_map_copy_value() in syscall.c.

13.6

Peek's prototype marks its buffer MEM_UNINIT, written by the call, which is true for a queue. For a bloom filter resolve_map_arg_type() turns it into a buffer the call reads, but stack liveness in v7.2, bpf_helper_stack_access_bytes(), reads only the prototype. It concludes that the key stored before the call is never read, poisons those stack slots when it cleans the state, and the argument check then refuses to read them. Mainline commit 830e4372de5c made liveness ask about bloom filter peeks, which is why a kernel with that fix loads the program.

13.7

The fetching OR becomes an atomic instruction that the x86 JIT cannot emit for arena memory: bpf_jit_supports_insn() refuses fetching AND, OR and XOR there, and the verifier, which asks the JIT, prints "BPF_ATOMIC stores into R1 arena is not allowed". A compare-and-swap loop does the same work and is accepted: read the counter, compute the value with the flag set, and retry __sync_val_compare_and_swap() until it succeeds; its return value says whether the flag was already set. A non-fetching OR, whose old value is discarded, is also allowed.

13.8

The arena, in most cases. It runs on the kernels the team already has, provided they support arenas and the atomics it uses, needs no change to the kernel, and leaves the team owning its code, its locking and its bugs; user space reads it without a system call. A map type needs the eight patches, maintainers who agree to a permanent uapi value and the kernels that carry it, which can take years to reach a fleet. A kfunc module gives kernel code and speed without a uapi change, but the team then maintains a module against every kernel it runs, since kfuncs promise no stability.
