Chapter 14

14.1

Four numbers, 81 tnums, 6,561 pairs; on five bits 59,049. x0x1 has two unknown bits, so γ holds 2 × 2 = 4 values: 0001, 0011, 1001 and 1011, which are 1, 3, 9 and 11. Each of four bits is 0, 1 or x, so there are 34 = 81 tnums and 81 × 81 = 6,561 pairs; five bits give 35 = 243 and 2432 = 59,049, the numbers the checker prints with --bits 5. Counting 24 = 16 tnums treats a tnum like a number and forgets the third state of each bit.

14.2

xxx0 is sound, 0xx0 is not, and tnum_add() returns xxx0. γ(01x1) = {5, 7}, so the real sums are 6 and 8. γ(0xx0) = {0, 2, 4, 6} misses 8, which is 1000 in binary, so a check that relied on it could pass when it should fail. γ(xxx0) holds all eight even numbers, both sums among them. By the code: the values add to 0110 and the masks to 0010, their sum is 1000, which differs from 0110 in 1110, and ORing the masks in leaves 1110 unknown and bit 0 known as 0. It is tempting to prefer 0xx0 as the tighter answer, but a smaller answer is worth nothing once it drops a real value.

14.3

No; it is a false alarm, the top right cell of Figure 14.1. The kernel's verifier is sound and incomplete by design, so some safe programs are refused, and the usual cure is a test the verifier can see, as in chapter 6, or a change to the program's shape. A soundness bug is the bottom left cell: an unsafe program loaded, for instance a read that the bounds said was inside the value when some input took it outside. Treating every surprising refusal as a kernel bug sends a report to the wrong place; such a report is a request for more precision, which then needs a soundness check of its own.

14.4

That no pair of well-formed 64-bit tnums and no values in them make tnum_add() miss a sum: soundness at 64 bits, for the formula as written. It proves nothing about precision, nothing about other widths, and nothing about the C code if the formula was copied wrongly, which is why the tnum paper ran its encodings against the kernel's C on random inputs (supplementary part D). Calling it "proved for every width" is the usual overreach; the 32-bit parts of the verifier need their own query or a proof on paper. It is also easy to read unsat as a failure, when for a negated claim it is the good answer.

14.5

A forbidden zone of erroneous states in the drawing of trajectories, and a proof must show that no trajectory enters it: the intersection of the concrete semantics with the zone is empty (section 4). Since the concrete semantics cannot be computed, the page concludes that the question is undecidable in general and moves to a computable superset. For the verifier the zone is every state that breaks a row of Figure 4.2, such as a read past the map value. Taking the zone to be the set of bad programs mixes the levels: the zone holds states of one program's executions.

14.6

Correct, which means no erroneous abstractions and so no forgotten errors, and complete, which means no false alarms. Section 13 says such an abstraction exists mathematically but cannot be computed, because of undecidability. That is this chapter's sound and complete, and the page's sections 11 and 12 add that the cost of soundness is false alarms. Reading "correct" as "precise" loses the point, since precision only reduces false alarms and can never remove them all.

14.7

Because it explores only prefixes of the trajectories, so an error after the bound is never seen and the method can report a program safe that is not (section 10). The kernel stops at the instruction limit too, but it then refuses the program, as copy (c) of chapter 5 shows with "BPF program is too large", so the limit produces false alarms and never a missed error. A walk that gave up and then accepted would make the mistake the page describes.

14.8

[1, 9], which also holds 4 and 5, values neither input allows. In section 6.1 intervals are ordered by inclusion, [l1, h1] ⊑ [l2, h2] when l2 ≤ l1 and h1 ≤ h2, and the join of section 4.2 is the least upper bound, the smallest interval above both. The join is sound and loses precision at once, which is the price of merging paths. A common slip is to answer with the two intervals side by side, which is not an interval and so not in the lattice.

14.9

Because the interval lattice has infinite height. Section 6.1 shows the chain [0, 0] ⊑ [0, 1] ⊑ [0, 2] ⊑ …, so the fixed-point iteration of section 4.4 may climb for ever, while the sign lattice is finite and the climb must stop. Widening applies a function whose results form a finite-height set, so the climb ends (section 6.2). On 64-bit registers the chain does end, after 264 steps, which is why it is tempting to think widening unnecessary there; Figure 14.3 shows that what matters is how many rounds the climb takes.

14.10

Section 12.5's complete means the analysis loses nothing beyond what its lattice must lose: its result equals α of the program's real behaviour. A complete verifier in this chapter, as in Cousot's section 13, raises no false alarm at all. An interval analysis can be complete in the first sense and still refuse a safe program, because intervals cannot express the fact the proof needs, as the sign example of section 12.5 shows with z = x − y. The papers use both senses, so it pays to check which one a sentence means.

14.11

sat, and a model in which Tie is false and Shirt is true. The three clauses can all be made true, and the model is one assignment that does it. In Figure 14.5 the same two calls would print the values of Pv, Pm, Qv, Qm, x and y that break the claim. It is easy to expect the model to be the only answer, but a solver returns one assignment among possibly many, so each run may show a different counterexample.

14.12

Because a solver looks for one assignment that makes a formula true, and validity means true under every assignment. If no assignment makes Not(fml) true, the solver answers unsat, and fml holds everywhere; the tutorial's own argument then shows by hand why that formula is valid. Figure 14.5 has the same shape, with "x + y is not in γ(R)" in the place of Not(fml). Asserting the claim itself and getting sat proves only that one input satisfies it.

14.13

By bit-blasting: every bit of every vector becomes a Boolean variable, and each operation becomes clauses, with addition encoded as the ripple-carry adder of Figure 2 and its carry bits. Multiplication needs a circuit of many adders, about one per bit of the multiplier, so the clauses grow far faster with the width. The tnum paper met this problem: the kernel's old multiplication was proved at 8 bits and gave no answer after 24 hours at 16 (section III-A). Expecting a solver to cost the same for every operation at a given width misses why the paper needed a proof on paper.

14.14

member(x, P) holds when x agrees with P on every known bit, x & ~P.m = P.v; wellformed(P) holds when no bit is both unknown and 1 in the value, P.v & P.m = 0. For 01x0 the mask is 0010 and the value 0100, so γ(01x0) = {x : x & 1101 = 0100} = {0100, 0110} = {4, 6}. A pair that breaks wellformed, such as value 0010 with mask 0010, has no member at all, because member forces every masked bit of the value to 0. wellformed states that condition on its own, so that a proof can require it of the inputs an operation is given and check that the result keeps it.

14.15

Addition, subtraction and the bitwise operators were proved sound at 64 bits in a few seconds each. The kernel's multiplication of that time was proved only up to 8 bits and did not finish after 24 hours at 16, because of its nonlinear arithmetic and unrolled loop. The authors then designed a new multiplication with a proof on paper for every width, which Linux merged in 2021 (Go deeper). It is easy to conclude that the old multiplication was unsound, but the paper shows only that the solver could not settle it.

14.16

μμ, written xx in the kernel's notation, which stands for all four values {0, 1, 2, 3}. The values 01, 10 and 11 disagree in both bits, so neither bit is known. A tnum with k unknown bits stands for 2k values, and three is not a power of two, so no tnum stands for {1, 2, 3} alone; the paper notes that α of this set soundly over-approximates it. It is tempting to answer 1x or x1, but each of those drops a member of the set.

Lab 14.1

By hand. iv_add_clamp([1, 2], [3, 4]) = [4, 6], and the real sums 4, 5, 5 and 6 all lie in it, so this pair proves nothing. With [1, 1] and [15, 15] the clamp answers [15, 15], but 1 + 15 = 16 = 10000 in binary, and a four-bit register keeps 0000, so the real result 0 lies outside.

$ python3 -I book/labs/ch17-check.py iv_add_clamp iv_add
iv_add_clamp  (broken on purpose), 4 bits
  136 values, 18,496 pairs, 665,856 concrete results, 0.24 s
  counterexamples: 14,500   wider than the best answer: 0
  first     [0, 1] + [1, 15] -> [1, 15], but 0 is a real result outside it
  smallest  [1, 1] + [15, 15] -> [15, 15], but 0 is a real result outside it

iv_add  (sound interval addition), 4 bits
  136 values, 18,496 pairs, 665,856 concrete results, 0.24 s
  counterexamples: 0   wider than the best answer: 3,060

Expected output. As above, from Python 3.14 on our machine, November 2026; the times will differ. first is the first failing pair in the checker's order and smallest the failing pair with the fewest input values.

What this shows. A bounds rule must follow the machine's arithmetic, which wraps (RFC 9669 §4.1); stopping at the largest number is sound only for saturating arithmetic. iv_add gives up instead and answers [0, 15] whenever the largest sum can wrap, which is sound but wider than the best interval in 3,060 pairs. v7.2's circular ranges (chapter 6) keep more in those cases, and book/labs/ch17-check.py cnum_add finds no counterexample among their 58,081 pairs.

Common wrong turn. Calling the clamp "conservative" because it rounds towards the largest number: an answer is conservative only if it holds every real result, and a wrapped sum lands at the other end of the range.

Chapter 15

15.1

1,048,576 cases, and the false step holds in 537,824 of them. Each bit of P with its member bit has four combinations (0 with 0, 1 with 1, and x with either), so there are 45 pairs (P, x) and 165 = 1,048,576 cases. The false step fails at one bit in 2 of the 16 one-bit cases, where one input is unknown and the other is 1, so it holds in 145 = 537,824, which python3 -I book/labs/proof/steps.py 5 prints. Counting 35 × 35 pairs of tnums gives 59,049, the checker's pairs, and forgets the values inside each tnum.

15.2

Z3 answers sat, for example with P and Q both the constant 11111111. With the mask α & β, every known 1 of the result is also marked unknown, so v & m is v and the result is not well-formed whenever v is nonzero. Such a pair has no members at all, so (x & y) & ~m, which step 4 of the proof makes 0, cannot equal a nonzero v. It is tempting to think more unknown bits can only be safer, but a bit that is 1 in the value and set in the mask would have to be known and unknown at once, which no number can be, and step 6 of the proof is the one the patch breaks.

15.3

The formula may differ from the C: an early return modelled in the wrong place, a signed comparison written with ULE, a 32-bit half compared at 64 bits, or code that runs after the function left out. Or the assumptions may be too strong, for instance an invariant the rest of the verifier does not in fact keep, or two assumptions that contradict each other, which makes every claim unsat. A third possibility is the width: a proof at 64 bits says nothing about the 32-bit path. A quick test for the second case is to drop the negated claim and check that the assumptions alone are sat; the tnum paper also ran its encodings against the C on random inputs.

15.4

v5.10 keeps [1, 1] for all four bounds, and __update_reg32_bounds() then makes them s32 [1, 0] and u32 [1, 0]; 5.13 gives [0, 0]. The result's tnum is (0x0; 0x100000000), whose low half is known 0, and R3's low half is known, so the 32-bit function returns at once, while R2 is not known in all 64 bits, so the 64-bit function does not reset the bounds. The update takes the larger minimum, 1, and the smaller maximum, the tnum's 0. cve.py --example prints these numbers. Expecting the update to repair the bounds misreads it, since it can only narrow.

15.5

That for every pair of registers whose tnums and 32-bit arcs hold their values, the arc this function computes holds every real low half of the AND: soundness of this function, as encoded, at these widths. It does not prove the 64-bit half, reg_bounds_sync() afterwards, the other operators, branches, or that the encoding matches the C; the encoding could be checked against the kernel on random inputs, as the tnum paper did. Treating one function's proof as a proof of the verifier is the overreach to avoid. The next chapter's Agni encodes every operator together with the shared tidy-up, which is how such proofs extend to the whole range analysis.

15.6

Because every p in γ(P) has at least the 1s of P.v, which is step 1 of this chapter's proof, and likewise every q, while the carry out of each position is the majority of three bits, which can only rise when an input bit rises. So setting every unknown bit to 0 carries least. Lemma 3 gives the most: Σ = (P.v + P.m) + (Q.v + Q.m), every unknown bit set to 1. A common slip is to take the mask of the sum to be P.m | Q.m alone, which is the broken tnum_add_nocarry of the refresher's checker; the carries that differ between the two extremes must be added.

15.7

Bit 1 is unknown in both inputs, so bit 1 of the sum may be 0 + 0, which carries nothing, or 1 + 1, which carries into bit 2; the minimum carries 10000 and the maximum 10100 differ there. The proof of tnum_add() must therefore follow carries across bits, and Lemma 5 shows that the kernel's mask (sv ⊕ Σ) | P.m | Q.m equals the one built from the carries. tnum_and() computes each bit of the result from the same bit of its inputs alone, so there are no carries to track. It is tempting to think the unknown carry comes from bit 0, but 0 + 1 there carries nothing.

Lab 15.1

def op(pv, pm, qv, qm):         # kernel/bpf/tnum.c:111, Linux v7.2
    v = pv ^ qv
    mu = pm | qm
    return v & ~mu, mu

def concrete(x, y):
    return x ^ y

$ $PY -I lab.py prove
prove, 64 bits: unsat in 0.005 s

# Part 2: mu = pm, so Q's unknown bits are forgotten
$ python3 -I lab.py check
check, 4 bits: 65,536 cases, 27,120 counterexamples, 0.01 s
  first: P 0000 x 0000, Q 000x y 0001: z 0001 is not in R 0000
$ $PY -I lab.py prove 8
prove, 8 bits: sat in 0.002 s
  P 11111111  x 11111111
  Q xxxxxxxx  y 11111111

Expected output. As above for tnum_xor(), on an AMD Ryzen 7 8845HS with Python 3.14.10 and z3-solver 5.4.1, 13 November 2026; times and the model's values will differ. tnum_or() gives the same pair of answers. tnum_sub() also has no counterexample at four bits and is proved at 64 bits in 2.7 s, and with chi dropped the checker finds 10,800 counterexamples.

What this shows. In the broken run every bit of Q is unknown, yet R claims to know all eight bits of x ^ y; Z3 chose y = 11111111, which flips every bit, so z = 00000000 disagrees with R everywhere. The dropped | qm would have marked those bits unknown. For subtraction the dropped term is the borrows, the counterpart of the carries in the reading above.

Common wrong turn. Writing concrete() as something other than the instruction's effect, such as x | y for XOR, which makes the real operation look broken. Another is copying tnum_sub() with a.mask and b.mask swapped in alpha and beta, which the checker catches at once.

Chapter 16

16.1

Twenty for a jump and five for an ALU instruction. A conditional jump refines both registers on both outcomes, and each register carries five descriptions, so 2 × 2 × 5 = 20, the count the paper gives under Equation 3; an ALU instruction writes one register, 1 × 5. Before 5.7 a register had three descriptions, since the 32-bit ranges came with commit 3f50f132d840, so the counts were 12 and 3, and Agni's checker changes its claims at 5.7-rc1. It is tempting to count the source register of an ALU instruction as an output too, but the kernel leaves it unchanged and Agni checks only the destination.

16.2

Not on that evidence. Inputs whose signed minima are 0 or more while their unsigned maxima pass 263 never come out of the tail, whose __reg64_deduce_bounds() cuts the unsigned maximum to the signed one, so the counterexample shows latent unsoundness. The test is the refined claim: pass both inputs through the tail and ask again, as repro.py does by default for AND, and Agni proved 5.14 sound that way (Figure 16.1). A search for a program should then come back empty. The case was still worth a patch, which 1f586614f3ff made in 6.10, but reporting it as an exploitable bug of 5.14 would be wrong.

16.3

Nothing about the multiplication or the access. Agni left multiplication out because its formula times out at 64 bits, checked it with 8-bit vectors only, and the repository marks it to be skipped. The offset into the map value is pointer arithmetic, which adjust_ptr_min_max_vals() handles, and every wrapper makes both registers scalars, so that code never enters a formula; nor does the access check of the section "A pointer plus a number, checked at the access". A passing run supports only that the encoded ALU and jump operators of the 6.6.y head it built were sound at 64 bits. Reading a green run as "the verifier is verified" claims far more than it shows.

16.4

Because the kernel's code reads across domains while it computes. scalar_min_max_and() takes the unsigned minimum from the tnum just computed and copies the signed range from the unsigned one, so it is neither an operator of one domain, which reads only that domain's inputs, nor a reduction, which takes finished outputs (Figure 2(b) of the paper). Agni therefore proved each instruction in one query. The 2024 split is of another kind, operator from tail rather than domain from domain. It became possible when commit 1f586614f3ff made AND, OR and XOR sound without the tail, since the soundness of the operator and of the tail then compose, which the --modular option relies on from 6.10.

16.5

That the public record holds no Agni verdict for v7.2. v7.2 keeps a tnum and two arcs per register (commit 256f0071f9b6), where Agni's checker expects four pairs of bounds, and Agni's daily run failed on bpf-next from April 2026 until GitHub switched it off on 14 May. The evidence that exists is narrower: CBMC checks of the arc operations by their author, Agni's checks of the branch operators cited by commit b254c6d816e5 for the earlier ranges, an SMT proof of tnum_step() (commit 76e954155b45), and the selftests. Even a full Agni pass would cover value tracking only. Quoting "proved sound since 5.13" for v7.2 stretches a result about other code.

16.6

Because a real program can start only from registers that hold constants or unknown values, and init() says that each operand's five descriptions are of one of those two kinds. Without it the solver could pick any input descriptions, including ones only the general claim admits, and the program would show a latent case that no run can reach. A model gives the concrete operands and their descriptions, so the instruction, with its operands loaded as constants or read from unknown data, is a program that runs and shows the mismatch. An unsat answer proves nothing about the bug; it only rules out programs of one instruction, which is why Equation 6 adds earlier ones.

16.7

Nothing on the value-tracking paths recurses or loops, so inlining every call ends, and each instruction becomes one function whose control flow is acyclic, with a finite path condition for every block. Memory needs no byte array because the functions touch it only through the fields of struct bpf_reg_state in two registers, so Agni models two disjoint trees of bit-vectors, indexed as LLVM's getelementptr indexes fields and versioned by MemorySSA. Tools such as SMACK and SeaHorn model memory as a linear array of bytes, which §8 calls a poor fit for kernel code. A common misreading is that loops are unrolled; there are none to unroll, and the current tool stops if one appears.

16.8

The first says that every bug in 5.5 needs an input description that no initial register has, such as a tnum known in some bits only or a range a branch has narrowed, so an earlier instruction must build it. The second has two readings, which §7 gives: a program of four or more instructions may reach the violation, which the enumeration timed out before trying, or the violation is latent and reported because the refined claim still admits impossible inputs. Figure 5(b) leaves 8 of 30 such cases for 5.5 and 3 of 21 for 4.14. Calling them false alarms of Agni's goes further than the paper, which leaves them open.

  ...
  out: var_off=(0x348405000002020; 0x9094942050804811)
     u64=[0x348405000002020, 0x8af9cb4b301068d1]
     s64=[236509692778520608, -8432485303485175599]

Expected output. As above, on an AMD Ryzen 7 8845HS with Python 3.14.10 and z3-solver 5.4.1, 13 November 2026. Times will differ, and so will the model's numbers in the runs without --small, but the verdict lines will not.

What this shows. In 5.12 both low halves are known after tnum_and(), since the masks of src and out are 0 in their low 32 bits, so the early return at lines 6544 and 6545 keeps the destination's u32 of [6, 6]. The __update_reg_bounds() at line 6600, at the end of scalar_min_max_and(), lowers the maximum to the tnum's 4 and gives [6, 4], while the real low half is 4; in 5.13 the same case is marked known as [4, 4]. The gen counterexample's dst has a signed range wholly below 263 beside an unsigned maximum of 0x8af9cb4b301068d1, above it. The tail would have cut that maximum to the signed one, so the verifier never holds such a register, and --synth finds no program for 5.13.

Common wrong turn. Blaming tnum_and(): the output's tnum, (0x4; 0x100000000), holds the real result, as the tnum column of the verdict line confirms. Another is to read the gen counterexample as a bug of 5.13 and stop there.

Chapter 17

17.1

About 28,684 instructions for Linux and 47 transfers for the fixpoint. The walk costs seven instructions a round plus twelve outside the loop, 7N + 12, which held at all four measured bounds, and the toy's walk, which matched those, counts 28,684 at 4,096; the kernel was not run at that bound. The fixpoint evaluates the eight slots before the loop and the four after it once, and the seven of the loop five times, for the four rounds of the climb and the descent and a last pass that records the states, whatever N is. It is tempting to scale the fixpoint's count with N as well, but N enters only as a constant in the exit test, and the climb ends after the same rounds.

17.2

Slot 13's r3 == 0x10 becomes r3 >= 0x10. The back-edge carries the states in which the test failed: "r3 is not 16" in the first form, which an interval cannot express, so the widened [0, +∞] survives, and "r3 is below 16" in the second, which cuts the back-edge to [1, 15] and the head to [0, 15]. Linux decides the test in every round from r3's known value, so either form ends its walk after sixteen rounds. A common mistake is to blame the widening alone; with the second form the same widening happens and the climb still ends at a safe state.

17.3

Nothing that can be relied on for Linux. PREVAIL proved the program safe under its own model of Windows' program types and helpers, with a different precision profile, and its parity notes say outright that matching Linux's decisions on every program is not a goal; Linux may refuse the program, as it refused the nine in the paper that PREVAIL proved, or need a different loop form. The team should load the object on each Linux kernel they support, with the verifier's log level set as in Lab 4.2, in CI. Reading a Windows pass as a portable proof would be a mistake.

17.4

The theorem is about eBPFPL, the model of §4, and the advisory is about the C++ code. In the model the packet's start and end are ghost registers that no store can reach, and a store outside the stack has no visible effect, so overwriting ctx->data and reloading it as a packet pointer is not a run the model contains. The code read those fields from the context while treating stores to it as no-ops, and release 0.2.4 now refuses such stores. The lesson, as with Agni, is to ask of any proof which model it covers and how the code was matched to it; "proved sound" says nothing about the matching.

17.5

Memory, first: the paper measured up to about 1.5 GB for its largest programs and called that unacceptable in the kernel, while Linux's walk keeps a few checkpoints. Precision, second: a fixpoint loses facts the walk keeps, such as a loop that ends on an equality test, and the 2019 developers also doubted that alignment checks and the defences against speculative execution fit the zone domain. What Linux took instead is a narrow widening, widen_imprecise_scalars() at iterator, callback and may_goto loops. Claiming that the move would cost nothing because the asymptotic complexity is better overlooks the constant factors the paper itself reports.

17.6

A pointer is a region and an offset, and the packet's start has offset 0, so data + r5 + 8 ≤ data_end becomes r5 + 8 ≤ the end's offset, a relation between r5 and one ghost variable. The interval domain keeps a range for each variable alone; from r5 in [0, 100] and the end in [0, 65,535] it cannot say that r5 + 8 lies below the end on every run, even when a check just established it. Only a domain with constraints on pairs, Zone among them, keeps r5 − end ≤ −8. One might think a narrower interval for r5 would do, but the end's lower bound would then have to rise with it.

17.7

The tags θ and the numbers d are may information, over-approximating what registers and cells can hold, so their join is the domains' own join. The set ζ of stack bytes holding only numbers and the set δ of cells holding a whole valid value are must information, true on every run that reaches the point. After paths meet, a byte is surely numeric, or a cell surely valid, only if it was on both paths, so the join intersects them. Taking the union would be the mistake: a pointer stored on one path could then be read back a byte at a time as a number.

17.8

Every program in the set had already passed the Linux verifier, and their authors had shaped them to fit its limits, unrolling loops and cutting bounds, so the set favours the walk; the authors say so. The experiments that escape the bias are those built from programs the kernel refused: the nine commits that reshaped code after false alarms, the six that cut loops or moved branches to fit the complexity limit, the two strncmp loops of Figure 11, and the six loops with variable bounds. Reading the speed result as a verdict on the two designs would ignore that selection.

Lab 17.1

$ python3 -I book/labs/prevail/toy.py once-ge 16 64 256
  ...
     N  fixpoint transfers  walk insns  checkpoints
    16                  47         124            4
    64                  47         460            9
   256                  47        1804           28
$ python3 -I book/labs/prevail/toy.py once-ge 16 --no-narrow -v
once-ge, N=16 (slots 0-18; len in [0, 65535])
    up 1: join       r2=[0, 255], r3=[0, 1]
    up 2: widen      r2=[0, +oo], r3=[0, +oo]
    up 3: stable     r2=[0, +oo], r3=[0, +oo]
  fixpoint  3 rounds up, 0 down, 40 transfers, 0.4 ms
    head 8: r2=[0, +oo], r3=[0, +oo]
    exit 18: r0=[1, 2]
    ALARM at 10: r4 = pkt+[0, +oo], len in [16, 65535]: may pass the end
    verdict: rejected
  path walk 124 insns, 4 checkpoints, 2 paths (0 pruned), 0.5 ms
    verdict: safe

Expected output. As above, with Python 3.14 on an AMD Ryzen 7 8845HS, 13 November 2026; each bound also prints 3 rounds up and 1 down for the fixpoint. Times differ from machine to machine; the counts do not.

What this shows. The walk's instructions and checkpoints, 124, 460 and 1,804 with 4, 9 and 28, equal the kernel's at each bound and grow with N, because each round is a new state. The fixpoint's 4 rounds and 47 transfers do not. The runs part in round 3: the back-edge brings [1, 15], the round's result [0, 15] lies within the widened [0, +∞], and the first run keeps it, which bounds the read at slot 10 by offset 15 against a packet of at least 16 bytes; --no-narrow keeps [0, +∞], and the read is refused.

Common wrong turn. Reading the alarm as a fault of widening alone. The widening is the same in both runs; what differs is whether the analysis takes the next round's narrower result, and the narrower result exists only because the test r3 >= 16 cuts the back-edge.

Epilogue

E.1

The counter's system-call tracepoint, a per-CPU hash keyed by cgroup ID, and batch reads. A tracepoint is the hook for a program that must outlive upgrades (chapter 8); it costs 127 ns empty and slows every system call while attached, getppid() from 320 to 354 ns. Many CPUs write each cgroup's key, so a shared hash updated by lookup and store loses counts, 66 per cent with eight writers (chapter 10); a per-CPU hash took 30 ns, at 209 bytes an entry on 16 CPUs that no cgroup is charged for. One batch reads the counts at 95 ns a key. Expect about the counter's 144 to 162 ns a run. It is tempting to take fentry for its 57 ns, but that holds only on kernels whose BTF has the function.

E.2

The loop and the arena need a fallback, and the kfunc needs a guard. Open-coded iterators arrived in 6.4 and bpf_loop() in 5.17 (chapter 4), so on 5.15 the loop must be a plain one with a small constant bound that the walk follows round by round, a dozen rounds or fewer by that chapter's rule. The arena arrived in 6.9, and before it the data has to live in a map with a slot per key (chapter 11). kfuncs exist from 5.13, but any one of them can be missing from a given kernel, so declare it __weak and call it only behind bpf_ksym_exists() (chapter 9). A common mistake is to expect CO-RE to cover all three, when it fixes field offsets and cannot supply what a kernel lacks (chapter 2).

E.3

That it is safe under the verifier's model of that kernel, and no more. Agni's proofs cover the range operators it encodes, on the kernels it ran on, and no public Agni run covers v7.2 (chapter 16); PREVAIL's theorem covers a model (chapter 17); and the SoK counts 325 memory-error bugs in the subsystem, 45 of them unfixed. The helpers and kfuncs the program calls are kernel C that the verifier never reads. What narrows the risk is control over loading: kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled at 2 (chapter 3), CAP_PERFMON only for a loader trusted with kernel memory (chapter 6), a token for a container, a signed loader on 6.18 or later, and bpf_jit_harden where untrusted users load (chapter 7). Reading Agni's result as a proof that the verifier is sound is the usual overreach.

E.4

On the capstone's workload of 100,000 light threads and four heavy ones, the hash of 1,024 entries took 83,968 bytes from creation and refused 296,940 inserts, silently unless the program checks for -E2BIG, and reading it took 100,004 bpf() calls and 69.5 ms (chapter 13). The LRU hash of the same size, 82,816 bytes, never refused a key, yet it kept 740 of the loader's threads and none of the four heavy ones, which had stopped writing and were evicted first. The count-min sketch held an estimate for every thread in 108,760 bytes, read with 1.5 ms of loads and no system call, each within its bound of 700 and the heavy ones within 0.1 per cent. It is tempting to expect an LRU hash to keep the busiest keys, but it keeps the most recently used.

E.5

Because a program is tied to its hook, its helpers and its maps as much as to its instructions. hXDP runs XDP programs on a network card, where the hook is the packet path and the hardware provides XDP's maps and helpers. The counter is a tracepoint program on sys_enter_write in the host kernel: its first call, bpf_get_current_pid_tgid(), asks which thread made the system call, which a card never sees, and its map is read by a loader on the host through bpf(). The instructions are the same, those RFC 9669 standardises, and Sephirot would decode them. Answering that an FPGA cannot run 64-bit eBPF instructions misses this, since Sephirot's four lanes execute eBPF instructions directly.

Glossary

Prologue

accumulator
the register most classic BPF instructions read and write
classic BPF
the 1993 filter machine: accumulator, index register, sixteen words of scratch memory, forward jumps
control-flow graph
a program drawn as instructions joined by its jumps
filter
a small program the kernel runs on each packet to decide whether to keep it, and how much of it
hook
a point on the kernel's own path where it stops to run code attached there
kernel extension
code added to a running kernel to change or watch what it does

Primer

ABI
the application binary interface: conventions compilers agree on above the ISA
callee-saved
a register a call must hand back unchanged; r6 to r9 in eBPF
caller-saved
a register a call may overwrite; r0 to r5 in eBPF
calling convention
where a call's arguments and result go, and which registers it may overwrite
frame pointer
a register holding a fixed address in the current frame; r10 in eBPF
immediate
a constant stored inside the instruction
instruction set architecture
the contract between compiled code and a processor: registers, memory addressing, instructions and their encoding
load/store architecture
an ISA whose arithmetic uses only registers and whose memory is reached only by loads and stores
opcode
the number that selects an instruction's operation
operand
a value or place an instruction works on
register
one of the processor's own named storage slots
spill
storing a register on the stack to free it; loading it back is a fill
stack
memory in which each running function keeps a frame for its locals

Chapter 1

bytecode
a program's instructions as stored in the object file and handed to the kernel
conformance group
a named set of instructions, such as base32 or atomic64, that a runtime supports whole or not at all
eBPF
extended BPF: the 64-bit instruction set Linux has run since 3.15
helper function
a kernel function a program may call by number
helper ID
that number, carried in a call's immediate
instruction class
the kind of instruction named by an opcode's low three bits: LD, LDX, ST, STX, ALU, JMP, JMP32 or ALU64
interpreter
code that runs a program by reading one instruction at a time and doing what it says; in Linux, ___bpf_prog_run()
map
a kernel object of keys and values that programs and user space both read and write
offset
a signed 16-bit field for memory addresses and jump distances
wide instruction
an instruction of two slots, sixteen bytes, that loads a 64-bit value: a constant, or a map or other address the kernel fills in

Chapter 2

back end
the target-specific part of LLVM; for BPF, llvm/lib/Target/BPF
BTF
BPF Type Format: a compact description of structs, fields, offsets and function signatures, written by clang for a program and by pahole for the kernel
CO-RE
compile once, run everywhere: field offsets recorded at build and corrected by libbpf at load
CO-RE relocation
a record in .BTF.ext that names a struct and field by name and says which instruction to patch
front end
the part of clang that parses C and writes LLVM IR
func info
a .BTF.ext record giving the BTF type of a function that starts at a slot
instruction selection
the back-end step that matches IR operations to BPF instructions
libbpf
the C library that reads an object file, creates its maps and programs, and attaches them
line info
a .BTF.ext record tying a slot to a source line, with the line's text
LLVM IR
the typed intermediate code that all LLVM targets share, with unlimited virtual registers each assigned once
register allocation
the back-end step that maps virtual registers onto r0 to r9, spilling to the stack when needed
tracepoint
a fixed, named hook that kernel developers placed in the source, such as sys_enter_write
vmlinux.h
the kernel's BTF printed as one C header by bpftool btf dump … format c

Chapter 3

anonymous inode
a file with no path that the kernel creates to give a process a descriptor for an internal object
bpf() system call
the single system call through which user space creates and controls BPF objects; its first argument is a command
BPF token
an object made from a delegating bpffs mount that lets a process in a user namespace pass the capability checks for the commands and types the mount allows; since 6.9
bpffs
the BPF file system, mounted at /sys/fs/bpf, where pins live
link
a bpf_link: a kernel object that holds one program on one hook; releasing it detaches the program
program type
the kind of program; it fixes what the program gets and may call
load
creating maps and programs in the kernel; nothing runs yet
pinning
giving a BPF object a file name, which holds a reference without any process
RCU grace period
the time it takes every CPU to leave any read-side section that could still see an object, after which the object can be freed
reference count
a counter in a kernel object with one unit per holder; the object is freed when it reaches zero
skeleton
the header bpftool gen skeleton writes: the object as bytes, plus open, load, attach and destroy functions
user reference
a reference held from user space, by a descriptor or a pin, counted in usercnt beside the map's ordinary reference count

Chapter 4

back-edge
a jump to an instruction still on the jump's own path; the shape of every loop
bounded loop
a loop whose last round the verifier can see; accepted since Linux 5.3
checkpoint
a verifier state saved at a prune point, for later paths to be compared with
global function
a function of the program without static, verified once for any arguments its BTF types allow
instruction limit
one million instructions walked, across all paths, before the verifier gives up
live
of a register or stack slot at an instruction: some path from there may read it before writing it
log level
how much the verifier writes: 1 for the instructions walked, 2 for the full state at each one, 4 for statistics
open-coded iterator
a loop in the program's own code that asks a kernel function for each next round, such as bpf_for(); since 6.4
path
one route from the first instruction to an exit, taking one side at each branch
pending branch
a side of a conditional jump that the walk keeps on a stack, with a copy of the state, to follow after the current path ends
pointer-or-NULL
a pointer that may be NULL, such as a map lookup's result; it cannot be read through until a test on that path
pruning
stopping a path where it matches a saved state already proved safe
register type
the kind of value a register holds: never written, a scalar, or one of many pointer types
scalar
a plain number, with bounds, that may never be used as a pointer
shape check
the verifier's first step: every jump lands inside the program and every instruction is reachable
verifier
the part of the kernel that walks a program at load time and refuses it unless every path is safe
verifier log
the text the verifier writes into the loader's buffer: each instruction walked, the reason it stopped, and statistics
verifier state
what the verifier knows at one instruction: a type, and bounds or sizes, for every register and stack slot

Chapter 5

BPF CI
the maintainers' automatic test runs, started from a pull request on GitHub
bpf tree
the git tree for BPF fixes
bpf-next tree
the git tree for BPF features, cleanups and improvements
patchwork
the web queue where patches sent to the list wait for review
selftest
a test kept in the kernel tree; the BPF ones live under tools/testing/selftests/bpf
test annotations
markers such as __failure and __msg(...) that tell the test runner what result to expect

Chapter 6

abstract interpretation
running a program on descriptions of its values instead of on the values
abstract value
the verifier's description of every value a register could hold at one instruction on one path
backtracking
walking back over instructions already verified to find which registers and stack slots a precise value came from
circular range
a first value and a count on a circle where the largest number is followed by 0; v7.2's form of the range
linked registers
registers and spilled stack slots that share an id, so that a bound learned on one reaches the others
precise
of a sound description: it holds few values the program cannot produce
precision tracking
the verifier's record of which scalars' bounds a check has relied on; only those are compared when pruning
range
the smallest and largest possible value, read as signed or as unsigned
sound
of a description: it holds every value the program can really produce
speculative execution
the CPU running ahead on a guess about a branch before it knows the outcome, and discarding the results if the guess was wrong
tnum
tristate number: each bit known 0, known 1 or unknown, stored as a value and a mask

Chapter 7

constant blinding
a rewrite before the JIT that replaces each constant with two random values whose XOR is the constant
direct tail call
a tail call to a constant slot, compiled to a five-byte jump that the kernel points at the slot's program or turns into a no-op
JIT
just-in-time compiler: translates a whole program into native code once, when it loads
JIT spraying
an attack that hides machine code in a program's constants and jumps into the middle of an instruction to run it
native code
instructions of the CPU itself, here x86-64
poke descriptor
a record of where in a program's machine code the jump for one program-array slot lies, so that the kernel can rewrite it
program array
a map whose values are programs, indexed by slot for tail calls
program pack
a 2 MB block of read-only executable memory that the JIT shares out among programs' images in 64-byte chunks
tail call
a jump from the end of one program into another, which reuses the first one's stack frame
trampoline
a short piece of x86 the kernel writes so that a kernel function's entry can call a program and continue

Chapter 8

attach
connecting a loaded program to its hook, so that it runs
attach type
the variant of a hook a program is for, sometimes fixed at load
context
what r1 points at when a program starts, shaped by its type
ELF section
a named block of an object file, chosen with SEC()
fentry
a program run through a trampoline at a kernel function's entry
fexit
the same at the function's return; it also sees the return value
kfunc
a kernel function offered through BTF, with no promise of stability
kprobe
a hook placed at run time on almost any kernel function, by name
LSM program
a program on a security-module hook; a negative return refuses
NMI
non-maskable interrupt, which can arrive while any lock is held
optimised kprobe
a kprobe whose breakpoint became a jump to a detour buffer
process context
the CPU running kernel code for a task, as in a system call
raw tracepoint
a tracepoint whose program gets the tracepoint's own arguments
sched_ext
the scheduler class, since 6.12, whose policy is a struct_ops set
softirq
interrupt work finished after the hardware interrupt returns
static call
a direct call whose target the kernel rewrites in place
static key
a no-op branch that the kernel rewrites into a jump when needed
struct_ops
a program set that fills a subsystem's table of function pointers
tc
a hook in the traffic-control layer, later on the packet path
XDP
eXpress Data Path, a driver hook that decides each packet's fate

Chapter 9

acquire kfunc
a kfunc flagged KF_ACQUIRE, which returns a pointer holding a reference that the program must release
BTF ID set
a list of BTF IDs, each with a word of flags, built into the kernel; registered for a program type, it makes the functions in it kfuncs for that type
helper prototype
the struct bpf_func_proto that gives a helper's address, flags, return type and argument types; the verifier checks calls against it
inlining
replacing a call with instructions that do the callee's work in place, as the verifier does for an array lookup
release kfunc
a kfunc flagged KF_RELEASE, which takes such a pointer and drops its reference
trusted pointer
a pointer the verifier knows to be valid and unchanged, such as a tracepoint's argument or an acquire kfunc's result; every kfunc wants its pointer arguments trusted

Chapter 10

arena
pages that a program and a process both map and address with pointers, since 6.9
bucket
one slot of a hash map's array: the head of a list of elements, with a lock
cache line
the 64-byte block in which a CPU caches memory, which moves to whichever CPU writes it
element
one entry of a hash map: list links, the stored hash, the key and the value
inner map
a map held in a slot of a map of maps, which must match the outer map's template
lost update
two writers read the same old value and each stores its own result, so one result is lost
map of maps
an array or a hash whose values are other maps, looked up in two steps
map type
the kind of map, which selects the kernel's table of functions for it
per-CPU
keeping one copy of each value for every CPU
perf buffer
an array of per-CPU buffers that programs write events into
resilient spin lock
a spin lock that returns an error on a deadlock or after a timeout instead of waiting forever; the hash map's bucket lock since 6.15
ring buffer
one event buffer shared by all CPUs, in order, since 5.8
wake-up
the kernel making a sleeping reader runnable again when data arrives

Chapter 11

address space cast
the instruction that converts a pointer between the arena's user form and the program's 32-bit form
allocated object
memory a program gets from bpf_obj_new() while it runs, typed by the program's BTF
BPF memory allocator
the kernel's per-CPU caches of free objects behind bpf_obj_new(), safe in any context
BPF stream
a per-program log, stdout or stderr, that programs and the kernel write and user space reads
kptr
a pointer field of a map value, marked in BTF, that owns the object it points to
non-owning reference
a pointer to a node in a collection, usable for its ordinary fields until the collection's lock is released
owning reference
a pointer to an allocated object that the program must drop, park or link before it exits
red-black tree
a binary search tree kept balanced by recolouring and rotating nodes, so that a lookup takes about 2 log₂ n steps at most

Chapter 12

bypass mode
sched_ext scheduling without the BPF scheduler, while one is enabled, disabled or failing
dispatch queue
a queue of runnable tasks that sched_ext keeps for a BPF scheduler, FIFO or ordered by a key
local DSQ
the dispatch queue of one CPU, from which that CPU always takes its next task
scheduling class
the set of functions through which the scheduler core asks one policy what to run
struct_ops map
a one-entry map whose value is a kernel table of function pointers, filled with programs
time slice
how long a task may run before it must give the CPU back
virtual time
a per-task clock that runs slower for heavier tasks; the task furthest behind runs next
watchdog
sched_ext's periodic check that ends a BPF scheduler when a runnable task has not run in time

Chapter 13

count-min sketch
d rows of w counters with one hash function per row, from which any key's count is estimated as the smallest of its d counters
cover letter
the message numbered 0 of a patch series, which explains the series before its patches
heavy hitter
one of the few keys that account for a large share of all counts
keyless map
a map created with a key size of 0, whose value is the item itself, reached by push and peek

Chapter 14

bit-vector
a fixed-width word whose arithmetic wraps round
completeness
of a verifier: it never refuses a safe program
concretization (γ)
γ(A) is the set of values the abstract value A stands for
counterexample
an input for which a claim is false
false alarm
a refusal of a program that is in fact safe
join
the smallest abstract value that holds two others
satisfiable
some assignment makes it true: sat, with a model
SMT solver
a program that decides if a formula can be made true
specification
a checkable claim about every possible input
widening
jumping a growing bound to the end of its range

Chapter 15

bit-blasting
turning each bit into a Boolean variable and each operation into clauses
bounded verification
checking a claim at one fixed bit width
invariant
a fact about the state that every step leaves true
membership relation
the test x & ~m == v: is x a value of the tnum (v, m)?
well-formed tnum
one with no 1 under its own mask, v & m == 0

Chapter 16

differential synthesis
a search for a program whose real run and abstract interpretation disagree
latent unsoundness
a wrong output for inputs that no program can produce
product domain
tuples of abstract values, one per domain; a tuple stands for the numbers all its parts allow
shared refinement operator
the tail every ALU operator ends with, narrowing each description by the others
trusted computing base
the software that must be correct for a proof to hold; for Agni, LLVM, Z3, its passes and its wrappers

Chapter 17

fixpoint
a state that one more round of a loop leaves unchanged
ghost variable
a variable the analysis adds, which the program never reads or writes
loop head
the point of a control-flow graph where a back-edge lands
narrowing operator
lowers bounds widening raised, never raises one
path-sensitive
of an analysis: keeping one state for each path to a point
relational domain
an abstract domain whose values relate several variables
zone domain
constraints x − y ≤ c on pairs of variables, with a bound for each

Epilogue

FPGA
a chip whose circuits are set by loading a design
high-level synthesis
making hardware from a software program
VLIW
a core issuing compiler-grouped instructions together
